Hasan benchmarks three encoder decoder networks: U-Net, U-Net plus plus, and DeepLabV3 plus. He also tests SeismoLabV3 plus, a tuned variant with a stronger backbone. The data set pairs five channel shot gathers with high resolution velocity maps. Results show the tuned variant achieved the best scores in the study. The work gives a guide for choosing networks for this task.
arxiv-2509-21431:
First light for a major upgrade to the Very Large Telescope Interferometer is reported by the GRAVITY+ Collaboration in a 2025 paper. The upgrade improves sensitivity, sky coverage, and contrast by orders of magnitude. Its adaptive optics system, GPAO, corrects wavefronts for all four large unit telescopes. It works with natural guide stars and laser guide stars, in visible and infrared light.

The paper presents the design, operations, and performance of GPAO. Commissioning observations from late 2024 show the gains. They include the first optical interferometry of a quasar at redshift near four. A very faint cool brown dwarf was also observed spectroscopically. The results open faint targets to interferometric study.
arxiv-2509-21531:
MRI scans take long to acquire, which raises cost and invites motion artifacts. Rohan Sanda and 5 co-authors extend a patch based diffusion method for MRI reconstruction in a 2025 paper. Diffusion models learn data driven priors that can fill in undersampled scans. Whole image models need large, expensive training sets. Patch based models learn priors from small data sets instead.

Their solver, PaDIS-MRI, handles complex valued, multi coil data. It was compared with a whole image diffusion baseline on sevenfold undersampled brain data. Models trained on as few as a few dozen k-space images beat the baseline on image quality metrics. Radiologist preference was also assessed. The work shows data efficient diffusion priors can carry clinical value.
arxiv-2509-21631:
Language models are black boxes, and high stakes users need reasons behind their outputs. Avash Palikhe and 6 co-authors survey explainable language models in a 2025 paper. Explainable AI methods were built for simpler models and strain against large architectures. Huge training corpora and broad generalization add further limits. Existing surveys miss challenges from architectural diversity and evolving capabilities, they argue.

The survey maps methods for interpreting internal mechanisms and decision processes. Stakeholder accountability in high stakes domains motivates the review. Architectural families are treated separately where their explanation needs differ. Gaps between explanation research and deployed language models are identified. The authors aim to bridge that gap toward transparent AI that users can audit.
arxiv-2509-21831:
Hesam Sarkhosh, Uzma Maroof, and Diogo Barradas survey how criminals wash money through Web3 in this 2025 paper, accepted at the APWG eCrime conference. Web3 finance runs on blockchains and smart contracts, with no central overseer. That open design gives users freedom, but it also gives launderers room to hide the source of stolen or illegal funds.

The survey sorts laundering schemes into a taxonomy, from high-level strategies down to the tricks beneath them. It shows how fake names, weak rules, and complex tools help move dirty money in secret. The authors also map what makes these schemes hard to detect and stop. They close with research directions meant to make Web3 finance more open to scrutiny, for scholars, lawmakers, and firms alike.
arxiv-2509-22631:
Debargha Ganguly and 8 co-authors built an AI agent that curates vision data sets on its own. Curating domain data is a bottleneck for robust vision systems, with trade-offs among quality, diversity, and cost. Their Labeling Copilot centers on a multimodal model that reasons in steps and calls specialized tools. Calibrated Discovery pulls relevant data from large repositories. Controllable Synthesis makes new data for rare cases, with filtering.

Consensus Annotation labels data by orchestrating several foundation models with voting and suppression rules. On the dense COCO data set, it proposed far more candidate objects per image than the ground truth holds. On Open Images, it found hundreds of new box categories despite heavy class imbalance.
arxiv-2509-22831:
Sean Trott asks when a mechanism found inside one language model can be claimed for others. Mechanistic interpretability names the parts behind a model's behavior, but the field lacks rules for generalizing its claims. Trott proposes five axes along which a claim might carry over. A mechanism might match in function, in when it develops, in position, in how it relates to other parts, or in weight-space structure.

He tests the frame on attention heads that look one token back, tracked through training in Pythia models of several sizes and seeds. Development paths were strikingly consistent, while positional consistency was weaker. Larger models showed earlier onsets and higher peaks. The paper closes with objections and replies.
arxiv-2509-22931:
Compact codes that keep key facts apart are prized for search and edge devices. Shreyas Gokhale presents MonoCon, a framework that earns such codes through function rules. A small monotonic network head sits on top of any pre-trained encoder. Monotonic means the head never reverses the order of its inputs. Contrastive training shapes both parts at once.

On CIFAR-100 image tests, MonoCon codes were about nine times smaller than the baseline codes. They were also about half again as robust, with near full accuracy kept. A sentence task showed the same trade at smaller scale. Gokhale frames MonoCon as a domain-free route to tiny, sturdy codes.
arxiv-2509-23131:
Comparing graphs by their structure is a basic need from chemistry to social networks. Matthias Dehmer and 3 co-authors build similarity measures from vectors of topological indices. Edit distance and kernel methods can be slow or miss fine detail. Index-based scores compute in polynomial time. Using several indices at once captures more structure than any single one.

Standard distance rules on those vectors give graph-level scores. Comparisons show the measures track subtle structural change well. Two demos apply the method in practice. One studies random graph models, and one scores molecular similarity among isomers. Early results look promising across fields.
arxiv-2509-23431:
Physical networks like brains and blood vessels cost material, yet their branching breaks the classic cost rules. Xiangyi Meng and 4 co-authors test local branching geometry across many such networks. Length and volume minimization forecasts fail in systematic ways. Their hypothesis: true cost needs the full 3D geometry, an intractable sum in general. A surprise mapping rescues the problem.

Surface minimization maps exactly onto Feynman diagrams in string theory. As links thicken, surface rules predict trifurcations and branching angles that match real networks. Stable orthogonal sprouts also emerge from the theory. Those sprouts help synapse formation and nutrient access in real systems.
arxiv-2509-23931:
Vision-language models read hundreds of image tokens when a handful might carry the answer. Hanshi Wang and 7 co-authors prune those tokens adaptively with AutoPrune, a training-free framework. Human vision explores broadly first, then narrows; their experiments show models do something similar. A fixed pruning schedule cannot fit inputs of differing complexity, so AutoPrune measures mutual information between visual and text tokens.

That signal is projected onto a budget-bound logistic retention curve shaped per task. Applied to LLaVA-1.5-7B, the method cut most visual tokens and three quarters of the compute while keeping nearly all accuracy. It also transferred to driving-oriented vision-language-action models.
arxiv-2509-24131:
Jian Huang and 2 co-authors report a link between magnetism and electric response in assemblies of magnetite nanoparticles. The link, called magnetoelectric coupling, held up at temperatures hundreds of times lower than in past studies. At the lowest temperatures the response stopped falling and leveled off into a plateau.

That plateau points to a quantum effect, the authors argue, not a size or surface artifact. The response also shifted form with magnetic field, from a squared curve to a straight one. The size of the squared part followed a power law in temperature that hints at a nearby quantum critical regime. The team presents these assemblies as a new platform for quantum magnetoelectric study.
arxiv-2509-24431:
Embeddings that fuse text, image, and sound are powerful but bulky to store and process. Eleonora Grassucci and 3 co-authors prove a strong link between shrinking the modality gap and the chance to compress such embeddings after training. The gap is the leftover separation between embeddings of different modalities that mean the same thing.

When the gap is small enough, same-meaning embeddings share a common region, and their centroid can stand in for all of them. Their method works direct on pre-trained encoders and replaces groups of embeddings with single centroids. On large multimodal tasks, it saved much memory without sacrificing performance.
arxiv-2510-00131:
Laura Escobar and Cesar Meza wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on matrix Schubert varieties. Fulton introduced these sets of matrices in 1992, defined by rank limits on their submatrices. A torus action lets each variety split into a core piece times a simple flat factor. The authors measure the core's complexity, meaning how far it sits from the nicest torus actions.

Building on earlier work, the authors pin down every complexity value the core can take. For an n by n setting, any whole number in the range can occur, with one small exception. The value one never occurs, no matter the choice of permutation. The result completes a classification question for this family of varieties. It also gives geometers a clean test case for how wild torus actions can become.
arxiv-2510-00231:
Alex Chen and four colleagues published this 2025 paper warning about a popular trick for speeding up language models. Compressing the KV cache shrinks stored attention data and raises throughput. Papers report almost no quality loss, but mostly on single-instruction tests. The team probed what happens when one prompt carries several instructions at once.

They found that cache eviction hits some instructions far harder than others, an effect they call eviction bias. A squeezed instruction can end up ignored by the model entirely. As a case study, they show system prompts leaking more often under compression. Instruction order and the compression method both change how bad the leakage gets. Two simple tweaks to eviction policy cut the damage greatly in their tests. Practitioners, they argue, should audit multi-instruction behavior before deploying compressed models.
arxiv-2510-00331:
Grzegorz Gutowski and three colleagues wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on drawing bipartite graphs with fewer crossings. Place the two vertex sets on two parallel lines, and crossings depend only on vertex order. In the one-sided version, one line's order is fixed in advance. A local variant asks not for fewest total crossings, but for the fewest crossings on any single edge.

Earlier work proved the weighted one-sided local problem hard and conjectured the unweighted case hard too. The authors confirm that conjecture: the unweighted problem is NP-hard as well. They also revisit the classic median heuristic of Eades and Wormald for this setting. With a specific tie-breaking rule, they prove the heuristic guarantees an approximation ratio of three. Results like these guide the layered drawing methods used in software such as the Sugiyama framework.
arxiv-2510-00631:
Zhang and a large team of co-authors report optical monitoring of the blazar OP313 during its strong 2024 flare, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Blazars are active galaxies whose jets point almost straight at Earth, so their light varies fast and brightly. The Fermi space telescope saw OP313's gamma-ray flux jump to about sixty times its average level at the peak.

The team followed the event with optical telescopes for about one hundred days. They found the source grew active roughly fifty days before the flare and stayed active afterward. During the flare its spectrum shifted from quasar-like to BL Lac-like, and its broad emission lines faded from view. The authors link the long active phase to changes in the accretion rate feeding the jet.
arxiv-2510-00731:
Gozzi and Perra model how to stop deception-based cyber-threats spreading through online social networks, in this 2025 arXiv paper on network science. Phishing-style attacks spread person to person, and defenders with a budget must choose whom to make aware and protect. The authors simulate activity-driven temporal networks where users differ in gullibility and interact with their own kind. Threats spread under a susceptible-infected-susceptible dynamic, much like a recurring epidemic.

They test four targeting strategies: random choice, picking the most active users, egocentric sampling through contacts, and security awareness tests. Targeting by activity proved effective at raising the spreading threshold. Egocentric sampling came a clear second despite needing no global knowledge of the network. Homophily among the highly gullible widened the conditions for outbreaks, yet it also shrank their reach. The authors warn that isolated gullible clusters can shelter threats for a long time.
arxiv-2510-01031:
Labarbarie, Itier, and Puech, at the University of Montpellier and IMT Nord Europe, make face anonymization reversible under a secret key in this 2025 arXiv paper on privacy. Face images leak identity and attributes to any vision system that processes them. Blurring protects weakly, while encryption destroys the image's usefulness, and diffusion-based anonymizers cannot be undone by anyone. The authors claim the first method that is secure, high quality, and reversible at once.

They merge a secret key into the diffusion model's latent representation of the face. A facial mask constrains generation so identity-irrelevant features, such as background and pose, survive untouched. Deterministic forward and backward diffusion then guarantees exact recovery with the correct key. Wrong keys produce wrong faces instead of leaking the original. The anonymized faces also looked less similar to the originals than prior methods achieved. No model retraining is required.
arxiv-2510-01331:
The Belle and Belle II Collaborations report a precision test of matter-antimatter asymmetry in a rare B meson decay. The decay emits a photon alongside three lighter particles, and its timing carries signs of CP violation. Two generations of Japanese electron-positron experiments contribute data to the measurement.

Analysts extract the asymmetry parameters separately for each experiment's dataset. Values from the older Belle data sit close to the no-asymmetry expectation within errors. The newer Belle II results run somewhat more negative, though uncertainties remain sizable. Combined scrutiny of such radiative decays probes physics beyond the standard model. Time-dependent measurement is the delicate part, since the mesons oscillate before decaying. Flavor tagging tells analysts which twin started each event. Hundreds of collaborators share authorship across the two experiments. Radiative penguin decays are the family this channel belongs to in particle physics.
arxiv-2510-01531:
Fang and Ke give language-model planners a habit that good human problem solvers share: ask before acting. Agents that plan under partial views often trust an inner model of the world that quietly disagrees with reality. Their framework, InfoSeeker, weaves information gathering directly into each decision cycle.

The agent plans probes that test its beliefs, detect changes, or check a guess before committing. A new text-based test suite stresses exactly this partial-view, shifting-world setting. Agents using the approach adapted their plans more accurately than planners that never questioned their model. Checking the world first makes later steps safer. Belief states update after each probe, so plans rest on fresher ground. Noisy dynamics punish agents that commit early and never look again. The benchmark varies how much of the scene stays hidden. Curiosity becomes a planned step, not an accident.
arxiv-2510-01631:
Kang and co-authors run over a thousand pretraining experiments to learn when synthetic data helps language models and when it quietly harms them. High-quality natural text is running out, and synthetic substitutes promise relief with murky scaling behavior. One unified protocol and scaling-law fits govern every comparison.

Rephrased synthetic data alone trains no faster than natural web text. Mixed at about one third, it speeds learning several-fold at larger budgets. Textbook-style synthetic data alone inflates loss, especially when data is scarce. Bigger generator models do not automatically produce better training data. One hundred thousand GPU hours bought the study its authority. Good mixture ratios depend on model size and budget jointly. Thirty percent rephrased emerges as the empirical sweet spot. Downstream domains punish textbook-only training hardest at small scale. Synthetic data is a seasoning, not a staple.
arxiv-2510-01831:
Williamson, Ji, and Dwyer uncover a pattern behind many math errors by language models in this 2025 paper. The models often solve a problem in one wording and fail the same problem in another. The authors call these failures syntactic blind spots. The issue is not missing math knowledge, but a brittle tie between surface wording and internal reasoning.

To test the idea, they rewrote wrongly answered questions using simpler templates from correctly solved ones. The rewrites kept the meaning but lowered the structural complexity, and models often answered correctly afterward. A complexity score based on Dependency Locality Theory predicted the failures well. Higher scores came with higher error rates across four benchmark sets. The authors argue that many reasoning errors are really alignment errors. Syntax-aware fixes could expose and reduce them without teaching new math.
arxiv-2510-02031:
Mao and Lecoanet compute exactly how internal gravity waves stir chemicals inside stars in this 2025 astrophysics paper. These waves ripple through the radiative zones of stars and slowly mix their chemistry. The amount of transport stayed uncertain because studies leaned on heuristics or hard-to-extrapolate simulations. The authors deliver the first rigorous asymptotic calculation in the small-amplitude limit.

A coherent wave packet turns out to transport chemicals at a rate scaling with the fourth power of wave amplitude. Numerical simulations verify that analytic scaling directly. A random superposition of waves behaves very differently, since transport is equally likely to run either direction. The net effect then scales with the eighth power of amplitude, far weaker than folklore suggested. That steep suppression matters for stellar evolution models that borrow mixing rates from simulations.
arxiv-2510-02131:
Brown and Erman compute sheaf cohomology over weighted projective stacks with exterior algebra methods in this 2025 mathematics paper. Sheaf cohomology measures global features of geometric objects, and computing it by hand is rarely feasible. A classic algorithm of Eisenbud, Fløystad, and Schreyer handles plain projective space through Tate resolutions. Weighted spaces, where coordinates carry unequal weights, break that machinery.

The authors generalize the algorithm using noncommutative modules. Koszul duality still moves the computation from a polynomial ring to its dual exterior algebra. Wholly new steps handle the weighted grading and the stack structure. The method computes these values for sheaves on weighted projective stacks and spaces alike. Fast computation matters because weighted varieties appear across modern geometry and mirror symmetry. A runnable algorithm turns abstract vanishing questions into routine sums. The paper extends a workhorse geometry tool to a broader class of spaces.
arxiv-2510-02331:
Ryu and co-authors generate fake shopping dialogues that stay true to a hidden user profile. Their 2025 paper tackles a data shortage in conversational recommenders. Systems that chat and suggest products need training dialogues. Public dialogue data is scarce and costly to collect. Simulators can invent users, but they often drift off character. The ICER method anchors each fake user to real ratings and tags. A behavior simulator keeps replies consistent with that anchor. Language model prompting then turns the exchanges into natural speech.

Human raters judged samples of the generated dialogues. They found them consistent, factual, and natural sounding. The dialogues cover both preference questions and example critiques. The full dataset is open source for other teams. Trained recommenders can learn from partial conversations this way. Synthetic data that respects a user state is the key advance.
arxiv-2510-02631:
Enescu and Sahbi teach generative models new tasks in sequence without erasing old skills. Their 2025 machine learning paper introduces a method called FunLoRA. Generative models spread fast across text and vision work. Retraining them on their own output is the usual defense against forgetting. That defense grows slower and degrades over time. Synthetic data lacks the richness of real data. FunLoRA conditions the model through low rank adaptation instead. It uses only rank one matrices at its core. Carefully chosen functions then raise the effective rank. Layer selection adapts only part of the backbone.

The design guarantees protection against catastrophic forgetting. Experiments showed clear accuracy wins over rival methods. It used far fewer parameters while winning. The method even beat approaches built on large pretrained models. Flow matching sped up sampling beyond diffusion speeds. Continual learning matters wherever models meet new domains weekly. Small, frugal adapters make that updating affordable.
arxiv-2510-02831:
Ofman and co-authors model waves that ripple through the Sun's outer atmosphere. The waves are called quasi-periodic fast magnetosonic waves. Space telescopes have watched them since 2010. They travel near a thousand kilometers per second. They fade fast as they move away from their source. Their patterns can reveal the strength of the corona's magnetic field. Earlier models used tidy, idealized magnetic layouts.

This team used a real active region instead. The region, AR 11166, was recorded on March 10, 2011. They rebuilt its magnetic field from surface maps. They added a layered atmosphere with realistic density and heat. Their three-dimensional simulation then launched waves from flare-like pulses. The model matched the observed wave direction, bounce, and fading more closely. Synthetic glow maps let them compare the run with telescope images directly. Better models sharpen coronal seismology, the art of reading the Sun through its waves.
arxiv-2510-03031:
Zhu and co-authors forecast where people will walk over the next minute. Robots and cars need such long-range guesses to stay safe. Learning-based forecasters often drift over long horizons. The team instead leans on Maps of Dynamics. These maps store motion patterns seen in each place. Flow direction and speed become features of the scene. A ranking step then picks the most likely path among candidates.

A new time-aware map adds the hour of the day. Crowd flow at dawn differs from flow at dusk, after all. Three map types were tested inside the same framework. Two real-world data sets supplied the trials. Map-based forecasts beat the learning-based rivals clearly. Average path error fell by up to half in the best cases. The time-aware variant scored highest overall. Uniform grids still limit how fine the maps can be.
arxiv-2510-03131:
Chen and co-authors build a regression framework that survives three flaws at once. Inputs are often measured with error in real studies. The regression curve itself may be the wrong shape. The error pattern may also be misjudged by the analyst. Their Bayesian nonparametric design tackles all three together. A Dirichlet process prior sits over the hidden data law.

Pseudo-samples of the true inputs refresh that prior with data. Estimators then pull the prior law toward the model's joint law. Users can tune how hard the prior and data each pull. Error bounds tighten when either piece matches the truth. Consistency survives even when neither piece is perfect. A gradient-based algorithm keeps the computation practical. Simulations and two real studies tested the design. It beat Bayesian and frequentist rivals on error size. Its answers also swung less when assumptions were bent.
arxiv-2510-03231:
Gehrmann argues that reward models and evaluation metrics are the same field wearing two coats. Reward models grade model outputs to train language models. Evaluation metrics grade outputs to monitor those same models. The two literatures grew up apart from each other. Duplicate terminology and repeated mistakes followed from the split. Both camps fight spurious correlations in their scorers. Both watch downstream gaming of the score itself.

An extensive survey maps where the fields overlap. Experiments show metrics beating reward models on some tasks. Data quality methods from metrics research transfer directly. Meta-evaluation practice is another shared weak spot. Preference elicitation offers a third bridge between them. Calibration-aware checking could harden both toolkits at once. The author warns against a monoculture of few benchmarks. Unifying terms and methods is the core recommendation. Reward hacking research would gain decades of metric wisdom.
arxiv-2510-03331:
Acharya presents a 2025 arXiv paper on fixing the iron triangle of United States health care. The triangle links access, cost, and quality, and gains in one corner usually hurt another. The United States spends more on care than any other nation, yet access and results stay uneven. The author proposes an intelligent health ecosystem that joins data, smart tools, and care teams into one coordinated system. Shared records, telehealth, and digital twins all play parts.

The framework adds a new value equation that counts all three corners at once. Tools like generative AI, federated learning, and common record standards support the design. The author argues that a coordinated system can cut waste and tailor care while widening access. Early real world projects offer some support for that claim. Hard problems remain, including privacy, bias, and training staff. The paper maps both the promise and the work needed to reach it.
arxiv-2510-03531:
Lu and Breheny present a 2025 arXiv paper on removing hidden bias from high dimensional regression. Confounders that no one measured can fake associations in genomics and other big data fields. Recent work shows adjustment is still possible when data carry many variables. The authors build a clean framework that splits signal, bias, and noise into parts they can dial separately. That control lets them stage fair contests between rival adjustment methods under known amounts of hidden confounding.

They compare plain LASSO, a principal components variant, and penalized mixed models. Both adjusted methods cut false positives and sharpened estimates over plain LASSO when confounding was present. The mixed model proved most robust overall, especially as confounding grew more complex, and it kept models sparser. Each rival still won in some scenarios, which the framework maps clearly. Analysts facing batch effects in lab data gain guidance on which shield to raise first.
arxiv-2510-03631:
Darzi and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper proposing QPADL, a post-quantum framework for private access to shared spectrum. Spectrum access systems let unlicensed users borrow licensed channels, but queries reveal location and transmission details. That exposure kills anonymity and invites spoofing and denial of service attacks. Quantum computers would break the cryptography as well. QPADL combines private information retrieval for queries, a post-quantum variant of Tor for anonymity, and signature schemes that verify location without exposing it.

Client puzzles and rate limiting round out the denial of service defenses. The authors give a formal security assessment of the design. Performance tests, sped up with graphics processors, show the system can scale to deployments. Building blocks offer different tradeoffs between security and speed. Regulators want spectrum sharing to grow, but users will resist systems that track them. A design that proves location while hiding it could unblock that tension.
arxiv-2510-04031:
Tan and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on whether counterfactual thinking helps language models explain their own text classifications. When a model labels a review as positive, users want to know which words drove the decision. The models act as black boxes, and calling them is expensive, so explanations must be cheap to obtain. The authors test whether asking for counterfactual versions of the text sharpens the model's word choices.

A counterfactual here is a minimally edited text that flips the model's verdict. The team introduces a decision changing rate to score how important the model's top words really are. It measures how often masking those words actually changes the classification. Experiments showed that reasoning with counterfactuals improved the model's ability to name the words that mattered. Better self-explanations could help prompt designers trim costly input text and give auditors a record of model behavior.
arxiv-2510-04231:
Dirnstorfer presents this 2025 arXiv paper on aligning two images with an algorithm short enough to fit in a dozen lines of Python. Image registration underlies stereo vision, optical flow, and change-tolerant comparison. Neural approaches work well but usually demand large datasets, long training, and heavyweight code. The proposed method takes a recursive, pyramidal route with a single small network.

Coarse alignment at low resolution seeds progressively finer corrections as the recursion descends the pyramid. The design is end-to-end trainable and learns from remarkably little data. A stereo vision demonstration trained on only seventy-four image pairs, using a small nineteen-by-fifteen input window. The compact network reached error rates comparable to established methods in continuous regions. The appeal is a lightweight, adaptable starting point for settings starved of data, time, or code budget. Simplicity here is the contribution, not a compromise.
arxiv-2510-04531:
Ravil Fatykhov and Sergey Sushkov wrote this 2025 paper on cosmic history in a modified gravity theory. Their theory couples a scalar field to gravity in two ways at once. One coupling ties the field to scalar curvature, and the other ties its motion to the Einstein tensor. A monomial potential for the field completes the model. The team asked which long term fates such a universe can reach.

They found the critical points of the system and tested each one for stability. With no potential, or with a shallow one, the early universe settles into a near de Sitter state that matches inflation. The expansion rate there matches values from earlier work on kinetic coupling alone. Some early regimes expand in a phantom way. Late time fates include power law growth, a radiation like stage where the effective Planck mass fades, and steady exponential growth for one exponent choice.
arxiv-2510-04631:
Anastasia Zhukova and three coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on adapting language models for factory text. Process plants log daily operations in short notes full of local terms and codes. General models read those logs poorly, and labeled training data in the field is thin. The team borrowed a method built for science papers, where links between documents form a graph. They fed graph embeddings into contrastive fine tuning of the text model.

Triplets for training came from the graph neighborhoods of each log entry, not from hand labels. The adapted model then ranked and matched plant texts on a private benchmark built for the industry. It beat a leading large text encoder by about ten to fourteen percent on that benchmark. The winning model carried about a third of the parameters of its rival. Graph structure thus substitutes for scarce labels in a niche domain.
arxiv-2510-04931:
Folkers and co-authors present a hands-on teaching tool for quantum physics in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their subject is quantum entanglement, the strange link between particles that defies everyday logic. Entanglement is hard to teach because it cannot be seen or touched. The team built electronic dice that mimic its behavior in the classroom.

Each die carries a display, motion sensors, and a wireless link to its partner. Rolling or turning the dice shows superposition, measurement, and linked outcomes in real time. Teachers can run lessons from basic entanglement demos up to quantum key distribution. The design is low-cost and open source, so schools with small budgets can build it. Early use suggests the dice help students form an intuitive grasp of the ideas.
arxiv-2510-05131:
Bowen Wei redesigns search inside a Head Start management platform in this 2025 arXiv paper. New staff must find the right task module among hundreds on the GoEngage homepage. Domain jargon and system-specific names defeat ordinary keyword search. Typos and varied word order make the mismatch worse.

Wei's hybrid system layers three retrieval methods. Typo-tolerant lexical search and embedding similarity first build a shortlist from the real module catalog. A constrained language model then re-ranks that shortlist, so it can never invent modules. Rationale augmentation widened semantic coverage well beyond lexical baselines. The full system reached production-grade quality on offline tests. Caching and graceful degradation keep it cheap and robust in daily use.
arxiv-2510-05231:
Dario Antolini, Guido Montúfar, and Alessandro Oneto define a new way to measure tensor complexity in this 2025 arXiv paper. Tensors can be built as entry-wise products of simpler pieces. Restricted Boltzmann machines in machine learning rely on exactly such products. The authors define the Hadamard rank of a point relative to a projective variety.

They prove that a generic point has finite Hadamard rank whenever the variety avoids coordinate hyperplanes and binomial hypersurfaces. For secant varieties of toric varieties, the maximum rank is at most twice the generic rank. A dimension bound for products of these secant varieties follows as well. The bound yields exact generic ranks for several Segre-Veronese families. The framework gives geometric meaning to decompositions used in learning models.
arxiv-2510-05431:
Yoo and colleagues at Macquarie University tackle a trust problem in automated patent sorting. Their 2025 paper proposes Self-Filtered Distillation, a method that learns from explanations written by large language models. Such explanations often contain logic errors, wrong labels, and terms that clash with patent classes. Training on them blindly can pass those flaws into the smaller student model.

The method scores each explanation with three checks that need no human labels. One check measures stability across repeated answers, and one tests fit with class definitions. A third check weighs whether the stated reasons support the assigned label. Scores then weight training samples, and the worst cases can be dropped. Tests on the USPTO-2M patent benchmark beat plain label training and standard distillation on accuracy and stability. The authors plan to extend the approach to medical and legal texts.
arxiv-2510-05631:
Abbrescia and colleagues write the first dedicated simulator for a new particle detector. The Resistive Cylindrical Chamber bends plate-chamber electrodes into coaxial cylinders. That geometry adds new freedoms, like electrode radii and voltage polarity. Their 2025 program models avalanche growth and signal induction in both geometries.

The code transports electrons stepwise through the gas gap. It approximates space-charge effects with a series of charged disks. Induced charge on external electrodes comes from explicit weighting fields. Validation against planar chamber data reproduces charge and efficiency well. In the cylindrical case, electric-field asymmetry shapes the avalanche development. Polarity flips therefore change detector behavior in measurable ways. The tool stays fast enough for parameter scans and design studies. Full microscopic simulations would cost far more computer time per configuration. Townsend coefficients as functions of the field drive the multiplication model.
arxiv-2510-05931:
AlKhamissi and colleagues argue that culture benchmarks need anthropologists. Language models now mediate translation, education, and public discussion across cultures. Benchmarks claim to measure cultural competence, yet treat culture as static facts. Their 2025 position paper examines twenty handpicked cultural benchmarks qualitatively.

A four-part framework sorts benchmarks by how they frame culture. The framings cover knowledge, preference, performance, and bias. Six recurring methodological issues emerge from the survey. Treating countries as cultures and ignoring within-culture diversity headline the list. Oversimplified survey formats flatten lived cultural practice further. Anthropology views culture as dynamic, historically situated, and enacted in practice. The authors propose narratives, community co-design, and in-context evaluation as remedies. Annotator disagreement should be treated as signal, not noise to average away. Sustained interdisciplinary collaboration replaces ad hoc benchmark fixes.
arxiv-2510-06131:
Mao and eight co-authors build one generator for medical images and reports in a 2025 machine learning paper. Medical generators usually specialize in one modality, blocking them from combining imaging, pathology, and notes. That fragmentation stalls progress toward genuine medical foundation models.

Their system, MeDiM, is a discrete diffusion model that learns a shared distribution across modalities with no modality-specific parts. A multimodal large language model serves as the backbone, contributing prior knowledge and cross-modal reasoning. Two changes adapt it: removing the causal mask allows bidirectional context, and timestep embeddings report the noise level. MeDiM reached strong image quality on MIMIC-CXR and PathGen and produced accurate reports for both. Jointly generated image–report pairs lifted downstream scores sharply, with BLEU-3 gains above 30 percent on PathGen. One model now translates, generates, and pairs clinical content coherently.
arxiv-2510-06231:
Zheng and nine co-authors build CML-Bench, a framework for judging machine-written movie scripts. Language models produce neatly structured screenplays, yet often miss the storytelling soul of good cinema. The team wanted metrics exposing exactly where generated scripts fall short.

They curated CML-Dataset, pairing summaries with segments from esteemed movie scripts in Cinematic Markup Language. Studying those scripts' continuity and narrative structure, they identified three quality dimensions. Dialogue Coherence, Character Consistency, and Plot Reasonableness became its scoring axes. CML-Bench gives human scripts high marks while pinpointing model screenplays' weaknesses. They also propose CML-Instruction, prompting with detailed guidance on dialogue and event logic. Models guided by it wrote better scripts, with improvements aligned to human preferences. The framework gives screenwriting AI a report card and a study guide.
arxiv-2510-06331:
Pedersen and five co-authors study a rapidly varying white dwarf, ZTF 1851+1714, with phase-resolved spectroscopy in a 2025 stellar astrophysics paper. The source swings by nearly a magnitude with a period of about twelve minutes. The team confirms it and interprets it as the white dwarf's spin.

Spectra show hydrogen and helium emission lines on a featureless continuum. The continuum grows redder whenever the source brightens. Emission lines show tentative Doppler shifts of a few tens of kilometers per second at the spin frequency. The hydrogen-alpha and hydrogen-beta lines move with different amplitudes, implying different formation regions. Potential orbital sidebands suggest a candidate orbital period of one hour. Everything fits the accretion curtain model. Material leaves a truncated inner disk and funnels along field lines onto the magnetic poles.
arxiv-2510-06431:
Tsuji and twelve co-authors measure whether the acceleration knots in SS 433's jets move in a 2025 astrophysics paper. The microquasar SS 433 drives parsec-scale jets into the W50 nebula. X-ray knots in its lobes likely match very-high-energy gamma rays from HAWC and H.E.S.S. With LHAASO's ultra-high-energy signal, the system is a jet-driven PeVatron candidate.

New and archival Chandra data span twenty years. The team searched for knot proper motion for the first time. No motion appeared at the three-sigma level. The innermost knots move below three percent of light speed, under ten thousand kilometers per second. With flow speeds, the shock-frame upstream velocity reaches tens of thousands of kilometers per second. That implies acceleration approaching the Bohm limit. The stillness points to a standing recollimation shock balancing jet and pressure at twenty to thirty parsecs.
arxiv-2510-06631:
Qiming Guo, Bishal Khatri, Hua Zhang, and Wenlu Wang aim to protect city water systems with artificial intelligence. Their 2025 paper focuses on underground water and wastewater pipes. Leaks and infiltration waste water, harm the environment, and cost cities heavily. Manual inspection is slow, while dense sensor networks cost too much.

Their framework deploys a sparse set of remote sensors along the pipes. The sensors stream flow and depth data in real time. A model called HydroNet reads that data on a graph shaped like the pipe network itself. Pipe traits such as material, diameter, and slope feed into its calculations. Tests used a real wastewater network on a university campus. HydroNet beat advanced baseline models on forecast accuracy across the metrics used. Its forecasts can support later tasks like leak detection. The design balances low sensing cost with network-wide prediction quality.
arxiv-2510-06731:
Xiaofeng Dong, Nesar Ramachandra, Salman Habib, and Katrin Heitmann test whether AI can imitate the growth of cosmic structure. Their 2025 paper benchmarks neural networks trained to evolve matter fields in the universe. Full cosmological simulations are accurate but slow. A fast learned substitute would help with error studies and parameter fitting.

They train a U-Net model on fields from two sources. One source is a simple analytic method, and the other is a numerical particle-mesh simulation. Judging the outputs takes more than pictures and basic statistics. The team applies higher-order correlations, conservation checks, and topological indicators. The network did well on some physical measures but not others. Accuracy degraded at small scales, where density varies over a huge range. A custom density-weighted training loss improved the small-scale results a great deal. The benchmarks give future AI surrogates a stricter standard to meet.
arxiv-2510-07131:
Xie and co-authors work on measuring how fast the universe expands, a value called the Hubble constant. Their 2025 paper is the second from the CURLING program. Strong gravity from a galaxy cluster can bend light from a distant exploding star into several images. Delays between those images reveal the expansion rate. The result depends heavily on how well the cluster's gravity is modeled.

Many modelers shrink each image to a single point to save effort. The first CURLING paper showed that this shortcut can bias the answer. Here the team models the full pixel pattern of the images instead. They test both styles on a fake system built to mimic a known lensed supernova. The pixel-based model gave a tighter estimate of the expansion rate. Sharper lens models matter because rival measures of cosmic expansion still disagree.
arxiv-2510-07231:
Lee and a large team build a demanding test of cause-and-effect reasoning in language models. Their 2025 benchmark avoids the fake, hand-made cases that weaken older tests. Instead, it mines causal claims from top economics and finance journals. Those claims rest on strong research designs used by social scientists. The test spans health, environment, technology, law, and culture. It holds nearly thirty thousand questions in four task formats.

Eight leading models took the test, and all struggled. The best of them answered only about three in five questions correctly. Bigger models did not reliably beat smaller ones. Even models tuned for step-by-step reasoning missed basic causal links. The authors see a wide gap between fluent answers and trustworthy causal judgment. That gap matters as models move into policy, medicine, and finance roles. The benchmark gives developers a hard, honest yardstick for progress.
arxiv-2510-07331:
Alpay and Alakkad introduce Truth-Aware Decoding, a scheme that checks language model output against a knowledge base while it is being written. Their 2025 paper borrows tools from program logic, the discipline of proving software correct. A lattice of semantic guards vets each candidate token at decode time. Only oracle-approved continuations survive. The authors give the scheme a formal semantics, casting filtering as a logical judgment rather than an engineering hack. That framing lets them prove properties, not merely measure them.

One theorem shows greedy selection keeps a local likelihood edge under sound and complete guards. An entropy-style invariant tracks factual risk through a notion of safe probability mass. Certified code artefacts in a proof assistant back the implementation claims. Case studies report fewer hallucinations with no loss of speed. The work bridges statistical models and formal verification, two cultures that rarely meet.
arxiv-2510-07431:
Van de Moortel constructs black hole spacetimes whose interiors end in two kinds of singularity at once. The 2025 paper extends his recent analysis of spherically symmetric charged black holes. Inside such holes, theory predicts a null singularity along the Cauchy horizon and a crushing spacelike one deeper in. Whether both can coexist in a complete, asymptotically flat spacetime was open. The author builds large classes of examples satisfying the Einstein-Maxwell equations with a charged scalar field.

Both one-ended and two-ended asymptotically flat examples are constructed. In each, the terminal boundary inside the hole has exactly the two predicted components, nothing more exotic. Near the junction between them, the spacelike singularity takes a Kasner form whose exponents degenerate to a specific limiting triple.
arxiv-2510-07531:
Strutz, Kiers, and Curtis optimize where to lay fiber-optic sensing cables so the ground reveals the most to them. Their 2025 paper concerns distributed acoustic sensing, which turns a fiber into thousands of vibration sensors along its length. Layout decides what the system can hear, yet deployments usually follow roads and convenience. The authors represent cable routes as splines that an evolutionary search can bend, subject to terrain, access, exclusion zones, and length limits.

A case study optimizes a layout for monitoring slope stability in the Swiss Alps at Cuolm da Vi. Both single-goal and trade-off searches run efficiently in parallel. Results show substantial potential gains in earthquake location accuracy and tomographic resolution from layout alone, with no new hardware.
arxiv-2510-08231:
Lei Li and co-authors use computer simulations in a 2025 arXiv paper to explain why merging black holes come in two favored mass groups. Gravity wave detectors keep finding pairs of black holes that merge and send ripples through space. The masses of these pairs cluster near two peaks, one light and one heavy. That pattern hints the pairs form in more than one way.

The team ran the MOBSE code, which simulates how pairs of stars live and die over time. Their models included a path called chemically homogeneous evolution, where stars mix fully as they burn. They found the light peak, near ten solar masses, comes from pairs shaped by shared envelopes or steady mass transfer. The heavy peak, near thirty-five solar masses, comes from the fully mixed path. Predicted merger rates varied widely with model settings, which the authors report in full.
arxiv-2510-08531:
Hongxing Li and co-authors train spatial reasoning in vision-language models step by step in a 2025 arXiv paper. Models still struggle to judge positions, distances, and multi-view relations in images. The authors blame a missing foundation: models jump to reasoning before mastering perception. Their SpatialLadder framework builds the skill progressively, from grounding to inference.

They first built SpatialLadder-26k, a dataset of twenty-six thousand six hundred ten samples across localization, single-image, multi-view, and video tasks. Training then runs in three stages: object localization for perception, multi-dimensional spatial tasks for understanding, and reinforcement learning for complex reasoning. The resulting three-billion-parameter model set state-of-the-art scores on spatial reasoning benchmarks. It improved on its base model by 23.4 percent on average, and beat GPT-4o by 20.8 percent on their measures.
arxiv-2510-08631:
Hanieh Shojaei Miandashti and Claus Brenner detect unknown objects in LiDAR scans using model uncertainty in a 2025 arXiv paper. Self-driving systems segment point clouds into known classes, but unseen objects get forced into wrong categories. Supervised detectors need extra outlier data sets, while unsupervised ones lean on predictive entropy. Entropy mixes model uncertainty with data ambiguity, mislabeling borderline known regions as unknown.

Their unsupervised method isolates epistemic uncertainty, the model's own ignorance, through hierarchical Bayesian modeling. Gaussian mixture model parameters in the network's feature space carry the uncertainty estimate. No auxiliary data or extra training stages are required. On the SemanticKITTI benchmark, the method beat existing uncertainty-based approaches clearly. Detection quality rose by eighteen percent in AUROC and twenty-two percent in AUPRC over the entropy baseline. False positive rates at high recall dropped from seventy-six percent to forty percent.
arxiv-2510-08831:
Haverals and Martin test whether readers favor writing they believe came from a human, in this 2025 arXiv study of literary judgment. Their test material was Raymond Queneau's Exercises in Style, a classic that retells one tiny scene in dozens of ways, plus versions generated by GPT-4. Humans and AI models judged the passages under three conditions: no label, a true label, and a false label.

Both groups showed a clear pro-human bias, rating identical text higher when they thought a person wrote it. The AI judges showed the bias more than twice as strongly as the human judges. A second study crossed many AI creators with many AI judges and found the penalty applied to anything labeled as machine-made, whoever made it. Labels even flipped how the same traits were judged. The authors say the models seem to have absorbed a human cultural bias from their training.
arxiv-2510-08931:
Kattamuri and co-authors build a detector that can tell whether a language model is recalling a test or genuinely solving it, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Benchmark scores lose meaning when the test questions leaked into training data, because the model may simply recite memorized answers. Surface checks cannot easily separate recitation from reasoning. The team's tool, RADAR, looks inside the model's workings instead.

RADAR gathers thirty-seven signals from each response, spanning simple confidence patterns and deeper traits like attention focus, circuit behavior, and how activation flows through the model. A team of classifiers votes on those signals. The detector reached ninety-three percent accuracy on a mixed test set. It was perfect on clear-cut cases and still managed roughly three quarters correct on deliberately ambiguous ones. The authors present the result as proof that watching a model's internals can police evaluation honesty.
arxiv-2510-09131:
Ghirlanda presents an algorithm that catalogs a family of geometric shapes completely in dimensions five and six, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The shapes are reflexive simplices, lattice polytopes whose mirror image through the origin is again a lattice shape. They matter because each one defines a family of geometric spaces used in string theory and algebraic geometry. Lower dimensions were enumerated long ago, but dimension five and beyond resisted a full census.

His method encodes each simplex by a matrix of degrees, a compact dual description that turns the reflexivity test into explicit conditions checked row by row. Early pruning by symmetry cuts the search sharply. The count comes to two hundred twenty thousand shapes in dimension five and just over three hundred million in dimension six. As a byproduct, the work gives explicit formulas for two key invariants of the associated spaces, their Picard group and Gorenstein index.
arxiv-2510-09231:
Coudreuse establishes a sharp gradient bound for a diffusion equation with interactions, both for the equation itself and for the step-by-step scheme used to approximate it, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The granular-medium equation describes a density that diffuses while being pulled by an external potential and by its own crowd effect. The Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality, born in heat-equation theory, bounds how sharply the logarithm of a solution can curve. Such bounds unlock many further estimates.

Coudreuse proves the inequality on the torus for the continuous equation and for its JKO approximation, the time-discrete scheme that moves the density by optimal transport steps. From the bound flow concrete dividends: Lipschitz control, uniform density bounds, and a quantitative Harnack inequality. Finally, the regularity proves that the scheme, applied to the Fokker-Planck equation, converges strongly in a local second-order Sobolev sense.
arxiv-2510-09331:
Rostyslav Serha, Carsten Dubs, and Andrii Chumak review magnetic materials for quantum magnonics in a 2025 arXiv paper. Magnonics studies spin waves, ripples that travel through a magnetic material, and a magnon is one quantum unit of such a wave. The field hopes to use magnons to carry and process quantum information, so materials that keep magnons alive a long time matter most.

The authors survey metals, Heusler compounds, antiferromagnets, altermagnets, organic and layered magnets, hexaferrites, and europium compounds. Yttrium iron garnet, known as YIG, stays the benchmark, since pure crystals hold magnons for long spans at very low temperatures. Thin YIG films on the usual base lose that edge, but films on a new matched base called YSGAG keep damping low. The review maps a path toward films that support lasting magnons for quantum networks.
arxiv-2510-09431:
Thomas Koopman and Sven-Bodo Scholz examine the numerical stability of Quickhull in a 2025 arXiv paper. Quickhull computes the convex hull, the tightest wrapping shape around a set of points in a plane. The algorithm is fast in everyday practice, yet its worst-case running time is poor when an adversary crafts the input points.

The authors show that the same pattern governs its numerical behaviour. Their question is forward stability, which asks whether the computed hull stays close to the exact hull of slightly perturbed input. They prove that Quickhull is usually forward stable, so ordinary inputs give trustworthy results despite floating-point rounding. The poor behaviour, like the poor running time, is confined to adversarial cases. The finding separates the algorithm's practical reliability from its theoretical worst case, and it gives users a firmer basis for trusting hulls computed on typical data.
arxiv-2510-09731:
Muhammad Munsif, Waqas Ahmad, Amjid Ali, Mohib Ullah, Adnan Hussain, and Sung Wook Baik survey multi-camera vision systems in a 2025 arXiv paper. Connected vision systems combine feeds from many cameras to serve vehicles, smart cities, surveillance needs, and human-robot interaction. Their power comes from multi-view analytics: tracking people across cameras, re-identifying them, and understanding their actions as one coherent picture.

Earlier surveys treated those tasks in isolation and mostly for single cameras, the authors argue, neglecting how integration changes the problem. Occlusions, shifting viewpoints, and variable environments all bite harder in real deployments. Their survey is, to their knowledge, the first to unify tracking, re-identification, and action understanding for multi-camera systems in one framework. A four-part taxonomy organises the field, and they systematically arrange the datasets, methods, results, and metrics for each part. Open challenges and emerging technologies close the review.
arxiv-2510-09831:
Ameya Patwardhan, Bas van der Geer, Jom Luiten, and Julius Huijts argue for permanent magnets in low-energy electron machines in a 2025 arXiv paper. Permanent magnet optics are already prized in high-energy accelerators for their simplicity and zero power draw. The authors list the gains of the same approach at low energies, where electron sources and diffraction instruments live.

Their designs use axially magnetised permanent magnets and deliver focal lengths of only a few millimetres. Because particles never start inside a magnetic field, the apparent emittance growth plaguing other designs is avoided. Applied to an accelerator on an ultracold electron source, the design preserves emittance at the shortest focus. Its beamline is only twelve centimetres long, limiting space-charge effects. Two remedies for making and alignment problems further improve the performance by suppressing stray defects.
arxiv-2510-09931:
Chaitanya Karamchedu, Matthew Fox, and Daniel Gottesman bound eventually universal gate sets in this 2025 arXiv paper in quantum computing. A gate set is eventually universal if, past some size, its gates can approximate any operation on any number of qudits, quantum units with more than two states, to any precision.

The definition sounds mild, but it hides a threshold question: how large must a system be before universality kicks in? The authors place bounds on that threshold for collections of gates. Their results clarify when a gate set that fails on small systems can still become universal at scale. Such bounds matter for designing quantum hardware, where the available native gates rarely form a tidy universal set.
arxiv-2510-10331:
Su and co-authors reformat customer support knowledge for language models in this 2025 arXiv paper from Airbnb's support operation. Support policies and workflows are complex documents, hard for a model to navigate reliably. The authors propose knowledge representation designed to be friendly to large language models.

Their Intent, Context, and Action format rewrites each policy around what the customer wants, the situation, and the step to take. Restructuring the same content in this form makes it easier for a model to find and apply the right rule. The approach is practical: no model retraining, just better-shaped source material. Clearer knowledge should cut wrong or inconsistent answers in automated support.
arxiv-2510-10731:
Yongxi Cao and four co-authors make trajectory prediction for self driving cars controllable, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Generative models such as conditional variational autoencoders predict where nearby road users will go. Accuracy is not enough: planners also need diverse predictions, because human behavior is uncertain. Random diversity, though, is less useful than diversity a planner can steer. Their framework, PrefCVAE, adds that control.

PrefCVAE learns from weakly labeled preference pairs, examples ranked by some trait. This imbues the model's latent variables with meaningful attributes that a planner can dial up or down. Using average velocity as the example attribute, the team shows the model produces controllable, meaningful predictions. Crucially, baseline accuracy does not degrade. The authors present preference supervision as a cheap way to make sampling based generative models more useful for safe planning, where asking for faster or slower hypothetical futures has clear value.
arxiv-2510-11031:
Yiwei Liu, Yucheng Li, Xiao Li, and Gong Cheng build a factory for logic plus arithmetic puzzles, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Language models struggle when a problem needs rule based reasoning and numerical computation together. Existing test sets use fixed rule collections and offer little control over difficulty, which limits their value for evaluation and training. Their LogiNumSynth system synthesizes natural language problems with dials for three things: the richness of the reasoning world, the depth of the logical reasoning, and the complexity of the numerical work.

The team uses the synthesizer three ways. It generates fully controllable joint reasoning tasks. It supports evaluation of both the final answer and the reasoning process itself. And its output serves as targeted training data to strengthen models. Experiments across multiple language models exposed persistent weaknesses in combined logical numerical reasoning.
arxiv-2510-11231:
Recurrent novae erupt every few years when a white dwarf's stolen surface layer ignites. Judhajeet Basu and co-authors studied the 2024 eruption of the Large Magellanic Cloud nova LMCN 1968-12a in this 2025 arXiv astronomy paper. The system erupts about every 4.3 years and hosts a massive white dwarf, and Swift discovered this eruption in August 2024.

AstroSat and Swift tracked the event in ultraviolet and X-rays. After a rapid decline, the light settled into a plateau modulated every 1.26 days, matching the orbital period, and supersoft X-ray emission appeared by day five with a double peak. The ultraviolet spectrum peaked near 20,000 kelvin from a source a few times the Sun's radius, too large and steady for the companion star or the nova photosphere alone. The authors conclude the light came from an irradiated accretion disk that survived and resumed activity within days.
arxiv-2510-11431:
Fermion wavefunctions must flip sign whenever two particles swap places, and representing that antisymmetry well is a central obstacle in quantum physics, chemistry, and materials science. Liang Fu introduces a representation that removes the obstacle in this 2025 arXiv paper. The trick is a lifting: any continuous antisymmetric function can be rewritten as a continuous symmetric function defined on an enlarged space.

Building on the lifting, Fu obtains a parity-graded representation in which symmetric feature variables encode the particle configuration and antisymmetric ones encode the exchange statistics. The representation is exact, not an approximation, and minimal. The number of features needed grows only polynomially with particle number. The exponent is set by the spatial dimension or better, depending on the feature maps. The result gives a foundation for neural network solvers of many-electron systems that improve step by step.
arxiv-2510-11531:
A Lyapunov exponent measures whether nearby paths of a system converge or fly apart; a negative top exponent means noise has steadied the dynamics. Alexandra Blessing Neamţu and Mazyar Ghani Varzaneh prove such steadying for equations driven by fractional Brownian motion in this 2025 arXiv probability paper. Fractional Brownian motion has memory, so the noise is non-Markovian and the standard ergodic tools for diffusion do not directly apply.

The authors build the machinery: they analyze the system the equation generates, build an associated random dynamical system, and find an invariant measure for it. Density estimates plus Birkhoff's ergodic theorem then show the top Lyapunov exponent turns negative once the noise is strong enough. The result gives the exponent's sign where computing its value is out of reach, aimed at a broader program on such dynamics.
arxiv-2510-12031:
Urvashi Kishnani and Sanchari Das audit the security of the world's top shopping apps. E-commerce applications carry global financial traffic, so their weaknesses matter. Their 2025 arXiv paper analyzes ninety-two top-grossing Android e-commerce apps, fifty-eight American and thirty-four international. Three automated scanners, MobSF, AndroBugs, and RiskInDroid, dissect each app's code, manifest, and certificates.

The findings are grim. About ninety-two percent of the apps used unsecured HTTP connections somewhere, and the average MobSF security score was roughly forty-one out of one hundred. Seventy-seven apps demanded more permissions than their function justifies. American apps showed fewer manifest, code, and certificate vulnerabilities than their international peers. Network-related weaknesses, however, were equally common in both groups. The authors call for stronger, standardized, user-focused security practices across all regions.
arxiv-2510-12131:
Haobin Ni, Robbert van Renesse, and Greg Morrisett put distributed-systems folklore on formal footing. Theorists argue for correctness in a gut-feel Hoare-like style, reasoning as if a messy asynchronous network were one tidy synchronous program. Whether that style is sound had never been fully proven. Their 2025 arXiv paper grounds it through twin languages.

Sync describes a spread system as a single synchronous data-wide program, kept syntactically tight so functional, Hoare-style reasoning applies. Async models the reality: interacting monadic programs, one per healthy node, with shuffled traces. Sync compiles into Async, and the authors prove any safety property proven for Sync survives the move into Async's operational world, Byzantine faults too. Built in the Rocq prover, the system verifies two fault-tolerant consensus methods, BOSCO and SeqPaxos. The payoff is runnable code carrying proof: engineers can reason in the comfy fiction and ship the async truth.
arxiv-2510-12331:
Bouin and Ziviani prove convergence results for kinetic Fokker Planck equations whose steady states cannot be written down explicitly, in a 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. Kinetic equations describe a gas or plasma through the distribution of its particles in position and velocity. Here space confinement is strong, velocity confinement is weak, and the local equilibria have fat tails, meaning unusually fast particles are not as rare as a Gaussian would suggest.

The authors extend earlier results to a wider class of such fat tailed local equilibria. They obtain convergence rates in a large family of weighted L1 spaces, which measure error while emphasizing chosen regions of position and velocity. Because the global steady state has no explicit formula, the analysis must characterize it indirectly. Simulations explore the shape of this non explicit steady state. The work clarifies how slowly such systems settle when velocity confinement is very weak.
arxiv-2510-12431:
Do and Norbury deform a famous recursion for the volumes of moduli spaces into a version depending on a parameter q, in a 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. Mirzakhani's recursion computes Weil Petersson volumes, which measure the sizes of spaces of hyperbolic surfaces, and revolutionized the field before her death. A related recursion by Stanford and Witten covers the super case.

The authors define q analogues of both recursions. Their starting point is recent work by Okuyama, who deformed a Gaussian matrix model so its outputs recover the Weil Petersson volumes in a rescaled limit as q approaches one. The q deformed volumes defined in this work agree with the top degree terms of Okuyama's quasi polynomials. The authors suggest this points to a variation of Okuyama's method that would cover the super setting. The paper links enumerative geometry, matrix models, and the combinatorics of surfaces through a single deformation parameter.
arxiv-2510-12531:
Cinque and Orsingher study pairs of counting processes whose components influence each other through migration, in a 2025 arXiv probability paper. Point processes record event times, such as arrivals or births, and interacting versions let one population's events affect another's rates. The authors examine two models with a migration type effect.

In the first model, two groups change state with rates depending only on time, and the vector process decomposes into independent non homogeneous Skellam processes. A general representation through independent Poisson processes follows. The second model adds births and deaths to migration. For linear death and migration rates, the vector at any fixed time equals in distribution the sum of two separate multinomial random variables. The distribution of a pure migration process follows as a byproduct. Finally they time change the processes with the inverse of a Bernstein subordinator, linking fractional equations to the wider class.
arxiv-2510-12931:
Byun and co-authors improve image captioning without any text labels in this 2025 arXiv paper. Vision-language models learn from huge labeled image collections, which limits how far they can scale and leaves most unlabeled photos unused. Their framework, ViZer, instead aligns the model's internal vision and language features directly during a short enhancement training.

Because no captions are needed as targets, an existing model can be upgraded without full retraining. The authors note that automatic caption metrics often punish correct details missing from reference captions, so they leaned on qualitative evaluation. Applied to two open models, SmolVLM-Base and Qwen2-VL, ViZer produced captions that were consistently more grounded and descriptive than the baselines. For example, it named a trekking hiker's backpack and poles where the base model wrote almost nothing. They offer ViZer as a starting point for broader zero-label adaptation.
arxiv-2510-13231:
Liu and co-authors explore coscattering dark matter in scotogenic models in this 2025 arXiv paper. Scotogenic models elegantly tie dark matter to the origin of tiny neutrino masses through particles odd under a discrete symmetry. The conventional candidate is squeezed hard by lepton flavor violation limits and direct detection null results. With two nearly equal-mass dark scalars, new production pathways open.

The authors map the parameter space where the lighter scalar's abundance is set by coscattering. In coscattering, collisions convert it into its heavier partner off ordinary matter. They contrast this with the coannihilation channel. They then apply constraints from Higgs decays, direct detection, and indirect detection. The heavier scalar's three-body decay affects predictions for big bang nucleosynthesis and the cosmic microwave background. It could also produce a displaced vertex signature at colliders, giving the scenario an experimental handle.
arxiv-2510-13731:
Khalaila and Cashman sketch a speculative grammar for designing charts that blind and low-vision readers explore by touch. Their 2025 arXiv paper, an accessibility conference contribution, starts from how tactile charts usually get made. Designers adapt visual charts directly, yet many visual encodings fail under fingertips. Readers instead measure with fingers, count ridges, and compare textures.

The proposed Tactile Perceptual Grammar links data analysis tasks to those physical strategies. Each task, like comparing values or spotting trends, suggests matching encodings and exploration moves. Speculative mockups show the grammar steering an accessible COVID-19 dashboard design. The choices aim to support comparison, trend detection, and judging proportions by touch. The authors stress the framework is not yet validated by studies. They close with design implications and plans for co-design and task-based evaluation.
arxiv-2510-13931:
Siying Liu, Shisheng Zhang, and Indu Bala test whether large language models let social details sway medical judgments, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The team studies drug-safety decisions, where a model predicts how likely a drug is to cause an adverse event, meaning a harmful side effect. Social traits such as education or housing should not affect that prediction.

Using United States adverse event reports, the authors gave two models, ChatGPT-4o and a biomedical Llama model, personas that varied by education, insurance, housing stability, and other traits. Disadvantaged personas were often assigned higher predicted risk than privileged ones. The team separates explicit bias, where reasoning text names the persona trait, from implicit bias, where predictions shift without any mention. They argue fairness checks are needed before clinical use.
arxiv-2510-14331:
Shivam Singhal and co-authors use language models as proposal engines for learning programs from a handful of examples, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Learning theory says a rule with a program description can be learned from few examples by searching the program class. But exhaustive search is exponentially slow. Gradient-trained networks need exponentially many samples for the same rules.

Their propose-and-verify recipe, LLM-PV, has a language model propose programs from its prior. Each program is executed and scored on a validation set, and the best is selected. There are no gradient updates and no feedback loop. Across algorithmic tasks including parity variants, pattern matching, and primality testing, the method recovered the rule from a labeled set. It generalized far beyond training sequence lengths. Transformer training, fine-tuning, in-context learning, and classical baselines fell short on the same tasks.
arxiv-2510-14531:
Onder and co-authors present, in a 2025 arXiv paper, the design of a silicon carbide radiation sensor called a low gain avalanche diode. Such sensors multiply a weak signal inside the device itself. That helps them register fast, faint events. The team's version uses a thin layer of the crystal form named 4H-SiC. Deep etched trenches help it survive very high voltages without breaking down at its edges.

All of the work reported is simulation, done with industry design software in a simplified geometry. The design fully depletes below five hundred volts. It gives controlled signal gain up to one thousand volts. After the authors tuned the guard structure around the edge, the simulated breakdown voltage rose above two thousand four hundred volts. They also checked that the design tolerates small changes in the gain layer. A first wafer run is now being made in Barcelona.
arxiv-2510-14731:
Rapaka and Riahi introduce, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a Generalized Fourier Series that handles functions which do not repeat, the classical weak spot of Fourier methods. A standard Fourier series assumes periodicity. Applied to a function that jumps at the boundary, it produces the Gibbs phenomenon: stubborn ripples near the jump that refuse to die as terms are added, plus slow convergence overall.

Their method splits a function into a periodic part and an aperiodic part. The periodic part uses ordinary Fourier modes, computed quickly with the Fast Fourier Transform. The aperiodic part uses adaptive, low-rank sinusoidal functions with non-harmonic modes, tuned on the fly to capture jumps and kinks at the boundaries. No artificial extension of the domain is needed. Numerical experiments show accurate approximations of functions and their derivatives in non-periodic settings. The overall cost keeps the favorable near-linear scaling of the fast transform.
arxiv-2510-15231:
Yuatyong Chaichana and four colleagues at SCB 10X and partner groups help audio-language models listen to long recordings without losing the thread. Their 2025 arXiv paper notes that models which hear sound and read text often accept only short clips, even though their text side handles long documents. Earlier context-stretching tricks had been tried on text-only models, never on audio ones.

Their first method, Partial YaRN, stretches only the positions of audio tokens, leaving text positions untouched so the model's reading skill stays intact, and it needs no retraining. A second idea, Virtual Longform Audio Training, simulates varied audio lengths during training so the model generalizes to recordings far longer than any it trained on. Tested on two systems, SALMONN and Qwen2-Audio, the training-free method already beat the originals in many settings. The training strategy added large further gains on long audio.
arxiv-2510-15431:
Francesco Colasanto and Pascal Steinke work out the fine asymptotics of a classic model of phase separation, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The Cahn-Hilliard functional assigns an energy to mixtures, favoring two pure phases separated by thin interfaces. As a small parameter shrinks, the energy's limit is studied through Gamma-convergence, a standard tool for such limiting problems.

First-order limits for this functional are classical, going back to Modica and Mortola. Colasanto and Steinke push to the second order, the next term in the expansion, under Dirichlet boundary conditions that fix the mixture's state at the edge of the domain. Their potential has a double-well shape with sub-quadratic growth near the wells, a weaker assumption than most earlier work required. The paper develops the second-order Gamma limit in this setting, sharpening what the energy predicts about interface behavior near walls.
arxiv-2510-15731:
Maximo Rulli and colleagues present a study in a 2025 paper. It examines attention patterns inside diffusion language models. These newer models generate text in parallel. Standard models generate one token at a time. The team looked for attention sinks. These are spots where the model dumps excess attention. Sinks are well known in autoregressive models. They were unexplored in diffusion models.

Diffusion models do show attention sinks. Theirs behave differently, though. The sink positions shift as generation proceeds. They do not stay fixed. Removing the sinks barely hurts these models. Autoregressive models degrade badly when theirs are masked. This is a basic difference in how the two families assign attention, the authors conclude.
arxiv-2510-15831:
Do Xuan Long and five co-authors present VISTA, a multi-agent system that improves generated videos by rewriting their prompts in a loop. Text-to-video quality hinges on prompt wording, and earlier test-time tuning methods struggle with video's many-sided nature. VISTA first breaks a user's idea into a structured plan over time.

After a video is made, a pairwise tournament picks the best version so far. Three specialist agents then critique that winner for visual, audio, and contextual fidelity. A reasoning agent merges the critiques and rewrites the prompt for the next round. On single-scene and multi-scene tasks, earlier methods gain inconsistently, while VISTA improves quality and fit to intent steadily.
