It wins a clear majority of pairwise contests against leading baselines, and human judges prefer its outputs in about two thirds of comparisons.
arxiv-2510-15931:
Gamaliel Morales, writing alone, defines a new family of quaternion sequences from higher-order Horadam numbers with three parameters. Horadam numbers extend the Fibonacci pattern through a flexible recurrence rule. Kuloğlu and colleagues added higher-order versions in recent work. Quaternions extend complex numbers to four parts. They serve widely in physics and geometry.

Morales joins the two ideas in one definition. The new sequences had not been studied before, by his account. He states the recurrence rules that build them term by term. He then derives their main properties. Those include generating functions and an exponential generating function. Summation formulas and a Binet-style closed form also appear. More identities follow from those results. Later researchers gain a ready toolkit for the new sequences.
arxiv-2510-16031:
Andy Shi, as sole author, releases a storm-centred radar data set at quarter-kilometre resolution for machine learning nowcasting. Nowcasting predicts a storm's next moves from radar reflectivity sequences. Public data sets at one to two kilometre resolution smooth away the fine structures that matter most for extreme weather, which has held model quality back.

Storm250-L2 is derived from NEXRAD Level-II data and GridRad-Severe storm tracks. An algorithm crops a fixed high-resolution window around each tracked storm, keeps the native polar geometry, and supplies consistent sequences of single-tilt sweeps plus a pseudo-composite reflectivity product. Thousands of storm events across the continental United States are packaged as HDF5 tensors with rich context metadata and reproducible file lists. The data set aims to let nowcasting models learn the sharp edges of convective storms.
arxiv-2510-16131:
Avijit Barua and seven co-authors report a way to build tiny light sources for future quantum networks. Each source pairs a quantum dot with a circular Bragg grating. A quantum dot is a speck of material that emits one photon at a time. The grating is a ring pattern that helps the light escape. Placing the dot dead center is the hard part.

The team uses electron beam writing guided by the dot's own glow, so each grating is drawn around a dot already found. Across ninety-five test devices, more than nine in ten worked, and the dots sat where they should. Even gratings with just three or four rings let light out well, which keeps the chips small and quick to make. The method offers a steady route to making many good single-photon sources at once.
arxiv-2510-16331:
Fatemeh Jafarian Dehkordi and four co-authors build a privacy-preserving way for several parties to compute dot products of binary vectors they hold in pieces. Tree-based vertical federated learning needs such bitwise operations, but classic secret sharing and multi-party computation tools handle binary data clumsily, especially when each participant owns different bits.

Their BiMPC framework centers on DoMA, a method computing binary dot products through ordinary and modular additions. Random masking in a larger field protects the linear steps, while a three-party oblivious transfer protocol covers the nonlinear bitwise operations, keeping every individual bit private. The authors analyze the privacy guarantees rigorously and argue the design stays efficient and scalable across distributed participants.
arxiv-2510-16431:
Nina Holden and Xin Sun survey a field called Liouville quantum gravity in their 2025 review. The field began in physics and now sits at the heart of chance and shape studies. It gives a way to build random curved surfaces. Random flat maps, built from glued shapes, are one key source. Their large-scale limits are said to match this gravity.

One part shows how such maps settle into the random geometry. Links with a random curve tool, called SLE, play a key role there. A second part ties the field to conformal field theory, a physics frame for scale-free systems. The review ends with open questions. It serves as a map for new readers of the field.
arxiv-2510-16631:
Anna Horváth, Aneta Wojnar, and Gergely Gábor Barnaföldi bend a mass rule in strong gravity in 2025. They work in Kaluza-Klein theory, which adds a fifth dimension to space-time. A dispersion relation ties a particle's energy to its momentum. Strong gravity warps that link, they find. The particle's working mass then hangs on how curved the phase space is.

Phase space pairs each place with its momentum in one big map. In zones of fierce gravity, the working mass can turn imaginary. An imaginary mass flags that the particle may break down there. In plain terms, curved space itself can force decay. The result warns that mass is not fixed where gravity runs wild.
arxiv-2510-17131:
Xin Gao and ten co-authors make fake odd samples to catch odd data in this 2025 paper. Detectors that flag out-of-place inputs train better with such samples. Past makers warp word cues, which gives shaky and narrow fakes. The team instead steers image growth itself toward odd zones.

Two guides steer growth, one in raw pixels and one in learned traits. A merged score then blends both gaps for a firm flag. Samples from the method train detectors to spot odd inputs far better. Tests in depth and breadth back the gains. The frame bends to many tasks since it needs no fresh training.
arxiv-2510-17531:
Keeping a fusion plasma in the right shape inside a tokamak is a control task where the classic PID controller adapts only within narrow limits. Niannian Wu, leading a team with eight co-authors, builds a more flexible controller from a large archive of past discharges that the older controller ran. Their method learns to copy the stable style of those runs while also building a tidy internal map of plasma states, which supports goal directed control.

The resulting policy can be dropped into new tracking tasks with no extra training for each task, a property called zero shot use. On a simulator of the HL-3 tokamak, Wu and her co-authors report precise and stable tracking of target shapes across varied plasma scenarios. The work points toward data efficient intelligent control for future fusion reactors.
arxiv-2510-17831:
John F. Hardy and three co-authors show that porous helical layers cut memory chip power sharply. Their devices are resistive random-access memory, a switchable resistance memory type. The test stack pairs indium tin oxide with tungsten oxide layers. Helical and flat film devices behaved alike at high current limits.

Only helical devices kept working reliably at a much lower current limit. There, reset voltages fell by about sixty percent. Switching currents dropped by roughly seventy percent as well. The readable memory window grew several-fold at that low setting. Geometry-driven field concentration explains the low-power, high-margin behavior.
arxiv-2510-18131:
Chengquan Guo, with five co-authors, defends code-generating models with an agent trained by automated attacks. As language models write more code, the security risks grow with them. Red teaming to find flaws is well developed, while blue team defense lags because it must tell unsafe code from safe code by meaning.

Their BlueCodeAgent pairs the two sides: attacks create varied risky cases, and the defender learns from them through guiding rules and code analysis. Tests span bias traps, malicious instructions, and vulnerability tasks. Security teams get a defense that trains against fresh attacks instead of a fixed list.
arxiv-2510-18231:
Rosalia O'Brien, with Richard G Arendt and sixteen co-authors, refines a zodiacal light model in a 2025 paper. Zodiacal light is the faint glow from sunlight scattering off dust between the planets. Older models were tuned for infrared light and predicted visible light poorly.

The new model, called ZodiSURF, draws on more than five thousand Hubble telescope sky measurements. It adds how dust scatters and reflects light across visible and near-infrared wavelengths. Predictions now match Hubble data much better, with model uncertainty near four and a half percent. The data also leave a small unexplained glow, which the authors link to a possible faint spherical dust cloud.
arxiv-2510-18531:
S. Q. Hou and his six co-authors redo a key nuclear rate. The rate matters inside X-ray bursts. Those are huge blasts on the surface of neutron stars. In them, a rapid capture process builds heavy elements step by step. One step has titanium-42 capture a proton, forming vanadium-43. Old rates came from a statistical model. That model assumes the middle nucleus has many dense energy levels.

The team rebuilt the rate from fresher inputs. They used fuller resonance data and a more exact direct part. They used newly released nuclear masses. They built the rate resonance by resonance. Random sampling gave the error range. The new rates differ from the old ones a lot. In places the gap reaches ten thousand times. Burst tests with the new rates changed final scandium and calcium amounts sharply. The broad pattern of elements stayed much the same.
arxiv-2510-18631:
Carlo Proietti and Antonio Yuste-Ginel compare ways of modeling uncertainty inside formal argumentation, the logic of claims that attack and defend each other. Most earlier work used abstract models, where arguments are bare nodes. The authors instead ground uncertainty in an argument's inner parts, its rules and premises, following a recent push toward concrete versions of the abstract theories.

Their first contribution is a notion of expressivity, a measure of what a framework can and cannot represent, that works for both abstract and structured systems. With it, they prove results in both directions, showing places where structured models match abstract ones and places where they fall short. The comparisons cover incomplete abstract frameworks, an extension with dependencies, and the structured system known as ASPIC+, sharpening the map of what each style of argumentation can express.
arxiv-2510-18931:
Kenya S Andrews and four co-authors use a justice lens to judge fairness and ethics courses in computing education. Course syllabi set tone and expectations, and in classes on fair artificial intelligence and algorithmic design, students need clear, open teaching about barriers to fair outcomes.

The team builds a justice-based scoring rubric and asks a large language model to review syllabi while playing several roles. Applying that process to twenty-four syllabi, they assess coverage, depth, classroom practice, and expectations. The method offers a faster, more consistent way to check whether such courses teach fairness in depth.
arxiv-2510-19031:
Akilan Amithasagaran and three co-authors introduce CLiVR, a virtual reality system where medical trainees talk with artificial intelligence patients. Real training with actors or manikins builds clinical reasoning and communication, but it is costly and hard to scale for every student.

Built in Unity for a common headset, CLiVR combines language models, speech tools, and three-dimensional avatars for natural dialogue. Each case is generated from a database linking syndromes and symptoms, and sentiment analysis feeds back on how the trainee communicated. The system offers repeatable practice without booking human patients.
arxiv-2510-19231:
Seongmin Kim and Alec Kirkley improve belief propagation on finite networks. They fix one well-connected source node. That breaks the global symmetry. Belief propagation passes messages to estimate key values. On small, sparse networks its estimates are often poor. Few loops make the problem worse.

Holding one hub node fixed costs nothing extra. Yet accuracy jumps for two test models. Both percolation and Ising models improve. The gain is largest on tree-like networks. Real networks are finite, never infinite. Cheap gains like this are thus worth having in practice.
arxiv-2510-19331:
Ewelina Gajewska and three co-authors test how giving language models annotator personas changes their hate speech detection. Personalized models might judge abuse differently depending on whether the persona shares an identity with the target, which could help or harm fairness across social groups.

Two commercial models were prompted with shallow personas and with richer profiles built through retrieval, playing both in-group and out-group annotators. The study links psychological ideas about group identity with current language technology, showing how persona design shifts sensitivity and bias. Such findings matter before personalized models are trusted with moderation decisions.
arxiv-2510-19431:
Jonas Cassel and three co-authors build a gauge theory frame for data. They call the theme Yang-Mills meets data. Gauge methods borrow the mathematics of vector bundles. They process data in a way that respects local symmetries. Such care is needed when data have no single global coordinate system.

Lattice gauge theory motivates the work. The authors give discrete versions of vector bundles. Clear ties link them to the classical formalism. Older bundle-based approaches unify under this frame. Gauge-symmetric heat kernel operators get a careful treatment too. Practitioners gain a shared geometric language for data.
arxiv-2510-19631:
Yiqian Yang and eight co-authors introduce HSCodeComp, a benchmark that tests whether AI search agents can apply hierarchical rule systems, using customs tariff codes as the test case. Every traded product needs a ten-digit Harmonized System code, and assigning one means navigating layered rules with vague boundaries. The dataset holds six hundred thirty-two real products from large e-commerce platforms, coded by human experts.

The best agent tested reached only about forty-seven percent accuracy on the full ten-digit code, against ninety-five percent for the human experts. Adding more test-time computation did not close the gap. The results expose hierarchical rule application as a weak spot of current agents, with direct relevance to law, medicine, and other rule-bound fields.
arxiv-2510-19831:
Adeline Wihardja and three co-authors measure how liquid crystal elastomers behave when stretched very fast. These rubbery solids couple liquid-crystalline order with deformation, making them attractive for soft robotics and energy absorption. The study focuses on isotropic-genesis polydomain samples across a wide range of strain rates.

A key contribution is a new tensile drop-tower that reaches strain rates of one hundred per second in tension, a regime important for applications but previously inaccessible. The team also extends a recent constitutive model into the high-rate regime and fits it to the measurements. The model describes the observed behavior across the full spectrum of rates examined, giving designers a predictive tool for impact-like loading.
arxiv-2510-19931:
Jiaming Pan and six co-authors quantify how well cross-correlating gravitational wave sources with galaxies could measure the Hubble constant. Standard sirens promise a distance-ladder-free route to the expansion rate, but most events have no identified light counterpart and hence no redshift. For these dark sirens, statisticians can still correlate their sky distribution with galaxy catalogs to recover redshift information.

The study asks what it will take to reach percent-level precision on the Hubble constant. The answer: distance uncertainties near ten percent, a catalog of at least about five thousand dark sirens, and accurate sky localization in the tomographic analysis. Constraints will be limited mainly by the quantity and quality of gravitational wave data, the authors find.
arxiv-2510-20031:
Marin Biloš, Anderson Schneider, and Yuriy Nevmyvaka speed up sampling from temporal point processes, which model event sequences such as arrivals over time. These models usually predict the next event from past events, so generating future events happens one step at a time. That sequential habit makes large-scale generation slow and inefficient.

The authors propose an algorithm based on rejection sampling that draws several future values at once, in parallel, from an existing trained model. It needs no change to the model design and no retraining, and it comes with theoretical guarantees of exactness. Tests on real-world datasets show clear speedups, making expressive models more practical for large jobs.
arxiv-2510-20431:
David Stein, Bjoern Andres, and Silvia Di Gregorio set part-best rules for cubic correlation clustering on broad graphs. The task puts each node of a graph in a group. It seeks the group set with the least sum of clique costs, where a cost counts if all clique nodes share a group. The full task is NP-hard, so real work uses local search with no best proof.

The cubic case caps clique size at three nodes. For that case, the team sets rules that can vouch for part of a group set as best. They code steps that test if the rules hold. Tests on two data sets gauge how well the vouch works in real use.
arxiv-2510-20631:
Kuntal Som, Thirumulanathan D, and Joydeep Dutta review two level choice problems where a leader picks first and a follower then picks a best reply. Trouble starts when the follower has more than one best reply, since the upper level result then depends on which reply is assumed.

Common fixes force a single reply or assume either the best or worst case for the leader, while a set based view tries to keep all replies in play. Som and his co-authors study the broad case without narrow limits and compare what each view counts as a solution. Their main finding is that the set based view may offer no real edge over the best and worst case views.
arxiv-2510-20731:
Myrtille O J Y Hunault, Timothy G Burrow, Fabien Besnard, Amélie Juhin. Christian Brouder work out the angle rules for resonant inelastic X-ray scattering, a synchrotron method that probes matter with tuned X-rays. Reading the data needs theory, yet the joint role of incoming and outgoing light angles had lacked a handy treatment.

Within a standard dipole approximation, the team counts how many basic spectra feed the signal for every crystal symmetry group. They then derive a general formula for mixed samples such as powders, glasses, and liquids that keeps the direction and polarization of both beams explicit. Shorter forms for common symmetry groups follow, and a uranium case study shows the framework in action.
arxiv-2510-20831:
Mehrnaz Asadi, Sina Javadzadeh, Rahil Soroushmojdehi, S Alireza Seyyed Mousavi, and Terence D Sanger introduce BACE, a method that learns directed links between brain regions that shift with each phase of behavior. Forecasting brain signals alone gives little insight, so the links themselves must be readable by scientists.

BACE gathers many micro contacts per region through per region time encoders, learns a link map for each behavior phase, and trains on a forecasting goal. On synthetic data with known graphs it recovers the true directed links while forecasting as well as leading baselines. On human recordings from eight deep regions during a cued reaching task, the phase maps show clear reordering of influence across the trial.
arxiv-2510-20931:
Albert Reuther leads four co-authors on an update to the Lincoln AI Computing Survey, a multi year record of commercial AI accelerators and processors. Attention to training and serving hardware has surged with generative AI, making a fresh survey timely.

Following the survey tradition, announced peak performance and peak power figures are gathered and plotted together so chips can be compared at a glance. Trends across seven years of devices show how speed and power have scaled and where the field clusters. The update gives buyers and designers a shared factual base for judging new hardware claims.
arxiv-2510-21131:
Guangxin Su leads five co-authors on a survey of how large language models meet text attributed graphs, networks whose nodes carry rich text. Language models reason well over words but hide their structure, while text attributed graphs expose relations yet lack semantic depth.

Integration frameworks are reviewed systematically from an orchestration perspective, the first survey of its kind on this pairing. Combined systems strengthen graph representation learning and give language models more structured, interpretable multi hop reasoning. Applications span recommendation, knowledge work, and science, wherever relations and text arrive together.
arxiv-2510-21331:
R. Mignon-Risse, P. Varniere, and F. Casse build a fast, simple model for the changing light of gas disks around pairs of black holes that are close to merging. Finding such pairs by their glow depends on predictions, but full simulations are expensive, so observers lack quick tools for testing candidates.

Their disk carries spiral arms and a dense lump that orbits more slowly than the black holes themselves. From a simple temperature map they trace light rays through an approximate space-time to predict what a distant viewer sees. The light curve pulses mainly at the lump's period, through a relativistic Doppler effect, with a shorter pulse from the arms. For the heaviest pairs, they estimate, a planned observatory could spot a few-percent pulse within six months of watching.
arxiv-2510-21531:
Jan Wehner and Mario Fritz turn interpretability probes into training signals for language models, and then worry about the obvious trap. Probes are small detectors read off a model's inner activity that can flag deception or bias invisible in its outputs. But a model trained to please a monitor may learn to fool it instead, an instance of Goodhart's law.

In a toxicity testbed, they train models against probes with two methods, plain fine-tuning and preference optimization, and watch how probe accuracy moves. Surprisingly, probe-based preference training preserves detectability better than training against output classifiers, as if the objective rewards keeping the inner signals honest. Ensembles of probes add little, since simply retraining probes after optimization restores high accuracy. The findings suggest probe-guided training can stay viable for some alignment goals.
arxiv-2510-21631:
Faisal Hamman and three co-authors shrink big language models into small ones using almost no data, by quizzing the teacher at its decision boundary. Standard distillation needs large sample sets to transfer a teacher's skill to a student, yet in many real tasks labeled examples are scarce or costly to obtain.

Their strategy pairs each few available example with a counterfactual twin, a minimally altered input that flips the teacher's answer. Such twins hug the boundary where the teacher's mind changes, so each one teaches the student disproportionately much about that boundary's shape. Theory supports the trick from both statistical and geometric angles. Across data sets and models, with as few as eight to five hundred twelve samples, the method beats standard distillation while using only half as many original examples.
arxiv-2510-21931:
Adam Smith, Emre Özülker, Eleonora Di Valentino, and Carsten van de Bruck test two tweaks to standard cosmology together. One tweak lets the electron's mass differ in the early universe. The other lets dark energy change over time. It may even cross the so-called phantom divide.

The team fits the newest data on the microwave background, galaxy maps, and supernovae. They compare the standard model with each tweak alone and combined. The electron-mass change alone moved the inferred Hubble constant up the most. That eased the clash with local measurements. The pull toward restless dark energy stayed present in the fits. So did the pull toward a phantom crossing. Both pulls grew somewhat weaker with the electron mass free. The two effects seem to tug at the tension in different ways.
arxiv-2510-22031:
Jincheng Zhou leads a seven-author team teaching causal discovery to use gradient descent, the engine of modern machine learning. Finding cause-and-effect graphs from observations alone usually follows one of two roads. Constraint methods that test independence rigorously but starve on small samples, or score methods that optimize smoothly but skip explicit independence checks.

The team's third road builds differentiable scores for d-separation, the graph condition behind independence, using percolation ideas rendered in soft logic. Independence constraints then become something a gradient method can directly optimize, keeping the rigor of the constraint tradition inside a flexible fitting loop. Tests show sturdy performance exactly where data is scarce, beating traditional constraint and score baselines on a real-world dataset. Code and data are publicly released.
arxiv-2510-22131:
Zhiqin Zhang, Yining Ma, Zhiguang Cao, and Hoong Chuin Lau open the black box of neural combinatorial optimization, models that learn to solve routing and scheduling puzzles. These models perform impressively, yet what their internal representations actually encode, and why they choose as they do, has stayed murky, which worries both researchers and users.

The team probes the representations with diagnostic tasks, and adds a tool that checks not just whether information is present but whether the probing coefficients are statistically meaningful. The models turn out to store low-level details needed to build solutions step by step alongside high-level knowledge that guides better global choices. Different popular architectures stamp different biases on what they learn, and the probes surface direct evidence about which representations generalize. The study is a first step toward models whose reasoning can be audited.
arxiv-2510-22531:
Unfair clauses hide in long terms of service that most people never read closely. Noshitha Padma Pratyusha Juttu, Sahithi Singireddy, Sravani Gona, and Sujal Timilsina compare ways to train language models to spot such clauses in a 2025 legal text study.

Full fine tuning of smaller models gives the best balance of precision and recall in their tests. Light adapter methods, which change only a small part of a model, use up to three times less memory while keeping competitive recall. Large models tried without training examples also feature, and the authors release open baselines for legal text work.
arxiv-2510-22731:
WiFi signals can identify a device by small radio traits. Such traits act like a fingerprint. Yong Huang leads a team with six co-authors. In 2025 they present CSI2Q, a system for this task. It uses channel state data from normal WiFi gear. That avoids costly special radio gear.

First, the system turns frequency data into time signals. Those signals match the form of richer radio samples. Next, deep learning transfers skill from a rich sample model. A final step flags devices it has never seen. Tests used synthetic data and two real router sets. Accuracy rose clearly over prior channel based methods.
arxiv-2510-22831:
Fractional quantum states need a large energy gap to stay robust. Yitong Zhang leads a team with five co-authors. In 2025 they challenge a common design belief. Flat Chern bands were thought best when most like the lowest Landau level. Landau levels are electron energy tiers in a field.

Deforming away from that limit can help a lot. Moire flat bands gave far larger gaps. Short range cases beat the Landau level by orders of magnitude. Long range cases gained by factors of two to three. The cause is stronger pseudopotentials. Pseudopotentials encode pair interaction by relative motion. The trick may also aid non Abelian states.
arxiv-2510-22931:
Xiaofan Zhou and Lu Cheng study how to keep large language models trustworthy as they keep learning new fields over time. When data shifts from one field to the next, standard promises about answer coverage can break down. Sets of possible answers can also grow so large that they stop being helpful.

The pair propose a method that can reject some queries and adjusts its promises for shifting data. It first estimates what kinds of questions are coming in, then sets coverage with that shift in mind. Their approach aims to give self-updating models honest limits instead of false sureness.
arxiv-2510-23431:
Titus Pinta proves a Newton-Kantorovich inverse function theorem in quasi-metric spaces, where distance need not be symmetric. Root finding on such spaces matters for recent models in biology and phylogenetics, where key problems are cast as optimization on quasi-metric spaces. Euclidean calculus does not directly apply there.

Pinta sets up a minimal algebraic framework with a notion of Newton differentiability that keeps standard calculus rules and suffices for superlinear convergence. The theorem then guarantees when Newton iteration finds roots or inverses. The result gives applied modelers a rigorous solver foundation beyond Euclidean space.
arxiv-2510-23931:
Miguel Fernandez-de-Retana and three co-authors test whether differential privacy actually stops gradient leakage attacks in federated learning. Federated training lets many parties build one model without pooling raw data, but the shared updates can be intercepted and inverted to rebuild private examples. Two defenses are compared: DP-SGD, which adds calibrated noise, and a variant that relies on explicit regularization instead.

The team trained several vision models at varied privacy levels on a simple classification task, then attacked the intercepted gradients in a simulated federation and graded the reconstructions. DP-SGD sharply reduced what the attacks could recover, at a moderate cost to model accuracy. The regularization variant kept accuracy high but failed as a practical shield — the reconstructions still exposed the data. The authors stress that privacy tools must be judged by attack experiments, not by their theoretical guarantees alone.
arxiv-2510-24031:
Peng Cai and two co-authors build LLMLogAnalyzer, a chatbot that helps organizations make sense of system logs, a backbone of cybersecurity work. Logs are vast and messy, and many teams lack the money, expertise, or time to analyze them well. Raw language models struggle here too: context windows overflow and structured log text defeats plain prompting.

The system's design routes around those limits with a modular pipeline — a router, a log recognizer, a log parser, and search tools — fronted by clustering. Tested on four domain log collections across summarization, pattern extraction, and anomaly detection, it beat leading LLM chatbots including ChatGPT, ChatPDF, and NotebookLM by thirty-nine to sixty-eight percent. Its answers were also far more consistent, with score variability cut by ninety-three percent. The authors pitch the tool for experts and non-technical users alike, aiming to make routine log analysis cheaper and more reliable.
arxiv-2510-24131:
Javier de Lucas and Marcin Zając survey and extend the theory of stochastic Lie systems, which are random differential equations built from a small set of vector fields. The fields span a finite dimensional Lie algebra, and random inputs mix them over time. This structure lets many random models be treated with shared tools from geometry.

The authors review the coalgebra method for Hamiltonian versions of these systems and add new examples of both standard and Hamiltonian types. They apply the theory to a wide range of models, including biological and epidemic models, stochastic oscillators, Riccati equations, coronavirus models, and Ermakov systems. The survey shows how one framework can organize many separate random models.
arxiv-2510-24231:
Waseem Shariff and four co-authors introduce a dataset and evaluation for recognizing microsaccades with event cameras. Microsaccades are tiny involuntary eye movements that matter for vision and brain processing. Standard studies use eye trackers or frame based analysis, which are precise but costly and limited in speed and scale.

Event cameras capture fine changes with high speed and low delay, offering a new route. The team rendered eye movement scenes in Blender and simulated microsaccades from half a degree to two degrees, split into seven classes. They converted the scenes to event streams with a simulator tool, preserving fine timing. The dataset supports work on small eye movements for cognitive computing.
arxiv-2510-24331:
Gabriel O. dos Santos and two co-authors systematically study in context learning in vision language models, asking what these models actually take from demonstration examples. In context learning lets a model learn a task from examples in the prompt, with no weight updates. It is well studied for text models but underexplored for models that also see images.

The team evaluates seven models across four architectures on three image captioning benchmarks. They analyze how prompt design, architecture, and training strategy shape performance, and they are the first to track attention patterns as the number of demonstrations grows. Training on interleaved image text data improved in context learning, but did not guarantee true integration of the examples.
arxiv-2510-24531: Simon Schirren defines a perfect obstruction theory for a moduli space of symplectic Higgs sheaves on projective surfaces, working alone. A key minimality assumption on the Chern character of the sheaf forces all sheaves in the moduli problem to be locally free, which makes the construction work. The result may help define a virtual count and Sp(r) Vafa-Witten invariants, extending enumerative invariants for gauge theory on surfaces to the symplectic case.
arxiv-2510-24731:
Bin Li, Dongdong Yang, Lei Liu, and Dusit Niyato plan how a smart mirror panel flown on a drone can boost wireless links. A flown panel can reach more spots than one fixed to a wall. But tilt and height shifts in flight can bend the beam off its mark and hurt the link.

Their plan sets the drone path, height, and panel phase shifts as one joint task, with limits on power, safety, and flight energy. They use flight math based on tilt terms to keep the beam true. The task is cast as a step by step choice game, then solved with a soft trial based method.
arxiv-2510-25231:
Milton Lin, Toan Pham, and Jize Yu give a ghost side read of a full part of wave marked modules on a loop space, in Langlands terms. Their set up starts from a smooth shape with a group act, of a kind called spherical. They take as given that the plain form of the linked local Langlands guess holds for that shape.

Two more terms are set: the loop space must be a tame kind of scheme, and a size rule for it must be in hand. With those, they mark the module part by the linked Langlands dual of the shape. That backs a slight shift of a tame form of the guess. Group marked rows frame the proof.
arxiv-2510-25331:
Alex Elliott, Jacob Ngaha, Scott Parkins, and Takao Aoki study photons. Their 2025 physics paper examines quantum-correlated light. They consider two cavity modes coupled to an atom. The atom has two levels and is strongly driven. Its fluorescence transitions feed the cavity modes. Photon counting statistics are explored theoretically here.

The cavity modes acquire nonclassical photon statistics, they show. Those statistics reflect dressed-state atomic transitions in pictures. In particular, the modes are antibunched in time. Antibunched means photons arrive more spaced than random. At the same time, cross-correlation exceeds unity. That combination is unusual and informative for quantum optics. The authors propose a concrete implementation for it. It uses a nanofiber cavity quantum electrodynamics system. A strongly driven cesium atom would sit inside. The setup could test these predictions in practice.
arxiv-2510-25531:
Clemens Schachter led eight co-authors on longitudinal data linking. Maren Hackenberg, Michelle Pfaffenlehner, and Felix B Tambe-Ndonfack helped. Thorsten Schmidt, Astrid Pechmann, and Janbernd Kirschner joined. Jan Hasenauer and Harald Binder complete nine authors. Their 2025 paper helps rare disease research study. Patients often switch therapies when new medications emerge.

Limited sample sizes complicate rare disease trials. Using all data sources is major. Reading instruments sometimes change during reading periods. Age-certain adaptations can cause such instrument changes. Resulting data trajectories become disjoint across instruments then. Classic mixed-effects regression struggles with disjoint trajectories. They map each instrument readings into latent space. Variational autoencoders embed item values into shared features. Time trajectories align across instruments in latent space. Mixed-effects regression then captures disease changes there. Treatment switch effects are estimated in that model. A novel testing method enables inference there. Spinal muscular atrophy patients supplied the use case.
arxiv-2510-25631: Sweta Das, Andrii Dmytryshyn, and Volker Mehrmann find standard forms for pairs of square complex matrices. Their 2025 paper works under two kinds of change rules for the pair. They stress cases where a product of the pair is the same when flipped, or flips sign. Those cases link to Lagrangian and Dirac spaces. They also link to systems in control work that lose energy in a clean way. The paper is a dense piece of matrix work for experts in the field.
arxiv-2510-25831:
Robin Eappen and Pavel Kroupa ask what past star formation histories could fit nearby galaxies, without fixing a shape in advance. A star formation history records how fast a galaxy made stars over time. Older models often force a smooth decline, which may miss the real variety in how galaxies grew.

Eappen and Kroupa generate large sets of random histories for each galaxy and keep only those that match its mass and current star making rate. Both the slope of the history and the time when half the stars had formed track the rate ratio strongly. Their results disfavor strongly declining histories for galaxies in the local volume.
arxiv-2510-25931:
Brendan Creutz, working alone, proves a result about rational points on varieties inside abelian varieties over function fields. An abelian variety is a higher dimensional analogue of an elliptic curve, and a rational point is a solution with coordinates in the base field. He assumes the variety has no positive dimensional isotrivial quotient, a technical condition that rules out constant parts after extension.

Creutz shows that any adelic point on the subvariety that is a limit of rational points on the ambient variety is already a limit of rational points on the subvariety itself. If the Tate Shafarevich group is finite, rational points are then dense in the Brauer set, a set cut out by a known obstruction. Similar results follow over totally imaginary number fields under a stated conjecture.
arxiv-2510-26031:
Zhaoqing Ding and Xuejiao Chen lead twelve co-authors in a study of how a magnetic material changes when sliced to a few atomic layers on a slanted crystal face. The material, SrRuO3, is a standard itinerant ferromagnet, meaning its magnetism comes from mobile electrons, in bulk form on the one one one plane. What it does in the extreme thin limit on that plane was largely unexplored.

As film thickness falls to a few unit cells, the system turns from a metallic ferromagnet into a semiconducting antiferromagnet, where neighboring moments oppose. Signs include vanishing remnant magnetization and a striking twelve fold pattern in magnetoresistance. First principles calculations confirm that an A type antiferromagnetic order is the stable ground state when thin.
arxiv-2510-26131:
Ali Caglayan, Nevrez Imamoglu, Oguzhan Guclu, Ali Osman Serhatoglu, Ahmet Burak Can, and Ryosuke Nakamura use network attention maps to improve indoor robot mapping with color and depth cameras. The task is SLAM, simultaneous localization and mapping, where a robot builds a map while tracking its own position. Good frame association, matching current views to earlier ones, is central to SLAM, and object awareness can help.

Class activation mapping, a visualization tool, shows where a neural network looks when it recognizes an image, using gradients to highlight salient regions. Caglayan and the team integrate layer wise attention from gradients directly into convolutional features, enriching them with task specific object locations. The goal is more reliable frame association for RGB-D indoor SLAM.
arxiv-2510-26331:
Guowei Dai and Yingxin Sun study a Robin eigenvalue problem, a maths question about special values tied to a wave equation inside a round ball. A Robin condition mixes the value of a solution on the edge of the ball with how fast it changes there. The pair ask which values can occur at all, and in what order they fall.

Dai and Sun work out the full list of these values, called the spectrum. For a positive edge constant they name the first two values in terms of zeros of Bessel functions, which are standard wave functions. For negative ranges they show that a set of negative values can appear, and they pin down the borderline case where zero itself joins the list. The result gives a complete map for later work on such problems.
arxiv-2510-26431:
Mihály Dobos-Kovács, Levente Bajczi, and András Vörös present CHCVerif, a solver for constrained Horn clauses. These clauses are a common middle format for program checks, such as safety tests, invariant finding, and analysis across procedures. Rather than build a new engine from scratch, the team routes the clauses to mature software verification tools.

Dobos-Kovács and his two co-authors run several such tools as a portfolio, so the strengths of each can cover the others. Their tests show moderate success on clauses about whole numbers. On bitvector benchmarks, which reflect low-level program detail, the results were modest but real. The paper argues the route is viable, above all when the portfolio is chosen with care.
arxiv-2510-26531:
David Leprich, with five co-authors, helps drones steer around obstacles while following a set path. Their frame is model predictive path-following control, which plans a short stretch of motion, flies part of it, then plans again. Obstacles are treated as ellipsoids, stretched ball shapes, in three dimensions, and they may sit still or move.

Leprich and the team give a fast, smoothly varying test for whether the drone's path hits such an obstacle. A two-stage optimisation step calms numerical trouble that the control problem tends to cause. They show the method in simulation and in real flights with a Crazyflie quadrotor. The paper calls this the first hardware run of a controller of this kind for such drones in a three-dimensional task.
arxiv-2510-26631:
Mikhail S Arbatskiy, Maksim V Kukushkin, Dmitriy E Balandin, and Alexey V Churov align biological data sets that measure different layers of a cell. Multi-omics integration tries to line up such heterogeneous data, measured on the same samples, along a shared diagonal structure. The team asks what the differences between data sets really say about biological variation.

Arbatskiy and his three co-authors study extremal trace problems for a coupled Laplacian, a matrix built from the data, on sets shaped like the Stiefel manifold inside complex space. They develop a gradient ascent method for the maximisation problem in classical functional analysis terms. On that base, they propose a new measure of how heterogeneous a data set is: the gap between the norm values at the maximum and minimum points. The approach is offered as a natural, unsupervised way to align such data.
arxiv-2510-26731:
Maria Acevedo, with eight co-authors, introduces the WHALES survey, which hunts Type Ia supernovae in and around galaxy superclusters. These exploding white dwarfs can serve as distance markers, and a sample around a supercluster can weigh it and test models of bulk flows, the drift of whole galaxy groups. No supernovae had been analysed toward the Shapley Supercluster before.

Acevedo and the team report the first two seasons on Shapley, which sits behind a large share of our local group's motion. Using SkyMapper they found twelve likely Type Ia supernovae there, eight confirmed by spectra, and they publish the first light curves, combined with ATLAS data. Simulations show about one hundred such supernovae would pin Shapley's total mass to twenty-five percent precision. The slow discovery rate argues for multi-year monitoring.
arxiv-2510-26831:
J Rodrigues, with six co-authors, presents AIRS, a system that helps airlines recover from disruption on the day of operations. When flights are delayed or cancelled, aircraft rotations, crew legality, maintenance windows, and airport slots must all be rebuilt at once. Their system models aircraft and crew recovery together on a time-space network and solves it as a mixed-integer linear program.

Rodrigues and the team shape the search space around the disruption and warm-start the solver, which keeps the combinatorics in check. A companion module re-accommodates passengers with greedy assignment plus a light evolutionary search, while respecting the aircraft and crew plan. Across realistic evaluations, AIRS met operational decision windows and cut recovery costs against manual or sequential methods. The authors pitch it as decision support for operations control centres.
arxiv-2510-27231:
H. W. Qu, H. T. Liu, and Y. C. Li review first-principles design of excitonic insulators, a quantum state proposed over sixty years ago but still unconfirmed. In this state, excitons, meaning bound electron-hole pairs, form spontaneously and condense so they become the ground state rather than an excited one. The scarcity of candidate materials is a key reason no example is yet recognized.

The review traces the field history, current status, and main challenges, then focuses on discovery through the first-principles Bethe-Salpeter scheme. A dark-exciton rule guides screening that opens routes in direct-gap and wide-gap semiconductors and reveals novel states such as half and spin-triplet variants. The authors close with computational and theoretical pathways toward the first recognized excitonic insulator.
arxiv-2510-27431:
Emanuele Greco sums up four years of results on exploded stars in this 2025 mini-review. A supernova remnant is the expanding wreck of a dead star, ringed by a shock front. Magnetic turbulence, a tangle of field lines, traps charged particles near the front. The trapped particles gain energy and shine in X-rays.

A new satellite, the Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer, reads the polarization of that X-ray light. Polarization is the slant of the light waves, and it maps the field's shape and order patch by patch. Greco reviews what the slant has shown across several remnants. Combined with plain spectra and images, it pins down the tangle's size and strength just behind the shock. That sharpens the picture of how remnants boost particles to extreme energies.
arxiv-2511-00031:
Shunsuke Matsuno studies gatekeeping experts, experts whose advice guides agents but who also hold veto power, as in financial audits, bank stress tests, and environmental regulation. Transparency invites gaming of the expert's rules, while opacity wastes the skill. That dilemma is the paper's focus, with financial audits as the primary setting.

Strategic blur settles the dilemma: showing just enough information guides pattern without giving a complete map to game. Economics readers get a formal logic for on purpose fuzzy sharing by controls and checkers. The result explains a common real practice that naive clarity arguments would condemn.
arxiv-2511-00131:
Shuhei Kobayashi gives a unified framing of the origin of the arrow of time in standard and quantum mechanics, starting from a one-dimensional three-particle system. That concrete system shows large-scale one-way flow arising from at small scale two-way motion. Abstracting the process finds coarse-graining, the dropping of small-scale detail, as the central part behind time asymmetry.

A general structural test for the thermodynamic arrow follows: when small-scale evolution forms a group but the induced large-scale evolution does not, one-way flow appears. Foundations of physics readers get a crisp process rather than a mystery. Three particles suffice to expose the logic, which then lifts to both standard and quantum settings.
arxiv-2511-00631:
Giovanni Tedeschi-Prades, Til Birnstiel, Klaus Dolag, Barbara Ercolano, and Mark Hutchison add dust dynamics to the OpenGadget3 simulation code, a workhorse for astrophysics. Dust steers processes from star formation to planet building, and particle-based hydrodynamics handles it well through the one-fluid model, which treats gas and dust as one mixture with internal drift. Their implementation improves on the original formulation in several ways.

Time-dependent artificial viscosity and conductivity join a new treatment of dust diffusion built from a pressure-like term. The code passes the standard dusty benchmarks, box, wave, and shock tests, the last extended to multiple dimensions, plus a dusty blast wave. Keplerian disks, protoplanetary disks, and shear instabilities stress it further. The diffusion term helps most where dust dominates and drag is weak, though limits of the one-fluid picture remain.
arxiv-2511-01031:
Mathieu Dubied, Paolo Tiso, and Robert Katzschmann present AquaROM, a pipeline for optimizing the shapes of soft robotic swimmers. Simulating soft bodies with finite element methods is expensive, and optimization needs many simulations, especially with the nonlinear forces that water and actuation produce.

Their algorithm rests on a tensor based parametric reduced order model, which compresses the simulation into a smaller space where solutions can be approximated fast. The tensor structure also yields analytic gradients inside a chosen reduced basis, speeding the search further. The team applies it to actuated soft swimmers. Internal and external nonlinear forces enter through a data free reduced basis. The method cuts computing cost sharply. It opens shape design for soft robots that was previously impractical.
arxiv-2511-01131:
Md Nahiduzzaman and colleagues make medical image diagnosis more interpretable without demanding costly concept labels. Concept based models explain a diagnosis through human ideas, such as lesion features, but training them normally needs experts to annotate those concepts on every image, which clinics rarely can do.

Their Prior-guided Concept Predictor uses class level concept priors, typical concept patterns for each disease class, as weak supervision instead. A refinement step with divergence and entropy penalties aligns the predicted concepts with clinical reasoning. On skin lesion and blood cell data sets, concept prediction quality rose by over a third against zero shot baselines. Diagnosis accuracy stayed competitive with fully supervised concept bottleneck models across four medical data sets.
arxiv-2511-01531:
Rodrigo Dourado and five colleagues tackle a practical headache in quantum devices: the states best protected against noise often exist only at tiny, hard-to-find spots in a device's tuning space. Their idea is to search for protection directly, by deliberately injecting noise and letting a learning algorithm hunt for the settings that shrug it off best.

The test bed is a short chain of quantum dots forming a Kitaev chain, a system prized for the Majorana bound states at its ends. An evolutionary strategy adjusts the settings to minimize the ground-state splitting under random fluctuations, and the system settles into a protected configuration. The method held up under magnetic fields, electron repulsion, uneven couplings, and different chain lengths.
arxiv-2511-01631:
Lakshmi S K and Saudamini Nayak extend a representation-theory construction, Weyl modules, to a twisted family of Lie superalgebras. Their objects are equivariant map superalgebras. These are algebraic maps from a scheme into a finite-dimensional Lie superalgebra. The maps must respect the action of a cyclic group. The field is algebraically closed and of characteristic zero.

The authors define global Weyl modules and Weyl functors for these algebras. Under an assumption on the target algebra's triangular decomposition, they prove the global modules are universal in their category. They also show the global modules are finitely generated over a certain commutative algebra when the source algebra is finitely generated. Local Weyl modules, defined through the functors, turn out finite-dimensional regardless of decomposition. The twisted local modules are exactly the images of untwisted ones under a twisting functor.
arxiv-2511-01931:
Eun Park's project sets out to determine all irreducible modules of a given modular Lie algebra, the building blocks of its representation theory in positive characteristic. Modular Lie algebras differ from their ordinary counterparts by carrying an extra structure, the p-mapping, which any classification must respect.

A key tool is the minimal p-envelope of the algebra, which is restrictable, together with a one-to-one correspondence between induced modules and certain of the original modules. By exploiting the properties of induced modules, the project aims to decompose a modular Lie algebra into its irreducible modules systematically. Worked examples demonstrate how such decompositions can be carried out for specific modular Lie algebras, illustrating the general method on concrete cases.
arxiv-2511-02031:
Elise Darragh-Ford and sixteen colleagues dissect how the Milky Way's dark matter halo is still ringing from the Large Magellanic Cloud's recent plunge through it. The infall drags a dynamical friction wake behind the satellite galaxy. It also shoves the halo's density center off the disk. These imprints encode the mass ratio, the orbit, and the halo's original shape.

Using basis function expansions on eighteen cosmological zoom-in simulations, the team separates the response into components. A dipole appears in every LMC-like merger. It comes from the displaced center and the halo distortion. Its amplitude grows with the square of the mass ratio. It peaks a few hundred million years after pericenter. A quadrupole depends mainly on the host halo's original axis ratios, with a wake contribution peaking just before pericenter. Measuring both patterns in the real stellar halo should recover the halo's pre-infall shape.
arxiv-2511-02131:
Benjamin Kwanen Tapley tackles a quiet failure mode of numerical simulation: standard methods for solving differential equations slowly corrupt quantities that should stay exactly constant, such as energy. Projection methods fix this by nudging each step back onto the surface where the invariant holds, but the nudging usually needs expensive iterative solving. Tapley's approach exploits homogeneous symmetries so the projection can be computed exactly, in closed form.

The result is a family of explicit, high-order integrators that preserve invariants while adding almost no cost over the underlying solver. Variants preserve several invariants at once to very high precision, and the scheme plugs into adaptive solvers for error-controlled stepping. Tests on a double pendulum, Kepler orbits, and two partial differential equations showed large gains in accuracy and efficiency over standard approaches.
arxiv-2511-02231:
Yuxi Lu and six co-authors reconstruct where the stars of the Large Magellanic Cloud were born, to read the history of its ongoing encounter with its smaller companion. The method infers each star's birth radius from its chemistry and age, after validation on a hydrodynamical simulation built to mimic the two galaxies' interaction. Birthplaces reveal how the disk's chemistry and dynamics evolved together across billions of years.

The cloud's metallicity gradient steepened about five, three, and one billion years ago. The timing matches bursts of star formation that started centrally, spread outward, and later flared across the disk with renewed central activity. Radial migration of stars strengthened at several epochs too. The most alpha-enriched stars formed two to three billion years ago across a broad span of radii, and unlike the Milky Way, the cloud shows no clear two-branch pattern in its chemistry.
arxiv-2511-02331:
Tianle Pu and seven co-authors make learned solvers for mixed-integer linear programming travel between problem domains. Such solvers predict good solutions quickly, but most are trained and tested inside a single domain, so they stumble on unfamiliar problem types. Their framework, RoME, is a mixture-of-experts model: a router reads a learned embedding of each problem instance and sends it to the specialist expert best suited to it.

Training uses distributionally robust optimisation at two levels, guarding against shifts between domains and perturbations within each domain. Surprisingly, training across domains not only improved performance on unseen domains but also within each training domain, apparently because the model learns more general combinatorial patterns. One model trained on three domains improved results by an average of 67.7 percent across five test domains, and it even gained on the hard public MIPLIB benchmark without further training.
arxiv-2511-02431:
Vladimir Dzhunushaliev and Vladimir Folomeev construct rotating wormholes, tunnels between separate regions of spacetime, inside a theory that combines gravity, electromagnetism, and a spinor field. The spinor field is complex and non-phantom. It is what holds the tunnel open with the topology it needs, while electromagnetic fields add charge and rotation. The resulting wormholes spin, carrying real angular momentum, yet stay regular at every point and flatten out to usual spacetime far away.

Each configuration is fixed in full by three input numbers: a throat parameter setting the tunnel's size, the spinor's frequency, and the electromagnetic coupling constant. The two mouths open into identical copies of Minkowski spacetime, although the two sides can in general carry distinct masses and distinct global charges. The paper works out the traits of these asymmetric, rotating solutions across that three-parameter space.
arxiv-2511-02531:
Munib Mesinovic, Max Buhlan, and Tingting Zhu survey a family of medical AI methods that try to learn causes rather than correlations. Hospital AI often degrades when moved between hospitals and can inherit biased patterns from its training data, partly because it learns statistical associations instead of causes. Causal graph neural networks combine graph views of biomedical data with causal inference, aiming at the mechanisms that stay invariant underneath.

The review covers structural causal models, disentangled causal features, and interventional and counterfactual reasoning on graphs. Applications discussed include psychiatric diagnosis from brain networks, cancer subtyping from multi-omics data, continuous monitoring of body signals, and drug advice, all feeding toward patient-specific causal digital twins. The authors are frank about obstacles: computing cost, checking beyond usual cross-checks, and causal-washing, where causal language is worn without causal evidence. A tiered framework separates causal-flavoured designs from validated causal discoveries.
arxiv-2511-02731:
Alvaro Sanchez builds a general method for studying representations of quivers, which are diagrams of points and arrows used across algebra. His 2025 paper works over abstract stable homotopy theories, a broad setting that covers rings, schemes, and ring spectra at once. The bridge is the Auslander-Reiten diagram, a classic map of how representations fit together.

For a finite quiver with no cycles, Sanchez proves that representations in this abstract setting match a mesh category built from a repeating version of the quiver. The construction uses reflection functors defined step by step. Symmetries of the diagram then yield universal autoequivalences, which form the spectral Picard group of the quiver. Classical tools like the Serre functor appear as special cases of the scheme.
arxiv-2511-03131:
Zeda Xu, Nikolas Martelaro, and Christopher McComb study how the form of a design changes which design people pick. Generative tools can flood engineers with drone concepts, so judging them well matters. Their 2025 study shows participants uncrewed aerial vehicle designs in three formats: visual renderings, numeric performance data, or both, then watches which designs get chosen for further work.

Format changed the choices. Surprisingly, numbers alone led to the best picks, beating pictures and the combined view. Participants also leaned toward visually conventional designs with mirror symmetry, even when those were not the strongest. The findings carry a warning for generative design workflows: the prettiest presentation can steer experts away from the best engineering.
arxiv-2511-03231:
Jie Zhu and Hao Li sort every still, round, empty-space solution allowed by a modified gravity idea called bumblebee gravity. In that idea, a background field picks a preferred direction and can point in space-like, light-like, or time-like ways. The authors work through the vacuum cases with a general background value and lay out a full classification.

One set of settings turns out to be flawed, leaving the solution free to take an arbitrary shape and marking the theory as ill-defined there. Another surprise is an exact match to the classic Schwarzschild solution even when certain matter is present, unlike standard gravity. That match, the authors note, would undercut solar system tests that assume such a match rules the new theory out.
arxiv-2511-03331:
Istvan Gaal completes an algorithm hunt for special generators in number fields of degree six that contain a quadratic subfield. A power integral basis lets every whole element be written neatly from powers of one generator, when such a generator exists. Earlier work handled limited shapes of the inner basis and left the general shape open.

Gaal extends those methods to the fully general case and works through the fresh technical hurdles it raises. Number theorists use such bases to test equations and to compute field traits with less bulk. Closing the general case means the sextic family with a quadratic part now has a complete procedure rather than a patchwork.
arxiv-2511-03731:
Fengming Liu and Shubin Yu present MimiTalk. It is a two-agent system that runs research interviews. One agent watches strategy and ethics. The other holds the chat and drafts each question. Written rules guide both agents at all times.

Three studies test the system in turn. First, twenty users rate how easy it feels to use. Next, its chats are matched against a large set of human chats. Scores cover richness, coherence, and stability of the talk. Last, ten scholars run both kinds of chats. They then judge themes with names hidden. Machine chats cut anxiety in these tests. They also scored higher on richness and stability. The authors still keep human oversight at the core.
arxiv-2511-03831:
James Enouen, Yujia Zheng, Ignavier Ng, Yan Liu, and Kun Zhang extend causal structure learning to systems where causes interact, not just act one at a time. Most discovery methods ignore such higher-order mechanisms, even though real processes often contain them.

Starting from the causal additive model, the team adds interactions and represents structure with a directed acyclic hypergraph instead of an ordinary graph. Definitions and identifiability results extend Markov equivalence to that setting. More restrictive assumptions can make the richer structure easier to learn, with better finite-sample behaviour. An extended greedy algorithm searches the hypergraph space and performs well in synthetic experiments reported here.
arxiv-2511-03931:
Iman Adibnazari and five colleagues compare data-driven ways to reduce soft robot models so that dynamic shape control becomes practical. A soft robot's whole body moves, giving very high-dimensional dynamics, and few general tools produce models that controllers can use. A simulated eel-inspired robot is the test case.

Three methods are compared: the eigensystem realization algorithm, dynamic mode decomposition with control, and Lagrangian operator inference. Each model drives model predictive control in three tracking tasks, from feasible reference paths to paths from a biological eel model and a physical analog. Lagrangian operator inference policies gave the lowest tracking errors in every experiment, marking a clear winner for this setting.
arxiv-2511-04031:
Mostafa Amini, Alireza Vahidi, and Fatemeh Ghanavati introduce new classes of modules in homological algebra, built under a special semidualizing bimodule over two rings. Catalog evidence left the creator field blank; the arXiv record supplies the three authors, and that record governs. Their classes generalize several known injective and flat module families at once.

Characterizations are given for the injective and flat classes, which are shown to be covering and preenveloping. Foxby equivalence relative to these classes is investigated. Over coherent rings of a stated type, the finite versions of both classes close under extensions, kernels of epimorphisms, and cokernels of monomorphisms, giving the theory a stable working shape.
arxiv-2511-04631:
Petr Kuznetsov and his co-author define dynamic concurrency for shared distributed data. Synchronization is the main brake on scaling, and it bites when operations conflict. Yet many operations conflict only in rare states, so constant strong locking wastes effort.

Under dynamic concurrency, an operation uses strong tools only when the current state forces arbitration. The authors then give a universal construction with that property. Any sequential object can, in principle, be built this adaptive way. The result points toward data structures that pay synchronization costs only on the rare steps that truly need them.
arxiv-2511-04731:
Greta Heine leads five authors putting graph neural networks on chips for the Belle II trigger. The Level-1 trigger must filter detector hits in real time at high rate. Their network reads spatial and temporal links among sense wire hits.

Quantization, pruning, and static graph building tune the model for FPGA hardware. Splitting the detector into parallel sectors lets the design cover the whole instrument. The system sustains a throughput near thirty-one point eight megahertz with latency in the hundreds of nanoseconds. It uses about a third of the chip's logic and no signal processors, leaving room to grow.
arxiv-2511-04831:
NVIDIA presents Isaac Lab, a GPU-accelerated framework for multi-modal robot learning. It succeeds Isaac Gym and pushes GPU-native simulation into the large-scale learning era. Physics, photo-like rendering, and modular environment design run in one platform.

Actuator models and multi-frequency sensor simulation are built in from the start. Data collection pipelines and domain randomization tools support both reinforcement and imitation learning. Example challenges span whole-body control, cross-embodiment mobility, and dexterous manipulation. By unifying best practices in one extensible system, Isaac Lab aims to make big robot learning studies easier to run and repeat.
arxiv-2511-04931:
Sebastian Petit and Geertrui Van de Voorde study how the twisted triality hexagon sits inside its natural projective space. The hexagon is a known incidence shape from finite geometry, and this work asks which subspaces can meet it, and in what forms.

The authors list the ways subspaces can meet the hexagon in that space. They then give tests on a set of lines that prove the set is in fact the line set of such a hexagon. The work extends past results on the split Cayley hexagon by Thas, Van Maldeghem, and Ihringer.
arxiv-2511-05031:
Zhuang Ma and co-authors build a full numeric frame to find and fix frequency clashes in superconducting quantum circuits. Such circuits are a lead path to large quantum machines, and wiggled control signals can spark stray links between parts.

Stray links form a dense web that caps chip performance. The authors ground their tool in Floquet theory and pair it with new analytic models for two wiggle schemes, one on qubits and one on couplers. The joined view lets builders spot harmful clashes early and tune designs to dodge them.
arxiv-2511-05131:
Fernando Berzal explains, in a technical report, how a neural network's output layer and its loss function must fit each other. The choice looks like a code detail, but he shows it rests on firm statistical ground.

The report reviews common output forms, such as linear, sigmoid, ReLU, and softmax, with their math traits and best uses. It then links loss forms like mean squared error, mean absolute error, and cross-entropy to maximum likelihood, a core rule for picking a model. The tie tells builders which loss a task truly calls for.
arxiv-2511-05231:
Saad Hamid and co-authors show how to calibrate agent-based models of supply chains far faster by making them differentiable and running them on graphics chips. Such models can trace how shocks spread through supply nets, a need made clear by COVID-19 and the war in Ukraine.

Calibration of these models is the hard part. With automatic differentiation, the authors report speed gains of more than a thousandfold over non-differentiable baselines in their tests. That jump opens the door to supply models at a scale that was out of reach, where each firm's links and buffers can be fit to data.
arxiv-2511-05331:
Pablo Peña and a co-author present EMPEROR, an open-source Python frame to find and characterize exoplanets from radial velocity data, the wobble a planet's pull stamps on its star. Orbit fitting is slow and noise in the wobble can mimic a planet.

EMPEROR joins dynamic nested sampling with adaptive parallel tempering Markov chains. It supports noise models like Gaussian processes and moving averages, and it ranks models by Bayesian evidence and a second criterion. Plots come out ready to publish. Tests check its planet finds against known cases, so users can trust its pace and care.
arxiv-2511-05631:
Genheng Zhao works on the Goldbach problem, the old question of whether every even number is a sum of two primes. Rather than attack the claim head-on, he counts the exceptions: even numbers below a bound that cannot be written that way. Bounding that exceptional set is a classic route toward the problem.

Zhao proves a new bound on the size of the exceptional set, though the constant in the bound cannot be computed from the proof. The same method also bounds the least prime in any arithmetic progression modulo a given number. That second quantity is tied to Linnik's constant, a long-studied value in number theory.
arxiv-2511-05731:
Xing Yao and co-authors ask what actually drives success when adapting a big segmentation model to ultrasound video. Segmenting ultrasound is hard: images vary between machines and patients, motion blurs frames, and labeled data is scarce. The foundation model SAM2 segments well in general, but its skill drops sharply on medical scans.

Instead of changing the model's design, the team varied the data and training plan. They tested training-set size, clip length, and augmentation styles across five model variants and three training schemes. Data scale and time context mattered more than model design or starting point. They also designed six ultrasound-specific augmentations, and found joint training a good compromise between fitting the modality and the task.
arxiv-2511-06131:
Giuseppe Calafiore and co-authors charge electric vehicles on a fossil-heavy grid while watching both the bill and the carbon. Smart charging can shift demand, but its climate value depends on when the grid burns what. The team couples a simple grid dispatch model, with hydro, thermal, and renewable sources, to a charging scheduler.

Hourly carbon intensity from the dispatch feeds a carbon-cost signal, combined with a local time-of-use tariff. Sweeping one weight traces the trade-off frontier between cost and emissions. In a three hundred vehicle scenario based on Vietnam data, their scheduler kept the full bill saving of a cost-only optimizer while cutting charging emissions. A sensitivity study on the hydro budget showed the scheduler stayed cheaper and cleaner than first-come charging throughout.
arxiv-2511-06231:
Henok Ademtew and Israel Goytom test whether emotion recognition can run privately on a wrist device instead of in the cloud. Cloud inference exposes sensitive body data and adds delay, both bad fits for real-time wearables. Their study compares model families on heart-related signals from a wrist sensor, using the WESAD stress dataset.

Classical ensemble methods clearly beat deep networks and transformers on this small body-signal dataset. The best method, ExtraTrees, scored far higher on combined features and still led on wrist-only features. Converted to an efficient format, the wrist model shrank to about four megabytes with very fast response, showing that private on-device emotion sensing is practical today.
arxiv-2511-06331:
Aldino Rizaldy and co-authors map individual trees in three dimensions while needing far fewer hand labels. Forest managers want per-tree structure and species data for precision forestry, biodiversity work, and carbon mapping. Laser scanning point clouds supply the raw detail, but labeling enough of them to train deep models is slow and expensive.

Self-supervised pretraining and transfer learning cut that labeling burden across three tasks: separating single trees, labeling tree parts, and naming species. Gains appeared on every task, with the largest jump in tree separation when self-supervision joined domain adaptation. A unified open framework runs the full pipeline, and pretrained models trimmed energy use and emissions by about a fifth.
arxiv-2511-06531:
Oluwadara Kalejaiye and co-authors bring four coastal Nigerian languages into language technology for the first time. Nigeria speaks more than five hundred languages, yet research concentrates on just four major ones, largely because text data for the rest barely exists. Anaang, Efik, Ibibio, and Oro appear in no major translation system or benchmark.

The ibom dataset extends a standard translation benchmark to those four languages and aligns the texts with topic labels from a classification benchmark. Tests show current large models translate these languages poorly with no examples and with only a few. Extra examples did steadily improve topic classification, charting a first path toward inclusive tools for Nigeria's minority languages.
arxiv-2511-07031:
Vivek Gusain, Mohd Zeeshan, and B K Mani design new thermoelectric substances on the computer before anyone synthesizes them. Thermoelectrics convert heat to electricity, and the guiding design ideal pairs glass-like heat blocking with crystal-like charge flow. Zintl phases fit that ideal well. The authors propose a family combining strontium and barium with silicon, germanium, or tin, and simulate their thermal and electrical transport from first principles.

The predicted lattice thermal conductivities are remarkably low, below one watt per meter-kelvin, traced to weak bonding from antibonding states, slow phonons, short lifetimes, and strong anharmonic scattering. The germanium member reaches a figure of merit near 2.0 at 700 kelvin, rivaling the benchmark substance SnSe. Similar performance for both doping types makes the family attractive for devices, and the authors invite experimental tests.
arxiv-2511-07331:
Theo N Dionne, Santiago Villodre, Mikel Iraola, and Maia G Vergniory find a way to describe Mott insulators in the everyday language of single electrons. The one-body picture explains weakly interacting solids beautifully but breaks down for strongly correlated substances like Mott insulators, where electrons freeze each other in place. Their system uses the single-particle Green's function and the one-body reduced density matrix to characterize correlated phases without abandoning one-body concepts.

Applied to the Hubbard diamond chain, and combining density matrix renormalization group with cellular dynamical mean-field theory, they construct symmetry-resolved effective orbitals and follow them across the Mott transitions. The purity of the density matrix serves as a single number flagging the phase boundaries. The tools promise a general route for extending one-body thinking into correlated substances.
arxiv-2511-07531:
Kyle Seyler and co-authors chase very fast magnetic walls for future memory devices. Domain walls separate magnetic regions, and moving them quickly could store and process data. Antiferromagnetic materials resist stray fields and promise extreme wall speeds, especially when pushed by coherent spin waves.

Making clean spin waves beside a single moving wall, then filming the motion, had blocked experiments until now. The team tackles both hurdles together. Spin-wave drive could in principle push walls near the magnon speed limit with little heating waste. Success would favor antiferromagnetic spintronics for dense, rapid, low-power memory and logic hardware.
arxiv-2511-07831:
Zewu Zheng and Yuanyuan Lin train game agents that survive the gap between simulator and reality. Policies polished in simulation often collapse under shifted dynamics. Robust learning answers by optimizing against worst-case environment changes, but online multi-agent versions with large state spaces resist fast algorithms.

A hardness result shows where the difficulty truly sits under shift assumptions. Using a minimum value assumption restores tractability, and a least-squares algorithm follows with linear function fitting. Sample efficiency with live data is the prize. Robust games matter for fleets, markets, and infrastructure where opponents and physics both drift.
arxiv-2511-08031:
Chende Zheng and co-authors build a system that both detects deepfakes and locates the forged parts in time. Modern generators make audio and video fakes realistic enough to threaten digital trust. Methods using only one channel miss cross channel clues and cannot pinpoint which segments were altered.

Their framework pairs a feature pyramid with a transformer, using pretrained WavLM for audio and CLIP for video. Multi scale blocks with local attention join temporal patterns across both channels. A dual head predicts forgery probability and refines segment boundaries, reaching a score near zero point seven five on a challenging benchmark test set.
arxiv-2511-08231:
Devin Hunter and Chinwendu Enyioha test a multi closeness leftover physics informed neural process for tracking the state of a robotic system in real time. Safety critical tracking needs not only forecasts but trustworthy error margins. Choosing the right motion model is a core difficulty, since simple models miss effects that complex ground truth dynamics contain.

The estimator learns the leftover gap between low closeness forecasts and high closeness conduct. Split conformal prediction supplies robust uncertainty guarantees inside training and inference for a hybrid online learning setup. Against unscented and deep Kalman filter variants, the method shows promising accuracy for live robotic tracking tasks.
arxiv-2511-08331:
Eunice Chan and Hanghang Tong study data poisoning attacks aimed not at accuracy but at the fairness of a machine learning system. Fairness research mostly measures and repairs bias, while the vulnerability of fairness itself to deliberate attack has received little attention.
