arxiv-2604-18131: Zhang and seven colleagues train language-model agents to explore unfamiliar digital environments on their own. No human rewards or rules guide the agent at run time. During training only, a reward measures how much the agent's self-written world knowledge improves later task success. The trained agent gains 20 percent on WebVoyager and WebWalker tests, and a compact 14-billion-parameter model beats an unassisted Gemini-2.5-Flash.
arxiv-2604-18231: Abdollahi and seven colleagues present AgenTEE, a system for running language-model agents privately on edge devices. Cloud hosting leaks latency and privacy, yet edge devices face software attacks and hostile owners. AgenTEE isolates the runtime, inference engine, and third-party apps in separately attested confidential virtual machines. Built on Arm's Confidential Compute Architecture, it keeps proprietary prompts and weights safe at near-native speed.
arxiv-2604-18331: Du, Grannen, Song, and Sadigh test whether a robot quadruped can work as an enjoyable running trainer. The SNOOPIE pacerbot runs interval sessions tuned to each runner's ability, competing against a wearable trainer in user experiments. Runners stuck to pace schedules about 61 percent better with the robot and held steadier speeds. Participants also strongly preferred the robot on ease of use, enjoyability, and helpfulness, suggesting physical presence adds real value to exercise coaching.
arxiv-2604-18631: Sole tests old metronome marks for Beethoven's five piano-cello sonatas against over one hundred recordings from 1930 to 2012. Czerny's and Moscheles's marks fall short of the whole set, with gaps of 15 to 39 percent. Kolisch's 1943 marks track recorded practice far more closely than either rival set. Allegro speeds stay steady across eight decades, since slow, middle, and fast habits live side by side, with the middle one on top. From the set's most common speeds, he offers new marks as ranges mirroring expert practice, not single fixed values.
arxiv-2604-18731: Bhagwat and three colleagues use SPICE simulations to test how bursty versus smooth stellar feedback shapes early galaxies, traced by the bright carbon-II line. All models tie carbon-II luminosity tightly to star formation rate, but bursty feedback gives lower luminosity at a fixed rate and larger scatter. Emission extends well beyond ultraviolet light, and fast outflows add little to it, so carbon-II kinematics can misread gas speeds. Gas kinematics still separates the models, with smooth feedback settling disks earlier and yielding higher disk fractions.
arxiv-2604-18831: Wu and three colleagues study whether indoor lidar semantic segmentation can be learned by distillation from a visual foundation model. Acquiring ground truth for lidar is costly, yet visual foundation models segment image frames well. The team couples lidar scans with a processed camera image to train a lidar model by 2D to 3D distillation. Evaluated on indoor SLAM data sets with pseudo labels, the distilled model reaches 56 percent mean IoU. Against real labels it reaches about 36 percent, showing cross modal distillation works without manual annotations.
arxiv-2604-19331: Cunningham, Greene, Cross, and Rago build a formal test for judging whether summaries of parliament debates carry their arguments in full. Debate volume and complexity strain outside audiences, and auto scores match human checks for truth poorly. Their approach, driven by computational argumentation, grounds argument structures in the contested proposals under debate. The test aims to make large-scale debate summary checks possible rather than merely fluent.
arxiv-2604-19431: Buda, Primiero, Ceragioli, and Antonelli introduce CTLF, a branching-time logic for reasoning about bias in generative AI output series. Generative AI amplifies biases in training data, yet inference-time fixes stay mostly empirical and lack formal guarantees. In CTLF, each world stands for a possible output at a given step. Modal operators check whether the output series respects an intended distribution over a protected attribute. The logic predicts the odds of staying within bounds as new outputs arrive, and counts how many outputs must be removed to restore fairness.
arxiv-2604-19631: Wang and colleagues propose MoSA, a motion-guided semantic alignment method for dynamic scene graph generation. Such work models objects and their dynamic interactions in video at a high level. Current methods struggle with fine-grained relationship modeling and tail links. MoSA encodes object-pair motion attributes like distance, velocity, persistence, and directional consistency, then fuses them with spatial features to yield motion-aware representations.
arxiv-2604-19831: Fazlollahi proposes an extension of general relativity based on the van der Waals equation of state, bringing non-ideal thermodynamic effects into gravity. Under Jacobson's thermodynamic reading of gravity, where field rules arise from the Clausius relation, the approach yields modified field rules with a varying effective coupling. That coupling evolves with the traits of the underlying system. It has major consequences in high-energy regimes, including a natural way to avoid the initial singularity of standard Big Bang cosmology.
arxiv-2604-19931: Singh and four colleagues compared three ways to teach data science students to write hints for faulty code. Students wrote hints alone, with AI help on demand, or with AI help held back until after a first draft. In a trial with 97 graduate students, the held-back design gave the best hints and helped students catch errors they would otherwise miss. Students prized the task for debugging practice and for learning to judge AI output with care.
arxiv-2604-20131: Subbiah and five colleagues study positionality and bias in LLM digests of life stories, asking how machine interpretation shapes study conclusions. Deductive coding can be checked against human labels, but abstractive thematic analysis resists such direct judgment. Their summary pipeline surfaces perspective-taking biases an LLM may employ, showing both race and gender bias with potential representational harm. The authors urge future LLM-interpretation studies to include a positionality portrait of the study's stance.
arxiv-2604-20531: Yeginbergen, Oronoz, and Agerri test multilingual medical question answering across high-resource languages, English, Spanish, French, and Italian, and low-resource Basque and Kazakh. They compare three evidence types: curated medical repositories, web-retrieved content, and explanations from a language model internal knowledge. Larger models lead in English at baseline, and English web-retrieved evidence helps high-resource languages most. For low-resource languages, combining English and target-language retrieval matches high-resource accuracy, showing that the best evidence strategy depends on language resources and model scale.
arxiv-2604-20631: Bianchi, Jacquier, and Sfragara work on the Ising model over a two-community stochastic block model, where spins split into two groups. They characterize the diagram and show that the model undergoes a uniqueness transition of the Gibbs measure. In the supercritical regime, the magnetization vector law converges to a mixture of Dirac measures. If alpha-n is much greater than 1/n, it sits on two points; if at most about 1/n, on four. In uniqueness, they analyze magnetization fluctuations in the subcritical regime and prove a quenched CLT.
arxiv-2604-20731: Vilkha, Służalec, Łoś, and Paszyński present a solver for CO2 sequestration. The solver uses IGA-ADS for the saturation field update explicitly, and CRVPINN for the pressure field. The study simulates the behavior of CO2 in porous structures, excluding chemical reactions, with the model based on Darcy's Law. CRVPINN is pretrained on the pressure configuration, and each time step update requires only 100 iterations of the Adam method. Compared with an IGA-ADS plus MUMPS baseline, the hybrid solver is over 3 times faster on a node.
arxiv-2604-20831: Chau, Zhao, Laflorencie, and Meng study the ground-state phase diagram of a spin-1 Heisenberg chain with staggered long-range interactions. They use a quantum Monte Carlo approach based on the split-spin representation. They resolve the continuous quantum phase transition between the gapped Haldane phase at large alpha and a gapless Neel phase at small alpha, where the continuous SU(2) symmetry is broken. From finite-size scaling and crossing point analyses, they determine the critical point at alpha_c equals 2.49 and extract critical exponents.
arxiv-2604-21131: Ari Azarafrooz exposes a blind spot in AI-agent safety: guardrails judge each message alone, so an attack split across dozens of sessions slips past every detector. His CSTM-Bench supplies 26 executable attack taxonomies with matched benign confounders across two 54-scenario splits. Both a session-bound judge and a full-log correlator lose about half their attack recall on the harder split, while a bounded-memory reader keeping the 50 highest-signal fragments survives both.
arxiv-2604-21431: James Hipperson, Jonathan Hargreaves, and Trevor Cox build JAX-BEM, a boundary element solver with gradient tracking that brings machine-learning-style automatic differentiation to acoustic shape tuning. Old-style tuning struggles with many goals and parameters, but JAX-style systems track gradients through fast linear algebra. Their solver matches existing BEM codes' error on a benchmark and enables gradient-based geometry tuning. Though shown acoustically, the concept extends readily to electromagnetic waves.
arxiv-2604-21731: Chai uses enhanced Langlands data to sort out irreducible representations of twisted p-adic general linear groups in unramified principal series. The paper defines standard ones and proves the twisted Kazhdan-Lusztig conjecture for counts in the Grothendieck group. It mainly follows Lusztig's connected-case work using graded Hecke algebra. The resulting parametrisation matches the Whittaker-normalized one. The work gives a complete list for this family of groups. That list helps researchers work with these groups in practice.
arxiv-2604-21831: Kawałek and Krzaczkowski build a single algebraic frame for circuit complexity beyond the Boolean domain. Old results focus on Boolean circuits, partly because computers are built that way. Richer circuit landscapes over larger domains get lost in that focus. Building on Barrington's branching programs and nonuniform deterministic automata, and on Idziak's wider version, they sort out which languages circuits over simple algebras recognise, and over algebras from congruence modular varieties.
arxiv-2604-21931: Wu and eight colleagues treat time as a learnable visual concept in videos. They learn, self-supervised, to spot speed changes and gauge playback speed. Those models then assemble the biggest slow-motion video collection yet from noisy in-the-wild sources. Slow-motion footage from high-speed cameras holds richer temporal detail than standard video. Using this data, they build models for temporal control, including generation conditioned on speed and super-resolution over time for blurry low-FPS videos.
arxiv-2604-22131: Benhaida, Drissi, and Saidi place the Haldane model on the dice lattice, changing next-nearest-neighbour flow and breaking inversion and time-reversal symmetries. They find point-charge particle symmetries at π/6 and 5π/6 and derive analytic quasi-energy forms. Gap closure at these points drives a topological transition, confirmed by Berry curvature and magnetic moment. Chern numbers for the valence, flat, and conduction bands shift with flux ties: equal fluxes give (2, -2, 0) then (0, 2, -2), while differing fluxes give (-1, -1) and (1, 1). Hall conductivity shows a quantized plateau of 2σ₀, a tilted plateau sliding from 1.50σ₀ to about 1σ₀.
arxiv-2604-22231: Mandal and Chaudhuri extend Jurin's law to fluids that make their own internal stress. The classic law gives how high liquid climbs in a narrow tube. Their theory adds an active stress term at the liquid surface. A new height formula then follows from activity strength and alignment at the meniscus. Depending on those factors, activity can raise, lower or fully suppress the climb.
arxiv-2604-22631: Herron and three colleagues typify two kinds of phoneme error in speech recognition systems. Modern speech recognition systems work better for certain speaker groups than others. One barrier to fairer systems is understanding errors, particularly embedding differences between high- and low-performance groups. The framework distinguishes random error, high phoneme variance, from systematic error, embedding bias. Training phoneme probes only on a single disadvantaged group sometimes improves performance for that group, evidence of group-level bias in phoneme embeddings. Speakers and groups with higher phoneme variance match lower-performance groups.
arxiv-2604-22931: Noonan and twelve colleagues report JWST observations of main-belt comet 457P/Lemmon-PANSTARRS, active in 2020 and again in 2024. Earlier JWST results on two outer comets supported water reservoirs as drivers, but 457P orbits closer in, within the 5:2 resonance with Jupiter. Despite dust activity in ground and JWST images, the team finds no water, carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, or methanol within tight limits. They suggest 457P is more depleted than its companions; wider surveys will tell whether it is an edge case or a distinct subclass.
arxiv-2604-23331: Wu and Beerel propose Branch Landing, a forward-edge control-flow integrity framework for RISC-V that replaces checks with Bloom filter queries. Two ISA extensions carry a source Section Identifier through a register and validate it at landings with latency independent of source count. Granularity spans type-based to CFG-derived policies. On 81 BEEBS benchmarks, overhead stays under half a percent and code growth near half a percent. The CFG-derived policy cuts equivalence class size by 32.5 percent against the type-based policy, with no failures.
arxiv-2604-23431: Scholl and colleagues reconstruct in-plane magnetization patterns in thin magnetic films from scanning NV magnetometry, a technique that maps stray fields above the sample. Because many magnetization patterns could produce the same field, they guide a simple autoencoder with spatial masks that narrow the search, needing no pretrained data. Aligning those masks well sharpens the result markedly, and tests on patterned Permalloy structures back the approach.
arxiv-2604-23531: Katanyukul simplifies Eigenmarking, a quantum search refinement that keeps answer states in the minority so Grover amplification can work, and flags the no-answer case with complementary states. Earlier schemes needed either two extra qubits or a hard multi-qubit controlled rotation, but his version needs only one extra qubit and a standard two-qubit controlled rotation. Two-qubit simulations show it beats both earlier marking schemes on both reported measures.
arxiv-2604-23631: Pizzuti and colleagues test chameleon gravity, a modified-gravity family with screening, using joint lensing and kinematic mass profiles of nine massive galaxy clusters. With cuspy mass profiles the combined constraints match general relativity and rule out large parts of the theory's parameter space. A cored profile instead hints at a mild departure, but the tension eases once dynamically disturbed clusters are excluded.
arxiv-2604-24131: Luo and five colleagues spot encryption loops in binary-only ransomware by checking the avalanche effect itself. Earlier work only checked a ripple effect, a necessary but insufficient sign, which attackers can fake. Their record-and-replay method tolerates sloppy input and output identification and resists evasion, backed by Shapiro-Wilk normality guarantees. Tests show no missed cases and 1.1 percent false alarms, and the tool analyzes every sample drawn from ten representative ransomware families.
arxiv-2604-24231: Filiot, Joseph, Pérez, and Sunny give the first complexity theory for Hanoi Omega-Automata, the standard omega-regular automata format for synthesis tools. Its succinct symbolic form, with Boolean transition guards and transition-based coloring, makes problems harder. Non-emptiness is NP-complete under standard conditions, with hardness from the Boolean guards. Language inclusion is PSPACE-complete mostly but EXPSPACE-complete for Emerson-Lei acceptance. The authors formalize Hanoi Omega-Games, with bounds from Pi-2-completeness to PSPACE-completeness, and extend techniques to symbolic games over decidable theories.
arxiv-2604-24531: The CMS team searches for Higgs bosons produced together with two vector bosons through vector boson scattering. The data come from proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV. Events were chosen with two forward jets, a large jet from a boosted Higgs decay to bottom quarks, and up to two charged leptons. The team excludes a range of values for the coupling modifier linking two vector bosons to two Higgs bosons, giving a new probe of that interaction.
arxiv-2604-24631: Zhang, Zhang, Ren and Yang apply a model-independent method for measuring the Weyl potential, which describes how gravity bends light, to KiDS-1000 lensing plus BOSS and 2dFLenS galaxy clustering. Fitting late-time observables in two redshift bins, they find one galaxy sample sits below the general-relativity prediction while the other matches it. A mild lensing-is-low hint appears, yet gravity tests overall show no significant preference for modified gravity.
arxiv-2604-25031: Amrollahi, Lopez and Barrett propose roundtrip checks for faithful formalization. Their approach formalizes a claim, translates it back, re-formalizes, and uses a tool to check match. Disagreement triggers stage diagnosis pinpointing the error step, with scoped repair attempting correction. They evaluate on the Texas Transportation Code and the Texas Parks and Wildlife Code, with two models and three baselines. Diagnosis-guided repair proves most effective, tied to diagnosis reliability. Under full repair, rules failing the equivalence check show up to 2.5 times more inference drift than rules passing it.
arxiv-2604-26631: Hinlopen and seven colleagues demonstrate a programmable superconducting diode built from the nematic superconductor FeSe. Ordinary diodes of this kind fix their one-way behavior in sample shape or crystal structure, making them static circuit parts. Here, vortices interacting with nematic twin boundaries yield gains up to about three quarters, and the domain-wall pattern encodes the diode behavior. Intense brief current pulses quench the nematic order at over ten million kelvin per second, reshaping domains to control direction and strength.
arxiv-2604-26731: Samanta decomposes spectral swings in heavy-ion collisions into thermal and geometric normal modes. The momentum spectrum of charged particles fluctuates event by event, mixing thermal and geometric swings of the initial state. A principal-part study of the joint covariance of normalized spectrum, mean momentum, and elliptic flow squared yields two leading modes. They explain over 99 percent of the total spread. Rotated by state constraints, the thermal mode alone drives the v0, while the geometric mode shapes v02 off-center, with a low-momentum flip.
arxiv-2605-00231:
Hussein Suprême and 5 co-authors propose a new way to plan growth of electric transmission networks. Older planning methods rely on snapshots and fixed assumptions, which miss how wind, solar, electric cars, and local energy resources change hour by hour. Their framework simulates a full year of grid behavior step by step.

The simulation tracks equipment behavior, control strategies, and the actions of local energy resources across all seasons. Applied to Hydro-Québec's projected grid for the mid-2030s, it exposed flexibility and limits that static methods overlook, under high wind and electric vehicle use. A storage control strategy in the model helps smooth wind swings. The authors argue planning should match how the grid will really run.
arxiv-2605-00531:
Qunying Song and 3 co-authors review autonomous driving system testing with the people who must use the research: industry practitioners. Self-driving systems now run in real traffic, but testing them is hard, since environments are open, scenarios are complex, and settled processes and metrics are lacking. Academic advances often fail to land in practice, which is the gap this rapid review attacks.

Working with twenty-one practitioners from a leading carmaker, the team identified twelve key challenges in testing. Practitioners ranked two as most critical: testing approaches for end-to-end driving systems, and knowing when testing is complete. The authors then analyzed seventeen relevant research studies, most about generating critical scenarios, and judged their relevance and applicability with the practitioners. They describe the study as the first practitioner-driven review of its kind, and call for more context-aware, industry-shaped research.
arxiv-2605-01031:
Siya Zhu and Raymundo Arróyave study how elastic strain changes phase separation in alloys whose split phases do not fit the same lattice. This strain term is often left out of phase diagram work, even though it can be large. The authors build a model that adds the strain term to standard CALPHAD chemical free energies, then apply it to the body-centered cubic niobium-vanadium system.

With the strain term included, phase separation is much weaker, the miscibility gap narrows, and the critical temperature drops toward measured values. The reading of the diagram also changes. The make-up of each phase now depends on both temperature and the overall alloy mix, so a boundary line no longer gives one fixed pair of phase compositions. The authors present the model as a general tool for alloys with mismatched lattices.
arxiv-2605-01131:
Steven Tang and nine co-authors introduce Forager, a lightweight testbed for continual reinforcement learning under partial observability. Continual agents must keep learning, acting, and exploring in a large world that is never fully seen. Most experiments instead add non-stationarity to classic fully observable tasks and focus on loss of plasticity. Partly that is because partially seen continual environments are often prohibitively expensive to run.

Forager has a constant memory footprint and supports in-depth study of agents. Experiments show agents do exhibit loss of plasticity. Proposed mitigations can help, but leveraging state construction helps most. A variant that generates an unending stream of new tasks highlights current agents' limits clearly. That gives researchers a practical environment for memory and recurrence questions.
arxiv-2605-01231:
Xiaorui Wang and eleven co-authors present CombinationTS, a framework for finding which parts of a time-series forecasting model truly drive its results. Models have grown complex fast, yet many reported gains are fragile or credited to the wrong part. The authors argue the field should move from picking whole models to testing parts one by one. Their framework splits a model into five modules: input transformation, embedding, encoder, decoder, and output transformation.

Each part is scored under shared test conditions by its average result and its stability, firmer than single point scores. In a large paired study, the team finds an Identity Paradox: once the embedding view is well designed, a simple encoder with no parameters often matches or beats complex backbones. Clear structural priors in the input step also give a better balance of results and stability than a more complex encoder.
arxiv-2605-02231:
TaeHo Yoon and Benjamin Grimmer develop a theory of the best fixed-step methods for a classic problem in optimization: finding a fixed point of a map that does not stretch distances. They study methods summed up by a lower triangular matrix, and ask which such methods are optimal in the worst case over a set number of steps.

The pair show that the optimal methods sit at a counted set of extreme points, each tied to an arc diagram that encodes its proof of convergence. Those diagrams let them join, split, and compare methods. They also study a dual operation that flips the matrix, and when it keeps optimality. From this base they build new optimal methods that stay robust even when the map breaks the no-stretch rule.
arxiv-2605-02731:
Ilkyoo Choi and three co-authors settle more of a graph theory question about cycles whose length divides evenly by a small number. A past conjecture held that any graph with high enough minimum degree has a cycle whose length is divisible by the degree bound. It is known true except in one open case. For lengths tied to three or four, stronger statements were already known.

The authors go further by characterizing all graphs above a degree floor, with few low-degree vertices, that avoid such cycles. From that full list, clean corollaries follow: with at most two degree-two vertices, a divisible-by-three cycle always exists. With at most three, and enough vertices, a divisible-by-four cycle exists. Characterizing the exceptions is stronger than just proving existence.
arxiv-2605-02931:
Jean-Pierre Magnot builds a framework for structures defined by pairwise comparisons, not absolute values. In many settings, from tastes to measurements, the raw data are ratios between pairs. Magnot defines cosurfaces whose values are matrices of such comparisons, over a general group. Its composition law treats upper and lower entries in opposite senses, which suits oriented gluing.

Starting from a directed family of finite grids, he builds finite spaces for each grid. Coarse-graining maps link a fine grid to a coarser one, through ordered refinement steps. The universal limit of that system then holds the global objects, which exist only through agreement across scales. Matching probability laws give meaning on the limit space. A measure of mismatch acts like discrete curvature, marking where global coherence fails.
arxiv-2605-03031:
Cristina Flaut and Bianca Liana Bercea-Straton describe linear and cyclic codes built over a family of special rings. Error-correcting codes are usually built over fields, but ring alphabets can offer useful extra structure for code design.

Their rings are formed from integers modulo a prime p, with an added element whose relation is set by a chosen shift value. The paper sets out how linear codes, which are closed under the ring structure, and cyclic codes, which are closed under cyclic shifts, behave over these rings. It adds a concrete new setting for algebraic coding theory.
arxiv-2605-03231:
Masafumi Oyamada, Kunihiro Takeoka, Kosuke Akimoto, Ryoma Obara, Masafumi Enomoto, Haochen Zhang, Daichi Haraguchi, and Takuya Tamura present cotomi Act, a browser agent that learns office work by watching its user. The aim is an agent that both runs multi-step web tasks reliably and keeps lasting knowledge of how an organization works.

For execution, lazy observation, compressed history, coarse actions, and best-of-N selection scored above the reported human baseline on a WebArena subset. Separately, passive watching is distilled into task boards and wiki pages in a shared workspace. A controlled test confirmed success rose as that learned knowledge grew.
arxiv-2605-03331:
Gordon J. Ross and Dean Markwick build a Bayesian model for extreme events whose rate and size both drift over time. Extremes often arrive in clusters, and nonstationary settings break models that assume a steady process.

Their model uses a self-exciting Hawkes process for event timing, with a flexible Dirichlet process form for the excitation pattern learned from data. Event sizes follow a generalized Pareto law whose parameters pool information across clusters, helping clusters with few events. Simulation checks and four real datasets gave the full model the best held-out predictions among variants tested.
arxiv-2605-03431:
Chao Xu and Mingdong Yang solve cardinality-constrained diameter partitioning, which splits items into two groups of set sizes while minimizing the larger group's diameter. Diameter here means the widest pairwise distance inside a group, so the goal is two tight, size-controlled clusters.

They give a quadratic-time algorithm with a matching lower bound for distance-query models, improving the best known runtime and solving all size splits at once. The method reduces to bottleneck two-coloring on the maximum spanning tree, handled by tree dynamic programming. For one fixed size with Euclidean distances, a faster subquadratic algorithm works in any fixed dimension.
arxiv-2605-03531:
Kenil Ajudiya's thesis reports work with the SPOTLIGHT collaboration hunting fast radio transients and radio pulsars. The sky was once thought static, but quasars, pulsars, and fast radio bursts revealed a violent time-domain universe tied to the end states of stars.

Modern GPU-driven instruments now probe microsecond timescales and produce data at rates that strain existing software. The thesis contributes to survey efforts for bursts and pulsars, joining instrument, computing, and search work. Open questions about neutron stars motivate the push, since each new transient class has reshaped what astronomers thought they knew about stellar remnants.
arxiv-2605-03931:
Kijun Park and four co-authors measure how well magnetite shields neutrons, with proton therapy centers in mind. High-density concrete and magnetite aggregates are common shielding choices around medical accelerators. Their behavior under neutron radiation must be characterized to keep doses safe. The team combined lab measurements with Monte Carlo simulations.

The lab results agreed well with the simulations, confirming the simulation approach. Attenuated neutron doses were computed for various shielding thicknesses. Dose ratios were then compared between the two materials. Magnetite provided superior shielding, with a shorter attenuation length than conventional concrete at the same barrier thickness. Neutron spectra typical of clinical proton therapy accelerators were studied for treatment rooms, primary and secondary barriers, and mazes. The results support better shielding design in medical and research facilities.
arxiv-2605-04031:
Dídac Martínez-Granado and Dylan P. Thurston study geodesic currents, a tool for describing curves on a curved surface in a broad, measure-based way. Each current assigns a number to every curve by counting how often the two cross.

The authors ask which assignments of numbers can come from a real current, and they answer with two simple rules about combining curves and smoothing crossings. From that answer they get fresh descriptions of measured laminations and length functions, plus a short proof of a classic result about group actions on trees.
arxiv-2605-04231:
Ji-Hun Oh and six co-authors report a failure of deep learning on scientific images, using medical tissue imaging as the test case. They compare normal stained tissue photos with infrared images, whose pixels carry rich chemical information across many channels.

Despite holding more information, the infrared data gave worse results. The authors trace the problem to a clash between the data's patterns and the models' bias toward simple cues, which led models to collapse their answers onto a narrow line. The finding raises safety concerns, since a model can look capable while barely using the rich signal it was given.
arxiv-2605-05031:
Honghu Pan and four co-authors generate computer-aided design models with a diffusion process that respects the discrete nature of design commands. A CAD model is a sequence of commands and values, and smoothing those symbols in a smooth space often produces invalid ones. Their framework therefore diffuses directly over symbol classes instead.

One stage generates the commands, and a second generates the values tied to those commands. Special step rules handle where things sit, sizes, and yes-or-no traits in ways suited to each kind. The cascaded design aims to produce valid, editable CAD sequences more reliably than step-by-step or continuous diffusion approaches.
arxiv-2605-05631:
An elastic polymer stretches through a random medium that changes with time but correlates across space. Gérard Ben Arous and Pax Kivimae study this model as the dimension of the environment grows without bound. They derive an explicit asymptotic formula for the free energy, the quantity that decides the polymer's typical behavior.

The formula runs through the distribution of the overlap between two sampled configurations, which they also characterize implicitly. Low- and high-temperature phases emerge in terms of the environment's spatial correlation. Wandering exponents follow for exponential and power-law correlations, completing a high-dimensional picture of the model.
arxiv-2605-06131:
Zhifang Du and Aleksey Sikstel study shock waves in multi-temperature models of compressible plasma flow. When detailed physics is compressed into such models, non conservative terms appear and shock solutions become ambiguous. More than one shock structure can seem allowed, and the equations alone cannot say which one nature picks.

The authors derive two distinct Hugoniot relations, one for the general multi-temperature case and one for two temperature plasma flows. Classical analysis shows both meet fitness conditions, proving a basic non uniqueness in shock structure. They link the two solutions to known numerical schemes, giving justified references for building approximations. Their conclusion is that microscopic physics or experiments must supply what the macroscopic equations leave open.
arxiv-2605-06231:
Fengze Guo and Yue Chang describe their system for a shared task on detecting online polarization across languages and cultures. The SemEval 2026 task covers polarized social media content in 22 languages, split into three subtasks: binary detection, target classification, and manifestation identification. Heavy label imbalance makes the classification harder, since polarizing posts are rare beside ordinary content in most feeds.

Their system ensembles two multilingual pretrained models of unlike designs, a mixed pairing meant to cover each other's blind spots. They test multi task learning, translation based data boosting, and class weighting as fixes for the imbalance. The findings favor modeling each task independently, combined with class weighting. The paper reports what worked for this multilingual, multicultural, and multi event detection challenge.
arxiv-2605-06331:
Yupeng Hou and five co-authors expose an expressiveness limit in generative recommendation and propose a simple fix. Such models recommend by generating an item's semantic identifier token by token, which arranges all items on a single decoding tree. Items sitting close on that tree receive strongly correlated probabilities for any user, so the model struggles to rank near neighbors by personal taste, the authors observe, however well it is trained.

Theory confirms the structural coupling blocks even simple preference patterns that classic collaborative filtering captures easily. Their modification, Latte, inserts a latent token before each semantic identifier. One tree becomes many latent conditioned trees, giving items multiple paths at varied distances and loosening the coupling. The change improved a standard ranking metric by an average of about three and a half percent.
arxiv-2605-06431:
Sheng Yang, Chengchang Liu, Lesi Chen, and John C. S. Lui design faster second-order methods for bilevel optimization where the outer problem is nonconvex and the inner one strongly convex. Their fully second-order method, FSBA, reaches a second-order stationary point of the hyper-objective with an accelerated iteration rate over first-order methods.

Second-order information is costly, so a lazy variant reuses it across several iterations and improves computational complexity by a factor tied to problem dimension. The same lazy idea yields a cubic-regularized Newton method for nonconvex strongly-concave minimax problems with better complexity than existing second-order options. The work targets problems where curvature information is worth its price.
arxiv-2605-06631:
Amir Ivry audits how audio compression affects large audio language models, which ever more reason over long clips where compression saves memory and time. A compression method can leave overall answer accuracy looking fine while badly harming certain kinds of questions, such as one query family users care about. Average scores therefore hide real harm.

His framework measures the rise in answer error against uncompressed audio for each required query family one by one. A pass rule caps that rise per family, and a workable test plan checks compression settings with statistical confidence. Across five audio question benchmarks and four models, the experiments expose compression damage that overall accuracy had concealed.
arxiv-2605-06831:
Muhammad H. Ashiq and five co-authors explain theoretically why the deterministic DDIM sampler hallucinates more than the stochastic DDPM sampler in diffusion models. Both reverse a noising process, one by an ordinary differential equation and one with added randomness. Analyzing both for a Gaussian mixture target, the authors prove that after a critical time the deterministic sampler can become stuck on the segment between the two nearest modes, fabricating in-between content.

The stochastic sampler's noise, by contrast, knocks it free of that trap region. Experiments confirm a significantly lower hallucination rate for the stochastic method whenever the trap is entered. Adding extra stochastic steps to the deterministic sampler also helps it escape, informing better sampler design.
arxiv-2605-06931:
Eshed Gal, Uri Ascher, and Eldad Haber attack the data choke point in learning to predict Boolean satisfiability. Machine learning for hard combinatorial problems needs labeled cases, but tagging satisfiability instances needs costly solver runs, which scales badly. Their target-aware framework builds correctly labeled satisfying and unsatisfying instances by construction, with no solver in the loop, while matching the structural traits of a chosen target benchmark.

A paired graph network feeds constraint-violation leftovers into its message passing, using the optimization structure of the problem. Together the pieces yield far faster data generation, and the synthetic, benchmark-aligned data usefully augments solver-labeled sets for graph-based satisfiability guessing. The authors argue data design matters as much as model design here.
arxiv-2605-07031:
Spenner settles a long open hardness question about deterministic finite automata, the simple state machines that read strings and accept or reject them. A machine is composite when several strictly smaller machines, combined by intersection, decide exactly the same language. It is prime when no such combination exists. Deciding which case holds, the Prime-DFA problem, was known since 2015 only to be NL hard and inside ExpSpace, a doubly exponential gap in difficulty.

The author closes that gap by proving the problem NP hard, using a reduction from propositional satisfiability, the classic problem of deciding whether a logical formula can be made true. The proof rests on a detailed characterisation of primality. It covers a class of automata broad enough to include every machine the reduction can produce. It is the first progress on the problem's complexity since its definition.
arxiv-2605-07431:
Murad Alim and Filippo La Mantia prove a modularity result for a Feynman integral that can be read as a period on a Calabi-Yau manifold. The integral in question is the two-dimensional conformal traintrack integral, whose modularity was asserted by Duhr and Maggio. The authors supply the mathematical proof of that assertion.

Their approach factors the associated Picard-Fuchs differential system into a tensor product of two Gauss hypergeometric systems. The factorization uses a gauge transformation due to Clingher, Doran, and Malmendier. The work also ties the result to Appell F2 systems, placing a physics-motivated integral firmly inside classical hypergeometric and modular mathematics.
arxiv-2605-07531:
Hippolyte Labarrière and three co-authors work on the theory behind black-box variational inference, a method that fits probability models by optimizing a lower bound with stochastic gradient descent. In this setting the gradient noise is unbounded, growing with distance from the optimum, which breaks the assumptions behind standard convergence proofs.

Focusing on a broad family of location-scale distributions, the team first proves that an optimal solution to the bound actually exists, a fact earlier work simply assumed. They then give finite-time and long-run convergence guarantees for projected stochastic gradient descent that grows its batch size over time and uses preconditioning. Numerical results back the theory, showing the combination delivers the promised behavior on modern inference tasks.
arxiv-2605-07631:
Sadegh Khorasani and three co-authors improve causal probing, a family of methods that test how a language model's internal states drive its behavior by intervening on them. Earlier interventions needed a separately trained probe classifier, which ties the method to one task and can clash with the model's own geometry.

Their method, HDMI, skips probes entirely: a gradient-based margin objective steers hidden states directly, raising the chance of a target continuation while lowering the source one. A lookahead variant supports text editing while preserving fluency. Judged by completeness and selectivity on two benchmarks and two model families, HDMI achieved higher overall reliability than prior probing methods.
arxiv-2605-07731:
Andrea Sassella and four co-authors benchmark EngGPT2, an Italian-oriented language model built by ENGINEERING Ingegneria Informatica, against comparable open-source models. The model is a mixture-of-experts design with sixteen billion total parameters and three billion active ones. The report tests it across reasoning, math, knowledge, coding, and long-context benchmarks, Italian and international.

Against other Italian models it performed as well or better nearly everywhere, with the longest-context result its standout, though one rival beat it on the Italian ITALIC suite. Against international mixture-of-experts and dense models the picture was mixed: it topped DeepSeek-MoE across the board and led on the math suites against several dense rivals, but trailed GPT-OSS-20B on most measures. Overall the authors call it a step forward for native Italian models.
arxiv-2605-07831:
Andreas Caduff and four co-authors extend a clear-by-design approach to fine-grained vehicle sorting for smart transport systems. Their earlier design replaced one opaque network with a part detector that finds vehicle parts strong in meaning, followed by feature building and a decision tree. That split made the system easy to extend and partly readable, but treated each part as simply present or absent.

The extension adds spatial awareness: a full probability map conditions each part's presence on the vehicle category being considered, and a softmax regression produces the final probabilities. The change made the classifier much more robust to false part detections, which matters in deployment. Head-to-head tests against a state-of-the-art end-to-end network showed comparable accuracy, challenging the assumed trade-off between accuracy and clarity.
arxiv-2605-08031:
Kaidi Jia and coauthors tackle machine unlearning for vision-language models, which may need to forget private or copyrighted content. Older methods retrain mainly the language part, so visual knowledge often survives and the model may invent objects that are not in an image.

Their framework, HFRU, works on the vision encoder to remove meaning at a deeper level. A two-stage design first disrupts alignment, then applies reinforcement optimization with rewards that favor valid substitute answers and punish hallucination. On object recognition and face identity tasks, the method reports over ninety-eight percent forgetting and retention with very little added hallucination.
arxiv-2605-08331:
Muaaz Bhamjee, Matthew Connell, Simon Connell, Emmanuel Igumbor, and coauthors simulate airflow inside the upgraded ATLAS inner tracker at CERN. The High Luminosity collider will push the detector harder. Its electronics must stay dry. If a cooling fault drops temperatures far below freezing, humidity inside could condense and cause damage.

The team uses computational fluid dynamics. They characterize the thermoflow of the dry nitrogen flushing scheme. The scheme keeps the tracker volume dry. The target is a dew point at or below minus sixty degrees Celsius. The simulations feed the monitoring and interlock design. They check that flushing keeps humidity in spec, even under fault conditions.
arxiv-2605-08431:
Emma Coletta, Massimiliano Todisco, Michele Panariello, and Antonio Faonio hide watermarks in speech by spinning its latent code. Their Latent Secret Spin method applies keyed rotations inside a neural codec's latent space. The rotations align to principal components. They leave a covariance mark that a detector can read. Listeners hear no change at all in the sound.

The scheme is blind. Detection needs no original recording. It needs no neural network training either. It works across datasets and keeps sound quality high. It resists common signal edits and accepts payload sizes that can vary. The authors present it as a clearer option than learned neural watermarking when the goal is to prove where audio came from.
arxiv-2605-08731:
Vladimir Iglovikov and Dmitry Kosarevsky benchmark JPEG decoders inside the data loaders that feed image model training, noting that the evidence title frames the same study around single thread claims. Fixing a PyTorch loader at eight workers, they compare twelve Python decoders against the standard Pillow library on four cloud processors and two photo workloads, repeating each setting five times in isolation.

On large camera originals, every decoder lands near Pillow speed. On a mixed workload with social media processed copies, three decoders run about forty percent faster, though the exact leader changes by processor. Practitioners learn to benchmark on photos like their own, since workload, not brand, decides the winner.
arxiv-2605-09031:
Thomas Tulinski works with three co-authors, Simona Cocco, Rémi Monasson, and Jorge Fernandez-De-Cossio-Diaz, on a solvable energy-based model of learning and generation. Their 2026 study examines the spherical Boltzmann machine, a flexible model inspired by statistical physics whose training behavior is usually hard to pin down. Working in the high-dimensional limit, they combine random matrix tools with dynamical mean-field methods.

The team solves exact equations for how training unfolds and computes a quantity that summarizes global traits of the trained model. They uncover chains of phase transitions during training, tied to the coupling matrix aligning step by step with patterns in the data. In a teacher-student setup they link those transitions to sampling effects, including double descent and biases from unfinished training. Tests suggest the same effects appear in standard generative systems, so the solvable model offers a window onto broader practice.
arxiv-2605-09131:
Giridhar Ganapavarapu and Dhaval Patel present MCP-Cosmos, a framework that gives tool-using language model agents a sense of foresight. The Model Context Protocol has standardized how agents reach outside tools, yet planners often ignore how actions play out, while reactive agents cannot see far ahead.

MCP-Cosmos plugs in world models, which simulate how the environment changes, so an agent can rehearse a plan internally before acting. Users can bring their own world model. Across more than twenty benchmark tasks, with two planning styles and three world models, the setup improved tool success rates and the accuracy of tool settings. The authors also add a quality measure for judging what world models contribute.
arxiv-2605-09231:
Rahman and three colleagues build a generative model for skeleton pose trajectories that ignores nuisance factors and keeps shape dynamics. Standard variational autoencoders waste capacity on camera angle, subject size, viewpoint, and pace, rather than shape geometry and motion. Their Elastic Shape VAE uses a transported square root velocity field code on Kendall's shape manifold, stripping translations, rotations, global scaling, and rate variability.

The encoder turns skeletal sequences into a low dimensional latent space with the Riemannian logarithm map, while the decoder rebuilds sequences with the exponential map. On gait cycles, the model predicts mobility scores and sorts subjects into healthy and post stroke groups. On the NTU RGB+D set, it handles action recognition, beating standard VAEs and several sequence baselines. The work offers a principled framework for generative models of longitudinal pose data, with better representations and downstream results.
arxiv-2605-09331:
Long and two colleagues study how the Muon optimiser leaves saddle points in the extreme high-dimensional terrain of large language model training. There, flat saddle points, not local minima, are the main block. Step-wise adaptive optimisers like AdamW are trapped by an O(D) dimensional curse, the authors argue, while Muon resists it through non-linear spectral shaping.

Extending matrix perturbation theory, they build a framework for Muon's non-equilibrium optimisation paths. Resolvent calculus and large-scale Cauchy contour math sidestep isotropic noise assumptions and Tracy-Widom edge spikes. Structural incoherence shields the path from side drift, giving a dimension-free saddle-point escape with a set O(1) discrete ballistic ejection under a wide enough spectral gap. The paper closes with a dimension-free escape bound for Muon, stated in algebra, spelling out the mechanics of its non-convex optimisation dynamics.
arxiv-2605-09531:
Gal and Nuer construct explicit equations for a special family of cubic fourfolds, shapes defined by a single cubic equation in five dimensional projective space. Such fourfolds matter in algebraic geometry for their rich Hodge theory and stubborn rationality problem. A fourfold is special when its cohomology lattice has rank at least two. Hassett showed the special ones form divisors indexed by a set of discriminants, and their common intersection is the Hassett maximal locus.

Earlier work by the authors fixed that intersection at dimension sixteen. But the link between the lattice and the geometry stayed unclear. Here they build a concrete family of cubic equations whose zero sets land in the Hassett maximal class. Using algebraic and arithmetic methods, plus a proved property for one ternary form, they show the lattice image spans the whole Hassett set. The result gives a geometric face to a formerly abstract component.
arxiv-2605-09731:
Chiriac and Jorza traced where the zeros of Miller basis modular forms lie, linking them to a logarithmic version of the Szegő curve. Miller forms look like q to the m plus higher terms, and their zero patterns matter for the theory of modular forms. The paper connects zero variation to the curve S with subscript delta, where delta is the ratio m over l.

When delta sits below 0.6194, all zeros lie on the unit arc for large weight k. When delta nears 1, all zeros lie on the log Szegő curve. The authors conjecture that in general zeros sit on the union of arc and curve, prove a partial result, and give conjectural thresholds for all-on-arc versus none-on-arc. They also list every algebraic zero of Miller forms with l minus m at most 25.
arxiv-2605-09931:
Zhang and ten colleagues improve tool-using language models at inference time, without any extra training. Tool-integrated reasoning lets a model call code interpreters and other tools mid-thought, yet failed tool calls drag answers down. The authors observe that errors usually clear within a few turns or not at all, with long retry spirals rarely helping. Their framework, PruneTIR, acts on that pattern.

Three components share the work. Success-Triggered Pruning cuts a trajectory once it succeeds, Stuck-Triggered Pruning and Resampling restarts stalled tool calls, and Retry-Triggered Tool Suspension stops tool use after repeated failure. Together they limit the damage from bad calls and keep models from circling failed fixes. Experiments show clear gains in Pass@1, the share of first answers that are right, plus better efficiency.
arxiv-2605-10031:
Bhangale and Zhang tackle the generalised min-sum set cover problem. Given hyperedges, groups of vertices each needing a set number of its vertices to appear, the task is to order the vertices to minimise total cover time. A hyperedge counts as covered once enough of its vertices have shown up. The previous best guarantee was 4.642, and the authors improve it to 4.509.

Their approach keeps the linear-programming framework of Bansal, Batra, Farhadi and Tetali. It sharpens the analysis, narrowing the gap toward the lower bound of 4 that holds if P differs from NP. The proof exploits the program's constraints in a non-trivial way. It develops new lower-tail bounds for sums of independent Bernoulli variables, results the authors note may interest readers beyond this problem.
arxiv-2605-10231:
Jonathan AD Wattis, Pilar R Gordoa, and Andrew Pickering analyze small, weakly nonlinear waves in a kagome lattice. That lattice, a pattern of hexagons and triangles, models systems such as nonlinear electrical lattices. Their 2026 paper, published in Physica D, uses Klein-Gordon interactions with a single scalar unknown at each node.

The dispersion relation, which links wave frequency to wavenumber, has three bands: a flat band plus two surfaces that may meet at Dirac points or split apart with a gap. Using multiple-scales asymptotic methods, the authors reduce the system to nonlinear Schrödinger systems, including the Townes soliton as a solution. Near the point where the flat band meets the upper surface, they find a novel coupled system, analyzed with Lie symmetries and supported by numerical simulations.
arxiv-2605-10631:
Parosh Aziz Abdulla and three colleagues study verification for Remote Direct Memory Access programs. Remote Direct Memory Access allows direct access from one computer's memory into another's, bypassing both operating systems. This enables high-throughput, low-latency networking for parallel computer clusters. Their 2026 paper studies reachability and robustness for RDMA programs.

The authors show reachability stays undecidable in general, even in a restricted fragment of the model. They then focus on robustness: whether a program behaves the same under RDMA and sequential consistency semantics. They prove decidability. Their result is a normal form for robustness violations. Any non-robust program has a violating execution of a form. This normal form yields a procedure reducing robustness to reachability in programs with counters. That gives an ExpSpace upper bound generally and a PSpace upper bound without poll operations. Both bounds are optimal.
arxiv-2605-10831:
Mingxu Zhang and five colleagues present SLIM, a framework that steers language-model molecule editors toward chosen properties without retraining them. Molecular editing tweaks a starting compound to improve traits like solubility while keeping its core, yet property signals tangle inside dense hidden states, so many edits fail or backfire.

SLIM splits hidden states into sparse, property-aligned features with a sparse autoencoder and gated importance, then steers only the features tied to the target trait. On the MolEditRL benchmark across four model designs and eight properties, gains reach more than forty points over baselines. Drug and materials teams get interpretable control knobs for edits that previously ran blind.
arxiv-2605-10931:
Albert Alcalde, Leon Bungert, Konstantin Riedl, and Tim Roith quantify how tokens cluster in deep encoder-only transformers at inference time. In the large-token limit, token motion follows a mean-field continuity equation, and the team proves the token spread collapses quickly onto a projected image of its starting shape.

The clustering holds steadily for moderate times, with Wasserstein distance bounded by a mix of a slowly growing term and a fast-decaying one. Stability estimates for the zero-temperature equation, its long-time limit, and a Laplace-type argument drive the proof. The result pins down the time scale, logarithmic in inverse temperature, over which tokens stay clustered. Theorists get a sharp picture of inference-time token geometry.
arxiv-2605-11131:
Elisha Dayag, Nhat Thanh Tran, and Jack Xin present USEMA, a hybrid UNet for medical image segmentation that merges convolutional local-feature extraction with Scalable and Efficient Mamba-like Attention. Vision transformers capture global interactions but pay quadratic cost in input size, a struggle for segmentation tasks.

SEMA avoids vanilla self-attention's dispersion through token localization via local window attention, keeping focus, while consistent arithmetic averaging captures global attention aspects. USEMA tests across modalities and image sizes show better efficiency than full self-attention transformers and stronger segmentation than purely convolutional or Mamba-based models. Medical imaging teams get a scalable segmenter that keeps both local detail and global context.
arxiv-2605-11231:
Abhishek Moturu, Anna Goldenberg, and Babak Taati present LiBaGS, a light method for picking targeted synthetic data through boundary gap building. Such data helps only when new samples cover missing parts of the training spread that matter for the downstream task.

LiBaGS scores tried samples by mixing decision-edge nearness, guess uncertainty, real-data density, and soundness, so picked samples are both useful and likely to stay on the real data manifold. A gap sharing rule targets sparse but true-to-life edge zones rather than simply adding more data or picking only the most unsure picks. LiBaGS also learns when enough samples have been added through an extra-value stopping rule and assigns softer labels near unclear edges. Data teams get data chosen for gaps, not volume.
arxiv-2605-11631: Zhao and four colleagues present GraphFlash, a fast elastic graph framework on serverless infrastructure. Graph systems usually rely on fixed clusters, giving poor elasticity and wasteful use under shifting workloads. Serverless computing gives automatic scaling and fine-grained billing, but current serverless systems suffer weak state handling and costly external-storage communication. GraphFlash uses a subgraph-centric model with shared external storage, plus rotating and pinned modes. Across varied datasets it beats prior serverless systems by up to 127 times and cuts resource use by up to 98 percent.
arxiv-2605-11931: Qihuang Zhong and five colleagues improve multimodal reasoning through vision-aware self-improvement training. Self-generated reasoning traces suffer data imbalance, with easy samples over-trained and hard samples under-trained, plus language prior bias that neglects visual cues. Their VISTA framework reuses partial correct traces through prefix resampling and scores visual focus with a vision-aware attention score. It boosted reasoning across models and tasks, gaining up to 13.66 percent on average for Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct.
arxiv-2605-12131: Charlie Masters, Ziyuan Liu, and Stefano Albrecht propose rollout cards to fix weak reproducibility in agent research. They audit 50 training and test codebases and find none log failed, errored, or skipped runs next to headline scores. They log 37 cases where scoring rules shift success rates, cost counts, or timings for the same evidence. A rollout card bundles the raw rollout record with its views, scoring rules, and drop lists. Re-grading saved outputs shows rule changes alone can move scores by 20.9 points and flip top model ranks.
arxiv-2605-12631: Egorov and four colleagues bridge variational and perturbation approaches to brittle fracture. Their model treats three-dimensional coplanar growth of sharp cracks in heterogeneous brittle solids under mixed-mode loading. Crack-front shapes come from minimising total energy, combining elastic stored energy from front bends with lost energy set by the fracture field. Energy and slopes are evaluated fast with the Fast Fourier Transform. A matrix-free Newton solver with trust region and physics-based tuning then resolves energy barriers and long-range elastic interactions.
arxiv-2605-12831: Benac and three colleagues measure missing notes behind expert actions. Inverse reinforcement learning infers rewards from demos, but data may omit the decider's notes. In clinics, that can make expert actions look poor even when near-best given info. Usual methods learn wrong rewards. The team finds smallest tweaks to notes making expert actions appear best, and builds a method. Synthetic routing, a cancer sim, and ICU data show its use for gauging gaps.
arxiv-2605-12931: Chan and four colleagues simulate collapsars, dying massive stars, in three dimensions to explain how relativistic jets get their large-scale magnetic fields. Starting from toroidal fields like those in pre-collapse stars, they find the disk dynamo seeds coherent poloidal loops that drift inward. They thread the black hole and launch wobbling jets lasting seconds. The jets sustain power comparable to long gamma-ray bursts, showing disk dynamos offer a robust jet pathway across progenitors.
arxiv-2605-13431: Keshav Bhandari and six colleagues present Text2Score, a framework that generates sheet music from text prompts. Text-driven music generation suffers from scarce aligned data and unreliable captioning. The first stage turns a prompt into a bar-by-bar plan of instruments, key, time signatures and harmony. The second stage turns that plan into interleaved ABC notation, a text format for music. The system outperforms a language-model agent and three end-to-end baselines, on objective measures and expert judgement.
arxiv-2605-13631: Kebin Contreras and three colleagues propose ProjGuard, safety monitoring for computer-use agents via low-dimensional projections. ProjGuard instead tracks behaviour trajectories, deriving a light scalar risk signal from interaction history at each step. It judges online whether execution drifts toward an unsafe region. That gives early warnings before harmful actions, and on alert an auxiliary vision-language model proposes a corrected next step. On OS-Harm, unsafe rates fall from 16 percent to 3 percent while task completion rises from 59 percent to 65 percent.
arxiv-2605-13931: Yang and six co-authors build a clean-up line that pulls pure, single-source sound clips from big open audio sets. A diffusion model first makes clean single-class sounds to build mixed clips with known parts for training. A trained audio encoder plus a sorting model then spots and drops clips that mix sources. Tests on FSD50K show the line works well against checks by human experts.
arxiv-2605-14031: Liu, Chasmai, Maji and Van Horn ask if masked autoencoders still pay off for bioacoustics when data is thin. Telling like-sounding species apart needs fine acoustic detail, yet big stores like iNaturalist often tag each clip with just one species. Masked autoencoders transfer well on huge audio sets, but modest bioacoustic use is less tested. The paper runs a systematic study of pretraining scale and domain fit for species sorting on iNatSounds.
arxiv-2605-14231: Huang and five co-authors introduce AudioMosaic, a contrastive audio encoder for general audio understanding. Self-taught audio learning seeks general-purpose codes from large-scale untagged audio, yet recent progress leans on generative remake while contrastive methods stay less explored. Two hurdles explain the gap: making effective audio changes is hard, and contrastive training demands large batches. It builds positive pairs with structured time-frequency masking on spectrogram patches, cutting memory use for efficient large-batch training.
arxiv-2605-14631: Eshwar and Pal introduce Action-Inspired Generative Models, a dual-network framework for bridge matching in generative modelling. Standard bridge methods weight every stochastic transition alike, even along incoherent paths. A small learned scalar potential scores bridge samples on the fly and reweights the drift objective, adding only about one and a half percent to the main network's size. The potential is dropped at inference, and generation quality is claimed to improve on fidelity and coverage.
arxiv-2605-14731: Zhan and team present UMo, a unified sparse motion model for real-time co-speech avatars in games, virtual production, and interactive play. Text, audio and motion tokens run through one formulation. A spatially sparse Mixture-of-Experts design plus a temporally sparse keyframe-centred design drive dense reconstruction in real time. Multi-stage training with audio augmentation is claimed to preserve fine speech-motion alignment under strict latency limits.
arxiv-2605-14831: Herrmann and team define interestingness as an inductive rule for future compression. The work tackles the block on the path to recursively self-improving systems. Using Kolmogorov complexity and algorithmic stats, they analyse profiles under Length, Algorithmic, and Speed priors. Past progress signals future discovery. Future gains depend exponentially on the recency of the last breakthrough. The Algorithmic Prior is far more hopeful than the Length Prior, yielding a quadratic rise in future discovery for the same profile. Results hold across three universal settings.
arxiv-2605-15231: Haoran Li and seven others present Mask-Morph Graph U-Net, a mesh-based surrogate for crashworthiness field forecast under large geometric change. Curved crash runs are true but too slow for repeat design. Graph neural surrogates help, yet edge-tied layers need fixed links. The new method morphs the coarse graph ladder to each input mesh via feature-aligned center-based parameterization before building cross-graph edges, masks nodes during pretraining, and freezes high-parameter layers during fine-tuning. Tests show lifted generalization.
arxiv-2605-15531: Hien Duy Nguyen derives explicit upper and lower bounds for the number of modes of a Gaussian mixture density. Normalizing the critical-point equations by a reference component yields two competing upper bounds, whose minimum, refined by a Morse-theoretic argument, bounds the finite-mode count. In the equal-variance case the bounds improve further, including a dimension-free form, while product and padding constructions supply lower bounds and a seed-closure principle packages them.
arxiv-2605-16131: Winter and three colleagues show that a local kinetic constraint can turn Dicke superradiance into a source of extensive mixed-state entanglement. Plain superradiance gives a collective burst of radiation but no entanglement in the emitters' mixed state. For any local Boolean constraint, they derive an emission-rate bound implying peak intensity scaling with N squared and peak time scaling with log N over N. The effect enables fast preparation of entangled dark states and survives atomic decay and collective dephasing.
arxiv-2605-16331: Jedryszek and Crook trace how the protein language model ESM2-8M predicts that proteins begin with methionine, a rule of life that almost always holds. The model does not spot methionine at the masked spot. Instead it pulls a methionine-leaning signal from the start token, with the output arising through contest with context-tied circuits. On chains that truly start with another amino acid, the model still predicts methionine, matching the average where biology differs. The finding suggests circuit-level checks will be needed for high-stakes calls.
arxiv-2605-16431: Taifour and eleven others present CT-DegradBench, a dataset and benchmark for spotting CT degradation and grading severity under single- and mixed-artifact settings. CT fixes are still largely evaluated with image quality metrics of limited clinical validity, while datasets focus on isolated restoration tasks, hindering unified benchmarking. The authors further propose SeSpeCT, mixing semantic priors from medical vision language models with frequency cues into a quality axis built without training from radiology prompts. Tests show SeSpeCT outperforms evaluated baselines in all tested settings.
arxiv-2605-16631: Braghini, Tognetti and Peet propose a new way to stabilize linear systems with several time delays using only measured outputs, not full state feedback. They extend a convex optimization approach for ordinary differential equations through a new state-space form. One problem solves state feedback, and a second uses a Projection Lemma lifted to partial integral operators. Comparisons with earlier output-feedback designs show a marked drop in conservatism.
arxiv-2605-17131: Kamal, Kumar and Prabhakaran survey deep learning for point clouds, the unordered sets of 3D points captured by sensors. Their review groups methods by backbone design, compares results on standard benchmarks, and weighs strengths and limits for classifying clouds and splitting them into parts and scenes. It closes by naming open problems for 3D scene understanding.
arxiv-2605-17231: Wang and colleagues trace brittle activation steering in transformers to a false premise: that hidden spaces are flat and Euclidean. The true geometry comes from the Fisher metric of the output layer, pulled back through intervening layers. Their FishBack method derives the steering direction that hits a target concept change with least side distortion. Tests on verb forms show off-target drift falling severalfold on small and large models alike.
arxiv-2605-17331: Il’yasov introduces a Rayleigh-quotient minimax method that finds maximal one-sided saddle-node bifurcations directly, without tracing solution branches step by step. A saddle point of a two-variable quotient on fixed cones yields the critical value, the bifurcation solution and the adjoint singularity rule at once. That direct pick replaces slow branch-by-branch tracking with one sharp test. The method gives Galerkin estimates, margin bounds and perturbation bounds for the critical value. Its assumptions are verified for elliptic systems, including non-potential ones.
arxiv-2605-17431: Hwang and colleagues propose MATE, a memory design for contextual Markov decision processes, where an unseen context shapes each task. Instead of tracking an intractable posterior belief over contexts, MATE keeps a sum-aggregated memory that exploits permutation invariance for proven sufficient expressiveness. It avoids transformers' growing rollout cost and recurrent nets' gradient troubles. Tests match sequence-model baselines on diverse benchmarks at lower compute cost.
arxiv-2605-18131: V. Adibekyan's 2026 study uses machine learning to infer star chemistry from motion and spectra where direct measures fail, notably for cool stars. The team trains on a large APOGEE sample of red giants and checks the models on a separate HARPS sample of near dwarfs. Motion alone recovers only a small share of the spread in iron content, with vertical orbit height the best single clue. Adding iron content sharpens forecasts of carbon, oxygen, magnesium, and silicon well beyond a plain baseline.
arxiv-2605-18331: Diego Coello de Portugal Mecke's 2026 paper presents Putri, a structured pruning method for large language models. Inference on large models stays costly for long contexts and small devices, motivating pruning of many parameters. Current methods cut less informative feed-forward nodes and whole attention layers. Putri instead updates surviving feed-forward weights to compensate for pruning error. It prunes feed-forward layers in sequence, accounting for earlier updates, and removes single heads rather than layers. The design extends to grouped-query attention and holds at extreme sparsity.
arxiv-2605-19131: Julian Becker and Konstantinos Panagiotou study consensus on a network where each vertex holds one of two opinions. Vertices sample neighbours at random and update by a rule such as k-majority, even with an adversary flipping a few opinions per round. They give limit laws for agreement time and the winning opinion, for many rules and any starting mix. Agreement time centers on a log scale formula, and its centered form never settles, turning periodic on both scales. For k-majority, they give the key constant in closed form.
arxiv-2605-19331: Takahiro Tanaka and Yuko Urakawa set a locality test for inflationary soft modes. After short waves are averaged out, the gradient expansion and separate-universe picture should describe long waves, yet hard-mode loops can spoil that picture. They require each local patch's hard-mode state to depend on soft modes only through values in that patch. When the test holds, dynamics stay local, loop corrections to horizon correlations stay suppressed, a generalized soft theorem follows, and infrared divergences vanish for gauge-invariant observables.
arxiv-2605-19531: Kuznetsov, Sutra and Toyos-Marfurt define conflict-freedom, a progress condition for shared objects. Obstruction-freedom promises progress only to operations running alone, yet the authors show mere overlap need not block progress: only clashing operations can do so. Conflict-freedom generalizes obstruction-freedom and suits objects with semantic overlap. As with obstruction-freedom, every sequential object gains a read-write conflict-free linearizable version, built from a commit-adopt object.
arxiv-2605-19731: Liang, Luo, Li and Yu examine neutron stars in quasi-topological gravity, a higher-curvature rival to general relativity, that can pack matter tighter than black holes allow. Testing several matter recipes and coupling strengths, they map equilibrium shapes and check radial stability. In the densest cores, exceeding the black-hole compactness bound becomes a universal pattern, and the new gravity terms can stabilise configurations that general relativity leaves unstable. The result makes such ultra-compact stars theoretically viable probes of strong gravity.
arxiv-2605-19831: Shastry, Sutherland, Mila and Rufino report the ground state entropy of a two dimensional Ising model on the Shastry-Sutherland lattice. This is a frustrated lattice, where rival interactions pull in different ways and block simple ordering at low temperature. The team also studies a wider version of the model that slowly lifts a constraint on the setups allowed at zero temperature. Together the two parts show how frustration shapes the lowest temperature states of this lattice model, and how easing the constraint changes what those states can be.
arxiv-2605-19931: Asiyabi and colleagues join two mismatched forest data sources to map tree mass above ground from orbit. Space lasers give shape at vast sites with no mass, while ground plots give mass at few skewed sites. Their StruMPL model trains all tasks jointly, corrects the skew in plot picks, and ties tasks with known size to mass laws per biome.
arxiv-2605-20131: Minh-Tâm Quang Trinh finds the graded Weyl character of cohomology of Lusztig varieties over the semisimple locus, for reductive groups and Weyl members. The formula links unipotent ones and yields an LLT model. Laurent polynomials indexed by irreps show how the formula breaks into Springer characters. He conjectures that type A ones have positive unimodal nonzero numbers, settling Haiman's 1993 question. He proves the matrix is triangular, with positive signs and unimodality stable under Levi nestings.
arxiv-2605-20231: John Moffat presents a realization of STVG-MOG, in which early scalar dynamics match Lambda-CDM without particle dark matter. Early-universe nonrelativistic excitations of the STVG field act as a collisionless component with density falling as scale factor to the minus three. On acoustic scales gravity nearly equals Newton's constant, so baryon-photon oscillations evolve as in the model and the third acoustic peak keeps its height. With Thomson scattering, recombination and diffusion unchanged, spectra can match Lambda-CDM once the vector sector supplies dust.
arxiv-2605-20331: Drudis and five co-workers present Bowtie VarQTE, a lean way to prepare structured quantum states. It simulates short real- and imaginary-time evolution, using classical computing where possible and quantum hardware only where needed. Causal light-cones trim the quantum work needed for gradients. On two-dimensional tests the method cuts quantum needs versus sample-based Krylov diagonalization, aiding state-preparation pipelines.
arxiv-2605-20531: Slim Barkallah and four colleagues propose pseudo-formalization, a middle path between informal proofs and fully formal ones. Formal proofs in languages like Lean are simple to check but hard to produce, especially from AI-written maths. A pseudo-formal proof splits an argument into modules, each stating premises, conclusion, and proof in natural language. Their block-verification method checks each module alone and beats judge-style baselines on error-finding precision and recall.
arxiv-2605-20731: Haonan Zhu and five colleagues release TASTE, a designer-annotated preference dataset for AI-generated graphic design. Text-to-image models now produce design at scale, yet supervision still comes from photo-style sets with one overall verdict per comparison. Designers instead judge typography, layout, colour harmony, and more as separate axes. TASTE has two cohorts of five professional designers each ranking outputs from four models across nine criteria, with hallucination flags per image.
arxiv-2605-21331: R. J. van Ruiten and colleagues test whether repeating fast radio burst FRB 20200120E could come from a millisecond pulsar making giant pulses. Its localization to a globular cluster challenges magnetar models based on core collapse. Comparing FRB bursts with giant pulses of the most energetic Galactic millisecond pulsar, M28A, using Parkes wideband data, they find broad spectra spanning seven hundred to four thousand megahertz with complex peaks. Known giant-pulse traits persist at this bandwidth, while a sub-band search finds no genuinely narrow-band giant pulses.
arxiv-2605-21431: Jun Zheng and co-authors introduce iTryOn, a method for interactive video virtual try-on with spatial-semantic guidance. Existing try-on methods mostly showcase garments in non-interactive scenes, overlooking active human-garment interaction. Interactive try-on, where subjects actively engage with clothing, adds challenges. One is resolving semantic ambiguity of interactions from pose data. Another is learning garment deformations from video where interactive moments are sparse and brief. The aim is try-on that keeps working when people move and touch clothes.
arxiv-2605-21731: Tarantino, Auricchio, and Giudici introduce I-SAFE, a post-hoc audit for scientific AI models. Strong benchmark scores can mislead, since a model may lean on shortcuts or quirks of its data rather than real domain structure.
