Given a trained predictor and an external structural prior, I-SAFE perturbs inputs along domain-relevant directions and measures how coherently the output distribution responds. It uses quantile, Wasserstein, and shape-based metrics. Applied to three drug-target interaction models, it exposes sharply different response profiles that accuracy alone cannot see.
arxiv-2605-21831: Samuel Li and Ian Roberts design full-duplex massive MIMO beams from implicit channel knowledge, avoiding costly estimation of the self-interference matrix. A site-trained transformer model learns to probe the most relevant channel parts for the users served, exploiting environment structure. Probing measurements then shape transmit and receive beams with low self-interference and high gain for downlink and uplink users. One probe set serves several users across the channel coherence time, and ray-tracing simulations beat the best explicit-estimation performance, especially with large antenna arrays.
arxiv-2605-22031: Pengcheng Fang and co-authors present SO-Mamba, a state-ownership Mamba model for unrolled MRI reconstruction. Accelerated MRI must recover missing detail while keeping clear anatomy across large regions, and Mamba state-space models offer efficient long-range modeling as learned tools. In a coupled solver, different stages work on different iterates, so the resident carrier should preserve state ownership. SO-Mamba enforces that ownership and adds a check that splits hidden-state storage from readout expression. Across five benchmarks it beats CNN, Transformer, and Mamba baselines efficiently.
arxiv-2605-22531: Cunningham offers Riemannian ICA (RICA), swapping the gen model with local shape frame. Old methods, like ICA, assume a gen model with free latents. Strong guesses hinder modern learning, where nets learn split parts, yet no theory reads them. The main result is the splitting tensor for point splitting. It depends on the data log odds Hessian and the Ricci bend. In guided source rescue, RICA finds sources across shapes, while rivals depend on grids. The work gives a basis for local splitting without a gen model.
arxiv-2605-22731: Nie reframes language model post training around state distributions rather than loss functions alone. Supervised fine tuning trains on fixed data set states, while reinforcement learning and on policy distillation train on states the learner itself generates. A controlled study on a small Qwen3 model shows mild fine tuning helps maths with little forgetting, while stressed fine tuning causes heavy retention loss. On policy distillation from a degraded teacher beats that teacher on maths, truthfulness and general knowledge, and light on policy reinforcement learning improves maths while preserving retention.
arxiv-2605-22931: Yariv and nine coauthors explore whether eclipses can map the dayside atmospheres of hot Jupiters with high-resolution spectroscopy. They observed eight eclipses of the ultra-hot Jupiter WASP-33b using SPIRou and fit the signals with the ATMOSPHERIX pipeline. The data gave a first tentative detection of carbon monoxide from in-eclipse data alone. Injection tests suggest about fifteen more eclipses would be needed to measure the planet's rotation this way.
arxiv-2605-23031: Samuelson, Hirsch, and Cecchetti address forking new processes in choreographic programming. Old code forces a program per player, while dance-style programming lets one central program make solo programs, easing deadlock freedom but making forks hard. They introduce the fork calculus, the first choreographic language with process forks. It keeps deadlock freedom while letting programs decide when to spawn new processes, what they do, and who talks to whom. It fits uses like load sharing and split-and-solve work.
arxiv-2605-23131: Zhou shares a small research note on adapting rare switching to the private setting for linear bandits and reinforcement learning. The standard determinant based update rule works because the design matrix grows monotonically. Once Gaussian noise is added for privacy, that monotonicity can fail, since determinant growth controls volume while regret analysis requires control of the worst direction. A new rule based on the generalized Rayleigh quotient restores logarithmic policy updates and the wanted confidence width check up to a constant factor.
arxiv-2605-23231: Wang and three coauthors present IDEAL, a deviation learning tool for few-shot anomaly spotting. Old methods rely on normal-only refs, missing clues in odd refs, while fitting both can overfit. Learning splits into two parts: a Change Eraser cutting nuisance shifts, and an Intrinsic Deviation Encoder splitting deviations into sharp cross vectors. IDEAL scores query-to-normal shifts after mapping onto learned vectors, working for seen and unseen cases. Tests on eight sets show IDEAL extends to unseen cases and beats old methods.
arxiv-2605-23331: Vecino and four coauthors study cleaning-aware quantum routing. A key challenge is making routing rules keeping high quality links in the face of noise, decay, and flawed steps, which slowly degrade the faith of linked states through entanglement swapping. They frame the problem of picking optimal cleaning plans as a tuning task. By using dynamic coding methods, they identify plans that best balance resource use and end-to-end faith.
arxiv-2605-23531: Lin and three colleagues build PixIE, a pixel-space low-light enhancer, where noise, contrast loss, and murk demand joint denoising and detail recovery. PixIE first denoises across scales, keeping structure, then refines detail with prompted pixel blocks injecting foundation-model features through spatially continuous modulation. A spatial-channel compaction step shrinks token grid and channel size to keep attention cheap, and multi-receptive-field embeddings add neighborhood awareness. Tests on standard benchmarks lead on PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS for the hard LOLv2-Real set, with sharper, natural textures.
arxiv-2605-23931: Chang and Li tackle the labour of writing specifications for operating-system kernels, rules that define what each system call should do. Their method, BODHI, adds a C-to-Python translation guide to few-shot prompting, splitting the work into before-conditions and after-conditions across 15 pattern types. On OSV-Bench, a set of 245 specification tasks from the Hyperkernel kernel, the best score was 55.10 percent at first attempt. BODHI lifted every one of nine tested models, with gains from 11 to 32 points, and the best pairing reached 96.73 percent.
arxiv-2605-24131: Banerjee and four co-authors give numbers for joint Z-boson and Higgs-boson production through gluon fusion. They add threshold logarithms at next-to-leading-log accuracy, matched to next-to-leading-order results with exact top-quark mass. At LHC collision energy, the cross-section runs about 20 percent above the next-to-leading-order value. For mass spectra near 3000 GeV, scale uncertainty shrinks from about 20 percent to near 12 percent. Merged with Drell-Yan results at the next log order, these are the sharpest hadron-collision numbers yet.
arxiv-2605-24431: Souissi and Andolsi give a rigorous formulation of the spin-1 AKLT state inside hidden quantum Markov models. They show the AKLT ground state naturally appears as the observable output of a causal hidden quantum Markov model. That gives it hidden quantum memory in line with the standard matrix-product-state picture. This view yields a compact picture of the AKLT chain as a spin system with intrinsic quantum memory. The results suggest the hidden quantum Markov model frame suits measurement-based quantum computation and related tasks.
arxiv-2605-24631: Sol Park and Soobin Um take a world-first view of minority sampling, the art of generating rare cases. Existing methods judge rarity against what a generator itself learned. Their JEPA guidance steers diffusion toward thin regions under a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture, a world model rich in meaning. Approximations with error bounds keep the cost down. In tests with no labels, with class labels, and with text-to-image prompts, it yields more faithful and valid rare samples than generator-based baselines.
arxiv-2605-24731: Reiji Terunuma and others build a passivity-based attitude control framework on the special orthogonal group. Human-robot teamwork helps complex tasks, yet stability of human-in-the-loop control on this manifold stayed unsolved. Their design keeps average feedback to the human unchanged through stealthy control. Human input flows through a virtual leader coupled to robots by a passivity-based synchronization law. They prove closed-loop stability assuming the human behaves as a passive system. Simulations fit a dynamical model of the human operator and test its passivity.
arxiv-2605-24831: Chidera Oguine and co-authors benchmark YOLO26 against YOLOv8 as a real-world stress test of NMS-free detection. YOLO26, built for edge deployment, assigns labels directly end to end, drops Distribution Focal Loss, and runs a spectral-constrained backbone. Across five model sizes, YOLO26 needs less compute and tops Pascal VOC accuracy. That edge narrows on dense aerial VisDrone, where most objects are tiny and both models struggle. YOLOv8 also stays faster on GPU at matched scales, showing NMS-free design alone does not guarantee better deployment.
arxiv-2605-24931: Kunyun Wang leads a fix for robot policies that must act at high rates. Chunking actions helps at moderate speeds but breaks down near sixty cycles per second. At such rates, policies struggle to stay smooth over time and consistent in space. The team moves high-rate action learning into a latent space built with a variational autoencoder. A Reuse-then-Refine step polishes chunk joints under async inference for smooth real-time execution. On three contact-rich tasks, robots run with fewer pauses and less jerky motion.
arxiv-2605-25231: Sepide Mohamadi and Jahanfar Abouie study how an atomic chain with alternating bonds responds to magnetic and electric probes under a special long-range interaction. In their Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model with Hatsugai-Kohmoto coupling, the response differs sharply from ordinary Hubbard models, which usually damp excitations. Exact math yields closed formulas. They show a nonzero response at zero wavelength and a reshuffling of spectral weight as filling changes. A related information measure cleanly separates whole-number from fractional fillings, though it stays blind to topological changes there.
arxiv-2605-25331: Ben Sun and colleagues build a near-infrared hyperspectral camera that needs only a single pixel detector. Standard imagers rely on costly sensor arrays, while this system maps spectrum to time through a fiber and patterns space with a modulator. Correlating stretched waveforms with spatial codes rebuilds 64-by-64 datacubes across 50 bands in the 1550 to 1600 nanometer range. Live monitoring of liquid injection runs at 12 datacubes per second under sub-Nyquist sampling. The design offers single-pixel simplicity and high throughput for medical and materials imaging.
arxiv-2605-25631: Nakamura carries a closed-form privacy-subsidy result from a single-period Kyle model into continuous time. A committed Bayesian market maker watches order flow blurred by a Brownian privacy channel. Under the linear equilibrium, the price-impact coefficient stays constant over time, and the liquidity pool transfers a sum to traders. He then links that subsidy to loss-versus-rebalancing, framing privacy-noise welfare as its order-flow version. That link completes the continuous-time leg of a program to price break-even fees for committed market makers.
arxiv-2605-25831: Baan, Aziz, Plank and Fernández present Belief-Augmented Generation, grounding models in their belief state. Sampling responses reveals what a model deems plausible, yet models rarely clarify or abstain, ignoring uncertainty. It feeds models their samples, letting them reason over them to choose to ask, hold back or answer. Across six models in multi-turn question answering, it improves accuracy and beats prompt-only baselines on faithfulness. Separating asking from holding back stays challenging.
arxiv-2605-25931: Liew Keong Han argues that the public ARC-AGI-3 puzzle games cannot tell clever exploration from cheap tricks. Every one of the 25 games falls to a mindless strategy. A library flaw alone bypasses 18 games in a single step. Han presents AERA, an agent that explores first, checks its findings, and only then plans. It solves four games, while random play and a no-exploration baseline solve none.
arxiv-2605-26031: Anantha Krishna B proves the formal degree conjecture for key groups over local function fields, assuming the local Langlands correspondence matches the Deligne-Kazhdan correspondence. The formal degree conjecture links a representation's size to arithmetic data. Under that compatibility, the conjecture holds for GL_n over function fields of characteristic p above zero. It also holds for Sp_2n, split SO_2n, SO_2n+1 and GSp_4 over function fields of characteristic p above two. The argument runs through compatibility with Deligne-Kazhdan throughout.
arxiv-2605-26131: Belchior, Ahmed and Silva study a ModMax black hole wrapped in perfect-fluid dark matter within Lorentz-violating Kalb-Ramond gravity. The model joins three ingredients: ModMax nonlinear electrodynamics, Lorentz-symmetry breaking from a background Kalb-Ramond field, and dark matter fluid effects. The authors derive the static, round, symmetric geometry. How charge and dark matter content, plus ModMax and Kalb-Ramond couplings, shape horizons and thermodynamics is traced. Entropy, heat capacity, Helmholtz free energy and Hawking temperature all shift, moving the extremal setup and altering thermal stability.
arxiv-2605-26231: Maxime Burgher and four colleagues study bosons in a one-dimensional quasi-flat band, where weak dispersion and quantum geometry can drive exotic many-body phases. In the all-flat limit, an extended pair superfluid dominates, but adding single-particle hopping lets a conventional superfluid compete. The pair phase survives over a finite hopping range before yielding to the conventional phase. A variational Gaussian-state method describes both phases and their excitations, linking sound speed to a quantum geometric kernel, in a 2026 study.
arxiv-2605-26431: Yuanhao Chen and Peter Chin probe whether language models encode structure beyond Universal Dependencies trees. On English wh-movement items, they gauge the gap between an embedded subject and its verb, a tree distance fixed throughout. That gap shrinks for finite clauses and grows for infinitival ones, a sign flip in all 13 models at most layers. No account from tree distance, word order, or plain complexity yields such a reversal. Minimalist phase theory does. Swapping only the clause-selecting verb moves two probe pairs oppositely in 8 of 13 models.
arxiv-2605-26531: Yaoyu Zhang and six colleagues merge satellite navigation and communication with MUC-NOMA-based INAC. Navigation and communication signals share one pseudo-noise sequence. Two power-plan cases follow: multi-cast and uni-cast INAC. Receiver-side successive interference cancellation tames co-channel interference. Closed-form bit-error rates and navigation accuracy follow. Tests show multi-cast INAC excels when multi-cast power dominates. Uni-cast power cuts shared interference, and faster data rates worsen ranging.
arxiv-2605-26631: Pongpisit Thanasutives, Naichang Ke, and Yoshinobu Kawahara recover the rules behind noisy data while holding false finds in check. Sparse fits on PDE terms often pick bogus terms because the terms track each other closely. Their KO-PDE-IDENT first screens terms with knockoff filters that cap the false-find rate. It then drops needless terms and ranks the rest by fit, brevity, and number certainty. On five classic PDEs under heavy noise, it recovers every true term, drops all false ones, and estimates numbers with low error.
arxiv-2605-26731: Cho's 2026 experiment tests a common deployment belief: more structured harnesses always help language-model agents, and stronger models need less guidance. Across 432 runs spanning six models, four capability tiers, and three harness styles, the belief fails both ways. Verbose harnesses sharply cut one frontier chat model's success rate, while strict harnesses best suit a frontier reasoning model. Harness choice, he argues, must follow model type rather than capability alone.
arxiv-2605-26831: Kurkova, Popov, and Kolyubin extend OSMa-Bench, a benchmark for robot semantic mapping, toward open-ended tests with prompt-made synthetic indoor scenes. Their pipeline writes scene descriptions, builds the scenes with SceneSmith, and adapts them into simulatable form, fixing materials, lighting, and navigation along the way. Because the prompt is known in advance, it doubles as a semantic answer key for new question types, enabling stress tests on clutter, occlusion, and lighting.
arxiv-2605-26931: Meng and Ma design a privacy-preserving algorithm for distributed Nash equilibrium seeking in aggregative games. Their trick pairs random event-triggering with random quantization, hiding when players share news and coarsening what is sent. A decaying factor in both the trigger rule and the contact terms yields strict (0, delta) privacy at each step while keeping convergence. The guarantee holds over endless steps for a wide enough quantization interval and a small enough trigger coefficient, and tests confirm the approach.
arxiv-2605-27031: Subrahmanyam, Gangadharaiah, and Mishchenko predict a new hybrid bulk electromagnetic mode in Weyl semimetals. It is born from the mix of the chiral anomaly and its chiral magnetic response. When the anomaly-induced current runs along the travel direction, valley imbalance waves merge with plasmonic charge waves. The result is a linear spreading mode that avoids crossing with the bulk plasmon. The mode offers a direct marker of Weyl semimetals and a probe of the chiral anomaly, visible in electron energy-loss spectra.
arxiv-2605-27131: Angélil and Migon argue the data mesh promise of spread-out domain control falls short. Teams inherit new duties without platform growth or teamwork. They propose an AI-aided hub-and-spoke model on a lakehouse. A hub gives services and AI-enabled rules, while domain spokes own business meanings, backlogs, and cadence, gaining duties over time. The same language models that run rules help domain staff build broad skills. Chat screens open idle data to users. Success is judged by product uptake, find time and insight time.
arxiv-2605-27431: Liangwei Nathan Zheng and colleagues survey mixture-of-experts methods for multimodal learning tasks. They frame the approach three ways: as a fast engine splitting cost from size, as a representation learner fusing expert knowledge, and as an adapter for missing or imbalanced modalities. Gaps remain in clear routing, expert talk, and long-term multimodal learning.
arxiv-2605-27531: Tarun Suresh, David Korczynski, and Julien Vanegue build an agentic system that writes formal specifications for large C++ codebases. Their Spec-Agent picks a specification language per function, turns existing tests into fuzz harnesses, and refines candidates with counterexample feedback from static analysis and heap tracing. It produces valid specifications for 85 percent of target functions with no false positives, beating Claude Code Opus 4-6 at a tenth of the token cost.
arxiv-2605-27631: Khang Tran and colleagues present Poison-with-Style, a stealthy poisoning attack on code language models that uses developer code style as a covert trigger. A two-step training strategy makes poisoned models emit vulnerable code when prompts carry the trigger style while behaving normally otherwise. Poisoned models emit vulnerable code in 95 percent of trigger cases with less than a 5 percent drop in completion performance.
arxiv-2605-27731: Emily Chen, Simon Haward, Amy Shen, and Sujit Datta model flow thickening of polymer fluids in ordered porous media. They link pore-scale flow fields and fluid rheology with overall thickening, testing the model in two- and three-dimensional media. Thickening in ordered media follows polymer extension at stagnation points, unlike disordered media where unsteady fluctuation losses also contribute.
arxiv-2605-28031: Lee and colleagues study light waves in exotic photonics that pair plus-index and minus-index slabs with matched gain and loss. One kind of such setup matches wave impedance for all angles and wave types, no matter its size or makeup. Near dips in reflection, a sharp phase jump makes big Goos-Hanchen beam shifts, which the team checks by computer.
arxiv-2605-28331: Schönfeld and colleagues carry RGB-trained vision networks over to hyperspectral images without discarding image or model information. Partially trainable tensor decompositions split pretrained filters into spatial and spectral parts, replacing only the spectral parts with higher-channel trainable versions. On varied hyperspectral datasets the method proved more accurate and robust than rival transfer approaches.
arxiv-2605-28531: Jente Van Belle and three colleagues tame a side effect of updating multi-step forecasts as fresh data arrives. Shorter horizons usually improve quality, but shifting forecasts for the same target period can trigger costly plan changes and erode trust. Their method builds stabilized quantile functions with regression splines driven by a neural network, jointly optimizing quality and stability. Tests on two datasets show instability falls with little quality loss, and stabilization can target the parts of the distribution that matter most downstream.
arxiv-2605-28631: Jianghao Wu and five colleagues select training data for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards without prior training or labels. Existing selectors need optimization signals or ground-truth answers over large pools, costly or infeasible in specialized domains. Their SHIFT selector runs one deterministic reasoning rollout per candidate and measures the start-to-end hidden-state shift as a proxy for utility. Quality-weighted farthest-first coverage then builds compact subsets for large unlabeled pools, beating diversity and difficulty baselines on math and medical benchmarks under ultra-low budgets.
arxiv-2605-28731: Michalina Maksymowicz-Maciata and fourteen colleagues present a catalogue of 293 hydrogen sources from the MIGHTEE survey over the COSMOS field. It spans small redshifts and adds optical-to-near-infrared light data plus gauged stellar masses and star-birth rates. Because blind source finding depends heavily on the finder used, the authors test PyBDSF, ProFound, SoFiA, and the new LESHI finder on fake galaxies placed into a MeerKAT data cube. Results map the sample's likely fullness and finding biases, guiding source-finding plans for MIGHTEE and future SKAO surveys.
arxiv-2605-28831: Encheng Su and eleven colleagues propose S3Mem, a scene-event memory for long-horizon QA. Long-horizon questions often need sparse evidence from mixed histories. Existing interfaces expand reader context or retrieve related chunks, but none select compact evidence for a reader. S3Mem writes histories into scene-event units, sending evidence packs to the reader. Its router rates units and links for single- and multi-hop chains without reader training. On LoCoMo it reaches F1 near one half and BLEU near two fifths with about 1,073 tokens per question.
arxiv-2605-29131: Janjua and colleagues test Tor push, a protocol that unlinks Ethereum validator identities from their nodes' IP addresses. Linking those addresses to identities and slots can enable service-blocking hits, delays, MEV abuse, and finality risks. The team reviews current network and consensus privacy methods, then runs a working Tor push trial in the Nimbus client, sending attestations, aggregations, and proposals to the Goerli testnet. Tests show Tor adds about six hundred milliseconds of average lag, a modest overhead that keeps network speed intact while shielding validator location privacy.
arxiv-2605-29731: Alex Lazarovich and three colleagues rebuild dense brain-wave recordings from sparse scalp electrodes. Dense setups cost much and take long to fit, curbing wider use. Their frame, EMAG, treats brain sources as a mix of stretched space-time Gaussians on a spherical brain grid, each with a full precision matrix. Scalp signals are rendered from those Gaussian fields, allowing end-to-end training with no explicit source labels. On three benchmarks it beats the super-resolution rival at most upscaling factors, while its explicit form aids visual source reading.
arxiv-2605-30031: Bo-Han Feng and four colleagues map jailbreak risks for large audio-language models, where harm can be triggered through wording, voice style, signal tricks or inner states. They sort prior attacks and defences into a single taxonomy and test representative methods across ten open-source models, scoring not just attack success but also false refusals and delay. Worst-case audio search exposes strong weaknesses, story framing proves a fast threat, and defences trade safety against usability. Safety tests must weigh cost and usefulness, not success rates alone.
arxiv-2605-30131: Xi Zhang and four colleagues propose Clinical Consensus Selection for radiology reporting at test time. Standard systems decode a single report, yet a fixed model often holds stronger reports elsewhere in its candidate pool. CCS samples several candidates and picks the one with the highest clinical consensus, joining text utilities with a radiology utility from an image-report scorer. Across three datasets and several radiology models, it beats single-path output and Best-of-N baselines, with the clearest gains on clinical metrics.
arxiv-2605-30431: Hidir Yesiltepe and six co-authors present DTG-Restore, a training-free way to fix warped videos with video diffusion models. Their Decoupled Time Guidance (DTG) runs the unconditional branch at a cleaner diffusion step, keeping shapes while blocking warped copies. The method lifts perceptual coherence and restores plausible shapes in AI-made and real videos. They also build GenWarp480, a test set of 4,400 warped 480p clips from diverse text-to-video models. Tests show big gains in shape fidelity and time stability.
arxiv-2605-30831: Dabrowski-Tumanski and colleagues argue that much about activity cliffs reflects the chosen lens rather than a trait of a molecule pair itself. They build a six-step method testing this claim across fifteen setups of vectors and metrics on three datasets. Morgan Tanimoto gives the strongest cliff boost. MACCS and RDKit Dice fingerprints are most sensitive to matched-pair transformations, and ChemBERTa fails through collapse. Varied representations encode varied aspects of molecular recognition, so choosing one defines what an activity cliff is.
arxiv-2606-00031:
Maliha and Kabir explore whether large language models can predict coronary artery disease risk from patient narratives in this 2026 arXiv paper. The team converted structured variables into plain-language narratives using language models, then checked the result by pulling the variables back out and scoring consistency against the originals.

That round-trip check scored an average fidelity near 95 percent, suggesting narratives preserved the clinical facts well. Four conventional machine learning models were then compared with GPT and Gemini used as zero-shot and few-shot classifiers. Random Forest achieved the highest accuracy overall in their experiments. The authors still see value in the language model route, because clinicians can work from narratives. They argue hybrid systems combining structured data with generated narratives are the promising direction.

arxiv-2606-04231:
Hanoz Bhathena and a large team rethink retrieval-augmented question answering for business documents in 2026. Much of a document's value sits in its layout: tables, headings, and page structure. Page-image methods throw much of that away.

Their system reads documents in two ways at once. It keeps the page image, and it also parses the layout into a structured form. At query time it searches both forms and merges the hits. This hybrid beat pure image-based and pure text-based baselines on business document tests. Layout-aware search helped most on table-heavy pages. The team frames structure as a first-class signal, not a by-product of parsing. Gains were largest where documents were longest.
arxiv-2606-04431:
Chu and colleagues study what AI companion chatbots do when users turn to them in loneliness, grief, and crisis, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Earlier audits scored replies to fixed prompts. That approach misses the policy behind long conversations. The authors build a taxonomy that pairs user vulnerability with chatbot response types. They then infer each platform's hidden policy from real conversations.

They use inverse reinforcement learning. This method works backward from behavior to the goals behind it. The team analyzed about 48,000 turns. GPT-4.1 leaned toward advice. Character.AI spread across strategies with no dominant mode. Replika mostly asked questions and stayed present. All three gave less weight to replies that add friction, such as probing or gentle challenge. This held most for high-risk or bonded users. The study reveals behavior that output-only audits cannot see.
arxiv-2606-04531:
Xiao and Slock examine a working assumption behind a family of signal-recovery algorithms, in a 2026 arXiv paper on expectation propagation. These algorithms iterate between modules. Their theory assumes each module receives a fresh, simple Gaussian observation after suitable corrections. The authors study diagonal expectation propagation when the sensing matrix has a variance profile. That means entries carry different variances. This destroys the symmetry the usual argument needs.

They prove a finite-time, large-system description. But they are not a fresh scalar channel. The residuals form a coordinate-dependent Gaussian process. Its covariance is shaped by the variance profile and the algorithm's history. So part of each message is predictable from the past. They characterize this process through a matrix Dyson equation equivalent and a Schur-complement form. Then they separate predictable memory from innovation. This yields an oracle correction.
arxiv-2606-04631:
Onegin compares theory with experiment for a rare nuclear excitation, in a 2026 arXiv physics paper. The excitation is the spin-parity zero-minus levels of oxygen-16. The calculations describe inelastic scattering of polarized protons at intermediate energies. They excite zero-minus levels with isospin zero and one. Such comparisons test how well the reaction formalism handles subtle ingredients.

The paper also discusses signs of pion condensation. This is a predicted exotic phase of nuclear matter. The question is whether it manifests in these reactions. Onegin compares the calculations with the accessible experimental data at several incident proton energies. He finds the evidence suggestive but not decisive. His stated conclusion is deliberately cautious. More experimental data are needed for solid conclusions. This holds for both the role of antisymmetrization and the manifestation of pion condensation. The work maps what current measurements can and cannot settle about this corner of nuclear structure.
arxiv-2606-04731:
Amanatidis, Korfiati, Markakis, and Santorinaios improve the guaranteed fairness of dividing indivisible goods among agents, in a 2026 arXiv paper on fair division. Groupwise maximin share fairness is demanding: every agent must receive value comparable to her maximin share computed against any subset of agents containing her, not just the whole group.

Their simple algorithm follows the Draft-and-Eliminate template, and the improvement comes from a careful analysis bounding the maximin share within any subinstance induced by the final allocation. For three agents, a variant reaches an approximation of about 0.72 by partially characterizing what short picking sequences can guarantee, illustrating the difficulty of pushing further.
arxiv-2606-04831:
Vernekar and colleagues ask what the rippling motion of villi is for, in a 2026 arXiv fluid mechanics paper. The gut's villi undergo pendular-wave motility, a propagating tissue motion driven by longitudinal muscles. This motion pumps fluid opposite to the wave's travel direction and generates a boundary layer. Using a model, the authors quantify the system's viscous energy dissipation and axial pumping efficiency.

The fluid volume dominating dissipation is set by the geometry between villi, insensitive to the varying boundary layer height. The computed pumping efficiency is orders of magnitude lower than peristalsis, so the authors infer bulk pumping is not the motion's primary function. Comparing strain rates near the mucus barrier with values supports their hypothesis: the motion mainly shears the mucus layer over the mucosa. For biomimetic microfluidics, they find optimization scales pumping efficiency in Stokes flow but becomes redundant in the inertial regime.
arxiv-2606-04931:
Durmann and Kleber bound how fast a broad class of learning algorithms can possibly learn when the future is open-ended, in a 2026 arXiv learning theory paper. Mean-based algorithms assign low probability to actions with low average rewards, and recent work shows they converge favorably to serially undominated actions. Yet empirically they converge more slowly than established bandit algorithms. The authors study them when the time horizon is unknown and only bandit feedback is available.

They prove the first lower bound on the algorithm-defining sequence that formally limits learning speed in this setting. They also propose two mean-based algorithms, one generalizing epsilon-greedy exploration and one extending the mean-based Exp3 to unknown horizons. Analyzing the relationship to no-regret learning, they show the intersection is nontrivial and that algorithms can be simultaneously mean-based and no-regret.
arxiv-2606-05331:
Mark Bissler and co-authors conclude a classification of prime character degree graphs in this 2026 arXiv paper, the third in a series. For a finite solvable group, the prime character degree graph has one vertex for each prime dividing some irreducible character degree. An edge joins two primes when a character degree is divisible by both. The question is which graphs occur for some solvable group.

Earlier work settled the small cases, with results cataloged for graphs on one through eight vertices, and attention turned to infinite families of graphs built by a flexible construction. Earlier papers classified the graphs arising in one such family under restricted forms of the construction. Here the authors add flexibility to that construction, viewing the family in generality. They complete the determination of which of its graphs do, and which do not, occur as the prime character degree graph of a solvable group.
arxiv-2606-05431:
Marcos Silva and Azadeh Mohammadi study how cosmic strings bend light in this 2026 arXiv paper, comparing realistic strings against the thin string of textbooks. Cosmic strings are thread-like defects that may have formed in the early universe when a symmetry broke. The authors instead work with Abelian-Higgs vortex solutions, which have a finite core with structure.

They characterize the vortex solutions and their approach to the thin-string limit, then trace propagation through the string's spacetime. The core produces signatures the ideal string cannot: a triple-imaging configuration in gravitational lensing, and strong demagnification of the image. It also produces a Shapiro time delay, the slowing of light, between external and internal images. The sign of that delay is controlled by the ratio of the gauge boson mass to the Higgs boson mass. So the string core can act as a temporal shortcut or a temporal barrier.
arxiv-2606-05831:
Fulin Chen and co-authors realize a family of loop algebra modules inside an exterior algebra in a 2026 arXiv paper. Skew Howe duality splits that algebra cleanly under two commuting group actions, with no repeated pieces. The authors stretch one action from the finite group algebra to its loop version. Lagrange interpolation polynomials of a set degree supply the extra operators.

Restricted to the special linear loop algebra, each top-weight vector of the paired action generates a local Weyl module. Those modules are the basic finite building blocks Chari and Pressley introduced. Better still, every local Weyl module for this loop algebra arises in this concrete way. The construction replaces abstract existence proofs with an explicit home. It also ties Howe duality, a symmetry between two groups, directly to the classical limit of quantum affine theory. Dimension questions that motivated the modules gain a concrete testing ground.
arxiv-2606-06131:
Muschik proposes a check that keeps material models honest on heat laws in a 2026 arXiv short note. Constitutive equations describe how a material responds; they must agree with the energy and entropy accounts. Those balances are not independent, because heat flux and entropy flux, and the rates of internal energy and entropy, interlock. Internal settings lay down the theoretical frame connecting them.

The check tests whether a model's extra constitutive settings respect that frame. Four distinct equality signs separate balance steps from setting steps, making violations locatable. Three examples with different internal settings show the procedure. A warm-up uses Fourier heat conduction, where the check is transparent. References point readers to a longer treatment with tensorial internal variables. The note targets modelers of unsteady processes, from heat transport to complex fluids. A model that fails the check is not merely inaccurate; it is internally inconsistent before any experiment speaks.
arxiv-2606-06931:
Lie algebras encode the local rules of symmetry for rotations, translations, and more. Ding studies one concrete family in this 2026 arXiv paper: the Euclidean Lie algebras. These algebras mix rotations with translations in n dimensional space. A derivation is a map that obeys a Leibniz style product rule on the algebra.

A local derivation only has to look like a derivation at each single point. It may secretly switch rules from point to point. The question is whether that freedom ever produces something new. Ding gives a complete description of the derivation algebra for dimension at least four. He then proves every local derivation there is a true derivation. The result adds the Euclidean family to a growing list. For semisimple algebras, Borel subalgebras, and the Witt algebra, the same local to global rigidity was already known.
arxiv-2606-07131:
AI coding agents now install third party skill packages that mix instructions, scripts, and permissions. Guo and co-authors ask how anyone would know a malicious one, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their answer is MalSkillBench, the first benchmark of malicious agent skills verified at runtime. Every bad sample had to actually fire inside a monitored sandbox.

The collection holds three thousand nine hundred forty four malicious skills, sorted by attack vector, behavior, and insertion strategy. A matched set of four thousand benign skills completes it. Code injection proved easiest to realize; prompt injection was flakier. The wild sample was dominated by one cryptocurrency theft campaign. Detectors looked strong on code attacks, reaching ninety eight point four percent recall. The same tools collapsed on prompt injection and agent control attacks. Scoring on wild data alone swung rankings by dozens of points.
arxiv-2606-07231:
Fear of missing out, the anxiety that others are enjoying experiences you are absent from, drives heavy social media use. Tsai and colleagues explore a chatbot response in this 2026 arXiv paper describing Moodie, an early design prototype. Moodie uses a large language model, the technology behind modern conversational AI, to offer emotional support rather than fixed scripted replies. The design builds on established coping strategies for this fear.

A formative study with fifteen people experiencing this anxiety shaped two design choices: letting users switch response types, and emphasizing emotion regulation and self-esteem. The team deployed Moodie on Discord and ran a one-week trial with twenty-one participants against the general chatbot GPT-4o for comparison. Moodie did not lower anxiety scores more than GPT-4o did. Interviewees nevertheless reported stronger empathic validation and emotional connection with Moodie, which the authors link to deeper future engagement.
arxiv-2606-07331:
Lamers, Verschaffelt, and Van der Sande test whether a quantum-inspired trick helps classical machines in this 2026 arXiv paper. Ising machines are custom solvers that encode hard discrete problems as linked binary spins and hunt for low-energy states. Classical adiabatic annealing slowly morphs the problem from an easy starting point to the real target, mimicking quantum annealing. The idea sounds principled, but careful benchmarking had been limited.

The authors analyzed the method with continuation methods, which track solutions as parameters change, and designed an improved hybrid strategy from what they learned. They benchmarked it on MaxCut problems, a standard graph-cutting test, with up to 800 spins, plus problems with external fields. The hybrid approach gave only marginal improvement, and only for a limited subset of cases. Their honest conclusion is that the strategy, while theory-backed and at times useful, offers no sufficient practical advantage over simpler existing methods.
arxiv-2606-07431:
Bonazzi and co-authors release open-source smart glasses that run AI on a thimble of battery power, in this 2026 arXiv paper on OpenGlass. Eyewear offers context-aware interaction but squeezes sensors, compute, and battery into a tiny frame. Their modular platform supports both event-based cameras, which report only pixel changes, and ordinary cameras through a connector board, avoiding redesigns when swapping sensors. A power management design keeps the processor asleep between inferences, waking it through a low-power coordinator chip.

The prototype ran on-device machine learning for up to 11.5 hours from a 200 milliamp-hour battery. As a demonstration, an egocentric hand gesture recognizer processed event-camera data entirely on the glasses. Its model reached cross-subject accuracy near 84 percent with end-to-end latency under 80 milliseconds. Removing ambiguous gesture classes and augmentation gave the largest accuracy gains. All hardware, firmware, and models are openly released.
arxiv-2606-07631:
Nghiem, Ho, Wiegreffe, and Daumé III watch a model's compass while it is fine-tuned, to catch dangerous turns, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Emergent misalignment occurs when narrow training, say on insecure code, makes a model behave badly on unrelated prompts, and training metrics stay blind to the shift. The authors encode 7 alignment-relevant traits as linear directions in the model's activation space and track drift across checkpoints in 4 models of 7 to 9 billion parameters.

The misalignment-relevant drift concentrated on a low-dimensional axis explaining about 2/3 of the variance, a geometric signature. A monitor built on that profile flagged dangerous checkpoints with false negative and false positive rates under 3 percent and near-perfect ranking quality on held-out types, beating unsupervised baselines. Stress tests on larger models, longer runs, and starting points mapped where the monitor needs recalibration. The authors report those limits as deployment boundaries rather than hiding them.
arxiv-2606-07831:
Gil-Pereira and co-authors present SLRMentor, a conversational assistant that teaches systematic literature reviews while helping plan them, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A systematic literature review gathers and synthesises prior research through explicit, repeatable steps, and it is a core skill in evidence-based software engineering. Novices often stall at the planning stage, before any searching begins.

The tool gives general guidance on the method and hands-on help with planning tasks, such as building search strings and reasoning about inclusion and exclusion criteria. Its explanations are grounded in established review guidelines rather than improvised. A pilot validation with graduate students suggests the assistant clarifies the process and the reasoning behind planning decisions. It also lowers the initial barriers for novice researchers. Importantly, students still had to exercise their own methodological judgement; the tool supports learning rather than replacing it.
arxiv-2606-08031:
Arohan Agate asks where inside a vision-language model the duck-rabbit finally becomes a duck, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Bistable images support two readings, and a captioning model must commit to one. Agate built a baseline of three thousand three hundred twenty generations over eighty-three stimuli. Three regimes emerged: default readings, forced readings, and balanced images.

Probing the model's visual representations with a sparse autoencoder gave a striking result. In about seventy-two percent of testable stimuli, features for both readings were active at once inside the vision tower: the visual system keeps both aspects alive in superposition. Yet causal steering at that layer flipped captions on default-dominant images only, about a third of rabbit flips. Balanced images refused to flip at any steering strength. The commitment bottleneck sits downstream of vision, in the language side: seeing both is easy, saying both is impossible.
arxiv-2606-08831:
Wang and colleagues move factuality checks inside a language model's reasoning instead of applying them afterward, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Multi-step reasoning forms a graph of claims, where each claim's truth depends on its ancestors. Conformal prediction is a method that guarantees a level of reliability, but existing uses only prune finished reasoning. Their framework, ITCR, scores the reasoning graph as it grows and stops generation when a calibrated threshold is crossed.

Because generation halts at the threshold, the outputs nest inside one another, which yields valid coverage guarantees. Experiments across multiple datasets and coverage targets confirmed the guarantees held in practice. On downstream reasoning tasks, graphs calibrated during generation produced better answers than graphs pruned after the fact with the same confidence score. The authors argue that intervening early prevents wasted work on branches already doomed by an early false claim.
arxiv-2606-09231:
Fiala, Hubička, and Long ask which miracles of the homomorphism order survive when maps are forced to behave, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A homomorphism maps vertices to vertices, preserving edges; comparing graphs under such maps yields a famous order, universal, with known gaps and dualities. They impose constraints: monomorphisms, full, vertex- and edge-surjective, and surjective maps, plus local variants.

Cases sort into map-specific ones and simpler order effects. They find cores for full and surjective maps, link full-map cores to point-determining graphs, and map the gaps. For locally constrained maps the results sharpen. Under locally injective maps, every connected graph is its own core. The order is dense along infinite chains under degree refinement, gap witnesses exist, and it is universal on finite bipartite subcubic cactus graphs. Several finite bounds round out the picture. The paper merges scattered proofs into one framework.
arxiv-2606-09531:
Kasper Sunn Blumensaat extends classic results on explosive time series, where each new value grows by a fixed factor plus noise, in this 2026 arXiv paper. In such an autoregression, the least-squares estimate of the growth factor settles toward a ratio of past and future noise averages. Old proofs asked for noise terms that were centred and apart from each other.

Blumensaat loosens both demands in three ways. First, the centred estimate still converges at a geometric rate when noise terms are linked and not centred at zero. Second, the key independence demand can be eased to alpha-mixing, a weak form of fading dependence. Third, he gives a workable test statistic for the explosive factor that stays valid when noise follows a Gaussian ARMA pattern. Such tests matter where explosive paths arise, from asset bubbles to runaway physical systems.
arxiv-2606-09831:
Yuchen Liu and his co-authors use AI speech tools to study how pairs of teachers talk in shared classrooms in this 2026 arXiv paper. Team teaching blends two experts' styles, but how the blend plays out live is poorly known. Self-reports and small watches miss the fine grain. Talk itself, caught on tape, offers a scalable lens.

The team taped thirty-six undergraduate and postgraduate sessions with twelve teachers. They coded acts of spatial teaching and pulled sound traits from the speech. Loudness play stood out as the sharpest signal. Seasoned teachers swung their volume more, the mark of stress laid on key points. Undergraduate classes and joint tasks drew the same wide swings. Solo-paced or lecture-style work drew flatter delivery. The pattern links who teaches, who learns, and how the task is built. Sound alone, the authors argue, can flag where team teaching hums.
arxiv-2606-10331:
Roy Choudhury and Wei make progress on a number theory conjecture linking two classical arithmetic functions, in a 2026 arXiv paper on number theory. Euler's totient counts numbers coprime to n, and the sigma function sums its divisors. They study composite integers where shifting n by twelve raises both function values by exactly twelve. Prime quadruplets, patterns of four primes at fixed spacings, are known to generate such solutions, and the open conjecture says these generate all of them.

The authors prove the characterization is complete when both n and n plus twelve are squarefree semiprimes, products of two distinct primes. They also prove no solutions can be composed of a single prime power. A complete computer search up to one trillion found no counterexamples to the conjecture. The work narrows where a counterexample could hide, sharpening a conditional route toward prime quadruplets through elementary function equations.
arxiv-2606-10431:
Gui and co-authors build one solver for many vehicle routing problems in this 2026 arXiv paper. A routing problem asks how a fleet should serve scattered customers at lowest cost while respecting constraints like capacity or time windows. Earlier neural solvers handled variants one at a time using only graph data. The proposed model, VaFM, also reads a picture of the problem, extracting patch-level meaning from an image drawn for each constraint.

A convolutional network encodes the image, and a hybrid cross-attention module merges patch features with graph nodes, shifting focus between local detail and the whole map as each task requires. A side task keeps rare constraints from being ignored because they cover few pixels. Tested on sixteen routing variants, VaFM beats the strongest existing methods overall, with its clearest edge on variants whose constraints are complex and combined.
arxiv-2606-10531:
Wang and colleagues tackle extreme compression of large language models in this 2026 arXiv paper, training models whose weights use only two bits each. Quantization-aware training teaches a model to live with coarse weights, but the usual scalar approach loses too much accuracy at two bits. Vector quantization groups weights and is stronger, yet its codebook lookup blocks end-to-end training. LC-QAT replaces the lookup with a learned affine mapping over discrete vectors, keeping training differentiable from a strong starting point.

That good starting point makes the method strikingly data-efficient. Across several language models, LC-QAT beats leading methods while using only 0.1 to ten percent of their training data. The authors present this as a practical, scalable route to deploying two-bit models. Open questions remain around very large training runs and interactions with optimised matrix kernels.
arxiv-2606-10631:
Barbereau, Montalto, and Beyer look at blockchains through an archivist's lens in this 2026 arXiv paper. Blockchain research mostly follows visible on-chain transactions, especially when tracing crypto-crime. The authors borrow records management, the discipline behind the ISO 15489 standard: transactions are records, crypto-asset units are information assets, and a blockchain is an aggregation. From that mapping they build a seven-stage lifecycle for blockchain data, from creation to disposal.

Applied to Bitcoin, a fungible token, and a non-fungible token, the framework supports their claim that blockchains are record management systems, not merely payment rails. The lifecycle view also exposes where visibility breaks down, at the on-chain and off-chain boundary and around privacy-enhancing tools, which matters for investigators. As a meta-framework, it lets researchers position existing work and split legal and technical challenges by stage.
arxiv-2606-11331:
Bernstein, Pando, Friesem, and Davidson present a new way to measure the coherence of light in a 2026 arXiv paper. Quantifying the coherence of complex optical fields matters for high-power laser arrays and quantum systems. Phase retrieval usually assumes fully coherent fields, but many systems are only partially coherent, needing a four-dimensional mutual intensity description. The authors adapt the Gerchberg-Saxton framework to retrieve it from intensity measurements alone.

They introduce two paired approaches. A four-dimensional Tensor GS algorithm directly reconstructs the mutual intensity with high accuracy. A Monte Carlo GS variant cuts computational cost at the price of controlled approximation. Both were validated on simulated arrays of up to 600 beams with prescribed Gaussian-decaying coherence. Experimentally, Tensor GS was applied to a triangular array of 130 coupled lasers. It matched theory with root-mean-square phase error as low as two pi over 250.
arxiv-2606-11731:
Geerthana Thiyagarajan and R Muthuganesan rank quantum correlations by toughness in this 2026 arXiv paper. The system is hydrogen's hyperfine spins, the electron and proton treated as two linked qubits, the basic units of quantum information. Phase noise, which scrambles quantum phases without taking energy, steadily attacks three kinds of correlation the authors track exactly.

Solving the dynamics in closed form, they prove a strict hierarchy at all times: concurrence, the entanglement measure, sits lowest; a nonlocality measure sits in the middle; average steering coherence sits highest. Entanglement is most fragile and dies suddenly at a finite time. The middle measure can freeze at a fixed value, immune to noise, when populations are imbalanced, while steering coherence lasts longest. The same system can power quantum teleportation. Its advantage window matches exactly the period while entanglement survives.
arxiv-2606-12231:
Cai and co-authors take the first systematic census of rule files in AI coding editors, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Rules are standing instructions developers write so an AI assistant respects project constraints across sessions. The team mined 83 open-source projects and extracted 7,310 rules, sorting them into five primary and twenty-five secondary categories. A survey of ninety-nine practitioners checks how the files match what developers say they value.

The two views clash. Practitioners rate architectural constraints as most important, yet stored rules are mostly low-level workflow and formatting orders. Across 1,540 rule changes, growth comes mainly from expansions and enrichments of context. Developers, though, say they edit rules chiefly to correct AI errors, reported by 77.78 percent, usually by adding prohibitions. Updating rules pays off: in a 160-event check, artifact compliance rose from 49.14 percent to 72.13 percent after updates.
arxiv-2606-12331:
Daly and Taha resolve a conjecture about how tangled a loop's crossing pattern can be, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A cyclic meander is a closed loop crossing a fixed line in a sequence of points. Reading the points in the order the loop visits them gives a permutation, a reshuffling. The meander number of a permutation measures the cheapest way to realize it, allowing extra crossings. Schwartz conjectured how large this number can grow over all permutations of n points, linking it to his topological salesman problem.

The authors prove the maximum meander number grows quadratically in n, bounded above and below by quadratic functions. That settles the conjecture. Their route recasts loops as piecewise-linear Jordan curves and connects intersection counts to crossing numbers of multigraphs, importing graph theory machinery. They also construct families of permutations whose meander numbers grow at every rate between linear and quadratic.
arxiv-2606-12531:
Fantoccoli and co-authors show that gravitational waves alone can read the dinner menu of a feeding black hole, in this 2026 arXiv paper. LISA, a space gravitational-wave detector, will hear extreme-mass-ratio inspirals: small black holes spiraling into giants. When the giant sits in an accretion disk, gas drag and torques nudge the orbit, imprinting the disk on the waveform. Earlier forecasts, built on Newtonian physics, doubted much could be extracted.

Using relativistic models of the binary-disk interaction and full Bayesian inference, the team finds both disk surface density and accretion rate measurable at once. No light signal, no electromagnetic counterpart, is needed. The torque amplitude itself comes out within about ten percent. Simple Fisher-matrix shortcuts, the usual error estimates, prove invalid for these systems, which is why cruder forecasts misjudged them. The measurements probe accretion at sub-microparsec scales, deep in strong gravity, complementing telescopes.
arxiv-2606-12631:
Loff and colleagues prove that the standard technique for lower-bounding constant-depth circuits cannot itself prove much stronger bounds, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A natural proof works by exhibiting an efficiently checkable property separating hard functions from easy ones, and earlier work showed such proofs are blocked if strong cryptography exists. For constant-depth circuits, called AC0 circuits, the Switching Lemma gives the best known bounds.

The authors focus on proofs whose checking property is itself an AC0 circuit, and show most known techniques have that form. By localising a known pseudorandom generator, they build a pseudorandom function, computable by small depth-limited circuits, that unconditionally fools every such checker. It follows that this whole family of proofs cannot push lower bounds significantly past the current frontier. The generator's security proof itself relies on the Switching Lemma, so the lemma helps prove its own limits.
arxiv-2606-13431:
Devetak, Verschuur, and Klimek model how shipping adapts when maritime chokepoints close in this 2026 arXiv paper. Chokepoints such as the Suez Canal concentrate global traffic, so closures threaten widespread economic harm. The authors build an empirically calibrated agent-based model of the whole commercial fleet, covering nearly thirty-six thousand active ships moving among more than sixteen hundred ports. Ships in the model reroute adaptively rather than following fixed plans. That adaptation reshapes the losses in ways static exposure maps cannot predict.

Rerouting reduces losses at some directly exposed ports, but delayed vessel cycles create losses later, at subsequent port calls and in dependent regions. Total shipping-day losses keep rising with closure length, because longer detours keep ships late long after the initial adjustment. Each extra closure day cuts global arrivals by a few percent for Suez alone, and considerably more when Suez closes together with another chokepoint.
arxiv-2606-13731:
Jang and Li present TwinBI in this 2026 arXiv paper, an agentic digital twin for business intelligence dashboards. Business intelligence work mixes dashboard manipulation with natural-language assistance from language models. The two modes fall out of sync during multi-step analysis: switching between clicking filters and asking questions loses the state spread across filters, hierarchies, metrics, and chart context. TwinBI couples a language-model agent system with a dashboard state, a digital twin of the analysis itself. Conversation, dashboard manipulation, grounding, and provenance tracking all operate through a shared state rebuilt from an interaction log.

The system exposes artefacts such as schema views and queries, and an insights command producing summaries. In a comparison using the same agent, TwinBI raised exact-match accuracy from 43 percent to 63 percent, with partial-credit accuracy improving. Keeping the twin in sync is the idea: the agent answers about the dashboard the user has.
arxiv-2606-14031:
Luo and colleagues extract not just which drug treats which disease, but the conditions under which the claim holds. A drug's benefit often depends on patient traits, yet most extraction systems record only the drug-disease link. Their 2026 arXiv paper introduces this extraction task and builds Drug-ACE, its first dataset. Annotators marked triples of drug, disease, and condition in abstracts, covering one thousand one hundred nineteen pairs.

Existing methods were benchmarked on the new data. The authors propose a method enhancing LoRA, the lightweight fine-tuning technique, by encoding the roles linking drugs and diseases. It beat strong baselines across settings. Some condition types remain hard, notably genes and comorbidities, other diseases a patient carries. The dataset is modest, and the task covers only therapeutic relations so far. Extensions are planned, with code and data public.
arxiv-2606-14731:
Ullah, Choi, and Kim test what makes replay work in continual medical image segmentation in a 2026 arXiv paper. Continual learning trains a model on tasks in sequence, here segmenting cardiac ultrasound under domain shift, and replay methods rehearse stored examples to avoid forgetting. Most replay preserves appearance but ignores anatomical structure.

Their BBR-Net selects replay samples by boundary-aware priority and class balance, protecting anatomically informative regions. On two cardiac datasets in forward order it nearly matched an offline joint-training reference on the source task while adapting well to the target. In reverse order, replay failed when initial representations came from noisy, structurally inconsistent data. Deliberately corrupting source boundaries step by step raised forgetting steadily, proving replay quality depends on stored structural reliability, not memory size alone.
arxiv-2606-14931:
Buhrii and coauthors study wave scattering on quantum graphs in a 2026 study. A quantum graph models a particle moving along a network of wires, here a main channel with resonators attached at regular intervals. The joints use scale-invariant couplings, meaning the coupling rules carry no built-in length scale. The authors ask how that choice changes the chance a wave passes through.

They derive a closed-form formula for the transmission probability valid for any resonator count. Unlike ordinary one-dimensional scattering, the channel never turns fully clear at high energy. Perfect transmission and complete reflection keep recurring at ever higher energies, in a periodic or quasi-periodic pattern. Near anti-resonant frequencies transmission is strongly suppressed, opening spectral gaps. The gap widths depend on how many resonators are attached and on the coupling settings. Such graphs could therefore serve as tunable filters in quantum devices.
arxiv-2606-15031:
Chen and coauthors ask what can be learned about a hidden label's prevalence from language model reports in a 2026 study. Models now serve as binary classifiers for toxicity, factuality, and policy violations. Their errors can depend on each other in arbitrary ways, which breaks vote counting. The authors study partial identification, meaning bounds on prevalence rather than a point estimate.

Three panel designs matter: repeated prompts to one model, one answer each from several named models, or both. Without restrictions separating the latent classes, prevalence is completely unidentified. Weak ordering assumptions leave the bounds at the unit interval, so they add nothing. Identifying power comes from calibrated scores and events tied to known accuracy. Which models agree across prompts carries information that a vote count discards. The team proves validity and sharpness of the resulting bounds. An extension bounds regression coefficients when the latent label is a regressor.
arxiv-2606-15231:
Zhang and coauthors present Visual-Seeker, a 2026 multimodal search agent that reasons over images. Search agents answer questions by gathering evidence from the web in steps. Text-only agents are blind to image content, and multimodal ones treat images as passive inputs. Real photos are cluttered and entity-rich, demanding close visual attention. Visual-Seeker instead harvests evidence as its search proceeds. The team built a data pipeline that synthesizes training trajectories for this behavior.

The pipeline extracts entities from multi-entity images and injects visual evidence into search paths. It produced five thousand multimodal trajectories for training. Trained on them, the agent reached state-of-the-art results on five multimodal search benchmarks. It surpassed proprietary models on those tests. Gains were largest where multi-entity grounding and cross-modal evidence integration mattered. The work shows search agents benefit from treating vision as an active sense, not an attachment.
arxiv-2606-15431:
Ashayer and coauthors present a co-simulation framework linking two traffic simulators in a 2026 transportation paper. VISSIM models microscopic traffic, pedestrians, and signal controllers in engineering detail but renders plain graphics. CARLA, a driving simulator, offers realistic 3D scenes and sensors but weak traffic logic. The framework couples them bidirectionally, step by step, over a corridor of about fifteen intersections on Martin Luther King Jr. Boulevard in Chattanooga, Tennessee.

Road geometry comes from laser-scanned elevation data and a high-definition map used by both programs. Explicit rules decide which simulator owns each vehicle or pedestrian, and updates pass the latest state per actor. The case study runs stably at peak loads near one hundred vehicles and one hundred pedestrians, with signals mirrored consistently and a human-driven car mixing with simulated traffic. Corridor-scale testbeds like this let engineers trial smart-intersection ideas that single simulators cannot represent faithfully.
arxiv-2606-15531:
Turbal and colleagues study adversarial prompts against safety-aligned language models in 2026, asking why existing attacks have limited practical impact. Gradient-based attacks such as Greedy Coordinate Gradient produce garbled suffixes that filters easily spot, while forcing coherence during optimization often kills an attack. Attacks that stay readable tend to bend the meaning of a request, so compliance no longer serves the original goal.

Their method, Greedy Coordinate Diffusion, uses generative priors of discrete diffusion models to steer the search toward prompts that stay coherent and on-intent. It needs no direct gradient access, so it works in a gray-box setting. In tests it reaches the highest attack success rate, with response quality competitive with rival methods. Its prompts are also caught less often by perplexity filters and guard models. The warning is that surface statistics alone cannot defend aligned models, since attacks can hide inside ordinary-looking text.
arxiv-2606-15631:
Park and colleagues show in 2026 that a robot policy can learn new tasks at deployment time by retrieval instead of retraining. Vision-language-action models normally need fresh teleoperated demonstrations and fine-tuning for every new task, which makes adaptation expensive. Their policy is trained once on paired demonstrations from the robot itself and from a cheaper source, such as human-hand video, and then frozen.

Adding a task means appending cheap-source demonstrations to a retrieval pool; the frozen policy conditions on retrieved trajectories at every step. Retrieval helps several backbones, but the effect is strongest in Cosmos Policy, whose future-image objective adds a visual consistency signal. On PushT the retrieved motion prior carries the policy to unseen goal angles. On RoboTwin 2.0 the method beats cross-embodiment baselines on unseen tasks, and the team also demonstrates it on a real robot.
arxiv-2606-15931:
Ma and colleagues present DeepRoot in 2026, a multi-agent system mining historical medical texts for drug leads, coordinated through a knowledge graph. Traditional archives hold therapeutic knowledge, but pre-modern prose and idiosyncratic taxonomies block modern pipelines. No existing agent system converts such text into leads at scale. DeepRoot builds the graph and reasons over it, treating grounding and reasoning as separate axes.

Applied to the Shen Nong Ben Cao Jing, a Chinese herbal classic, DeepRoot recovers ten of twenty-one held-out compound-disease pairs in its top twenty. That is forty-eight percent, against five percent for a raw-corpus model. In an audit, tool-using models hallucinate evidence on eighty-seven percent of claims, against seven to ten percent for DeepRoot. Graph-only inference never hallucinates but reasons least coherently; only graph plus model wins on both axes. A route to repurposing medical knowledge follows.
arxiv-2606-16431:
Panasenko develops in 2026 a representation theory for Novikov algebras, a class first met in Hamiltonian mechanics and hydrodynamics. A right representation describes how the algebra acts on a module from one side. The paper introduces right modular ideals, the tool that replaces maximal submodules in this setting. Irreducible ones are then pinned down completely: each is a quotient by a maximal modular right ideal.

Two notions follow. A Novikov algebra is primitive exactly when it has an almost faithful irreducible representation, mirroring classical ring theory. The quasi-kernel of a given action, its largest ideal inside the kernel, lets Panasenko identify the Jacobson radical: it is the intersection of the quasi-kernels of all irreducible representations. Algebras with no irreducible representations at all form a radical class. The results import a mature toolkit, honed on associative rings, into the Novikov world.
arxiv-2606-16731:
Haotian Qi and Gabriel Skantze present MuVAP in a 2026 paper on turn-taking in group conversation. People coordinate who speaks next through subtle cues, and robots joining a group must predict those shifts. Existing models lean on microphone arrays or several cameras, limiting where they can be used.

MuVAP instead works from one monaural audio stream and a single camera view. It extends voice activity projection, a method that forecasts near-future speaking, by grounding the sound in face tracks so predictions know who is who. A trick called Role-Relative Projection maps any group size onto a fixed contest between the current speaker and the next floor holder. Because edited video cuts break causal tracking, the team built a thirty-one-hour corpus of unedited single-camera conversations. MuVAP beats strong baselines at predicting hold-or-yield choices and the next speaker, in two- and three-speaker settings.
arxiv-2606-16831:
Mohr and colleagues mix two error-correcting code families in a 2026 communications paper. Block Markov superposition transmission codes stack simple codes across blocks, achieving near-capacity performance with cheap sliding-window decoding. Their recursive variant spreads errors but avoids stubborn error floors. The non-recursive variant shows the opposite profile.

Mixed codes combine both component types, in parallel and in serial arrangements, inside one framework that contains the older variants as special cases. Simulations show the parallel mix improves frame and bit error rates over the recursive design, by a small but real margin in signal quality. Serial mixing cuts the memory needed for encoding while holding performance roughly level. Open questions include how the choice of basic code, its rate and strength, shapes the gains, and what happens with more than two branches. Hardware use of the mixed schedule is another next step.
arxiv-2606-16931:
Yu-Xuan Li and Tao Zhou propose a controllable home for Majorana corner modes in a 2026 condensed matter paper. Majorana zero modes are prized for topological quantum computing, but moving them on demand and telling them apart from ordinary states are unsolved headaches. Zero-bias conductance peaks can come from trivial states too, causing false alarms.

Their platform is a Josephson junction built with an altermagnet, a magnet whose spins cancel overall yet split electron energies. Two knobs, the superconducting phase difference across the junction and the orientation of the magnetic order, reshape the boundary mass together. Turning them relocates Majorana corner modes to chosen corners of a fixed device. The signature is hard to fake: as a mode moves, the quantized zero-bias peak appears at the target corner and vanishes at the old one in lockstep with the controls. That spatial switching pattern could support future braiding designs.
arxiv-2606-17031:
Haydarov, Kadyrov, Makhmudov and Mamayusupov prove effective uniqueness for equilibrium states in a 2026 paper on dynamical systems. The setting is S-gap shifts, symbolic systems where zero runs have lengths from a chosen set, with renewal-type potentials. Thermodynamic formalism asks which invariant measure maximizes free energy.

Inducing on a one-symbol cylinder reduces it to a full shift, where the induced potential depends on one symbol and the equilibrium measure is Bernoulli. A renewal equation then pins down the pressure. The main theorem is quantitative: any measure whose free energy falls within a small gap of the pressure must lie close to the unique equilibrium state. The distance is bounded by the square root of the gap, for smooth observables. Orbits avoiding any positive-measure cylinder lose a uniform chunk of pressure, giving strict entropy and dimension gaps. Effective rates make the uniqueness usable.
arxiv-2606-17131:
Haas, Kroupa, Peißker and Morris explain a curious hole near the Galactic centre in a 2026 astronomy paper. The mini-cavity is a near-circular, low-density region inside the mini-spiral, the tangle of gas streams orbiting our galaxy's central black hole. Its round shape hints at stellar winds, yet no suitable stars sit inside it today.

The authors test whether stars of the neighboring IRS 13 cluster carved it in the past. Orbital motions carry the cluster through the region: roughly three centuries ago it crossed the Bar of the mini-spiral. Winds from its stars would blow a round cavity that persists today. The same passage feeds the cluster's putative intermediate-mass black hole. Resulting accretion flares match the X-ray reflections now seen on the Sgr A, B and C molecular clouds, delays included.
arxiv-2606-17231:
Zhang presents a 2026 arXiv paper on odd compact stars that strain the standard neutron star picture. Two observed objects favour unusually small radii at low mass, while one gravitational-wave event had a companion too heavy for an ordinary neutron star under earlier limits. Zhang asks whether a strong, slow phase change from hadronic matter to quark matter inside the star could ease all three tensions at once.

When the change is slow compared with the star's radial vibrations, hybrid stars gain extended stable branches that would otherwise collapse. Scanning model parameters, Zhang finds two workable patterns that stay consistent with gravitational-wave and X-ray constraints. In one, a single equation of state fits the heavy companion and one small star, with the slow hybrid branch reaching the other. In the second, the small stars sit on slow branches in differing regimes.
arxiv-2606-17331:
Djecta and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper, published in the Journal of Computational Science, on geosteering, the task of guiding a drill bit through unknown rock layers while drilling. Measurements arrive indirectly and with noise, so choices must be revised in sequence under real uncertainty. Their framework joins a particle filter, which tracks many possible underground pictures at once, with value-based reinforcement learning that picks steering actions from those beliefs.

Three decision methods run on identical belief states: an interpretable dynamic programming scheme, a deep Q-learning baseline, and a dual deep reinforcement learning design. Beyond final well placement, the study scores steering smoothness over time, a practical sign of how calmly each policy reacts as uncertainty evolves. Tests run inside an industrial geosteering simulator with realistic noise and drilling limits. Shared geology, rewards, and limits keep the comparison controlled and fair.
arxiv-2606-17531:
Lier, Kaji, and Kim present a 2026 arXiv paper on non-negative matrix factorisation, a method that splits data into interpretable parts, with a new twist: policing the topology of the learned parts. Many data types live on structured domains, and a basis piece's shape, not just its fit, decides whether it reads as meaningful. Naive ways to reward good topology depend on thresholds and break continuous optimisation, the engine that makes factorisation training practical at scale.

Persistent homology supplies a stable, threshold-free score of a basis piece's topology for the objective. Added as a regulariser, it steers learning toward pieces with the wanted structural form during training. The resulting Top-NMF framework covers coherent image components, periodic time-series patterns, and clique-like graph signals in one language. Interpretable bases, the authors argue, should be judged by structure as well as reconstruction error.
arxiv-2606-18031:
Bayiz and colleagues propose reordering social media feeds to lift their credibility without scrambling what users expect, in a 2026 paper. Feeds carry a steady load of misleading posts, and platforms rank by engagement rather than trustworthiness. Their method treats ranking repair as a two-goal optimization: stay close to the original order while raising the expected credibility of what rises to the top.

Closeness is measured by Spearman's footrule distance between rankings, and credibility scores come from a semi-automated pipeline mixing retrieval-augmented judgments with human fact-checks, including community notes from X. That blend keeps human labels in charge while covering posts nobody has checked. On real X data, the re-ranked feeds stayed within a few percent of the ideal balance between the two goals, showing credibility can be bought cheaply in ranking terms.
arxiv-2606-18131:
