Yi Cai and a large team present a 2026 study of a light-activated molecule shaped to attack tumor DNA directly. Immune alarm pathways that sense loose DNA can rally the body against tumors, but switching them on safely is tricky. Their V-shaped compound binds double-stranded DNA and produces reactive oxygen under low-power white light.

Treated tumor cells suffered damage to both nuclear and mitochondrial DNA, spilling fragments that triggered the alarm pathway. Cells also died in inflammatory ways that further alert the immune system. In a mouse breast cancer model after surgery, one treatment during the operation prevented local regrowth, built immune memory, and slowed distant tumors and lung spread. The approach turned a local light treatment into a body-wide response.
pmc-13242131:
Bagdonas's team at Jena priced what German cancer patients pay for complementary therapies insurance ignores. A 2024 multicenter questionnaire reached two hundred nine patients in all. Users detailed their chosen modalities, monthly spending, and distress levels. Most German CAM sits outside insurance reimbursement.

Over half the patients used complementary medicine alongside standard oncology care. Seven in ten users paid out of pocket, averaging well over one hundred euros monthly. Blood cancer patients spent the most, near two hundred thirty euros. More modalities meant proportionally higher monthly bills, feeding financial toxicity risk.
pmc-13242831:
Vinay Sharma, Aruna Arya, and Padamjeet Panchal catalogued unusual branching of the arm's main artery found during routine dissection. Their cadaver study appeared in Cureus in 2026. The brachial artery normally splits into radial and ulnar branches at the elbow, but variants matter for surgery and blood sampling. Over fourteen years, two anatomy departments dissected 116 arms from 58 cadavers and recorded every departure from the classic pattern.

Nine arms, just under one in twelve, had a terminal branch arising much higher than usual. Two arms formed a rare pair: a superficial ulnar artery springing from the armpit artery on both sides of one body. Seven arms carried a high superficial radial artery, which consistently kinked where it crossed a tendon sheet near the elbow. Distal circulation stayed intact in every case. The authors tie the patterns to early development and warn clinicians to expect them.
pmc-13245531:
Camila A Picchio and colleagues review care models for hepatitis B and C across Europe in a 2026 Series paper. An estimated 29 million people in the WHO European region live with chronic infection. Deaths from viral hepatitis now pass those from HIV and tuberculosis combined.

The review covers models put in place from 2015 to 2025. Simpler testing and treatment, wider vaccination, harm reduction, and prison programs have all moved elimination forward. Point-of-care tests and services based where patients already are show clear gains. Big gaps remain: many infections stay unfound, and at-risk groups face unfair access. The authors say 2030 goals need faster case finding and broader care.
pmc-13248031:
Siddiqi, Javaid, and Kumar pooled the early trials of ketone supplements for heart failure, in this 2026 World Journal of Critical Care Medicine meta-analysis. Ketone bodies, especially beta-hydroxybutyrate, are alternative fuel the failing heart may use efficiently, and small trials have tested giving them directly. The team searched four databases and trial registries for randomized studies comparing ketone supplementation with placebo on heart pumping measures.

The pooled trials, few and short with small crossover designs, showed short-term improvements in selected measures such as cardiac output and ejection fraction. The authors refuse firm conclusions: the evidence base is thin and brief. They call for larger, longer randomized trials to settle dosing and whether the early hemodynamic gains translate into outcomes patients can feel.
pmc-13248531:
The EFSA Panel on Food Enzymes updated its view of a second starch enzyme in this 2026 opinion. This enzyme also comes from a genetically modified Bacillus strain made by Novozymes, and it had cleared review for three food processes. The applicant sought three additional processes, bringing the total to six.

Because the enzyme residue is removed in two processes, the panel estimated dietary exposure from the remaining four. The highest estimate was about half a milligram per kilogram of body weight each day in European populations. Judged against the earlier safety work, the panel found no concern under the revised conditions of use.
pmc-13249631:
Nagai and colleagues present iPatax, an iPad app that measures shaky coordination in ataxia, in a 2026 study. Doctors still grade cerebellar ataxia mostly with stepped rating scales, which can miss small changes. Twenty-eight patients and twenty-seven healthy volunteers traced targets on the tablet in three tasks, some stop-and-go and some continuous.

Two numbers worked best: how unevenly speed varied in straight tracing, and how far the finger strayed in circular tracing. Both separated patients from controls well, and both tracked the standard clinical scale's scores. Healthy users improved with practice, a learning effect the authors account for. They propose the app as a cheap, objective companion to rating scales in clinics and trials.
pmc-13249731:
Blackledge and colleagues grew pancreatic cancer neighborhoods in miniature, in a 2026 Angiogenesis study. Pancreatic tumors are packed with fibroblasts, support cells that come in tumor-promoting and tumor-restraining flavors with opposite effects on survival. The team placed each fibroblast type into chip-sized 3D systems with blood vessel cells to watch how the neighborhoods behave.

Chips with restraining fibroblasts grew more new vessel networks and remodeled their surrounding matrix more heavily. Chips with promoting fibroblasts sprouted vessels differently and drew in more monocytes, immune cells that can aid tumors. The authors say mapping such subtype behavior is groundwork for therapies aimed at the tumor's support staff rather than the cancer cells alone.
pmc-13250231:
Verswijveren and co-authors sort Australian children into daily movement profiles and check how each profile relates to body fat and well-being. Their 2026 BMJ Open study reuses data from the TransformUs school trial in Victoria. Nearly eight hundred children aged seven to eleven wore activity trackers that captured sitting, light activity, and vigorous play.

Four profiles emerged, from highly active children with short sitting bouts to mostly seated children with long unbroken sitting. The most active group had healthier body measures than the long-sitting group at the start of the study. No profile predicted later body or well-being changes over twelve months of follow-up. The authors say vigorous play matters most, though patterns with less sitting and more light activity may also support health.
pmc-13250631:
Jackson Drew and colleagues study shrub neighbours in Arctic Alaska in this 2026 paper. Two tundra shrubs are spreading as the Arctic warms: dwarf birch and Siberian alder, the region's only tall shrub that adds nitrogen to soil.

The team cut birch stems near alders and away from them and read their growth rings. Birch near alder grew under deeper snow, which delayed its season by days but shielded it from early frost. Those sheltered plants also grew taller, made more catkins, and held more nitrogen in their leaves. Alder seems to feed and protect its neighbour, a help that could shape how tundra greens as it warms.
pmc-13252731:
Rajat Das Gupta and colleagues examine wealth, schooling, and blood pressure in Lesotho in this 2026 study. The southern African country is urbanising fast, and high blood pressure is rising with the lifestyle shift, but the role of money and education was murky.

The team analysed a 2023–2024 national health survey of 5,457 adults aged 18 to 49, using matching methods to balance the groups being compared. About 21 percent had hypertension. Adults from non-poor households had clearly higher odds of hypertension than poor adults, a pattern the authors tie to changing diets and activity in better-off homes. Schooling was examined alongside wealth for its separate and joint effects.
pmc-13253431:
Jia-Wen Liang and colleagues evaluate patient-specific 3D-printed guides for vertebroplasty in a 2026 retrospective study. Vertebroplasty injects bone cement into fractured vertebrae, a common treatment for osteoporosis-related spinal fractures. Success hinges on threading the needle through the narrow pedicle accurately, traditionally under repeated X-ray guidance.

The study reviewed 106 patients treated at a Yan'an University hospital between 2020 and 2022, fifty-two with printed guides and fifty-four with the conventional freehand method. The guide group finished operations and punctures faster and needed fewer X-ray checks during surgery. Cement leaked less often, and complications including nerve root injury, cement displacement, and needle paths breaching the pedicle wall were all rarer with guides. Pain and disability scores were tracked with standard scales for both groups. The authors conclude that a guide printed from the patient's own scans makes this one-sided approach to the spine safer and more precise.
pmc-13254231:
Seongjin Park and colleagues test a combined heart surgery approach in a 2026 study. Patients had atrial fibrillation, an uneven heart rhythm, plus heart failure. Surgery used a scope-based ablation, which burns faulty rhythm paths, with or without closing the left atrial appendage, a small heart pouch where clots form.

Among 127 patients, only 13 did not get the closure. Rhythm relapse leaned higher without closure, and major heart events were more frequent, at 23.1 versus 8.8 percent, though not firmly. Vein reconnection was clearly higher without closure, and heart pumping improved either way.
pmc-13254931:
Megan Patton and colleagues examine whether a patient navigator raises transition readiness in youth moving to adult care in a 2026 Alberta study. Young people with chronic conditions transfer from pediatric to adult services between sixteen and twenty-one, often feeling unprepared. This sub-study of a randomized trial tracked scores on a validated readiness survey in 129 participants over two years.

Readiness rose a lot in both the navigator and control groups, from baseline to twelve months and again by twenty-four months. Access to the navigator, however, made no significant difference to the trajectory; the groups started level and climbed together. The authors suggest readiness may grow mainly through lived experience of the transfer itself. Both arms also received shared transition resources throughout, which may have lifted everyone. Fifteen youth partners with personal experience of transition reflected on the findings alongside the researchers.
pmc-13255031:
Franziska Klaucke and co-authors present a 2026 modeling study of how Germany might keep the power supply secure as wind and solar grow. The country is weighing schemes that pay plants to stand ready as backup. The authors compare a central capacity market against a reliability reserve that kicks in at a fairly high price.

Using a detailed expansion model set in 2030, they found the capacity market caps wholesale prices and thereby dulls the urge to invest in flexible demand. The reserve design prompted seven times more flexibility investment in energy-hungry industry and double the investment in district heating storage. Supply stayed secure at similar overall cost. The authors suggest the reserve could help new flexibility tools mature on the path to climate neutrality.
pmc-13255231:
Huilong Chen and co-authors build a tool that predicts bacterial growth acidity from genomes in a 2026 paper. The best pH for growth shapes enzyme work and where bacteria can live, but lab testing is slow and misses most species. The team built a dataset of 3,476 samples linking measured pH values to genome data.

Their model, served on a free web platform called BactoGenopH, predicted growth pH with about 89 percent accuracy within one pH unit on held-out data. Analysis flagged key genes for ion transport and pH balance. The authors say the tool speeds trait-driven microbe research and design.
pmc-13255531:
Hao Xu and a large team report a 2026 physics study of FeTe, an iron-based material whose bulk form orders magnetically instead of superconducting. Grown as thin films, though, it can carry current without resistance. Earlier routes to that state relied on oxygen or interface effects that muddied the mechanism.

The team grew clean FeTe films on a strontium titanate base and varied the amount of extra iron sitting between layers. Removing that surplus iron suppressed the magnetic order, sharpened the electronic behavior, and switched on superconductivity above 10 kelvin. Careful reheating restored the iron and reversed the change. Calculations pointed to a fluctuating magnetic ground state under the film's strain. The authors say precise composition is the real key.
pmc-13256431:
Giuseppe De Santis and co-authors review six years of studies using the INFOGEST 2.0 laboratory digestion protocol on milk and dairy products in a 2026 paper. This standardized bench model mimics human digestion so researchers can estimate how foods break down and release nutrients. The team analyzed fifty selected studies published since 2020.

The protocol reproduced broad digestive trends reliably, including peptide fingerprints after protein breakdown and consistently high protein digestibility. Fat and mineral release depended strongly on the dairy matrix, as in real digestion. Weaknesses included a heavy skew toward cow's milk, varied local tweaks that hurt comparability, and simple follow-on models that limit absorption claims. The authors chart a path toward dynamic, harmonized versions covering more dairy species, aiming at predicting true nutrient availability rather than describing breakdown alone.
pmc-13257131:
Chao Sun leads a 2026 scan study that sorts a rare lung cancer type before surgery. This mucus-forming type can look like other lung cancers on scans, yet care plans differ. Two hundred patients treated in Tianjin from 2018 to 2025 gave data, with thirty-seven of the rare type.

Clinical facts, scan measures, and deep learning traits were merged in one model. A filter kept ten traits, most of them from the scan measures. A forest-type classifier did best, and the merged model beat each single-source model in the test group. Checks of choice value and score fit backed real-world use. Scan doctors gain a non-cutting aid for planning. Proof in other hospitals must come before routine use.
pmc-13257631:
Alessander D'Ascoli and co-authors audit an automated infection surveillance system after knee replacement in a 2026 French study. Chart review of more than eleven hundred primary knee replacements from 2016 to 2018 was set against the national ISO-ORTHO automated indicator at one university hospital.

Full clinical follow-up found five prosthetic joint infections over an average of about forty months. The automated system, once running, counted fewer procedures and caught only one of three infections in its window. Local rates still informed national monitoring usefully. Infection control teams get a balanced verdict: automation scales surveillance, but gaps against chart truth are real. Pairing automated flags with long clinical follow-up is proposed so deep infections surfacing late are not missed by either method alone.
pmc-13257731:
Monique Greiner and colleagues tag polypropylene with germanium nanocrystals that glow under laser reading in a 2026 feasibility study. Recycling rules increasingly demand reliable plastic identification, and invisible tracers could sort streams automatically. Crystals coated with oily ligands were blended into the plastic at several loadings and molded.

Raman spectroscopy found a sharp crystal signal clearly separated from the plastic's own bands. Signal strength rose steadily with tracer content, and mapping showed even spread with slight clumping at high loads. The tracer survived normal melt processing temperatures. Sorting technology developers gain a working marker chemistry for one major plastic. Digital material passports could pair such tags with product data, helping recyclers separate food-grade material from lower grades at speed.
pmc-13258031:
Keigo Takagi and co-authors wrote a 2026 case report on eye surgery in two highly myopic, meaning very short-sighted, eyes. Long eyeballs can make vitrectomy, surgery inside the back of the eye, harder because standard entry points sit far from the retina. In both cases the surgeons shone a light from inside the eye. It marked the back edge of the ciliary body, a ring of tissue near the front. They used that mark to guide instrument entry.

One eye had surgery for a macular hole and the other for a macular hole with retinal detachment, where the retina pulls away. In the second case, a first light mark proved misleading, and a second darker band about nine millimetres from the corneal edge marked the true boundary. The authors say the light method may help surgeons place entry points more safely in such eyes.
pmc-13259031:
Lei Zhang and coauthors blend learning control with a fixed deadline sliding controller for robot arms in a 2026 paper. Factory arms must track paths precisely and finish within set times despite disturbances. Standard deadline controllers need large switching gains that make actuators chatter.

A delayed feedback surface guarantees error settles inside a time the user picks in advance. A learning agent estimates unknown dynamics online, reducing reliance on harsh robust gains. Stability proofs support the combined design under stated conditions. Simulations under parameter mismatch and shifting disturbances showed precise, smooth tracking. Chattering fell clearly against a standard terminal sliding controller.
pmc-13259431:
Roberto Petrucci and coauthors recycle plastic bushes from railway sleepers into new composites in a 2026 study. The contaminated parts were cleaned and pelletized, then assessed for environmental cost over their life cycle. Flow problems from the uneven recycled plastic were eased with additives.

Carbon fiber waste raised stiffness, heat stability, and electrical conductivity of the blends. One blend reached well over triple the stiffness of the plain recycled matrix. A compatibilizer balanced strength best, while bottle cap plastic preserved conductivity better. Yield strength held up across the fiber loaded recipes. Rail suppliers gain a circular route for parts now sent to landfill.
pmc-13260031:
Şimşek Çelik and co-authors wrote a 2026 study of frailty and short-term death in older patients with multiple trauma in an emergency department. Frailty means reduced physical reserve that makes recovery from injury harder. The prospective study enrolled patients aged sixty-five and over between July 1 and August 31, 2024. Frailty was scored with two tools, PRISMA-7 and a trauma-specific frailty index, and compared with standard trauma severity scores.

In total, 144 patients were included. Frailty was significantly associated with death within twenty-eight days, more intensive care admissions, and longer hospital stays. Mortality rose with age, reaching 30.0 percent in patients aged eighty-five and over. Frailty scores also rose with age, while the standard injury severity score did not. PRISMA-7 performed comparably to other scores, and the authors recommend it as a quick screening tool.
pmc-13260131:
Johanna Elisabeth Willker and Ralf Dringen wrote a 2026 cell study of oxidative stress in astrocytes, the brain's support cells, which have strong antioxidant defenses. They exposed cultured rat astrocytes to beta-lapachone, a compound that triggers oxidative stress through an enzyme called NQO1. The team tracked key molecules for cell energy and redox balance, meaning the balance of oxidation and reduction reactions, including NAD-related compounds and ATP, the cell's main energy currency.

Exposure rapidly oxidized those molecules and drained total NAD content over time, while the cells stayed alive. Treated cells partly lost ATP and could not raise lactate production when their breathing chain was blocked. Blocking certain enzymes called PARPs lessened the NAD and ATP losses and preserved that backup energy response. After the stress ended, cells given a NAD precursor restored their levels and function.
pmc-13260431:
Mengyao Ma and co-authors fed in 2026 adult beagle dogs a supplement of postbiotics made from Bifidobacterium animalis for 42 days. Postbiotics are non-living bacterial products that may benefit health without the storage problems of live probiotics. Dogs received a plain diet or one of two supplement doses.

Growth and routine blood measures did not change, yet several health markers improved. Antibody levels rose, while inflammatory signals such as tumor necrosis factor fell in both dose groups. Defense enzymes against oxidative damage climbed, and bone formation markers rose at the higher dose. Coat quality improved, with smoother hair cuticles and richer amino acid content. Stool chemistry and gut bacteria also shifted toward a friendlier mix, with more helpful species and fewer potential pathogens.
pmc-13261431:
Jianlong Wang and colleagues tested in 2026 two additives for water-based drilling mud used in a troublesome Pakistani shale. Drilling mud must carry cuttings and limit fluid loss, yet the Ranikot shale swells and sheds sand when wet. Their mix paired a zinc oxide and carbon nanotube composite with a natural biopolymer, tuned through thirteen designed experiments.

Raising the composite dose cut fluid loss volume from 26 milliliters to about a quarter of that amount. Shale swelling likewise plunged from over seventeen percent to under six percent at the top dose. The composite's long fibers thread into tiny pores and bridge them shut, blocking water entry. The biopolymer added little, and too much of it tangled and clumped, undoing the even spread. Statistical checks confirmed the composite drove both gains.
pmc-13261631:
Rui Wang and colleagues assessed in 2026 whether gene sequencing of patient samples helps diagnose invasive fungal infections in intensive care. Many such infections strike patients without the classic risk factors, and standard tests miss fungi often. Their review covered 106 adults treated between mid-2022 and early 2025, split by immune status.

Two thirds of the patients had working immune systems, though many carried other illnesses. Sequencing found most of the 81 pathogens identified overall and excelled at rare fungi and mixed infections where standard tests fell short. Its results changed care for seventy-five patients, about seven in ten. Fluid washed from the lungs gave the most useful samples, while blood gave the least. The authors back sequencing as a strong add-on, with specimen choice shaping the benefit.
pmc-13263331:
Shunyu Xiang and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on a smart gel that fights bacterial wilt, a destructive tomato disease. The disease is caused by the bacterium Ralstonia solanacearum and is hard to catch early. The team's hydrogel, a water-holding jelly, has two linked networks that respond to acidity.

When soil turns acidic, as it does in diseased fields, the first network loosens and releases an antibiotic plus zinc. The second network then falls apart, adding an amino acid and more zinc. One root application protected plants for up to fourteen days. In field trials, control lasted up to thirty days and largely preserved the tomato yield.
pmc-13263731:
Paisit Kosum and colleagues describe a fatty heart tumor hiding in a spot never before reported: the right atrial appendage. Cardiac lipomas are benign and usually silent, found by accident. Their 2026 case began when a sixty-year-old woman arrived with a pulmonary embolism and scans caught a small moving mass.

Magnetic resonance imaging confirmed the lump was fat, consistent with lipoma. It had not caused her embolism, but its mobility in a slow-flow pocket raised fears of blockage and clots. Surgeons removed it through a minimally invasive operation, adjusting cannula plans around the appendage. Tissue examination proved the benign diagnosis.
pmc-13263931:
Lei Li and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on mouth bacteria as noninvasive markers for esophageal cancer, cancer of the food pipe. Early detection matters, yet the standard test, endoscopy, is invasive and costly. The team sequenced bacteria from tongue-coating samples of 440 people: patients with the cancer, healthy controls, and patients after radiotherapy.

Cancer patients carried a more diverse oral community, with more Veillonella, Streptococcus, and Actinomyces and less Porphyromonas and Rothia. A six-marker classifier separated patients from controls with about ninety-four to ninety-five percent accuracy. Radiotherapy shrank diversity, and a separate marker set predicted which patients would progress within six months with about ninety-nine percent accuracy.
pmc-13264031:
Soon Yi and co-authors present a 2026 modeling study on predicting how long therapeutic messenger RNA lasts in solution. RNA breaks down mainly by hydrolysis, a chemical reaction with water, and structure can shield vulnerable sites. Broad measures such as overall folding energy miss local weak points along the molecule, so predictions have stayed imprecise.

The authors show that fine-scale pairing odds for each position add information beyond global measures. Combining local and global features gave a compact four-feature model named STRAND. It cut prediction error by more than half compared with earlier machine learning approaches and held up across different transcripts. Designers gain a simple, interpretable tool for choosing more stable RNA sequences.
pmc-13264431:
Nelson M H Teo and co-authors wrote a 2026 case report and literature review on cystic squamous cell carcinoma, a skin cancer that grows as a cyst rather than a solid lump. Its mild look often delays care. The paper aims to clear up how this form shows itself and how it should be handled.

Their patient was a 55-year-old man with a scalp lump that had no clear bad signs. He wanted it removed because it bothered him. A first cut-out showed the cystic cancer under the microscope, so a wider cut followed, and he healed well. The authors note that case reports are rising, and they urge wide removal and scans once lab tests confirm this cancer.
pmc-13264531:
Mei Zhang and a large team report a 2026 trial of a glucose sensor worn for 15 days by adults with diabetes in China. The device tracks sugar levels all day without finger pricks. The team checked its accuracy and safety at many sites, on both the upper arm and the belly.

Seventy-four people took part, each wearing four sensors. Readings on the arm differed from lab values by 8.44 percent on average, and on the belly by 8.91 percent. Agreement within set limits topped 94 percent at both sites. On standard error grids, almost all readings fell in the safe zones. The authors say the system stayed accurate and safe across the full wear period.
pmc-13264731:
Shutong Shao and colleagues develop a nomogram to predict serious pancreatic leakage after major pancreatic surgery in a 2026 study. Over one thousand patients having pancreatic head removal were split into training and validation groups. Variable selection and regression identified five independent predictors: soft gland texture, narrow duct, higher body weight index, longer operation and absence of diabetes. Inflammatory blood markers, though examined for association, did not survive into the final prediction tool built for bedside use.

About eighteen percent developed the clinically relevant leak. The visual score discriminated far better than two existing fistula risk scores in both groups. Surgeons can estimate risk before and during surgery to plan drainage, monitoring and feeding strategies. External validation in other centers is still needed before general adoption.
pmc-13264831:
Mario Andrea Latorre and co-authors wrote a 2026 study on inflammatory bowel disease unclassified, the label used when gut inflammation cannot be sorted as ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease. Doctors did not know how often that label sticks over time. Using records from a large Leeds hospital unit, the team followed such patients to 2025.

The group held 153 patients, with a mean age of 46.6 and mean illness length of 13.1 years. Their drug patterns sat between the two named diseases: more use of one gut drug and more biologic use than colitis, but less than Crohn's. Steroid use and health care use ran higher than in both named diseases. At the end, 88.2 percent still carried the unclassified label. The authors call it a lasting form in its own right.
pmc-13264931:
Abi Woodward and colleagues map research on social prescribing for minority ethnic groups in the United Kingdom, in a 2026 scoping review. Social prescribing connects patients with community support instead of medicine alone. Minority groups face unequal access to many services. How well these programmes reach them was unclear.

Seventeen papers met the inclusion rules. Common offers included advice, arts and culture, nature activities, and exercise. Cultural fit, strong community links, and link worker support helped people engage. Language problems, low awareness, logistics, and stigma held people back. Reporting of ethnicity was often patchy. The authors call for clearer reporting and more culturally tailored designs.
pmc-13265231:
Luqiao Li and colleagues look for markers that predict immunotherapy benefit in advanced melanoma in China, in a 2026 study. Single-drug immunotherapy helps only a limited share of Chinese patients. Records covered 62 patients treated at one Nanjing hospital from 2019 to 2022. Tumour gene testing and blood measures were collected.

More than five spread sites, liver or bone spread, and certain blood patterns linked to shorter time without progression. Combined chemotherapy improved survival. Common gene changes included NRAS and CDKN2A. One mutation, in KMT2A, independently predicted shorter benefit. The findings help sort patients into risk groups.
pmc-13266131:
Jason P Murphy and the team identify required competencies for expert infection nurses in Sweden, in a 2026 consensus study. Infection threats and drug resistance are growing system challenges. Formal evidence on essential skills for these nurses was lacking. Thirty-one academic and medical experts completed three rating rounds.

Agreement, set at three-quarters, was reached on sixty-two of seventy-four proposed skills. Agreed areas spanned microbiology knowledge, medical judgement, prevention, collaboration, and leading during extreme events. Person-centred care and mentoring also featured. Cross-culture care, green goals, and ethics items missed agreement. Those gaps are flagged for future work.
pmc-13266231:
Lijun Pan and co-authors review in 2026 why meat and meat products develop unpleasant off-flavors, and how producers can limit them. They name the main chemical culprits, including aldehydes, ketones, sulfides, and amines that produce fishy, stale, or strong animal odors. Examples range from boar taint in pork to the sharp smell of mutton.

Formation routes covered include lipid oxidation, protein breakdown, microbial action, and the build-up of compounds from feed or the environment. Control options span physical, chemical, and biological methods, plus combined approaches used during breeding, processing, and storage. Food scientists and processors get a single map linking odor chemistry to practical quality control.
pmc-13267231:
Adrian Treves, Sedona Chinn, and Miha Krofel wrote a 2026 paper about research findings that will not die. Science does not correct itself on its own, they argue, and wrong results can keep being cited with approval. They add a new label, vampire articles, next to the known idea of zombie articles, which are retracted papers that keep being cited.

A vampire article must meet two tests: its result cannot be reproduced, and it is still cited with approval in policy, papers, or private messages. The authors sort repeat attempts into four types and suggest how many failed repeats should trigger action. Two cases, on shooting coyotes from the air and on predicted overfishing, show the harm. They urge sharper retraction rules.
pmc-13267531:
Mario Romeo and colleagues present a 2026 case report on treating a bowel cancer spread in the liver. Their patient was a 52-year-old woman whose rectal cancer had been treated with drugs, radiation, and surgery. One liver spot, about 17 millimeters wide, sat near a large vein and bile ducts in a liver full of cysts, making standard imaging unclear.

A contrast ultrasound scan showed rim brightening and fast washout, signs of living tumor. Surgery and heat-based burning were judged poor fits for the spot's position. Doctors instead used electric pulses, a method that kills cells without heat, guided by ultrasound. The scan right after showed full coverage. Six months later, scans showed no leftover or returning disease in the liver.
pmc-13267731:
Yucui Ding and colleagues report a 2026 study of a nano-sized drug carrier built to overwhelm breast cancer cells with calcium. Drug resistance and spread limit chemotherapy for breast cancer. The carrier wraps a plant compound, oridonin, in a manganese-based mineral sheet inside a fat shell aimed at tumors. Once inside a cell, it sets off a self-feeding loop of stress.

Stress in the cell's protein workshop forces calcium into its power plants, which then fail and burst out damaging oxygen chemicals. Manganese adds more of those chemicals and wakes an immune alarm pathway. Immune cells inside the tumor shifted to an attacking mode, and killer T cells moved in. In mice, the carrier strongly shrank tumors with no clear whole-body harm.
pmc-13267831:
Ji-Seong Jeong and colleagues present a 2026 rat study of silica nanoparticles breathed in during pregnancy. These tiny particles are among the most made nanomaterials, used in industry, medicines, and consumer goods. The nose and lungs are a main entry route, yet pregnancy risks were little studied. Pregnant rats received the particles through the nose daily in mid-to-late pregnancy, at four dose levels including none.

Treated mothers showed mild inflammation and healing changes in the breathing passages. No mothers died, and no general poisoning appeared. Checks of the litters and unborn young found no harm to development at any dose. The authors say the particles hurt only the surfaces they touched under these conditions. They still urge more studies, since particle types and exposure patterns vary widely.
pmc-13268231:
Mehmet Beler and Yusuf Bilal Çelenk present a 2026 study of insomnia in people aged 80 and over. This oldest group grows fast yet is rarely studied for sleep. The team enrolled 419 patients at a Turkish city hospital's advanced age unit in late 2025, using a standard insomnia severity questionnaire; a score of eight or more counted as insomnia.

About 38 percent had insomnia. It was more common in women and in those with low income. Past falls, high blood pressure, diabetes, and taking many medicines all linked to insomnia. Severity rose with the number of chronic diseases and the number of drugs taken. The authors argue insomnia at this age is not normal aging but a treatable problem, and that routine sleep checks belong in care of the very old.
pmc-13268631:
Xingyu Zhang and colleagues present a 2026 machine learning study predicting lab test orders in emergency departments. Lab testing guides emergency care, but overuse wastes money and time. The team analyzed 13,115 adult emergency visits from a 2021 national US survey. They built models from structured record data, from free-text complaint notes converted by a language model, from both together, and from an averaged ensemble.

The combined model predicted test ordering best, clearly beating either data type alone. The ensemble also did well but did not top the combined model. Older age, ambulance arrival, abnormal vital signs, and chronic illness predicted testing; injury visits predicted less testing. The authors say joining structured and text data could power decision support that trims unnecessary tests without missing needed ones.
pmc-13269031:
Celina Wojciechowska and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on death risk after removing heart device leads. They tested two simple scores, first built to judge stroke risk, as tools to predict death after the procedure. The scores add points for age, sex, and common health problems.

The study followed 3,822 patients treated between 2006 and 2023 at busy centers. Patients scoring three or more died more often at 30 days, one year, and three years. That cut point caught 80.6 percent of later deaths, with 62.3 percent exactness for survivors. Each extra point on the newer score raised death risk by 11.7 percent overall.
pmc-13270031:
Long Jing and co-authors published a case report and literature review in 2026 about a 50-year-old woman treated for a brain aneurysm, a bulge in a brain artery. She had a stent-assisted coiling procedure through blood vessels, which went smoothly. The next day she developed continuous seizures, a medical emergency called status epilepticus.

A brain scan showed mild swelling on the right side, pointing to brain injury from the imaging dye used in the procedure. Prompt seizure drugs and supportive care followed. She recovered fully, with no lasting deficits. The authors summarize how this dye reaction presents when seizures dominate, to help clinicians spot and treat it early.
pmc-13271331:
Shuang Liu is lead author of a 2026 journal article on FTL008.16, a bispecific antibody designed to switch on T cells only inside tumours. Drugs that activate the 4-1BB receptor on T cells can fight cancer but have been limited by liver damage. This antibody also binds 5T4, a protein found on tumour cells, so activation needs both targets.

In cell tests, the antibody boosted T cell growth, signal release, and tumour killing only when 5T4 was present. In two mouse tumour models it beat a standard 4-1BB antibody, fully clearing tumours in one model. In monkeys, even a high dose caused no rise in liver enzymes, suggesting a safer profile.
pmc-13271431:
Ticiana De Francesco is lead author of a 2026 multicentre study comparing two tiny drainage devices for glaucoma, the Xen63 gel stent and the Preserflo microshunt. Both lower eye pressure by draining fluid. Both were implanted alone, with a drug to limit scarring, in this study looking back at past cases.

At twelve months, complete success was about sixty-two percent for Xen63 and about seventy-four percent for Preserflo. Complete success meant pressure controlled without glaucoma medicines under strict rules. That gap was not statistically clear. Complications were more frequent with Xen63, at about sixty-two percent against about twenty-nine percent. Reoperations were also more common, at about seventeen percent against four percent. Pressure reduction and medicine burden were otherwise comparable.
pmc-13271931:
Rui Tang and coauthors pool in 2026 animal studies on ginseng extract as a supplement for weakened bones. Ginseng is widely used in traditional practice, and its active compounds may protect bone. The team wanted firm numbers on whether the extract improves bone strength in osteoporosis models.

Across 28 controlled animal studies, the extract raised bone mineral density and improved the inner spongy bone structure. Treated bones also bore higher loads before bending, and blood markers of bone building rose. Benefits looked stronger in female and naturally aged animals at moderate doses. The authors note that animal success still needs testing in people.
pmc-13272231:
Riccardo Maria Borgo is lead author of a 2026 cross-sectional study linking retinal damage to cognition in multiple sclerosis. In that disease, immune attacks on nerves cause brain shrinkage and disabling thinking problems. Eye scans called OCT measure retinal layer thickness quickly and cheaply. They offer a possible window on brain degeneration.

One hundred people with multiple sclerosis had thinking tests, brain MRI scans, and retinal scans of several layers. Thinner retinal layers tracked with smaller brain volumes and lower cognitive performance. One layer, the ganglion cell layer, showed the strongest links, especially with processing speed and executive function, and was the only retinal predictor left in statistical models. Patients with impaired cognition had thinner ganglion and nerve fibre layers.
pmc-13272331:
Jialei Chen and coauthors track in 2026 how age reshapes blood immune measures and gut microbes in adult broiler chickens. Gut microbes steer immunity, but most poultry studies stop at young birds. Yellow-feathered broilers aged one to four years gave blood and fecal samples for immune assays and microbial sequencing.

One blood protein peaked at one year, while antibody IgG climbed steadily with age. Overall microbe community structure did not separate cleanly by age, though spread within groups did. A few microbe-immune correlations appeared, including one gut genus rising alongside IgG. The authors label those links exploratory pending confirmation.
pmc-13272731:
Kendra Rodeghiero leads a 2026 longitudinal study of bacteria in the lower airways of pigs, comparing animals with and without lung lesions. The lesions matched infection with Mycoplasma hyopneumoniae, a common swine pathogen. Samples of airway mucus and lung tissue were taken from nursery through slaughter.

Pigs without lesions showed richer and more diverse bacterial communities during finishing, while pigs with lesions had lower diversity and less change over time. Only 18 bacterial variants appeared in all phases in both groups. Two candidate marker types were flagged for each group, but the authors treat those links as preliminary and specific to this data set, needing further checks.
pmc-13273231:
Ritam Das wrote a 2026 article on improving phage therapy with antidefense proteins taken from the environment. Phages are viruses that kill bacteria, and doctors used them against infection long before antibiotics spread. Rising drug resistance has revived interest in this old approach.

The opening sections trace the history from the first observations of phages in the early twentieth century through early treatments for dysentery and cholera. Use faded once mass produced antibiotics arrived, though work continued in parts of Europe. Das frames the modern problem as bacteria defending themselves against phages, much as they resist drugs. The article's stated aim is to show how antidefense proteins found in nature could help therapeutic phages break through those defenses.
pmc-13273631:
Khan and colleagues report a 2026 journal article on cutaneous leishmaniasis in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan. This skin disease is spread by sand fly bites. The study links hospital records with a household survey. It asks where cases cluster and which habits raise risk.

The team counted 5,123 confirmed patients at 17 district hospitals during 2020. They also surveyed 576 households about schooling, family size, knowledge, and spray use. Big families, low schooling, and poor knowledge were tied to more cases. Spray use was tied to lower risk. The authors tested new sticky traps for sand flies. Most flies were caught 30 to 121 centimeters above the ground. That height detail can guide where teams place traps and spray.
pmc-13274131:
Siyao Liu and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on a fat-handling protein that helps an aggressive breast cancer grow. HER2-positive breast cancer spreads readily, and disordered fat use inside tumors may fuel it. The protein STARD10 moves lipids within cells, but its role in this cancer was unclear.

STARD10 levels were higher in HER2-positive tumors and marked a poorer outlook for patients. In two lab cell lines, extra STARD10 sped growth, movement, and invasion, and fat droplets built up. In mice it sped tumor growth and spread to the lungs. The effect ran through a signaling chain named cAMP, PKA, and CREB1, which the authors propose as a drug target.
pmc-13274831:
Ahadul Hassan Bhuiyan Konok and colleagues report a 2026 journal article on adverse birth outcomes across Bangladesh. Using the national Demographic and Health Survey, the team analyzed pregnancy outcomes for 10,254 ever-married women. They counted four problems: stillbirth, early birth, low birth weight, and death in the first month of life.

Low birth weight was commonest at 14.3 percent of pregnancies, followed by early birth at 8.9 percent, with stillbirth and newborn death each at 1.3 percent. The authors report about one in seven births involved at least one problem. Twin births, household wealth, place of delivery, and the mother's wish for the child recurred as linked factors. They recommend equity-focused maternal care and stronger women's decision-making power.
pmc-13275531:
Yves Moreira Ribeiro and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on how the natural estrogen estrone, a pollutant in farm runoff and sewage, harms fish reproduction. Zebrafish were exposed for forty-nine days to three estrone levels found in real surface waters, from twenty to two thousand nanograms per liter. The team then examined ovaries, hormone levels, and spawning success.

Exposure reshaped the ovary: more immature egg cells and withered follicles, more inflammation, and fewer support cells. A related hormone and a growth factor signal rose at the lower doses, while a nitrogen stress marker climbed at the higher ones. Egg production fell in every exposed group, and fertilization rates dropped significantly at the two higher doses, even at common environmental levels.
pmc-13275631:
Luis Parmenio Suescún-Bolívar and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on tiny plastic bits in water and the germs they may carry. The team studied recycled PET, the plastic used in drink bottles, cut into microplastics. They asked how Escherichia coli, a common gut bacterium, sticks to and changes on these plastic surfaces.

The team checked the plastic with light-based tests and microscopes before and after contact with the bacteria. The tests found nine clear chemical bands for PET, and neither cleaning nor bacteria changed the plastic much. Microscope views showed bacteria clinging to the surfaces and forming biofilms, thin layers of living cells. Colonies also fermented lactose, a milk sugar, less well. The authors propose their setup as a model for tracking how plastics move microbes in water.
pmc-13276231:
Wang Yi and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on a better endoscopic fix for bleeding-prone veins in the stomach. Gastric varices are swollen veins caused by liver cirrhosis, and their bleeding can be deadly. Standard banding treatment often grips the vein incompletely, so rebleeding is common.

At one Chinese hospital, ninety-nine patients had either standard banding or banding assisted by a metal clip. The clip method cleared the veins in a single session for about seven in ten patients, versus about half with standard care. Early rebleeding hit none of the clip group but about one in eleven of the standard group. Death rates and side effects were similar. The authors caution that the rebleeding benefit is exploratory and want larger, forward-looking trials to confirm it.
pmc-13276431:
Sunyan Hong and colleagues present a 2026 vision system for spotting defective green coffee beans automatically. Hand sorting is slow, tiring, and inconsistent, yet bean quality drives prices worldwide. Their system builds on the YOLOv10 detection model and targets fast factory use.

Three design changes cut computing load while sharpening fine detail and wider context. The dataset covered seven defect types graded to speciality coffee standards. Five-fold testing gave detection scores above ninety-eight percent for precision and recall, with answers in about two milliseconds. The model was also smaller and faster than a newer baseline, which suits sorting lines with limited hardware.
pmc-13276531:
Mariana Arino and co-authors present a 2026 case report on a rare, poorly understood degeneration of the cornea's edge. Peripheral nodulocystic corneal degeneration forms clear blister-like nodules around the cornea's rim. Only one similar case had been reported before, leaving its course and treatment undefined.

Their patient was a fifty-two-year-old woman with joint aches throughout her body and a past history of LASIK eye surgery in both eyes. She reported worsening dryness and discomfort in the left eye. Examination found multiple blister-like nodules in both eyes, mostly along the upper and outer edges. Scans showed cyst-like spaces under the surface layer and mild loss of the cornea's inner cells. She declined surgery, and symptoms eased with anti-inflammatory and lubricant eye drops plus a pressure-lowering drop. The authors discuss how degeneration, body-wide inflammation, and prior surgery may interact.
pmc-13277231:
Islam El-Malky leads a 2026 hospital study of brain bleeding in older patients, from a stroke care unit. The bleeding, called spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage, starts inside the brain without an injury. The team compared 71 patients aged seventy or older with younger patients among 238 cases, tracking recovery and death.

Older patients more often had high blood pressure, worse stroke scores, and lower alertness scores on arrival. They also more often showed signs of a vessel disease linked to aging. Their one-month death rate was higher and their three-month function was worse. Higher alertness and lower stroke severity scores predicted a better outcome. Age alone was not the whole story, the patterns suggest.
pmc-13277631:
Yuanxia Wang and co-authors compare two bacterial strains for fermenting mulberry juice in a 2026 food study. Mulberries are rich in vitamins and protective plant compounds but spoil very quickly. Fermentation with lactic acid bacteria can extend use and add function.

Juice fermented with Lactobacillus plantarum or a bulgaricus strain was stored at room warmth and in a fridge. Fermentation lowered sugar, acidity measures, and protein while raising phenols and flavonoids, plus antioxidant strength. Those gains faded during storage, more slowly when chilled. The plantarum batch kept the strongest antioxidant activity and richer flavour mix. Sugars from the fermented juice also showed enzyme effects relevant to blood sugar control.
pmc-13278331:
Viraj Deshpande leads a 2026 study of readmission after knee replacement with hypoallergenic implants, implants made for patients sensitive to metals. Metal sensitivity is a growing concern in joint replacement, and earlier work suggested lower quality of life with these implants. The team reviewed 6,954 knee replacements from 2019 to 2022 in a Mayo Clinic database.

Only 320 operations used hypoallergenic implants; the rest used standard ones. Readmission within thirty days was about two point two percent in the hypoallergenic group versus about zero point seven percent with standard implants. No link appeared with body weight, illness burden, heart disease, diabetes, alcohol, smoking, or medical complications. Extra vigilance for this group is the authors' practical advice.
pmc-13278831:
Aryana T Far leads a 2026 proof-of-concept study of a chatbot that turns plain-language questions into database queries for liver cancer research. Clinicians often cannot use structured research data without coding skills. Built on a secure university platform, the chatbot writes SQL code, runs it, and returns both code and results, keeping protected health information inside approved systems.

Clinicians posed thirty questions, and outputs were compared with a data scientist's code. The chatbot read the intent of about seventy-three percent of prompts correctly. Its generated code and final outputs were each accurate in roughly fifty-three to sixty-three percent of cases. Errors clustered around group comparisons, ambiguous variables, and open-ended exploration.
pmc-13279031:
Mohammed Amer Khan and colleagues published a 2026 study grading how well large language models answer patient questions about blood-thinning medicines. The team posed 11 common questions covering warfarin and four direct oral anticoagulants to ChatGPT-4.5, Gemini Pro 2.5, and DeepSeek-V3. Blinded clinical pharmacists then scored each answer for accuracy, clarity, and completeness against responses written by cardiologists and pharmacists from standard references.

ChatGPT-4.5 earned the highest mean ratings overall, with its clearest edge in completeness. Differences between sources reached statistical significance across all three scoring domains, and the sharpest gaps appeared on warfarin questions, where dosing and monitoring details are tricky. For the newer direct anticoagulants, the three chatbots scored broadly alike. The results suggest patients can get reasonable plain-language answers from these tools, but expert checking still matters for high-risk therapy.
pmc-13279331:
Jiale Yin and colleagues published a 2026 review on how gut bacteria act on three signaling pathways in depression, and how traditional Chinese medicine acts on them. The gut and brain talk through the microbiota-gut-brain axis. When gut communities fall out of balance, the intestinal barrier weakens and inflammation spreads to the brain, a process the authors treat as a core driver of depression. Three pathways, MAPK, NF-κB, and Nrf2, regulate much of that activity.

Herbal formulas and their active compounds reshape gut bacteria, strengthen the barrier, and dial down inflammatory messengers such as TNF-α and IL-6 through those pathways. Calmer brain signaling means less overactivation of microglia, the brain's immune cells. Because traditional formulas hit many targets at once, the authors see them as well matched to a disorder with intertwined causes. They present them as a complement to standard drugs that often disappoint.
pmc-13279531:
Yu Luo and colleagues published a 2026 machine learning analysis of a ten-year HIV cohort in Chongqing, China, asking how movement interacts with progression. Residence-based follow-up systems struggle when patients relocate, so the team built a cohort of 5,213 people followed monthly from 2016 to 2025. They separated local cases, prevalent cases, and incoming migrants, then modeled who would move away during care and who would progress to AIDS or death.

Their migration model reached an AUC of 0.849, and analysis singled out migrant status and injection drug use as the strongest markers of unstable residence. Survival modeling showed incoming migrants fared significantly worse than both other groups. Risk of progression climbed in steps after diagnosis ages of 30 and 50, and unemployed or homebound patients carried the highest risk. The authors argue management must shift from static local registration toward shared data across regions and support that follows patients when they move.
pmc-13280031:
Caroline Kim and colleagues published a 2026 study comparing recovery self-reports between young athletes in individual sports and team sports after knee ligament reconstruction. Surgery for a torn anterior cruciate ligament sidelines teenagers for months. The team reviewed records at one center for patients under eighteen who had surgery between 2019 and 2024. Patients filled in standard forms on anxiety, mood, mobility, fatigue, peer relationships, and pain across the first year.

The cohort held 70 individual sport athletes and 556 team sport athletes, with a mean age of fifteen. At four to six weeks after surgery, individual sport athletes more often reported moderate to severe anxiety, 24 percent against 12 percent, and fatigue, 34 percent against 21 percent. At three months they also reported worse physical mobility scores more often. Later time points showed no significant gaps. The authors suggest early recovery support may matter most for athletes who train and compete alone.
pmc-13280331:
Mehmet Goktug Esmer and colleagues published a 2026 animal study of whether low-frequency electromagnetic fields help skin flaps survive after reconstructive surgery. Random-pattern flaps often die back at their far edge for lack of blood. Twenty-one rats received a dorsal flap operation and were assigned to no treatment, a low dose, or a high dose. Exposures ran twice daily for fifteen minutes over fourteen days. The team measured surviving flap area, tissue structure, inflammation, and genes for vessel growth and cell death.

The low-dose group kept more flap alive, about 76 percent against about 55 percent in the other groups. Its tissue showed better regrowth, more new vessels, tidier collagen, and fewer inflammatory cells. The high dose brought no benefit and suppressed vessel-growth gene expression. One inflammation marker moved in opposite directions at gene and protein levels, which the authors attribute to timing. They call the work exploratory.
pmc-13280531:

It rests on joint acts of circulating tumour cells, platelets and vascular endothelial cells, the cells that line vessels. It lowered CD29 levels on tumour cells and curbed platelet activation, shown by lower P-selectin. Tumour cell and platelet clumps formed less as well. It also blunted TNF driven rises in endothelial adhesion molecules. Blocking spread without cell kill is the strategy on test.
pmc-13280831:

Shrinkage as concrete dries drives cracking and long-term durability problems, and conventional checks sample it too sparsely to catch its course. The authors assembled 79,008 hourly observations across sixteen mix designs and several curing regimes, then trained ensemble and neural models on inputs.

Random forest, extra trees, nearest-neighbor, and neural network models all predicted shrinkage with accuracy near an R-squared of 0.99 on held-out data. pmc-13280931:

pmc-13281231:
Cadu Klier and Luciano Grüdtner Buratto tested whether practice quizzes shield memory from stress in a 2026 study. Fifty-six men learned pairs of words in Swahili and Portuguese by testing themselves. Some pairs were easy and some hard, with extra practice to level the start. Two days later, half faced a stress test with cold water and judges. Then all took a final recall test.

An earlier claim, that stress hits hard items in a special way, did not hold up here. The authors say strong practice may armor memory against stress, whatever the item's difficulty.
pmc-13281431:
Marta Martínez-Guitián and colleagues published a 2026 study charting how the antibiotic linezolid damages mitochondria the longer a patient takes it. Forty patients were grouped by treatment length, from days to over two weeks, and their blood immune cells were tested for respiration and protein damage.

Functional decline and molecular losses agreed, strengthening the causal story beyond the known complex IV effect. The authors suggest mitochondrial readouts could one day warn clinicians before linezolid toxicity becomes clinical, though monitoring tools remain a research prospect.
pmc-13281631:
Britta K Matthes and colleagues mapped how tobacco firms react after health laws pass in a 2026 study. Industry meddling while laws are written is well logged. What firms do once laws take force is less clear. The team scoured journals and news records across six databases. They kept three hundred eight sources from about fifty countries. Recurring moves were coded and grouped into a playbook of five tactics.

One tactic strikes before a law starts, through stockpiling goods or early package tweaks. After the start, firms may simply ignore the rules. Or they may stage token compliance that looks real but blunts the law. A fourth path bends around rules through product, design, or sales tricks. That dodge was the most logged move of all. Firms also lean on shops, bars, and officials to soften enforcement. The playbook aims to help enforcers spot the next move early.
pmc-13281931:
Pierre Ollitrault and colleagues published a 2026 case report of a brain injury caused by air traveling the wrong way through veins after a leadless pacemaker implant. Leadless devices avoid the wires of conventional pacemakers and are usually threaded from the leg, but this team used the right internal jugular vein for catheter control. Their patient, a 77-year-old man with high blood pressure and diabetes, had an uneventful implant.

When staff sat him up at thirty degrees, he collapsed, scoring 6 of 15 on the coma scale. Ultrasound showed air bubbles in the right side of the heart, and brain scans found air in the cerebral veins, floated up against the blood flow. Treatment combined head-down positioning, oxygen, and a hyperbaric chamber. He recovered substantially but kept a left-sided weakness fifteen months later, though the pacemaker worked. The authors list preventive steps.
pmc-13282131:
Manol B Sokolov and Angel N Arabadzhiev report a 2026 case where three gentle surgical methods were combined to treat a complex tunnel near the anus. Such tunnels, called fistulas, are abnormal channels that drain from the bowel to the skin. Cutting one fully open risks damaging the muscle ring that controls bowel movements. In complex cases that risk of leakage is high, so sparing the muscle matters.

Their patient was a thirty-four-year-old woman with a highly complex fistula. The team combined a laser method, a tract-tying method, and a flap repair, shortened to FiLAC, LIFT, and TAFR. Together they treated side branches, cut off the tract, and cleared the inner opening. Eleven months later she had no return of the fistula and no loss of bowel control. Combining muscle-sparing methods, the authors argue, offers the best chance of cure.
pmc-13282531:
Richard J Paulson wrote a 2026 author's reply in the debate over the term unexplained infertility, standing by his editorial's conclusion. Critics had argued the label honestly marks testing limits and warned against calling the condition mainly mechanical. Paulson agrees couples understand the diagnosis in varied ways, which he sees as part of the problem with an imprecise label. He restates his view that the cause is primarily mechanical.

His argument rests on treatments that simply bring egg and sperm together. A past procedure placing both into the fallopian tube often worked without changing hormones, immunity, or the womb. Modern IVF, which unites egg and sperm in the lab, achieves conception rates in unexplained cases matching those in blocked-tube cases. If other hidden factors dominated, he argues, a mere mechanical bypass should not succeed so well.
pmc-13282731:
Won Hyuk Chang and co-authors present a 2026 analysis asking which subacute stroke patients benefit most from robot-assisted walking training with a wearable exoskeleton. The work is a prespecified analysis, planned in advance, of an international randomised trial. Fifty-eight patients received robot training and sixty-nine received conventional gait training, each five times a week for four weeks. Independent walking right after treatment was the target outcome.

Regression models hunted for traits predicting success in each group. For robot training, two factors stood out: preserved thinking ability at the start and strength in the affected leg. For conventional training, leg strength mattered too, but so did time since stroke onset. The authors say robot training's benefit depends less on how soon it starts within the early subacute window, provided cognition is intact.
pmc-13283031:
A painless cheek lump in a nine-year-old girl turned out to be an exceedingly rare gland tumor, reported by Giorgio Novelli's team in 2026. The tumor is sialoblastoma, with only about 60 cases noted in past reports. It most often strikes children and usually grows in the main cheek gland.

The patient was a healthy 9-year-old girl with a painless lump inside her cheek. Needle sampling, a tissue biopsy, and MRI scans guided the diagnosis. Surgeons removed the tumor and rebuilt the area with a cheek fat flap. Tests confirmed the tumor came from small saliva glands. Later scans showed no return or spread, and no added therapy was needed after full removal.
pmc-13284831:
Abdirasak Sharif Ali, Yahye Ahmed Nageye, and Kizito Eneye Bello report a 2026 laboratory study of oyster mushroom extracts from Somalia. The edible mushroom holds nutrients and possible germ-fighting compounds, relevant where poor diet and gut infection meet in mothers and children. Water and alcohol extracts were tested against five foodborne bacteria, and food content was measured.

The alcohol extract slowed all five germs in dish tests, with strongest action against Staphylococcus aureus at the top dose tested here. Broth tests showed modest strength for a crude extract. Dry mushroom held solid protein, fiber, iron, and zinc levels. Chemical profiling and docking work were exploratory. The authors frame the mushroom as a food candidate needing more study.
pmc-13285331:
Liver cancer outlook may hinge in part on RNA marks called pseudouridine, argue Zeying Gan and co-authors in a 2026 gene study. Liver tumors vary a lot in course and drug response, and the role of genes tied to this RNA change was murky. The team pulled tumor gene and outcome data from three large public sets and built a risk score.

Patients split into high and low risk groups with unlike survival, and the score held up after adjustment for other traits. Groups also split on mutations, immune traits, and drug response hints. Turning down two named genes, DKC1 and PUS1, slowed tumor cell growth in lab tests. The authors offer the score for prognosis work.
pmc-13285631:
Zofia Nowek and fellow authors review how a gut worm of sheep and goats has become resistant to a widely used class of deworming drugs. The 2026 review focuses on Haemonchus contortus, a blood-feeding parasite that harms farm animals worldwide. Benzimidazole drugs are cheap and easy to give, so heavy use has driven resistance to spread.

The review compares ways to detect resistance, from animal and laboratory tests to DNA methods such as real-time PCR and deep sequencing. Pairing molecular monitoring with careful parasite control, the authors say, can slow further spread and protect remaining drugs.
pmc-13285831:
Devi Nair and a large team test a deep learning tool for heart ultrasound from inside the heart in a 2026 multicenter study. Doctors guide catheters with this imaging during rhythm and structural procedures, but reading the views takes rare skill. Their program, called Auto-Contour, learns to outline heart structures on its own in real time.

Experts sorted more than five thousand video loops from 249 procedures into 20 standard views and marked key structures by hand. The trained model matched expert outlines best on large chambers such as the left atrium. Smaller parts, from the appendage to the valve cusps, also scored at usable levels. Each frame took a tiny slice of a second to process, fast enough for live guidance during a case.
pmc-13285931:
Shuang Zhang and colleagues trace weight gain paths and heart risk in young children in a 2026 cohort study from Tianjin, China. Weight gain during pregnancy and growth speed after birth both shape later health, but their joint weight was unclear. The team sorted mothers by gain pattern and children by growth path, then read blood fats and sugar at age six.

The study held 39,169 mother-child pairs from a city health cohort. Children whose growth sped up after age three, about one in five, were nearly all overweight or obese by age six. That late rapid path predicted the worst blood fat and sugar readings, far beyond any pregnancy gain pattern. Mother's gain shaped risk mostly by steering the child's own growth, which marks the preschool years as the key window to watch.
pmc-13286231:
Samuel Mann and colleagues follow alcohol-free drink use among young adults in California in a 2026 longitudinal survey study. Zero- and low-alcohol beers and wines now crowd store shelves, and fans claim they help drinkers cut back. Two yearly waves of a long-running cohort let the team test whether use of the drinks lined up with lighter drinking then, and with change a year later.

About one in four of the 877 young drinkers at the first wave had used such drinks in the past month. Their social urge to drink ran slightly lower than non-users, with other drinking measures sitting level between groups. A year on, baseline users showed a modestly higher chance of full abstinence from alcohol. Hints of more quit tries appeared too, though binge drinking and harms stayed alike, a mixed picture the authors frame with care.
pmc-13287031:
Elissa Maalouf, Eva Lopez, Bruno Coutard, and Remi N. Fourteen clinical and environmental strains from two hospitals matched the standard method's groupings, and family trees built from each agreed closely. Accuracy faded when strains differed at many points. As a first-line screen during outbreaks, the method could speed infection control.
pmc-13287331:
Sandra Stankovic M and co-authors reported in 2026 a boy aged 17 months whose kidneys could not hold water, causing very salty blood, dehydration, vomiting, and poor growth. Early clues pointed the wrong way: he partly responded to a hormone medicine, and a brain scan seemed to fit a hormone shortage instead.

Treatment shifted to water-retaining tablets, anti-inflammatory drugs, and low salt intake. Progress was slow. The authors urge early gene testing when infant urine problems stay unclear.
pmc-13287431:
Fatema K and co-authors describe in 2026 six infants seen at a university neurology unit in Bangladesh whose severe epilepsy was traced to changes in KCNT1, a gene for a potassium channel. Each child had brain wave testing, brain imaging, and gene sequencing.

Seizure types varied widely, covering focal attacks, spasms, and prolonged seizures. Most children showed global developmental delay despite normal birth histories. The authors set the seizure patterns against current classification guidance. With only six cases, the report mainly adds regional case detail to a rare condition. It also shows the value of gene testing when infant epilepsy resists standard explanation.
pmc-13287531:
Qian Yang and co-authors describe in 2026 an ultra-thin patterned material that soaks up low-frequency microwaves across a wide span, from P band through C band. Low-frequency absorbers usually must be thick, a limit set by wavelength rules, which blocks compact designs.

Their design pairs stacked patterned layers with a coupled surface that replaces the usual solid backing plate. Local electric fields and loss regions are shaped together so energy is trapped and drained in thin layers. Stacking layers in a cascade lifts performance further without the zero-transmission constraint of older designs. The authors aim the approach at flexible shielding and stealth uses where thickness matters.
pmc-13287731:
Shyh-Chi Chen and a large team tested in 2026 whether daily swings in air humidity can set body clocks in insects, much as light and temperature do. Species from several insect orders were kept under wet and dry cycles, then under steady humidity to see whether rhythms held.

Many species timed activity to wet or dry phases, or to the change between them. Most kept the rhythm for a while after the cue vanished. Fruit flies shifted to new humidity cycles and held them. Flies with broken clock genes or broken moisture sensors lost much of the pattern. The authors name humidity a likely clock-setting cue for small land animals.
pmc-13289131:
Stacie Hodge and colleagues test arm exercise checks before leg surgery in 2026. One center in Greater Manchester hosted the work. Patients had severe leg artery disease. Most cannot do leg-based fitness tests. An arm crank test offers a way around that.

Sixty patients did the bedside arm test. Most inpatients met the entry rules. Most who were asked agreed to take part. Nearly all finished the test to exhaustion. No major harm came during or after tests. Most tests ran within 48 hours of the decision. Surgery was not delayed by testing. Patients found the test acceptable overall.
pmc-13289331:
Diane Zinkeng Tongwa led a 2026 survey on malaria knowledge and habits in Kumba and Muyuka, Cameroon. pmc-13289731:

Genes for carbohydrate use, stress handling, signaling, transport, vitamin making, and energy filled the functional profile, supporting probiotic potential. Clusters for making protective compounds varied, richest in products from Sikkim, Manipur, Meghalaya, and Nagaland as named. Resistance genes stayed low overall.
pmc-13289931:

pmc-13290531:

pmc-13290931:
Splitting factory work between microbial partners beats one overburdened strain, Fatma Gizem Avci and Volker Wendisch review in 2026. Loading a whole multi-step chemical pathway into a single microbe strains its metabolism, so engineers increasingly build synthetic consortia that divide the labor.

pmc-13291331:

pmc-13291731:

pmc-13291831:

pmc-13291931:

pmc-13292331:

pmc-13292431:

pmc-13292531:

pmc-13293331:

pmc-13293631:

pmc-13293731:

pmc-13293831:

pmc-13294631:

pmc-13294931:

pmc-13295031:

pmc-13295531:

pmc-13295931:

pmc-13296331:
Victoria Sherwood and co-authors survey ten years of change in how new antibodies are found, in a 2026 review. Antibodies are proteins the immune system makes to bind one target. New tools let teams study huge numbers of single B cells, the cells that make antibodies, and link each one's gene code to what it binds. Tiny fluid devices screen the cells at high speed, and gene reading recovers both chains of each antibody at once.

Work has shifted from simple binding tests toward tests of what an antibody can do. Computer methods, from machine learning to shape models, feed results back into the next round of lab work. Lab and computer steps thus refine each batch of candidates together. The authors say such loops promise faster, more hands-off routes to antibodies for tests and treatments.
pmc-13296631:
Sukjoo Cho, Katherine Shelmidine and Jason T. Yustein review, in 2026, why osteosarcoma, the main bone cancer of teenagers, varies so wildly within and between tumours. Treatment has barely changed in forty years, and this patchwork biology is blamed for stalled progress.

Causes span unstable genomes, broken tumour suppressors, extra copies of growth genes, inherited risks and a varied tumour neighbourhood, plus shape-shifting cells and chemical tags. Answers proposed include marker-guided risk sorting, better lab models and combined drugs hitting growth, immunity and metabolism. Maintenance therapy ideas are also weighed.
pmc-13296831:
Hervé Tshikomba Mbuyamba and colleagues present, in 2026, a rare surgical emergency in a forty-seven-year-old woman: a gallstone that escaped through a channel into the bowel and blocked it. She arrived after a week of cramping pain, four days without stool, vomiting and a swelling belly.

Gallstone blockage causes only a small share of bowel obstructions yet kills a notable fraction of patients, partly because signs are vague and diagnosis drags. The case review covers classic scan clues and the debated surgical options. The authors stress thorough checking when obstruction has no clear cause.
pmc-13297131:
Linzhu Fang and colleagues identify a wheat switch gene that boosts the waxy coating on leaves in a 2026 plant study. That cuticular wax shields the crop from drought and other stresses. Turning down the switch gene, called TaMYB46, left plants with less wax and leakier leaf coatings.

A second gene, encoding an enzyme that activates fatty building blocks, proved central to making the wax. The switch protein was found sitting on that gene's control region and turning it on. Silencing either gene cut wax accumulation in the experiments. The pair forms a tidy regulatory module that breeders might exploit for hardier wheat.
pmc-13297931:
Ioana Maria Marinescu leads a large team reporting a 2026 antibacterial hydrogel platform for soft tissue and wound care. Polyacrylamide gels are biocompatible yet lack germ-killing action and can be weak in strength. Their design adds cellulose nanofibers carrying silver nanoparticles, with the fibers also helping form and stabilize those particles.

Analysis found two particle populations that may give both quick bacterial contact and a longer release of silver ions. Adding more hybrid material changed swelling, stiffness, and surface wetting in tunable ways. Colony counting confirmed germ-killing activity in the higher-silver formulations against several pathogenic strains. The team positions the material as an adaptable candidate needing further development.
pmc-13298231:
Yu Zhang and a team report clinical features and prognosis for growth hormone-secreting pituitary tumours, in a 2026 retrospective study. These tumours cause acromegaly and serious complications, and surgery is the main treatment. Their analysis covered 344 patients, searching for factors tied to hormone non-remission or recurrence after removal.

Recurrence itself, high hormone levels before surgery, and higher Knosp grades, which grade tumour invasion toward nearby vessels, emerged as key risk factors. The team also built prediction models for non-remission and recurrence risk. They propose the results can sharpen patient stratification and follow-up planning, though the study rests on past records from clinical care.
pmc-13299231:
Why do health staff in South Africa pick their jobs, and why do they quit them? Modupe Busisiwe Makwarela and her team put both asks to the field in a 2026 talk-based study. They spoke with ten staff from the fields of drugs, food care, mind care, and ward care, in state, paid, and school posts, till the tales ran dry.

Kind hearts, kin sway, past life, pay and job safety, and school marks all shaped first picks, as did the lack of a guide. Shifts took many forms: deep skill in one field, a switch of field, a full exit from health work, or side work past health. Staff, shop-floor, and red-tape strains drove the moves. The team call for rule change that serves those who stay as well as those who train next.
pmc-13299931:
Seung-Woo Baek and others frame bladder cancer drug resistance as a staged molecular evolution rather than simple mutation selection, in a 2026 review. A gemcitabine-resistant cell model supplies the time course. Early adjustment quiets cell-cycle and sugar-burning routines while raising epigenetic give and rewiring energy use toward mitochondria and lipids.

Later, resistance hardens through matrix reshaping, growth and stress signalling, and immune-metabolic exchanges inside the tumour surroundings. Mapping a resistance score onto patient tumours suggested similar patterns occur in patients. The authors argue treatment should strike the passing adaptive states before resistance settles, opening a timed window for treatment.
pmc-13300031:
Yoshihito MATSUZAKI and colleagues treat a stroke caused by a torn middle cerebral artery with clot removal as the first move, in a 2026 case report with literature review. Such dissection is a rare stroke cause with no settled management. Their young adult patient arrived with headache, vomiting, weakness on one side, and language loss.
