Combined stent-retriever and suction thrombectomy fully reopened the vessel, and balloon widening then fixed the remaining narrowing without a permanent stent. Later vessel-wall imaging confirmed the tear. He recovered well with no further damage over six months. Careful device choice and long imaging follow-up are stressed.
pmc-13300531:
P Mahajan and co-authors review four years of left bundle branch pacing at one center in a 2026 retrospective analysis. The physiologic pacing method has spread quickly, but long-term safety and durability data remain thin. The team gathered 271 patients implanted between January 2019 and November 2023 who had complete electrocardiogram, device, and ultrasound follow-up, all with confirmed selective capture of the bundle at implant.

Average procedure time was seventy-five minutes. Among patients who began with left bundle branch block, the paced QRS width trended narrower over four years without reaching statistical significance, and pumping function likewise held steady rather than improving. Thresholds stayed acceptable, with only two patients above two volts at four years and no lead revisions needed. One in five patients showed a persistent right bundle pattern at four years. The authors call the technique reliable and low in complications over the long term.
pmc-13300631:
D Parfianowicz and colleagues compare ultrasound-guided venous access with fluoroscopy-guided access for implanting cardiac electronic devices in a 2026 retrospective study. Ultrasound may skip radiation at the puncture step, yet hard outcome data are limited. The review covered 514 implants at a large center during 2023, with 297 patients in the ultrasound group and 217 in the fluoroscopy group, compared with models that adjust for other factors.

After accounting for the number of leads placed, neither procedure time nor total radiation exposure differed in any clear way between approaches. Complications were nearly absent, with none in the ultrasound group and a single collapsed lung in the fluoroscopy group. The authors conclude ultrasound access is safe and sound, while noting a puzzle: sparing radiation at access did not shrink the overall dose, which comes mostly from later steps.
pmc-13300831:
Blood thinners face a stiff test in cardiac amyloidosis, where clots and bleeding both threaten. Hussein Abdul Nabi and colleagues compared warfarin with newer direct oral anticoagulants in a 2026 multicenter review of 422 Mayo Clinic patients who had both amyloidosis and atrial fibrillation. Median follow-up ran 4.3 years.

Twenty-one patients suffered a thromboembolic event. Yearly rates came out low and close, at 0.83 percent on warfarin and 0.67 percent on the newer drugs, a gap without statistical weight. Major bleeding touched 9.9 percent of patients overall, again without a clear winner. Pauses in therapy longer than five days raised clot risk, the sharpest warning in the data.
pmc-13301031:
Two lichens new to science emerge from Anhui Province in a 2026 taxonomic study by Yi-Shan Feng and colleagues. The crustose genus Lecidella gains Lecidella biformis and Lecidella versicolor, named from combined evidence of form, chemistry, and DNA phylogeny. Both species grow in the southeastern Dabie Mountains.

Together with L. albida, the pair forms a well-supported branch marked by tiny fruiting bodies under half a millimeter and the compound atranorin. Biformis shows two-toned discs and an extra chemical, while versicolor shifts from yellow youth to nut-brown maturity. Full descriptions, photographs, and a key to all Chinese Lecidella species round out the account.
pmc-13301431:
Wojciech Ł. Grześkowiak and Martyna Wienke test sheep wool grease as a green wood preservative in a 2026 materials study. Scots pine samples were coated with four lanolin emulsions, some fortified with boric acid, then challenged with water behavior measurements and decay fungi, molds, and microfungi. The question was whether the wax could push water off the surface and starve the organisms that rot timber.

Treated wood turned water repellent: droplet contact angles climbed from about fifty-eight degrees untreated to between eighty-five and one hundred five degrees, on par with paraffin and carnauba wax coatings. Decay slowed, with mass loss cut by up to roughly thirty percentage points against the brown rot fungus, though gains against the second test fungus were small. Boric acid strengthened fungal resistance while trimming the water repellency slightly. The authors position lanolin emulsions as a sustainable alternative to conventional hydrophobic treatments.
pmc-13301531:
A trainee's ultrasound hand steadies with practice, María Teresa García-Martínez and colleagues show in a 2026 learning-curve study of plantar fascia measurement. Eighty-four adults, half with plantar fasciopathy and half pain-free, were scanned twice each by an expert sonographer and a supervised student. Agreement and drift over time were the points of interest.

Across the whole span, the two examiners' thickness readings matched at group level. Sliced by period, though, real gaps appeared in the first two months, November to December 2024, then faded from view. Agreement crept upward descriptively as the student logged supervised scans. The authors frame the pattern as exploratory evidence for structured training and oversight in ultrasound teaching.
pmc-13302231:
N Augustin and co-authors track, in a 2026 study, how pacing thresholds evolve after implantation of a leadless pacemaker in the heart's upper chamber. The atrial device, approved in Germany in 2024, pairs with a ventricular unit to form a fully leadless two-chamber system. Thresholds at implant looked high even when positioning seemed perfect.

Fourteen patients implanted between August 2024 and October 2025 were compared with fifty recipients of the matching ventricular device. Atrial thresholds started significantly higher than ventricular ones, then fell markedly and settled at low, stable levels over six months. Ventricular thresholds barely changed. The authors blame swelling at the contact point, proportionally larger in the small upper chamber, and call for work on the mechanism.
pmc-13302331:
Giuseppe Neri and a large team review, in a 2026 review, how safely invasive procedures can be done while adults are supported by ECMO. The machine oxygenates blood outside the body. These very ill patients often need surgery or bedside procedures, yet the blood thinning ECMO requires raises both bleeding and clotting dangers.

Forty-six studies met the criteria, grouped into six procedure families from airway work to major abdominal and chest surgery. Airway and scope procedures generally succeeded in chosen patients, though registry data showed bleeding in about a quarter of tracheal cases. Emergency chest and abdominal operations carried the heaviest burden of bleeding, transfusion, and death. The authors urge procedure-specific planning with blood-thinning management matched to each patient.
pmc-13302531:
Fungicides are learning to aim, Xiyu Wu and colleagues survey in a 2026 review of targeted discovery against crop fungi. Resistance and tighter environmental rules are squeezing the old broad-spectrum chemistry, so researchers increasingly design compounds around chosen weak points. The review sorts the new strategies into three families and weighs each for selectivity, durability, and the risk of fresh resistance.

One family attacks processes the fungus cannot live or infect without. A second disarms virulence, blunting the tricks pathogens use to slip past plant defenses. A third recruits the plant itself, switching on or redirecting its immunity. Repurposed drugs, structural biology, and AI-assisted design speed the search, the authors note.
pmc-13303331:
Sarah Jane Harrison and colleagues review, in a 2026 paper, the case for starting long-acting injectable antipsychotics early in schizophrenia rather than reserving them for crisis. Injections every few weeks keep drug levels steady and remove daily pill burden, yet clinicians often wait until repeated relapses prove pills are failing. The first five years after diagnosis are framed as the critical window.

Evidence gathered here links early injection use to fewer relapses, better daily functioning, and lower overall care costs. Barriers include negative views among clinicians, patients, and families, plus thin guideline support and limited education. The authors propose teaching programmes and guideline updates to normalise early use. Gaps in direct evidence for first-episode patients are acknowledged plainly.
pmc-13303431:
Nicolo' Monti and colleagues report a 2026 cohort study of growth problems in children adopted across borders. The group studied 1,955 children seen at a large children's center in Italy between 2015 and 2025, most aged one to nine years.

Growth was judged with World Health Organization standards for stunting, underweight, and thinness. About one child in eight showed stunting or underweight, and thinness was less common. Anemia, age one to four years, Asian origin, and fetal alcohol spectrum disorder raised the risk of poor growth. The results point to early screening and nutrition support soon after adoption.
pmc-13303931:
Po-Sung Chen and colleagues craft light, strong titanium alloys in a 2026 materials study. Swapping niobium for zirconium in a medium-entropy mix lowers weight while keeping the toughness that transport and energy uses demand.

Four mixes with rising titanium shares were cast and checked. All held a single crystal structure, and more titanium traded some strength for slightly better stretch. Rolling plus fast heating then lifted performance a great deal. One mid mix heated at the lowest tested level paired very high yield strength with good stretch and low density, marking it as a strong candidate for light parts.
pmc-13304631:
Tao Liu, Clementina Manera, and Francesca Gado argue, in a 2026 review, that natural product research works best when discovery, mechanism, and supply advance together. Plant and microbial molecules like paclitaxel and artemisinin occupy chemical ground that synthetic libraries rarely reach, yet the useful ones hide as trace ingredients in messy mixtures. Older isolate-and-test pipelines kept rediscovering known compounds.

Modern campaigns instead map extracts by mass spectrometry and molecular networking, spotting known scaffolds before any bench work. Genome mining predicts what silent pathways could produce, while protein-target methods read a compound's targets inside living cells early enough to guide priorities. Organoids grown from patient tissue test relevance in realistic settings. Finally, engineered microbes ferment scarce products at scale, turning a rare extract into a supply that factories can make.
pmc-13304831:
Madeline R. Bolding and co-authors build a lab method for raising antibodies against membrane fats rather than proteins in a 2026 study. Fats change little between germ strains, so they may offer broad targets that protein hunting misses.

Tiny lipid discs carrying bacterial surface fat served as bait in phage and yeast display screens. Rival and subtraction steps cut sticky false binders, and winners were sharpened for stronger signals. The same setup then fished out antibody fragments that bind discs made from plague germ membrane fat, with some selectivity over control discs. More work must pin down exact targets.
pmc-13305331:
Ragini Gopagoni and colleagues describe a 2026 case of lung scarring in a man with celiac disease, paired with a review of lung problems in that condition. Gut illness from gluten can reach many organs, yet lung links remain rarely reported.

The 55-year-old had well-controlled celiac disease before breathlessness and cough grew. Scans were unclear, so surgical biopsy confirmed the usual interstitial pneumonia pattern of scarring. Immune blood tests stayed negative and no other cause surfaced. Despite diet lapses being addressed and a scarring drug, disease advanced to lung transplant. The link stays unproven and needs study.
pmc-13305431:
Juan Song and co-authors study how added microbes reshape root chemistry in the sweetgum tree Liquidambar formosana in a 2026 experiment. Roots leak compounds that feed soil life, and the two-way exchange may steer tree growth itself.

A bacterium, a root fungus, and both together were added to young trees. Combined dosing lifted growth most and eased stress chemistry in roots. Chemical profiling showed broad shifts in amino acids, acids, and sugars, with one sugar falling in both roots and leaks, hinting at lower stress demand. Richer carbon leaks may strengthen helpful microbe partnerships.
pmc-13305631:
Hui Lu and co-authors offer a 2026 plain language summary of a survey on treatment preferences in hemophilia care. People with the bleeding condition and caregivers of affected children in the United States and United Kingdom weighed made-up treatment options online.

Choices varied benefits, risks, and delivery style, from vein injections to newer under-skin shots. Adults and caregivers mostly agreed on what mattered. Taking treatment less often ranked highest of all features. Respondents would accept somewhat higher risk or lower benefit in exchange for fewer doses, a trade-off that drug makers and clinics should weigh when planning care.
pmc-13306231:
Higor Antonio-Domingues studied pollen from Madagascar members of the plant genus Vernonia in a 2026 survey. Light and electron microscopes documented 37 of 44 known island taxa, a broad sweep for a group famous for tangled classification.

Measured traits split the pollen into two types, a split backed by statistical pattern analysis in the reported results. A pore structure never before recorded for the genus also appeared during the survey. Further joint studies across Africa and Madagascar will test whether these pollen marks stay useful for naming species and tracing family history.
pmc-13306431:
Kexin Guo proposed a self-taught system for reading machine health from many sensor streams in a 2026 study. Noise, timing mismatch between streams and hand-made labels have limited earlier tools, especially under extreme faults.

Environmental, device, network, behaviour and log signals are treated as one state view, learned through masked time modelling and contrastive training without manual labels. Error scores of 0.0167, 0.0856 and 0.1291 on three standard measures beat rivals including LSTM and Transformer models in reported tests. The authors present the features as stable, transferable and readable for later tasks.
pmc-13306731:
Maria Breygina compared flower chemistry in two tobacco lines with differing seed output in a 2026 study. Fortune plants grow longer flowers, larger fruits and more seeds than Samsun, and stigma fluids guide pollen growth in both lines.

Samsun stigma fluid carried higher overall oxidative power and possibly more nitric oxide in spectrometer checks. Fortune held more of a protective enzyme in stigma tissue and more abscisic acid in its fluid in reported measures. Young style growth checks added enzyme activity patterns, linking redox balance to pollination success. The gap in fluid traits may help explain why one line sets far more seed.
pmc-13307431:
Yanhui Tian and co-authors examine in 2026 how a ring shaped carbon fibre part hardens, pairing computer models with strain sensors built into the part. They first measured how the LD-2184 resin cures, its stiffness when fully hard, and how much it expands with heat.

Rings were wound wet with fibre, and tiny fibre sensors tracked pull along the axis during curing. The model joined heat flow, cure chemistry, and shape change in one frame. Measured and modelled strain differed by 7.15 percent in the final check, which backs the model. Left over stress came mostly from resin shrinkage and from cooling under mould restraint.
pmc-13307631:
Betsy Armenta-Leyva and colleagues pool 145 studies in 2026 on detecting viral genetic material from samples dried onto commercial filter papers. They promise cheap collection, transport, and storage for human and animal testing. Thirty-nine paper types appeared, led by cellulose brands such as Whatman and FTA products.

Detection success varied widely, from under half to nearly all expected positives depending on paper type. Virus target mattered too, with rates spanning a broad middle range. Storage temperature, drying time, and humidity could shift recovery, yet many studies reported those conditions poorly. Polyester and glass fibre papers appeared less often in the literature. The authors call for head-to-head designs that compare papers across conditions honestly. Without such rigour, they warn, field programmes may trust a paper beyond its proven limits.
pmc-13308631:
Raphiel J Murden and co-authors develop in 2026 a probability based take on JIVE, a method that splits shared and solo patterns across data sets taken from the same people. Their version, ProJIVE, learns both parts at once through an expectation step that seeks the best fit for the full model.

Joint fitting can beat step wise rivals on accuracy, since each part is shaped with the other in view from the start. Tried on brain shape and thinking scores in Alzheimer disease, the joint scores tied to dear lab markers of the illness. Code is shared in public, so other teams can test the method on gene, scan, and chemistry data sets.
pmc-13308731:
Xiaona Liu and Wei Zhao review in 2026 nano sized tools that aim to retrain the immune system in allergic rhinitis, a long term nose ill that burdens many lands. Shots that teach tolerance are the sole care that can change the course, yet they take years and vary a lot by person.

Tiny carriers such as polymer bits, fat bubbles, and cell shed packets can ferry allergens to the right cells with tight release control. Nano vaccines and nano sized binders add fresh ways to calm the skewed response at its root. Smart systems that sense local cues may lift both gain and safety at once. Human proof still trails the lab work by a wide margin.
pmc-13309131:
Helena M Swinkels, Mary A Georgilas, and Steven Keeler argue in 2026 that town pool closures in Canada cut a core health tool, not a mere luxury for towns. Pools are often first on the block when budgets pinch, yet swim cover has not kept pace with growth, and many pools near the end of their working life.

Swimming loads most muscle groups, spares joints, cools people in heat waves, and teaches a skill that guards against drowning in lakes and seas. A fresh federal fund of 30 billion dollars for town builds gives a chance to fix and grow the pool stock. The authors urge that pools rank high when that cash is shared.
pmc-13309431:
Dan Adler and colleagues argue in a 2026 theory article that science splits into law-finding work and history-tracing work for a basic reason. Laws work when each event can be treated as separate, with past events leaving the rules unchanged. Evolution breaks that habit, since each step changes the next step.

A simple formal model shows how objects that merely persist longer can build population-level change without genes or copying. Placed beside law-based science, the model yields a four-part map of kinds of inquiry. The authors claim that history-based fields need their own building style of explanation. The piece speaks to readers who study how evolution should be explained.
pmc-13310631:
Mélina Côté and colleagues rebuild in 2026 the full nutrient makeup of packaged foods from their labels and ingredient lists, filling a gap in food data banks that mostly cover generic items. The data covered 5,371 packaged products sold in Québec across 17 categories. A language algorithm matched each ingredient to its closest entry in the national nutrient file.

A maths model then solved for ingredient shares that match the declared label values. Over half the ingredients matched their data bank matches with high closeness scores. Median error stayed under twenty percent for energy and the ten label nutrients, within the leeway rule-makers accept for labels. Six food categories did strongly, while three categories gave poor figures on several nutrients. Complete profiles for packaged foods would sharpen dietary studies, since such products supply nearly half the energy in many countries.
pmc-13310931:
Qi Wang and a large team offer a practical lab test for nerve disease antibodies in a 2026 study. Live cell tests best detect antibodies tied to optic and spinal cord attacks, yet they are costly and hard to standardize. Fixed cell tests are easier but miss more cases, so a cleaning step for blood samples was built.

A lysate product soaks up interfering matter before the fixed test. In blind tests with 818 people in two cohorts, the cleaned fixed test matched or beat the live test for both antibody types, with near perfect accuracy on controls. Wider labs could adopt the method for routine diagnosis.
pmc-13311331:
Horace Cheuk Wai Choi and co-authors model the costs and gains of widening HPV vaccination in Hong Kong in a 2026 analysis. Since 2019 the city has offered two doses to schoolgirls aged 10 to 12.

The model weighs the current girls-only plan against vaccinating boys too, in one or two doses, over a 100-year span. Two doses for both sexes cost too much per health gain at the stated prices. One dose for both sexes came out cost-saving or good value in all runs, if boys' uptake passed half and one dose guarded for 30 years. The results guide a cheaper path to wider cover.
pmc-13311631:
Jiayu Zhang and colleagues detail a 2026 interview study on involving awake intensive care patients in shared decisions about their care. Staff views on the practice were gathered at one accredited hospital in Hangzhou, China.

Sixteen ICU doctors and nurses, aged 23 to 45, were interviewed between September and November 2024. Three themes emerged. Staff saw patients as often not ready, with shifting capacity, raw emotions, and limited grasp of choices. Doctors acted more as advisors, nurses felt sidelined, and team talk was patchy. Involvement could protect or burden patients. Clearer roles and structure are urged.
pmc-13311831:
S Knaga and co-authors present a 2026 study on dosing broiler chicks before hatching. Chicks got a prebiotic or a fatty acid donor in the egg, and gut microbes were read at six weeks of age.

On day twelve of incubation, 1068 fertile Ross 308 eggs were split into four groups. The groups were untouched, salt-water, galactooligosaccharide, and sodium butyrate. Gut contents from the small intestine and cecum were gene-sequenced at day 42. The prebiotic raised microbe variety and favored Lactobacillus and kin. The butyrate reshaped communities more sharply, cutting Lactobacillus and lifting other groups. Early dosing, it seems, steers the gut for weeks.
pmc-13311931:
Maxime Pichon and co-authors report a 2026 comparison of gut microbiome testing offered by French medical biology laboratories. Interest in self-testing is rising. Yet the scientific validity and clinical meaning of commercial kits remain in question. Acting as an ordinary patient would, the researchers chose five laboratories through standard internet searches in June 2024. They sent each one portions of a single pooled stool sample from a fictitious healthy 40-year-old man.

Even at the kit stage, the laboratories differed widely. Contents ranged from collection instructions and questionnaires gathering basic personal or clinical details to promotional material with no biomedical purpose. The team set out to compare packaging safety, data handling, and final reports as well. They treated the exercise as a national-scale check on standardization. Their findings already show a market with little common structure, which complicates any advice patients might draw from results.
pmc-13312031:
Ronja Hugg, Marc Stegger, and Bo Söderquist report a 2026 study on whether long-term dalbavancin treatment breeds resistant staphylococci in patients. Dalbavancin is a long-acting antibiotic used for prosthetic joint and other implant infections, and laboratory work had warned that low drug levels can select resistant strains. The team sampled nose and perineum swabs from 19 patients treated for at least twelve weeks and from 25 control patients awaiting elective joint surgery.

Cultures grew on plates containing graded dalbavancin doses, and resistance was checked against standard breakpoints. Four of the 19 treated patients carried resistant Staphylococcus epidermidis, with minimum inhibitory concentrations from 0.38 to 0.75 in the reported units, while no control sample yielded resistant staphylococci, a statistically significant contrast. The authors conclude that resistance genuinely emerges during prolonged treatment in the body, a caution for reusing the drug when infections recur.
pmc-13312131:
Wenyu Tang and co-authors examine, in a 2026 study, how the severity of tooth-root lesions relates to thickening of the sinus lining in people with severe gum disease. Both advanced periodontitis and apical periodontitis can swell the membrane of the nearby maxillary sinus, a detail that matters when planning surgery or implants.

The team analyzed cone-beam scans from 330 patients with stage III or IV periodontitis plus apical disease in upper back teeth. Sinus lining thickening appeared in both stages, spread across both sides, and rose modestly but significantly with lesion grade. Thickening was strongest at the upper first molar, which sits closest to the sinus floor. The authors offer the findings as support for careful preoperative checks of the sinus before dental work in this area.
pmc-13312531:
Yunfeng Zheng and co-authors report a 2026 study of copper-molybdenum nanozymes designed to clear infected burn wounds. Burns strip the skin's barrier and invite bacteria, while spreading antibiotic resistance weakens standard drugs, and copper-based nanozymes had been held back by dose dependence and bacterial defenses.

The hollow Cu2MoS4 particles, made by a simple hydrothermal route, mimic several enzymes at once and burst out reactive oxygen species that kill bacteria directly. Gene analysis showed the particles also shut down a gene that lets copper escape, trapping copper inside cells until a cuproptosis-like death follows. They further dulled the bacteria's energy production inside biofilms and, through the molybdenum part, suppressed antioxidant defense genes. In animal wounds, inflammation fell, new blood vessels and tissue grew, and healing sped up.
pmc-13312631:
Md Fojle Rabby and a large team report a 2026 qualitative study of community views on mass malaria vaccine and drug administration in Bangladesh's Chittagong Hill Tracts. A trial there is giving preventive medicine and vaccine to mostly healthy people to speed malaria elimination. It is a socially delicate move among indigenous and marginalized communities, where trust and history shape whether people take part.

Between September and October 2024, the team ran focus groups and interviews with 105 people in two sub-districts. They ranged from villagers and traditional healers to pharmacists, religious leaders, and local officials, all new to formal research. Conversations covered how locals understand malaria, where they seek care, and what they make of the mass campaign. The authors aim to feed these perspectives into community engagement so the elimination drive is designed with, not merely delivered to, the people it targets.
pmc-13312831:
Carlos Abraham Herrera-Amante and colleagues set out, in a 2026 cross-sectional study, to build a body fat equation made for elite Mexican women footballers and check it against the reference DXA scan. Precise body composition guides training and nutrition at the top level, but DXA machines are rarely at hand, and existing skinfold equations were never validated on this population.

Twenty-seven players from the Mexican Women's National Team were measured during a training camp with DXA and standardized anthropometry. The team derived a regression equation from the sum of eight skinfolds and waist girth. They checked its statistical assumptions, and judged it by error measures and agreement analysis against DXA. Leave-one-out cross-validation tested the equation internally. Six historical equations were refitted to the same players so their predictor structures could be compared on equal footing.
pmc-13314231:
Roostita L. Balia and a large team screen, in a 2026 study, dairy cow milk in Pangalengan, West Java, for Mycobacterium bovis, the agent of bovine tuberculosis. The disease can reach people through raw milk, and Indonesia reports no official clinical cases, which makes silent surveillance the only way to know the coast is clear. Sixty milk samples from lactating cows in three villages underwent DNA extraction and conventional PCR targeting two gene regions specific to the bacterium.

Every sample tested negative. No target band appeared in any lane, while the positive control amplified cleanly, confirming the assay itself worked. The authors conclude there is no current evidence of the bacterium in Pangalengan's dairy milk and that the zoonotic risk through this route looks minimal for now. They still recommend continued molecular surveillance, since a single negative sweep cannot guarantee a region stays free.
pmc-13314331:
Shirley B. Pariona-Rodas and colleagues test, in a 2026 feeding study, two alternative forages for guinea pigs raised in Peru's high Andes. Guinea pigs are a major protein source and income stream for highland families, fed on lucerne. Chicory and plantain had succeeded in other species. Over six weeks in Andahuaylas, groups of five guinea pigs received diets blending each forage at thirty or fifty percent against lucerne, plus a lucerne control. Growth, intake, and carcass yield were compared.

Both newcomers earned their place. Chicory diets at inclusion level improved weight, weight gain, feed conversion, and hot carcass weight over the control. The thirty percent plantain diet improved weight, dry matter intake, feed conversion, and carcass weight as well. The authors conclude that chicory and plantain can beat the all-lucerne ration on the measures producers care about, widening the forage options for a thin-margin livelihood.
pmc-13314631:
Hongbin Li and Shengxuan Geng study what drives student engagement in AI-aided English writing in their 2026 paper. They focus on learners in ethnic minority regions of China and on three inner drivers: growth mindset, the ideal future self in the language, and enjoyment.

Survey data came from 519 university learners of English as a foreign language, modeled with structural equations, as counted in the report. Interviews with 20 of them then fleshed out the numbers. All three drivers tied positively to engagement, by the results reported. Growth mindset also fed engagement through the ideal self and through enjoyment, singly and in a chain. The study tells teachers that belief in growth, a clear future image, and fun in class jointly power effort with AI tools.
pmc-13314731:
Josef Finsterer writes a 2026 letter that disputes a diagnosis of Miller Fisher syndrome in a published case. The case told of a 67-year-old man with double vision from weak eye muscles. He was labeled with the syndrome on the basis of lost reflexes and unsteady gait, and he gained from immune globulin therapy.

Finsterer argues the label fails its own rules. Muscle strength was first called normal, which hints weakness came later, a course that fits Guillain-Barré syndrome with cranial nerve spread better. No levels of GQ1b antibodies were given, though those antibodies rise in nearly all true cases, as the letter notes. No nerve conduction study was reported either. His plea: use the name only when the full triad is met and all other causes are ruled out.
pmc-13315131:
Haoyun Hong and co-authors investigate, in a 2026 study, whether a patient's housing status sharpens cardiovascular risk prediction and mirrors wider burden of chronic disease. Standard tools such as the PREVENT equations use measures alone, while renting versus owning tracks economic and neighborhood exposures that clinics miss. The team worked with records pooled from thirty American health care organizations. They linked records to housing and income data, focusing on adults without prior cardiovascular disease who had risk variables from 2010 to 2016.

The analysis asks two things: whether it improves on established prediction, and whether it parallels disparities in non-cardiovascular conditions as well. The design matters because health systems increasingly screen for social needs without knowing which data points change decisions. By testing a linkable fact, ownership, against both heart risk and general chronic burden, the study probes when such data earns a place in the model.
pmc-13315431:
Pan Li and a large team present in 2026 a blood-based way to spot the best germline chimera chickens early, without harming the birds. Making gene-edited chickens through transplanted primordial germ cells is slowed by having no gentle test of how well donor cells settled before the birds mature.

The team made male germ cells carrying a secreted luciferase reporter and a green marker, then placed them into embryos. The cells reached the gonads and produced working chimeras. Reporter activity in blood matched how many donor cells were in the testes, giving a repeatable, non-invasive readout that could cut blind rearing time and cost.
pmc-13316131:
Shay Nemet and a large team studied in 2026 which factors send young children with community pneumonia to emergency care or hospital. Their population-based case-control study covered all children aged 1 to 6 years diagnosed in three districts of a health organization from 2014 to 2020, excluding preterm and chronically ill children.

The cohort held 59,662 children, of whom 3,685, or 6.2 percent, visited emergency departments and 2,026, or 3.4 percent, were hospitalized. A third of emergency visitors were admitted, versus 1.4 percent of community-diagnosed children. Minority sector membership, lower income status, and higher white cell counts and C-reactive protein each raised the odds independently.
pmc-13316231:
Andrew Gillikin and colleagues studied in 2026 weight and heart outcomes when incretin drugs follow bariatric surgery, using a nationwide United States record cohort. Long-term weight control after metabolic surgery stays hard, and GLP-1 and dual GIP and GLP-1 drugs raise interest as add-on therapy after operations.

The study compared patients who took semaglutide or tirzepatide for at least a year after surgery. They were matched by dose, timing, and surgical anatomy, drawn from records covering 43,104 people in the source dataset description. Further matched checks weighed major adverse cardiovascular events between drug users and non-users over the long term.
pmc-13316631:
Pål Nicolay Fougner Rydning and co-authors, in a 2026 follow-up study, report long-term outcomes for survivors of neck spine fractures linked to ankylosing spondylitis. That inflammatory disease fuses the spine into a rigid structure that can break even in a low fall. Surgery is usually advised, although deformity and other illnesses make operations difficult.

Survivors were assessed with function scores and later computed tomography. Long-term disability was generally low, and most patients kept independent daily function. About half of those who had spinal cord injury improved to the best grade on the impairment scale used. Follow-up scans showed high rates of bony fusion at the fracture site, offering reassurance about healing in this fragile group.
pmc-13317731:
Qirui Zhao and a large team review, in 2026, smart nanoparticle delivery systems for osteoarthritis, a wearing joint disease driven partly by immune and metabolic upset in the joint lining and cartilage. Standard drugs spread through the body and reach the joint poorly, so benefits are small and short-lived.

Smart carriers release cargo in response to acidity, reactive oxygen, enzymes or heat, and can be aimed with molecular tags that home in on cartilage or immune cells. Animal studies with metal frameworks, breakable particles and liposomes show joint effects on inflammation, metabolism and tissue repair. The authors discuss safety, manufacturing and regulation, and propose camouflaged membranes, patient grouping from multi-omics data and computer-run trials as next steps toward tailored joint therapy.
pmc-13318731:
Lin Liang and co-authors report a 2026 retrospective study of a muscle disease marked by anti-NXP2 antibodies. They compare patients who develop weakness in the hands and feet with those who do not. Records came from adult patients in China with follow-up data. The antibody defines a subtype of myositis.

Of 110 patients, 53 showed distal limb weakness. That group started disease younger, at a mean of 38.40 years against 46.26 years in the comparison. They also had higher disease activity, more severe weakness, and more swelling, swallowing trouble, and abnormal heart tracings. Steroid pulse treatment was far commoner in that group. Relapses numbered 32 overall, and nine distal-weakness patients died, mostly from infection. Survival itself did not differ.
pmc-13319731:
Elin Wik and co-authors trace a brain seeking antibody drug in mice in a 2026 study tied to Alzheimer care. The drug was built to latch onto clumps of a sticky brain protein, first in loose form and later in hard plaques. How fast it moves through brain fluid and shifts between those pools in the first day was not yet mapped.

Fine tubes drew brain fluid from awake mice across 24 hours after one dose, and brain tissue was split by clump type after death. The drug cleared from fluid fast and shifted over time from loose clumps toward plaque bound pools. Loose clump levels fell within 12 hours of dosing. Hard plaque clearing will need longer care, the team notes.
pmc-13320231:
Théo Servan-Schreiber and colleagues ask, in 2026, whether dialysis disequilibrium syndrome is missed more often than doctors assume. The syndrome brings neurological symptoms when dialysis starts, and textbooks blame rapid urea removal. Prospective adult data on frequency and risk factors have been thin.

Forty-eight patients starting haemodialysis at one centre were scored before and after each of their first four sessions during 2021 and 2022. Nearly a quarter developed the syndrome, and two patients had repeated episodes. Linked factors included certain centrally acting drugs, fluid overload and blood acidity measures. Urea level before dialysis, surprisingly, did not predict episodes. Blood pressure rising during dialysis emerged as the one independent predictor in adjusted analysis, suggesting pressure and acid-base dynamics matter more than urea alone.
pmc-13320331:
Sara Varanese and co-authors present a case series from 2026 on extra movements in people with parkinson like illness. Jerky or twisting extra moves are rare in this family of ills and may hint at gene based leanings. Three people with clear extra moves had full gene panel reads, and their results were set next to eleven peers without early extra moves from the same center.

All three carried single copy changes in two genes tied to vessel health, swelling, and brain protein buildup, though the wider family picture stayed early and small. Cases ranged from late onset illness with severe jerky flings to young onset twisting illness that answered dopamine drugs very well. Brain scans backed a dopamine fault in each. The genes may act as risk shifters rather than sole causes.
pmc-13320431:
Amy L Mihalchik and co-authors run safety tests on a brew made sweetener from monk fruit compounds in a 2026 study. The mix, made by a tuned yeast, is rich in one sweet compound that is rare in plain fruit extracts sold to date. Since brew made forms had never had a full safety pass, gene harm tests and rat feeding trials were run to set safe intake.

No gene harm showed in bacterial or cell tests at the top doses used, run to trade lab standards. Rats fed the mix for twenty eight days and for ninety days showed no ill effects even at the top diet share tested, which sets the safe floor for intake math. With expected eat levels far below that floor, the mix reads as safe for food use.
pmc-13320731:
Brian T. Gillis and colleagues describe a pilot sleep programme for low-income families in a 2026 trial report. Poor sleep in such families often stems from daily habits and from bedrooms that are noisy or too warm or cold. The Good Nights Sleep Program pairs teaching with behaviour change steps that parents and children choose and track themselves.

Parent and child pairs joined a randomised pilot, with a mean income to needs ratio of 1.68 reported for families. Children in the programme slept longer by wrist sensor measures than waitlist controls. Parents fell asleep faster by their own reports and woke at more regular times. The team presents the model as a workable, empowering route to better family sleep.
pmc-13321031:
Clement Jose and colleagues present, in 2026, a rare clotting disease that blocked blood flow to several organs at once. Nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis forms sterile growths on heart valves in people whose blood clots too easily, usually because of cancer or autoimmune disease. Most patients present with brain emboli or heart symptoms, and overall mortality is high.

Their patient was a 63-year-old woman with no known medical history who arrived with two days of on-and-off pain and weakness down her right arm and leg after a long flight. Stroke and vein clots were first considered. Evaluation revealed simultaneous ischemia in the upper limb, lower limb and liver, an unusual combination. With help from several specialties, the team diagnosed the valve condition and treated it, offering guidance for vascular surgeons who may meet it first.
pmc-13321231:
Phruet Soipetkasem and co-authors track breathing effort in ventilated patients in a 2026 prospective study. Breathing too hard on a ventilator can injure the lungs, while breathing too weakly can waste the diaphragm. The Effort-I study measured drive and effort at the bedside during the first 48 hours of ventilation.

A total of 206 adults with acute respiratory failure were enrolled at one centre. Patients whose measures stayed in set target ranges had more days free of the ventilator over 28 days. Low or high drive, low muscle pressure, and high lung driving pressure each predicted fewer free days after adjustment. Simple bedside measures may help staff tune support early.
pmc-13322031:
Mokhtar Salah Eddine Belhadj and co-authors mine the genome of a Bacillus strain for new antimicrobials in a 2026 study. Drug resistance drives the search for fresh natural products. Strain F11, named Bacillus halotolerans, was picked for strong germ killing, and its whole genome was read as one circular chromosome of 4.15 million letters.

Mining predicted 10 gene clusters for making bioactive compounds, including a full fengycin cluster. Comparing clusters across strains showed fengycin recipes diverging, with two letter changes in the F11 version and a hybrid form in a sister strain. Chemical profiling found 9719 metabolites and matched two compounds, bacillaene and bacillibactin, to their gene clusters.
pmc-13322831:
Sanjay Kumar, Alfred Veldhuis and Farzaneh Yazdani test where sensory problems in ME/CFS arise in the brain, in a 2026 study using event-related potentials. Their group included 31 people with ME/CFS and 30 healthy matched controls.

Patients reported far more sensory problems than controls in daily life. On a paired-click task, early brain filtering, measured by P50 suppression, did not differ between groups. On an oddball task, the later P300 response was clearly smaller in patients, pointing to higher-order control systems rather than early sensing. The authors argue that help for sensory trouble in ME/CFS should target those later brain systems, not the senses themselves.
pmc-13324131:
Colin J Driver and colleagues report endoscopic disc surgery in two dogs with far-lateral disc extrusions, in a 2026 veterinary case report. Both middle-aged crossbreed dogs showed sudden pain calls, pelvic limb lameness from nerve root pressure and marked back tenderness, with imaging confirming L5-6 extraforaminal extrusion in each.

Medical care failed, so surgeons used a single-portal endoscope docked on the transverse process, opening a muscle-sparing side corridor to free and remove the disc material in pieces without bone removal. Operations took 25 and 30 minutes in the two cases. Post-surgery scans confirmed decompression, pain scores stayed low without opioids, and both dogs left within a day and walked soundly by three weeks.
pmc-13324431:
Tabassum Elahi, Saima Ahmed, and Muhammed Mubarak review the metabolic fallout of kidney transplant and its threat to graft life. Their 2026 paper notes that transplant improves how long people live and quality of life in end-stage kidney disease, yet such disorders are common afterward and endanger both graft and patient. Post-transplant diabetes strikes up to 30% of patients within a year, while transient high blood sugar affects 60% of nondiabetic patients after surgery.

Dyslipidemia, obesity, high uric acid, and secondary hyperparathyroidism add cardiovascular, bone, and graft risks, and immune drugs including corticosteroids, calcineurin drugs, and mTOR drugs contribute a lot. The review weighs lifestyle change, drugs such as SGLT2 drugs and GLP-1 receptor agonists, bariatric options, and close weight monitoring as countermeasures. Evidence gaps remain, above all in managing hyperparathyroidism, and the authors call for tighter tracking after transplant.
pmc-13324531:
Ke-Ting Duan and co-authors describe three new leafhopper species from Guizhou Province, China, in a 2026 taxonomic paper. The insects belong to Minucella, a boldly marked genus known only from China with just two valid species before this work.

Named Minucella dilatata, Minucella angustata, and Minucella elongata, the species are drawn and told apart by body form and male genital parts. The authors also give a fresh genus description, a diagnosis, and a key covering every known species. Study used dry male specimens under a microscope, with genital parts softened in sodium hydroxide and photographed in detail. Type specimens rest at the Institute of Entomology, Guizhou University, in Guiyang.
pmc-13326331:
Shoba Ramanadhan and team reviewed how power is conceptualized and operationalized in implementation science. Their 2026 scoping review asked how far research on evidence-based implementation examines power. It also asked how power is defined and measured in those studies, and what opportunities exist to intervene on power relations. The field emphasizes context and aims to address health inequities, yet attention to power has stayed insufficient.

After a six-step scoping process, the review applied Fung's liberatory framework and four levels of power, everyday, policy, structural, and ethical, to map the literature. It found a dearth of studies fixing power in implementation research. Openings exist to weave power theories and frameworks into projects, so teams can see how power shapes implementation systems and results and can use power deliberately to improve them. The authors present the review as a guide for making power a visible, workable part of implementation science.
pmc-13327031:
Mingdong Zhang and team sized up a new screw route for side-entry lower back fusion surgery. Their 2026 study tested the anterolateral transpedicular transverse process screw route, built to beat long surgery, heavy blood loss, and soft tissue harm. CT scans in 40 people tested how often screws placed well and key spine measures. A bone model set three fixation builds against each other. Twelve people gave clinic results.

A spine width above 10.21 mm foretold placement, and the route worked best low in the back, safest at L5. In the bone model, the new build matched two-sided pedicle screws in sound bone and beat front add-on fixation. In weak bone it beat add-on fixation but fell short of pedicle screws. Twelve people felt much less pain and disability. Three-month CT scans showed fusion. The team calls the route safe, workable, and strong at six months.
pmc-13328031:
Darragh Doyle and colleagues measure skin barrier change as young Atlantic salmon prepare for the sea in a 2026 study. Smoltification remakes the fish in form, body chemistry, and behavior, yet skin function across the shift was untested. Electrical measures on skin from parr, smolt, and post-smolt stages gauged leakiness and ion transport.

Parr skin leaked more and carried a different current than smolt skin under matched conditions, and seawater raised skin voltage in post-smolts while freshwater raised current in smolts. Gene messages for tight junction parts did not differ between stages, so other channel types or later control steps must drive the change. The authors advise guarding skin health during and after sea transfer on farms.
pmc-13330531:
Nurin Yasmin Mohd Khairudin and colleagues give a step-by-step guide to staining artery plaque in mice in a 2026 methods article. The en face Oil Red O method colours plaque along the opened aorta in ApoE knockout mice. Results vary between labs due to cutting, imaging, and counting habits, so a shared routine helps.

Steps run from aorta harvest and trimming through staining, mounting, photo capture, and counting in Adobe Photoshop. A standard digital camera suffices for imaging, the authors note. Each step carries photo guidance for new users. The routine aims to make plaque shares comparable across labs in early heart disease studies with mice.
pmc-13330631:
Nguyen Van Khanh and a large team chart bone cancer spread at single-cell scale in a 2026 study. Osteosarcoma survival has stalled due to spread and genetic tangle. The team profiled 40,401 cells across four stages: untreated, after chemotherapy, returned disease, and lung spread.

A spread-rich malignant group stood out, steered by ADAMTS12 in the reported analysis. Silencing that gene cut cell movement in two cell lines and lowered growth signals. Spread tissue also held distinct immune and vessel cells, tied together by shared signals. High ADAMTS12 marked worse survival in checks. The network map may guide risk grading and new drug aims against spread.
pmc-13331131:
Rajalakshmi Rajendran and colleagues present a 2026 protocol for a review of womb lining screening in women with polycystic ovary syndrome. Long oestrogen exposure without progesterone balance can drive lining overgrowth and cancer, and the syndrome raises that risk. Yet guidelines do not back routine screening for women without symptoms.

The review will search databases from the start to February 2026 under standard reporting rules. Two reviewers will screen, extract, and grade studies, with a third settling disputes. Findings will be summed in words, with pooled analysis where apt using a standard review tool. Spread checks and subgroup work are planned. No ethics approval is needed for published data.
pmc-13332831:
Louise Nicolette Mendoza and colleagues report a 2026 case of recurrent spontaneous pneumothorax in an 18-year-old man, raising a preventive-surgery question. Primary spontaneous pneumothorax means air collects in the pleural space from within lung tissue without trauma, and it can stay stable or become a tension emergency. Clinical suspicion drives diagnosis, with chest X-ray as the main tool. Care ranges from needle aspiration to chest tube drainage, with surgery weighed for repeat cases.

The young man suffered three X-ray-confirmed episodes over seven months. The pattern was notable for recurrence on the opposite side after pleurodesis on one side, in an otherwise healthy adolescent. The case underscores the difficulty of idiopathic recurrence and the need to check for genetic or structural predispositions. It also asks whether preventive pleurodesis on the other side should be considered for patients with recurrent disease.
pmc-13333231:
Seung Soo Lee and colleagues update 2026 imaging assessment of pancreatic cancer for judging resectability. Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma is highly lethal, and imaging guides diagnosis and management, with treatment largely set by tumor stage and resectability at first diagnosis. Pancreatic CT protocol is the preferred first-line imaging method, while MRI and PET/CT serve as problem-solving tools. In non-metastatic disease, anatomic resectability turns mainly on tumor-vessel contact, classed as resectable, borderline resectable, or locally advanced.

Treatment decisions have traditionally relied on anatomy alone, yet growing evidence highlights the limits of that approach. An expanded concept now adds biological and host-related conditional factors, including carbohydrate antigen 19-9 levels, imaging tumor phenotype, and lymph node patterns detailed in the full paper. Radiologists and surgeons gain a current frame for judging not just whether a tumor can be cut out, but whether surgery fits the tumor's biology.
pmc-13333331:
Zequan Lin and co-authors present a refined protocol in 2026 for creating an Alzheimer's-like state in zebrafish larvae with aluminum chloride. Zebrafish are cheap, breed fast, and have transparent young, making them attractive for screening candidate drugs and genes, but published recipes vary so much that results are hard to compare.

The sticking point is acidity: aluminum chloride breaks down in water and drops the pH, harming larvae on its own. In trial runs, 100 μM gave unstable effects while 150 μM killed or deformed many larvae, so the team settled on 150 μM with tight pH control at 4.8 to 4.9, reached by careful alkali titration and fresh daily solutions. The protocol walks through breeding embryos, choosing and treating larvae, running improved behavior tests, and analyzing the data. The authors say the tighter standardization should yield a consistent disease-like picture across laboratories.
pmc-13333431:
Mindong Mi and colleagues mined urine for early warning markers of diabetic kidney disease in a 2026 study, since the standard albumin ratio catches damage late. Catching the disease at its silent stage matters because it drives a huge share of kidney failure worldwide.

The study enrolled 200 people: 50 healthy controls and 150 with type 2 diabetes split evenly by albumin level into normal, mildly raised, and heavily raised groups. The team screened classic urinary proteins, 20 amino acids, and the full protein catch from mass spectrometry. Two classic proteins, transferrin and immunoglobulin G, scored AUC values of 0.926 and 0.916, and all 20 amino acids together reached 0.928, beating any single amino acid. One protein stood above the rest: SERPINA1, confirmed by a targeted test at an AUC of 0.964. The authors nominate urinary SERPINA1 as a leading candidate for early diagnosis and staging.
pmc-13333731:
Emma Scudero and co-authors assessed tooth decay risk in toddlers in a 2026 cross-sectional study, using intraoral cameras alongside microbe tests and family surveys. Twenty-one mother-child pairs took part, with toddlers averaging 3.9 years of age.

Camera images were scored with an adapted international caries detection system, and agreement between scorers was good for healthy teeth but poor for moderate to severe decay. Most toddler teeth were sound, with about one in ten showing mild decay. Streptococcus mutans appeared in 45 percent of toddlers and Lactobacillus in 19 percent. Brushing more often went with lower levels of both bacteria. The study also probed transmission from mothers and habits such as soda drinking to build a fuller risk picture.
pmc-13335831:
Yewei Li and co-authors worked out how much potassium a zinc battery electrolyte needs in a 2026 study. Adding potassium ions helps aqueous zinc-ion batteries, but cathodes of zinc hexacyanoferrate slowly dissolve, and nobody had a rule matching dose to lattice form.

The team set a current-dependent critical dissolution concentration as the reference point, mapping how cathode dissolution depends on potassium level through thermodynamic analysis. Microscopy and X-ray diffraction showed that too little potassium leaves the lattice underexpanded while the right amount steadies it under current. Cycling tests at graded concentrations and currents then pinned down the optimal potassium ratio for each working current. The rule turns electrolyte tuning from guesswork into a formula for longer-lived zinc batteries.
pmc-13336031:
Jiawei Zhou and co-authors turned a cancer driver into a drug delivery handle for childhood sarcomas in a 2026 study. These childhood tumors vary widely yet share excess MDM2 and lack targeted treatments.

MDM2 harms cells two ways: breaking down the guardian p53 and sitting on chromatin to keep growth programs switched on. The team built MDM2-recruiting degrader molecules, PROTACs, aimed at the CDK9/Cyclin T gene-copying complex. Their lead, dCDK9-010, beat the parent CDK9 inhibitor and the MDM2 antagonist alone or combined, striking the MDM2-p53 axis and super-enhancer copying at once. Breaking down that machinery dismantled the programs these tumors are addicted to. The approach shows how an excess oncoprotein can be drafted to destroy the very machinery it sustains.
pmc-13336131:
Jing Wang and colleagues study 2026 epitope-mapped digital SERS mapping of shape-shifting targets via a multi-epitope two-target immune frame. Digital Raman scatter immune tests turn epitope binding events into digits to achieve very sensitive protein finding. However, current setups mostly rely on single-epitope spotting, yielding a 1D molecule view of antigen structure and hiding how shape variety or mutation-induced changes affect targets.

This limit cannot be fixed simply by combining multiple single-clone immune proteins, as mixed linking and wild binding collapse epitope-mapped signals into pooled, mixed signals. The authors present EpiCount-SERS, a multi-epitope digital SERS frame that enables epitope-mapped immune mapping. The platform employs nano-body-based two-target immune pieces that pair epitope-mapped nano-bodies with a unified anti-PEG linking domain, enabling aim-controlled sticking to color-coded SERS tags.
pmc-13336731:
Chansik Kim and colleagues test a fat-stripping liposome idea in a 2026 liver cancer study. Extra cholesterol in cell membranes blocks drug entry and weakens treatment for hepatocellular carcinoma. Their cholesterol-carrying liposomes act like a laundry for membranes, pulling cholesterol out and letting drugs in more freely.

Drug uptake and killing improved in cancer cells, three-dimensional spheres, and patient liver tissues kept alive on perfusion chips. Water-hating drugs gained more than water-loving ones. In mice with fatty livers, the liposomes alone cut liver fat, inflammation, and scarring. Cell studies traced the path: swallowed liposomes collect membrane cholesterol inside sorting bubbles, which then pass it on for processing.
pmc-13337431:
Øyvind Bjerke and Thomas Priqueler map research on outdoor school physical education in a 2026 scoping review. Outdoor settings are praised for activity, wellbeing, and sustainability learning, yet the literature is scattered across traditions. Following standard scoping methods, the team gathered peer-reviewed empirical studies from 2005 onward in English, French, or Norwegian.

Forty-one studies published between 2005 and 2025 qualified, mostly from Western Europe and the United States and aimed at primary and lower secondary pupils. Outcomes clustered into physical, psychological, social, and environmental domains. Activities ranged from fitness games and orienteering to cycling, adventure challenges, and water-based sessions in grounds, parks, forests, and beaches. The map shows where evidence is thick and where gaps remain.
pmc-13337631:
Danilo Bontempo and colleagues test a psychological chain behind compulsive social media use in Generation Z in a 2026 study. Social platforms are where young adults build identity and friendships, and problematic use is a rising public concern. The team surveyed 520 daily users aged 18–25 years online, measuring borderline symptoms, defense styles, and social media addiction.

Immature defenses, unconscious habits for dodging hard feelings, carried the link between borderline personality traits and problematic use. The mediation held after accounting for age, sex, education, and other defense types. In plain terms, borderline traits may drive overuse partly through immature ways of handling emotion. The authors discuss therapy angles that target those defenses, alongside the study's limits.
pmc-13337931:
Yitao Ren leads a 2026 survey on first choice of care in highland farming areas of Qinghai. Mountain barriers and local culture may shape where residents seek care first. Anderson's model sorted influences into background, enabling, and need factors.

Data from 1,443 residents were analyzed with regression and a Shapley method that ranks each factor's share. Overall, 62.7 percent preferred primary care sites as reported. Older age, having insurance, and better self-rated health each raised that preference. Ranking the factors helps officials decide which levers, such as insurance reach, matter most for guiding patients to local care first.
pmc-13338831:
Yunus Emre Tütüneken and Elif Kabasakal study jaw function links in temporomandibular disorders in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Fifty-four adults with a prior diagnosis took part. Jaw limits were compared with pain, mouth opening, neck disability, and quality of life.

Jaw function scores tracked strongly with pain at r equal to 0.87 and with neck disability at 0.71 in the reported correlations. Worse function also meant narrower opening and lower quality of life across all domains, most sharply for physical health. The tight jaw, neck, and pain links argue for treatment plans that address the neck and daily function together, not the jaw alone.
pmc-13339031:
Ezzat E. E. Gabar and colleagues report a 2026 case of covering exposed brain lining after skull bone infection. A 35-year-old man had post-injury occipital bone infection with hair-loss scarring and a full-thickness defect. Free flap surgery carries vessel risks the team wished to avoid.

Their single-stage method stacked three layers: a dermal substitute called Matriderm, a rotated scalp layer, and a shifted skin flap on one stalk. The donor area received the substitute plus a thin skin graft. Outcome satisfied both function and appearance as reported. The approach offers a salvage option for medium defects in patients unsuited to free flaps.
pmc-13339231:
Fazhi Yang and a large team test a simple blood ratio for survival after severe heart attack in a 2026 study. Urea nitrogen divided by albumin blends kidney strain and nutrition into one score. Patients had emergency artery opening at a Kunming hospital from 2018 to 2023.

Records covered 1,099 patients treated with primary stenting as reported. Higher ratio values tracked with worse long-term survival in curve and regression analyses. After adjustment the ratio still predicted death overall and from heart causes. Accuracy checks support adding this cheap score to risk talks after ST-elevation heart attacks.
pmc-13340431:
Heating bio-oil compounds with carbon dioxide is the focus of a 2026 reactor study by Maria Virginia Manna and colleagues. Acetol, furfural, phenol, and syringol stood in for biomass pyrolysis oils, with methane and propane as plain hydrocarbon comparisons, all run in a tubular flow reactor at 800–1350 K.

Gas products were tracked online and liquid leftovers checked by chromatography and water titration. Breakdown dominated at lower heat, while true dry reforming took over above about 1200 K for the oxygenated feeds. Carbon dioxide conversion passed 50% and reached 100% at the highest temperatures. Phenol boosted hydrogen yield without shifting the reforming start point.
pmc-13340731:
A milk-filled cyst growing in armpit breast tissue is described by Abdulrahman Mohammed Abdulrahman Abouh and research partners in a 2026 case report. The 33-year-old breastfeeding mother noticed a steadily enlarging, mildly painful lump in her right armpit, while both breasts looked normal.

Ultrasound suggested a galactocele, and needle aspiration drew thick milky fluid that settled the diagnosis. Because of its size and her preference, surgeons removed the cyst together with the accessory breast tissue. She recovered well, kept breastfeeding, and had no recurrence. The case warns that such cysts can imitate lymph node swelling, lipoma, or even cancer.
pmc-13341531:
Arterial stiffness readings shift with posture and mental effort, in a 2026 study by Barbora Czippelova and colleagues. Twenty-three healthy adults averaging 22.3 years underwent tilt sequences and a mental arithmetic task while the Cardio-Ankle Vascular Index was recorded with pressure and gravity corrections.

The adjusted index rose progressively as tilt went from head-down to 40° head-up, exceeding both lying flat and head-down values. Heart rate, blood pressure, cardiac output, and vascular resistance were tracked alongside to explain the shifts. Since stiffness measures are meant to reflect vessel walls, knowing how posture and stress bend them matters for honest interpretation.
pmc-13341731:
Student PE teachers describe internship stressors in a 2026 grounded theory study by Chao Wang and colleagues. Deep interviews with 30 elementary physical education student teachers in western China were coded in three levels to build a model linking stress events, appraisal, coping, and outcomes.

Stress centered on teaching itself: complex tasks and interpersonal friction, rooted in resources failing to meet demands. Appraisals sorted into challenge, threat, and helplessness types, each steering coping toward gaining, protecting, or draining resources. Outcomes ranged from stronger professional identity to burnout, and fed back into later appraisal. Interventions, the authors suggest, should target the resource imbalance upstream.
pmc-13344431:
Sophie L Campman and colleagues compared in 2026 how often people from six ethnic groups in Amsterdam took a PCR test for SARS-CoV-2 before vaccines arrived. Testing was a central tool for slowing spread, yet uptake may have differed by group, shaping who was found, isolated, and protected.

The team linked a large urban health cohort to the city testing register, covering 19,006 adults, and defined uptake as at least one PCR test before early September 2021. Uptake ranged from about one quarter among Ghanaian participants to about one half among Turkish participants. Adjusted models then weighed age, sex, and group-specific factors, aiming to show where outreach and access failed and where future testing drives should focus first.
pmc-13346031:
Satoru Okada and colleagues reviewed in 2026 the biology of thymic epithelial tumours and how immune features should shape treatment. These rare chest tumours include thymomas, often linked to autoimmune diseases such as myasthenia gravis, and the more aggressive thymic carcinomas.

Complete surgical removal remains the mainstay for all types, with radiation and drug therapy playing larger roles in advanced or recurrent disease. Drawing on a broad literature search plus their own research, the authors contrasted how thymoma and carcinoma differ in immune behaviour and drug sensitivity. The synthesis aims to match each tumour type to the strategy most likely to help, including immunotherapy choices where autoimmune risk must be weighed carefully.
pmc-13348131:
Masahiro Hayashi and colleagues report the first complete genome for a seawater Francisella species, in an announcement published in 2026. Strain GTC 22824 came from coastal water off Osaka, Japan, concentrated and grown on rich agar. Paired long and short reads closed the genome, since the species was known from wild and clinic sources yet lacked a finished sequence.

The circular chromosome spans 1,991,123 base pairs in the reported assembly, giving a solid anchor for a genus that includes serious pathogens. A finished wild strain genome helps labs tell harmless sea kin from dangerous relatives and track how the group spreads in coastal water.
pmc-13349931:
Yaoyao Chen and fellow authors reviewed the liver-brain axis in 2026, the two-way signalling network linking the liver with the central nervous system. Signals travel by nerves, blood-borne factors, and immune routes.

Far from passively obeying the brain, the liver actively senses and shapes immune and nerve responses across the body. The review contrasts human and mouse biology, including barrier structure and liver immune settings, then ties axis failure to obesity, diabetes, heart and vessel disease, anxiety, and depression. New treatments aimed at the axis for fatty liver disease, its inflamed form, and related mental conditions are surveyed as a growing field.
pmc-13350331:
Heidi Tranter and colleagues argued in a 2026 paper that people with disabilities must sit at the centre of usability testing for digital mental health tools. Their example is a referral tool for child and adolescent mental health services in the NHS, co-built with a pan-disability accessibility group whose members all had lived experience of disability.

Workshop feedback changed the login security steps and reworked wording and navigation across the tool. Web accessibility rules set only a floor, the authors say; skipping inclusive design widens the digital divide for the very people services aim to reach. They describe how the group was formed and run.
pmc-13350531:
Tang QinLi and Li Li studied male-oriented live-action romance games in a 2026 mixed-methods analysis of player reviews. These interactive dramas boomed in 2023, yet how they generate emotional pull and turn it into praise and spending was unexamined.

Reviews of four representative titles across platforms were coded by content analysis, emotion scoring, and topic modelling, backed by online fieldwork. Emotional interaction drove ratings most, story came second, while body representation and technical topics sometimes backfired through objectification complaints or performance disputes. Oddly, category patterns held for whole works but weakly for single reviews. Designers chasing word of mouth should invest in the relationship, not the spectacle.
pmc-13350631:
Lukasz Dorobisz and co-authors measured in 2026 blood flow in external carotid artery branches. These branches are possible donors for microsurgical brain revascularisation. Bypasses linking the superficial temporal artery to cerebral arteries treat picked cerebrovascular states. Yet donor vessel flow capacity in healthy people was not fully mapped.

Ultrasound measures in 157 adult volunteers with no vessel disease were taken. The group was split evenly by sex. Peak systolic, end-diastolic, and mean velocities were tallied, plus minute flow. Heart risk factors were also noted. Stats charts of normal values give surgeons a reference for picking donor vessels and forecasting bypass flow. The base line data back safer planning for brain bypass operations.
pmc-13354231:
Wei Zhang led a 2026 nationwide survey of physicians' openness to AI that prescribes drugs. Drug-giving AI has advanced slowly, and it is unknown whether keeping a doctor in the loop would raise acceptance, or in which settings physicians see such tools being used first. The survey studied views, perceived roles, and likely rollout contexts.

Physicians across China answered questions about AI giving, with designs that require human approval at each step. Replies reveal where doctors welcome assistance, where they demand oversight, and where they resist automation altogether. Developers and policymakers gain a grounded map of the trust problems that must be met before giving AI reaches routine care.
pmc-13355531:
Jia-Jin Chen led a 2026 real-world study of GLP-1 target agonists in dialysis people with type 2 diabetes. These people face extremely high heart and deaths risks, yet evidence for effective care in this group is limited. Whether GLP-1 drugs help people on dialysis, as they do in broader diabetes populations, was unclear.

Using TriNetX records from 2013 to 2022, the team built 1,688 propensity-matched pairs of new GLP-1 users and new DPP-4 blocker users. Major adverse heart events formed the primary outcome, with secondary results also tracked. The study gives nephrologists comparative evidence for choosing diabetes care in a people often excluded from trials.
pmc-13355731:
Yining Chen and co-authors pooled brain scan studies in 2026 on lasting white matter harm after traumatic brain injury. White matter carries signals between brain areas, and diffusion scans can reveal hidden damage months after injury. The team kept 27 studies of people at least three months post-injury, excluding sports and combat cases, and compared them with controls.

Scans showed weaker signal direction and freer water movement across many pathways, a sign of damaged wiring. Effects were larger after moderate to severe injury, and strongest in the corpus callosum, the bridge between brain halves. Age, sex, and scanner strength swayed results, so the authors urge tighter controls in future work.
pmc-13356631:
Majid Jafari and others showed that an N-end amphipathic helix governs action and shape moves of Nramp metal transporters, in 2026. Nramps are proton-coupled transporters of divalent metals key for homeostasis. In humans, Nramp2 mediates iron uptake, while Nramp1 exports metals from phagosomes to support anti-germ defence.

Surveying solved Nramp parts, the team found the helix and tested its role in transport action and shape change. The helix proves central to how these transporters move metals across skins. The work shows a fundamental way of metal homeostasis, with relevance to iron illnesses and host defence against illness.
pmc-13356731:
Hisako Kushima and co-authors compared heart tracing features in 2026 between two rare lung scarring diseases. One disease, IPPFE, scars the upper lobes and flattens the chest, yet its heart tracing pattern was poorly defined. The team reviewed tracings, heart ultrasounds, and chest scans for 20 patients with that disease and 18 with the more common lung fibrosis.

The IPPFE group showed a clear rightward shift in the heart's electrical axis and a shorter PR interval, still in the normal range. Scans showed the lung roots pulled higher. The shift did not track with chest shape or heart measures, so the authors think changed heart position from chest deformity is the likely cause, and tracings may aid recognition.
pmc-13357331:
Changhong Zhang and co-authors report a 2026 study on breast cancer care in China. They built a tool that uses ultrasound scans to guess how fast a breast tumor is growing. The key marker is Ki-67, a protein that shows how quickly cancer cells divide. Doctors now check Ki-67 with a needle biopsy, which can hurt and can miss parts of the tumor.

The team studied 558 patients at two hospitals and pulled fine detail from their ultrasound images. They mixed those image traits with basic facts like age and tumor size to build three models. A chart form of the best model, called a nomogram, let doctors read off a risk score. The work points to a gentler way to plan care before surgery, without a needle test first.
pmc-13358731:
The Journal of Thoracic Disease issued a 2026 retraction notice for a paper it had published in 2020. The paper, led by Xueqiang Wei, had reported that a small RNA called miR-107 slows lung cancer cells by acting on the STK33 and ERK signals. All of the authors asked for the paper to be withdrawn.

The notice states the reason plainly: the study's data were in dispute. The authors agreed to the retraction and apologized for the trouble caused. Retractions like this one form part of the public record, warning later readers not to build on results the authors themselves no longer stand behind.
pmc-13358831:
Thomas Birdas wrote a 2026 editorial on what counts as success in esophagus cancer surgery. Removing the esophagus is among the hardest operations, above all in older patients. Registries track short-term results well, but long-term survival and later health care use have stayed murky. A study by Blasberg and colleagues linked a national surgery registry with Medicare records to fill the gap.

Their analysis covered nearly 5,000 patients aged 65 and older operated on between 2012 and 2020. Birdas argues the fuller picture, of survival, readmission, and risk over years, should reshape how surgeons and hospitals judge value in this demanding operation.
pmc-13359431:
Jianli Shi and co-authors report a new pig virus in China in a 2026 paper. The virus is a reshuffled form of porcine sapelovirus, a gut virus in the same family as polio. This recombinant strain does something alarming: it causes severe disease and crosses the blood-brain barrier, the wall that normally shields the brain from germs in the blood.

The team identified the virus, mapped its mixed genome, and showed its effects. A pig virus that reaches the brain raises the stakes for farm biosecurity, since such viruses spread fast through herds. Early warning and monitoring can help veterinarians contain outbreaks before they widen.
pmc-13359731:
Lucas Alexander Knøfler and co-authors build a transparent forecast for hospital stay after liver surgery in a 2026 study. Patients with colorectal cancer that has spread to the liver often have the deposits removed. Stays vary widely, and a good advance estimate helps counsel patients and plan beds. No trusted tool existed for this forecast.

In a multicenter study of 915 patients in Denmark, they built a model whose reasoning doctors can audit step by step. How the surgery was done, plus tumor size and count, proved the strongest predictors of a long stay. The model's accuracy matched that of less transparent rivals.
pmc-13360631:
Akio Goda and co-authors present a 2026 study of thinking skills and movement in healthy older adults. All took a standard memory test and scored near the top, so the usual screen showed no problems. The team used a phone-style app version of a color and word pick-out test that taps planning and focus. Scores were adjusted for age before the group was split and compared.

Two movement measures stood apart clearly between the score groups: a timed stand-and-walk test and top walking speed. Both gaps held up after strict checks across 70 measures. Other links, like balance on one leg and step length, faded under those checks and count as early hints. The authors say the app can spot movement-linked thinking gaps that normal screens miss.
pmc-13361831:
Nam Xuan Vo and co-authors reviewed the cost-effectiveness of a newer statin in a 2026 paper. Faulty blood fats drive heart and vessel disease and a heavy global cost. Statins are the main defense, and pitavastatin is the newest of the class, matching stronger rivals at lowering bad cholesterol. The team searched three databases for economic studies through November 2025.

They compared pitavastatin with atorvastatin and rosuvastatin, the two most used statins. The main measure weighs extra cost against extra health gained, counted in quality-adjusted life years or cholesterol cuts. Study quality was graded with current reporting and bias tools.
