Health systems must choose which statin to fund, and pooled economic proof helps them spend wisely.
pmc-13362231:
Insafe Mezjan and co-authors reappraised surgery strategy for multilevel spine narrowing in a 2026 study. Many patients needing surgery for lumbar stenosis show narrowing at several levels on scans. Opening every level is a bigger operation; opening only the level that truly drives symptoms is gentler. The team used a two-portal endoscopic method that allows precise, targeted decompression through small openings.

They reviewed consecutive adults with at least two narrowed levels treated from December 2022 to July 2025 at one center. Only the symptom-driving level was decompressed in this strategy. Outcomes were then judged against the case for full multilevel surgery. If one level is enough for most, patients gain shorter operations and faster recovery. The study adds real cases to a live surgical debate.
pmc-13362431:
Ibrar Ahmad and colleagues introduce a 2026 computer vision study that sorts mangoes into five shelf-life stages, from unripe to spoiled. Sorting by eye is slow and uneven, and poor sorting wastes a large share of the crop in poorer countries. Their model reads a photo and judges ripeness from color and skin texture, using a design built to run fast on small devices.

Trained on 4,428 mango photos, the model sorted the stages with about 98 percent accuracy in repeated tests. It beat other light models while staying quick and lean on memory. Photo maps show it looks at the same skin cues a human grader would. The tool could suit packing sheds with cheap hardware.
pmc-13364331:
Hui Li and co-workers propose a 2026 plan for the fastest safe path of a servo motor used in fine machines. Old plans use steady state torque and speed caps. Those caps waste the short bursts of extra force such motors can give off when cool.

The team maps a moving cap zone shaped by heat and turn angle, then ties it to an energy use model. A fast solver picks the best path in a flash of time. Tests in sim and on real gear back the plan. The gain is quicker moves with no loss of care for heat.
pmc-13368831:
E Meyer and others fully surveyed fascial closure ways at stoma undoing, ran the network meta-study in 2026. Incisional hernia after stoma undoing is frequent, yet optimal fascial closure remains unclear. Prophylactic mesh reinforcement adds another choice that random evidence could clarify.

Searching MEDLINE and CENTRAL through October 2025, random trials in adults comparing closure strategies and reporting hernia or op site illness were summed with random-effects frequentist and Bayesian network meta-studies. The study ranks closure ways and mesh strategies comparatively. Surgeons gain a comparative evidence base for closing the belly wall at stoma undoing.
pmc-13369631:
Roberta Giorgione and colleagues run a small pilot study of bees exposed to smoke from a landfill fire in a 2026 paper. Bees were sampled in May, before the fire, and again in June, after it. The bees were split into three groups: untreated controls, bees fed the plant Quassia amara, and bees fed probiotics. Lab tests measured markers of cell damage and gene regulation.

Across all bees, the markers showed no clear change after the fire. In untreated bees, one damage marker rose sharply, while bees given Quassia amara showed a clear fall in that same marker. The authors stress that the sample was small and the results are early leads only, but the work points to diet as a possible shield for pollinators facing dirty air.
pmc-13371731:
Conchita Sisí and co-authors probed links between heavy social media use and sharp thought in a 2026 study. They tested 943 young adults in Spain, aged 18 to 35. Each person filled in a scale on problem use and did two quick screen tasks on focus and self-control.

Heavy use went with slower times on the focus task, but daily hours of use told the story best. The self-control task showed no clear link. The tie was stronger in women than in men. The authors say that hours spent may matter more than a problem label, and that focus, not control, is the skill most at stake.
pmc-13373231:
Hinrich Gronemeyer wrote an obituary in 2026 for Pierre Chambon, a giant of gene science who died on May 5, 2026. Chambon taught in Strasbourg, France. Early in his career he found a cell enzyme that adds a chain to proteins, work that much later led to a class of cancer drugs.

The piece traces his path from that find to his lead role in how genes are read and switched in cells. It notes his eye for the big ask of his time and his force as a lab head. For readers new to the field, it is both a life story and a short tour of how modern gene science was built.
pmc-13375531:
Peter C Kahr and co-authors give long-term news on a heart protein drug in a 2026 study. The drug is a lab-made immune tag that seeks stray protein laid in the heart wall. In the first human trial it was safe and cut marks of that load over one year.

A group of 23 men from that trial kept on with the drug in an open next phase. They got a mean of ten more drips, for a top of 24 in all. Most also took a pill that steadies the same protein. Long checks of heart shape, marks, and harms will tell if load cuts turn to real gains.
pmc-13380931:
Josephine N Rioki and co-authors argue in a 2026 perspective that East Africa should rebuild breast cancer control around cell testing and genetics in national policy. Care in the region has long reacted to symptoms rather than acting early on risk. Breast cancers there often appear younger and behave more aggressively.

The proposal draws on a multi-year Kenyan research program covering cell patterns in breast samples, risk factors, and inherited gene faults. The authors recommend using needle-based cell sampling as a first triage step, then adding genetic screening into primary care. That shift, they argue, could move the region from late diagnosis toward precise, preventive public health.
pmc-13382931:
Lukas Goede's team mapped action and rest tremor to distinct motor cortex networks, in a 2026 brain stimulation study. Both Parkinson disease and essential tremor respond to deep brain stimulation, yet whether the two tremor types share a target was unclear. The team used stimulation network mapping across patient cohorts and targets.

Rest tremor linked more strongly to effector-specific zones along the motor strip, while action tremor favored inter-effector territories, in both disorders. Clinical programming choices aligned with symptom-specific engagement. The split supports tailoring stimulation to the tremor type rather than aiming at one generic motor target.
pmc-13383131:
Shoeb Bin Islam's team compared hepatitis knowledge and infection between Rohingya refugees and host residents in Bangladesh, in a 2026 study. Teknaf hosts over a million displaced Myanmar nationals alongside local Bangladeshis, both facing hepatitis B and C risk. The team surveyed and blood-tested 654 adults at a Teknaf hospital between April 2021 and March 2022.

Overall 3.52 percent tested positive for hepatitis B or C, but refugees carried far more hepatitis C at 17.24 percent versus 1.01 percent. Passing knowledge reached only 5.17 percent among refugees versus 12.25 percent among hosts, and no refugee knew of hepatitis B shots. The gap calls for targeted teaching and screening in camps.
pmc-13383431:
Charles Prendergast and co-authors relate sugary snacks and soft drinks to allergy outcomes in Polish children in 2026 work. Data came from the Polish arm of the Global Asthma Network, covering 4,647 children aged 6 to 15 years. Parents reported how often children ate sweet snacks and drank soft drinks.

Frequent sweet snack intake tied to higher odds of lifetime hay fever and eczema, but not to current symptoms. Soft drink results pointed both ways, with lower odds for some allergies yet higher odds of current wheeze. Girls and children exposed to traffic fumes showed higher symptom odds throughout, which the authors note as firm background factors.
pmc-13385431:
Zong Chen and co-authors find that precursor cells in fat release a factor that keeps the tissue in balance in 2026 mouse work. Fat precursor cells were isolated from marked animals and proved eager to mature into fat cells. Gene profiling hinted they both promote fat formation and calm inflammation at once.

Follow-up work pinned those effects on clusterin, a secreted protein the precursors release. Clusterin fed back to aid the precursors' own maturation and raised resistance to oxidative stress in nearby cells. Mice lacking clusterin in the right cells lost fat tissue balance, which marks the protein as a therapy lead.
pmc-13386931:
Yang Liu and Yue Liu track gain and loss of plasmid-borne resistance genes across nearly 7,000 bacterial genomes in 2026 work. Plasmids shuttle drug resistance between Enterobacteriaceae lineages at high speed. A family-tree aware model measured gain, loss, growth, and shrinkage for plasmid genes across 6,895 genomes.

Resistance genes changed hands at rates like other plasmid genes, but expanded and shrank far faster. Lineages already carrying resistance on their chromosome gained more plasmid resistance and lost less than their sister lineages. Effects depended mostly on species, not drug class, which marks chromosomal resistance as a warning sign.
pmc-13387031:
Sofia Prada and colleagues report autoimmune pancreatitis mimicking cancer in a young man in a 2026 case report. A 32-year-old with asthma had three weeks of upper belly pain spreading to his back, without jaundice. Scans showed several ill-defined pancreatic masses with gland enlargement, raising strong concern for a tumor.

Blood tests showed raised total IgG and mildly raised IgG4, with tumor markers negative. MRI features, including a capsule-like rim and a preserved main duct, pointed instead to autoimmune disease. Steroid treatment, started after team review, brought rapid improvement and a symptom-free taper.
pmc-13389031:
Abigail E Calder leads a 2026 placebo-controlled crossover trial asking whether a single dose of LSD leaves lasting effects on brain function and learning. Forty-five healthy adults, including 24 women, each received 100 micrograms of LSD and a placebo on separate occasions.

For up to a week after dosing, the team measured brain responses with scalp recordings and magnetic stimulation, tracked a blood factor linked to brain growth, and tested typing-based motor learning. Learning between practice sessions improved the day after LSD, and reported stress was lower one week later. Readers interested in psychedelic science get a cautious human test of claims first raised in animal work, with both brain measures and lived experience covered.
pmc-13391731:
Wei Xu and colleagues compare, in 2026, three non-drug brain stimulation methods for Alzheimer's disease in a network meta-analysis of randomised trials. Current drugs offer only modest and short-lived benefit, so non-invasive stimulation has drawn strong interest.

The study weighs three ways to spur the brain: light, weak direct current, and pulsed magnets. It weighs how well each works, how easy each is to give, and how safe each is. The maths blends head-to-head trials with indirect proof. Doctors gain a ranked view of methods that have met in one trial all too rarely. The ranks help them pick which path merits a large, firm test next.
pmc-13392631:
Brook M Jensen, Alden S Estep, and Silvie Huijben traced how three mutations in a mosquito nerve channel combine to blunt insecticide sprays. They bred the yellow fever mosquito Aedes aegypti into six genetic combinations using parent strains from one Florida site, then dosed males and females with the spray chemical deltamethrin on the skin.

Mosquitoes carrying all three changes in double dose withstood over fifty times the dose that killed a standard laboratory strain, while other combinations fell in a lower band. Two resistant gene pairings behaved as partly recessive traits. Modelling showed the benefit of resistance rises and falls with dose and with how common the trait already is. Once body weight was accounted for, males matched females in resistance, which suggests males could serve in field monitoring.
pmc-13393231:
Ghaffar Kiani reviews fifteen years of Iranian work on genetically modified rice. The crop is pressed by drought, salty soils, and pests in a country that leans heavily on it for food security. A national research programme has moved from gene discovery to field trials, and Kiani maps that path through a systematic search and thematic reading of the literature. Insect-resistant Bt lines headline the results.

Field data show the engineered lines holding stable inserted genes, stacking several traits, yielding more, and needing less pesticide with a smaller environmental footprint. Yet planting remains blocked by a biosafety framework that does not function and by public scepticism. Contrasting Bangladesh, where modified crops reached farms, Kiani argues science alone cannot close the gap. Working regulation is one missing piece. Public engagement that frames home-grown modified rice as a sustainability tool is the other.
pmc-13393331:
Herrera-Luna and colleagues developed a light-driven method in 2026 to make aryl boronate esters, building blocks prized for assembling new molecules and medicines. Their recipe uses visible light alone, with no light-absorbing catalyst and no metal, and runs inside a gel open to the air. The starting materials are common aryl halides, ring compounds carrying a halogen atom that is easy to swap.

The gel gave the fragile reaction a stable setting. The method worked across halides bearing many other groups, such as alcohols, amines, and esters, in some cases giving the product in full yield. Light-absorption tests and magnetic resonance experiments showed the partners first join in a ground-state complex held by hydrogen bonds, weak links between molecules, and computer models backed that picture. The authors present the route as a greener way to a key class of reagents.
pmc-13393931:
Qingqing Zhang and others pilot village-doctor care with cash perks and video links for old rural adults with sugar illness in a 2026 chance-assigned trial. Rural sugar care lags for want of funds, spotty sugar checks, and scarce doctor advice.

Six Baima Township village clinics were split by chance into plain care or joined care with cash perks plus video help. Among 215 finishers, the joined-care group cut its long-term sugar mark more over three months than plain care did. The pilot backs scaling doctor-led, perk-backed video care to lift rural sugar control.
pmc-13395431:
Johannes Malm and colleagues pilot, in 2026, daily tracking of dementia behaviour symptoms in Swedish nursing homes. Such symptoms swing by day and setting, yet notes are often rare. Staff at four units logged symptoms each shift for eight residents over ninety days. A digital form held both a standard scale and personal items.

Nearly twenty-two thousand entries were logged in all. Staff kept up the routine on about three quarters of shifts, though rates varied by resident and worker. Each entry grew faster with practice, halving in time by the last month. Symptom counts swung widely within one person across days. Staff found the routine easy to fit in.
pmc-13396031:
Colin R. Tosh and co-authors used a computer model to test whether trees planted in fields shield crops when bad weather strikes early in the season. Their 2026 study simulated one hundred years at Wakelyns, a farm in southeastern England known for alley cropping with rows of trees.

The Hi-sAFe model grew winter wheat and peas under two climate paths, a middle course and a very high emissions course, from 2001 to 2100. Yields were checked for steadiness and for losses in years with harsh early weather. The results support the view that the shelter, shade, and water effects of trees can soften climate shocks at the growth stages when young crops are most at risk.
pmc-13396331:
Wei Li and co-authors compared two look-alike forms of early lung cancer that both appear as solid masses on scans, in a 2026 study. Mucinous adenocarcinoma, which makes mucus, may behave differently from the common non-mucinous kind, and telling them apart early could shape care.

The review covered 579 patients with stage I disease, averaging about 60 years old. Clinical features, scan traits, gene changes, and relapse patterns were set side by side for the two groups, and survival curves were compared with standard methods. Models then tested which factors predicted relapse or death, giving surgeons a clearer picture of whether the mucus-making type needs different handling.
pmc-13396431:
Xin Li and co-authors combined genetics with lab checks to hunt for blood chemicals that cause, rather than merely accompany, the foot deformity called hallux valgus, better known as a bunion. Their 2026 study used Mendelian randomization, a method that treats inherited variants as a natural experiment.

Screening 1,400 serum metabolites flagged two tied to lower bunion risk: the amino acid cysteine and a bile-related compound. No reverse effect of the deformity on their levels appeared. Following cysteine, the team predicted 548 genes it may act on and found 47 shared with bunion-linked genes. Those shared genes clustered in known signaling pathways, giving drug hunters concrete targets.
pmc-13396631:
Zhao and co-authors enable, in 2026, high-voltage lithium metal batteries with ether electrolytes by adding a trace of lithium borohydride, 0.05 molar, to create dihydrogen bonds. Ethers suit lithium metal but normally decompose above 4.0 volts. The borohydride's hydridic hydrogen bonds to the solvent's slightly positive hydrogens. That weakens lithium-solvent binding, speeds lithium shedding its solvent shell at the anode, and shields the solvent's weak sites at the cathode from oxidation.

The modified electrolyte stayed oxidatively stable to 5.54 volts while keeping ionic conductivity above 16 millisiemens per centimeter at 30 degrees Celsius. Lithium cells against NCM811 cathodes retained 87 percent capacity over 400 cycles, while the conventional ether electrolyte collapsed to 5.6 percent retention under the same cycling. Full cells with thin lithium and loaded cathodes ran stably over 100 cycles at a 4.5-volt cutoff. The authors present dihydrogen bonding as a simple, synthesis-free route to high-voltage ether electrolytes.
pmc-13396731:
Leong and team map, in 2026, the absorption landscape of far-red Photosystem II, the machinery some cyanobacteria rebuild to harvest light beyond the visible range. In far-red mode, swapped subunits install chlorophylls, types f and d, that catch longer wavelengths. For the complex from Chroococcidiopsis thermalis and a Calothrix species, they combined cryo-electron microscopy, sequence checks, and charge analysis to assign each pigment its site and wavelength.

The C. thermalis structure revealed a subunit found only in far-red mode, PsbH2-prime, forming part of a chlorophyll f site, and the analyses assigned four chlorophyll f sites. Calothrix lacks the subunit and carries two of the four chlorophyll f sites found in its relative. Assigning wavelengths to red-shifted chlorophyll gives modelers the tools to simulate energy transfer through the far-red complex. The authors highlight shared features that let these microbes survive where white light barely reaches.
pmc-13397331:
Madhusudan Channappa and co-authors tested whether a plant protein drink taken before a sugar load blunts the blood sugar spike that follows, in a 2026 crossover study. Fourteen people with already-compromised blood glucose control took part.

Each volunteer received the Nutrilite All Plant Protein as a preload before a standard 75-gram glucose drink. It was served in 250 milliliters of spiced buttermilk. Each volunteer also had a control session without it, in a fixed order. Because every participant served as their own comparison, the design isolates the preload's acute effect despite the small group. A protein that softens post-meal spikes could earn a place in dietary care for early diabetes.
pmc-13397531:
Neel Vishwanath and fellow authors revisit whether men bleed more than women after facelift surgery under modern care. Their 2026 study matches male and female patients of one senior surgeon from January 2014 to January 2024. Men were long thought riskier because of thicker skin, richer blood supply and habits such as drinking or smoking.

Each man was paired with a woman of similar age, body size, smoking and health profile, and all shared one strict routine to prevent blood collections. That routine used set cutting methods, careful sealing of vessels and local tranexamic acid where noted. If rates now match, the old sex gap may reflect outdated care rather than the patients themselves.
pmc-13397631:
Xavier Perafita and others offer a poverty-normalized spatial Bayesian model beyond the Gini index in a 2026 study. The Gini index is widely used for income inequality, but it compares poorly across areas with different socioeconomic builds and wobbles in small populations.

Adding the poverty rate as an offset within Bayesian spatial modeling sharpened precision and comparability of small-area estimates. On income data for 8,043 Spanish municipalities in 2022, the normalized index bared inequality patterns the stock index missed. Researchers gain a fairer map of territorial inequality for small areas and for funding choices.
pmc-13397731:
Eng-Kean Yeong and co-authors test whether stem cells from the placenta can lift early survival after severe burns when basic care falls short. Their 2026 animal study responds to settings where fluids and warmth, the twin pillars of burn care, may arrive late or in short supply. The cells are known to calm inflammation, which drives much of the early danger.

Sixty male rats received standard full-thickness burns over 40 percent of the body, then were split into six groups mixing fluid dose, warming method and cell treatment by vein. Survival was tracked for 14 days, with blood levels of three inflammation markers also measured. Design lets the team judge whether cells help on top of, or in place of, ideal support.
pmc-13398131:
Quanxing Yao and colleagues craft a transistor that thinks and changes colour at once, copying how chameleons shift skin tone. Their 2026 study pairs a plastic semiconductor, P3HT, with an ion gel so voltage-driven ions tune both electric flow and colour. Robots and embodied machines need sensing, processing and feedback in one loop, and a device that shows its state could serve all three.

Ion entry creates charge carriers that reset the plastic's energy levels, flipping its light absorption in step with its conductance. The colour swing is strong and reversible, echoing a synapse's graded response in the same motion. Such dual behaviour could let robot skins sense, compute and signal without separate display hardware bolted on.
pmc-13398531:
Nick Patterson and co-authors read ancient genomes from a Himalayan cave to date a meeting of peoples. Their 2026 study sequences ten individuals from Old Lady Spider Cave in Ladakh, 4,000 metres up, buried about 1,500 years ago. South Asia's past is hard to reconstruct because ancient DNA from the region is scarce.

The ten genomes look alike and carry a rare blend: roughly half ancestry like today's North Indians and half like ancient Tibetans. Measuring the length of inherited blocks dates the mixing to at least 50 generations before these people lived, around 2,800 years ago. A high crossroads of trade routes, Ladakh kept that blended heritage while surrounding populations shifted.
pmc-13399331:
Mohamed Mowafy and colleagues built a flat, circuit-board style power combiner able to handle kilowatt pulses for L-band radar, reporting in 2026. Solid-state radar transmitters gang several amplifier modules together to reach high peak power. The Gysel design suits this job because its isolation resistors bolt to ground, giving heat a direct escape path. It has usually been built in bulky waveguide form.

The team's four-way planar version, etched on RO4003C substrate, reached a 3 kilowatt peak output. Their optimization adjusted line impedances and lengths while accounting for current flow, heat dissipation, and manufacturing tolerances. The prototype covered 1.2 to 1.4 gigahertz with input return loss better than 15 decibels and isolation above 25 decibels. Bench results matched simulations closely, which the authors offer as proof that planar construction can serve kilowatt-class radar.
pmc-13399631:
Wen-Cheng Shi and colleagues compared two forms of bupivacaine for a chest-wall nerve block in older patients having keyhole lung surgery, in a 2026 randomized trial. Liposomal bupivacaine packages the same drug in tiny fat bubbles that release it over up to three days. The team tested whether it eases pain and opioid use after video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery.

A total of 116 older patients were allocated to standard or liposomal bupivacaine, with the block placed before anesthesia began. Pain scores matched at most time points but ran significantly lower in the liposomal group at 24 and 36 hours after surgery. That group scored higher on the QoR-15 recovery questionnaire at 24 hours, pressed the pump fewer times, and used less sufentanil between 24 and 72 hours. Rates of side effects and postoperative delirium did not differ. The authors say the long-acting form buys a real, if time-limited, advantage for this age group.
pmc-13399931:
Angelo A. Mattos and colleagues review how a disturbed gut microbiome helps drive acute-on-chronic liver failure, the catastrophic flare of cirrhosis that fills hospital wards, in this 2026 article. Drawing on clinical studies and meta-analyses, the authors put gut bacteria escaping into the body at the center of the story.

Their account runs from imbalance to catastrophe: cirrhosis skews gut microbes, the skewed community inflames the intestinal wall, and the leaky barrier lets bacterial products flood the portal blood. That flood ignites the inflammation that tips a compensated patient into organ failure. Because dysbiosis sits upstream of the cascade, the review tours microbiome-directed treatments as candidate therapies, from probiotics and rifaximin to fecal transplants. The authors present such treatment as a plausible way to change the disease's course rather than a proven one.
pmc-13400131:
Soh Yamamoto and colleagues report three adolescents whose chronically low platelets unexpectedly surged after taking the influenza drug oseltamivir, in a 2026 case series from Japan. Across four influenza episodes, every one treated with oseltamivir, platelet counts climbed sharply about a week and a half after the antiviral started.

The median count rose from 9.1 to 26.7 in units of ten thousand per microliter, peaking at a median of 11.5 days after oseltamivir began. One girl's count overshot to 93.1 in the same units before settling. Two episodes forced the team to cut or pause eltrombopag to avoid excessive clotting risk, and counts drifted back to baseline over a median of 57 days. No thrombosis, major bleeding, or other harm occurred. They advise planned monitoring when children with chronic ITP on eltrombopag receive oseltamivir.
pmc-13400531:
Fan Yang and colleagues review, in 2026, how the stiffness and softness of lipid nanocarriers shape their fate in the body. These tiny fat-based packages, including liposomes and lipid nanoparticles, ferry drugs to targets. Yet their behavior at the boundary with cells and tissues varies widely, slowing clinical use.

Mechanics, the authors argue, is a key hidden variable. The review gathers measured mechanical traits for three carrier types, the structural features that set them and the ways stiffness affects uptake, travel and delivery. It also covers tools for measuring mechanics and engineering tricks to tune them. Building a shared database, they say, would let designers craft carriers by mechanical design rather than trial and error.
pmc-13400631:
David Bescoby and co-authors release, in 2026, a global dataset mapping the exact boundaries of coastal World Heritage Sites. Coast heritage faces flooding and erosion, worsened by sea level rise and development. Risk modeling was held back because site boundaries existed only as rough points or not at all in digital form.

The Glo-CoH dataset digitizes 1,250 individual sites that sit along coasts below 20 meters elevation, spanning cultural, natural and mixed listings and a vast total area. Boundaries were drawn from site plans and satellite imagery. A validation exercise on a sample found over nine in ten digitized sites reached top accuracy grades. The free dataset is aimed at researchers and planners judging climate exposure.
pmc-13400731:
Yan-Bo Li and colleagues report, in 2026, a reaction that swaps a single boron atom for a carbon atom inside a ring molecule while keeping everything else in place. Such single-atom skeletal editing lets chemists isolate the effect of one atom change, a prized tool in drug design. Methods for it in aromatic systems are rare.

Their process converts ring compounds called benzazaborines into quinolines, using glyoxylic acid as the carbon source. The group originally attached to boron is caught and reattached to the product, making this a true single-atom swap rather than a rebuild. The reaction tolerated many functional groups and worked on late-stage derivatives of natural products and drugs. Detailed mechanism studies accompany the method.
pmc-13400831:
You-Fan Peng and colleagues ask, in 2026, whether eating more cholesterol raises the odds of prediabetes, the borderline blood sugar state that precedes diabetes. Many nutrients have been tied to prediabetes risk, but dietary cholesterol itself was unexamined. Data came from a United States national health and nutrition survey spanning 2011 to 2016.

Based on day-long dietary recalls, people with prediabetes reported higher cholesterol intake than those with normal blood sugar. Intake also tracked modestly with fasting glucose and long-term sugar markers across all participants. After adjustment, higher cholesterol intake was independently linked to prediabetes, with odds roughly a quarter higher. The authors suggest limiting dietary cholesterol may help prevention, while noting survey data cannot prove cause.
pmc-13400931:
Faranak Behnaz and colleagues run, in 2026, a randomized trial comparing two sedation drugs during stereotactic brain biopsy, a needle procedure done through a fixed head frame. Dexmedetomidine calms patients while easing blood pressure and stress responses. Remifentanil is a very short-acting opioid. The trial weighed sedation depth, vital signs, pain and recovery.

One hundred forty patients were assigned to one drug or the other under single-blind conditions. The remifentanil group reached deeper sedation scores. The dexmedetomidine group kept higher heart rate and blood pressure readings during surgery. Afterward, that group reported less pain and needed significantly less morphine in recovery. The authors present a trade-off: deeper sedation with one drug, better pain control with the other.
pmc-13401131:
Sonia Baumard and co-authors use, in 2026, a case of typhoid fever with a dangerous immune overreaction syndrome to ask how that syndrome should be treated when typhoid triggers it. The syndrome, called HLH, is a life-threatening state where immune cells stay switched on. Guidance exists for tuberculosis-triggered cases, but not for typhoid.

Their illustrative case involved an eighteen-year-old French man of Senegalese ancestry. Alongside it, the authors reviewed past published typhoid-linked cases. They asked two questions. Is specific immune treatment always required on top of antibiotics? And if so, should steroids or intravenous immunoglobulins be preferred? Standard scoring helps diagnosis, while steroids, immunoglobulins and chemotherapy drugs remain the main first-line options in general practice.
pmc-13401531:
Jingchen Jia and co-authors ran a 2026 split-mouth randomized trial on laser treatment for pain after orthodontic tooth movement, comparing pulsed Nd:YAG laser settings against a continuous-wave laser. Soreness after braces are fitted or adjusted hurts the patient experience and compliance.

Ninety-six first-time fixed-appliance patients were assigned to four groups of 24: pulsed laser at low, medium, or high frequency, namely 10, 15, or 20 hertz, or a continuous-wave semiconductor laser. Within each patient, one randomly chosen side of the mouth received active treatment while the other side got a sham procedure, making every participant their own control. A digital pressure algometer measured pressure pain thresholds. The team aimed to find the best frequency and firm evidence for pulsed laser pain relief in orthodontics.
pmc-13401631:
Julia Stalder wrote a 2026 patient perspective piece on ductal carcinoma in situ, the so-called stage zero breast cancer, drawing on her own diagnosis. The condition is non-invasive, yet standard care brings surgery, radiation, and hormone therapy, a mismatch she calls a distressing paradox.

Research increasingly suggests many DCIS cases would never progress to invasive disease if left alone, but clinicians cannot yet predict reliably which ones will. Stalder examines how inconsistent language between providers, uneven risk communication, and a shortage of balanced educational material shape the choices patients face, especially without access to specialist centres. Her recommendations target transparency, shared decision-making, and patient-centred support, with continued research and better risk stratification tools.
pmc-13402231:
Singh and Chattu assess, in 2026, the Seventy-eighth World Health Assembly, held under the theme One World for Health, and its push for health equity. The Assembly adopted the Pandemic Agreement and resolutions on health financing, air pollution, and traditional medicine. This came against a backdrop of the United States' planned withdrawal from the World Health Organization and a 600 million dollar budget shortfall facing the agency.

A headline commitment sends 20 percent of pandemic-related products, tests, treatments, and vaccines, to the WHO to pass on to low-income countries under the agreement. The health financing resolution, adopted on May 24, 2025, responds to an expected 40 percent cut in external health aid and rising out-of-pocket costs for patients. The authors recommend health diplomacy, stronger regional cooperation, shared digital systems, and local drug manufacturing to convert the Assembly's commitments into fair outcomes on the ground.
pmc-13402831:
Hao-Yu Lan and colleagues shrink monolayer semiconductor ribbons to a few dozen nanometers wide and find the transistors get better, not worse. Future chips need channel widths in the tens of nanometers, yet most devices from atom-thin transition metal dichalcogenides stay micrometer wide. The team narrowed molybdenum disulfide ribbons from hundreds of nanometers down to about 30 to 40 nanometers.

Median on-current density rose about 42 percent and subthreshold swing fell about 16 percent on narrowing, with a champion device hitting 995 microamps per micrometer at the stated voltages. Clean edges, stronger gate grip at ribbon edges, and better side contacts shared the credit, cutting contact resistance from about 860 to 270 ohm-micrometers. The platform extended to tungsten disulfide and p-type tungsten diselenide, the latter reaching 357 microamps per micrometer, backing ribbons as a route to ultra-scaled electronics.
pmc-13403031:
Feras Al Lami and co-authors show how descending necrotizing mediastinitis, a lethal spread of deep neck infection down into the chest, was beaten without surgery in their case. The disease usually starts from dental or throat abscesses. It races along neck tissue planes. Older series lost about half their patients. Modern mortality still runs 40 to 60 percent when drainage lags.

Their patient was diagnosed from laboratory findings and clinical examination. He recovered on an appropriate medical approach alone, against the usual insistence on operative drainage by routes from thoracotomy to thoracoscopy. The authors do not dismiss surgery. They use the success to argue recognition speed and immediate broad antibiotics decide survival first. Drainage strategy, they note, remains contested territory. The case adds a data point for carefully chosen nonsurgical management.
pmc-13403731:
Yongfeng Liu and colleagues found a greener way in 2026 to cook up glowing crystal dots for light amplifiers. The dots, made of a lead halide crystal, shine brightly yet lose much light to waste paths. Their recipe uses lecithin, a natural fat-like coat, plus a simple solvent.

One batch yielded over 10 grams of dots, with room to scale up further. The coat calmed surface flaws and slowed clumping during growth. Dots kept shining under air, heat, strong light, and harsh solvents. Light output reached about 95 percent efficiency in their tests. Amplifier thresholds fell to levels the team calls record-low for plain dot films.
pmc-13404931:
Jordan L Hickman and team mapped how direct electrical stimulation of the neocortex engages neurons in three dimensions. Their 2026 work uses three Neuropixels probes set at right angles in mouse visual areas to record voltages and spikes around a stimulation source with sub-millisecond detail. Brain-surface stimulation underpins neuroscience and neuromodulation, yet how fields recruit tissue and shape perception had stayed unclear.

Evoked potentials spread unevenly and grew less than linearly with amplitude, shaped by anatomy. Higher amplitude raised the density but not the reach of directly responsive neurons, with fewer than 5 percent switched on directly. Fast-spiking interneurons fired nearer the source, pyramidal neurons fired unevenly by direction, and sparse direct spikes drove large responses in over half of neurons at higher amplitudes. Mice weakly sensed single pulses, with no gain from amplitude. The work argues that patterning, not spike count, governs impact.
pmc-13406631:
Kazushige Migita and colleagues describe gallbladder surgery in a man kept alive by an implanted heart pump, in a 2026 case report. The man in his fifties had carried a HeartMate II pump for six years while waiting for a donor heart. Fever and upper belly pain signalled an inflamed gallbladder with stones.

Blood thinners, pump hardware and the risks of inflating the belly for keyhole surgery all complicated action. Doctors first drained the gallbladder through the liver to cool the infection. Delay carried its own danger, since infection could seed the pump and end transplant hopes. The case shows the staged reasoning such patients demand, in a field with thin formal evidence.
pmc-13406731:
Małgorzata Chojak and Marta Czechowska-Bieluga use brain wave markers to guide support for children from alcohol-affected families, in a 2026 study. Such children grow up with chronic stress that can disturb attention and body tension. Resting brain recordings offer an objective window beside teacher and parent reports.

The theta-to-beta ratio separated the groups most strongly among all markers tested. Frontal alpha asymmetry, another popular marker, lost significance after correction for multiple comparisons. Children from affected families showed weaker attention regulation and higher physiological arousal in the reported profile. The authors rank markers into a hierarchy so schools and social services can match interventions to each child's measured needs.
pmc-13407831:
Chenqi Liao, Danyang Sun, and Xiong Wang review, in 2026, delivering Alzheimer's medicines up the nose to reach the brain. Many candidate drugs never reach useful levels in the brain. They also cause body-wide side effects. The nose offers smell-nerve and trigeminal routes into the head. These partly bypass the blood-brain barrier, especially when drugs ride in engineered nanocarriers.

The review sorts many cargoes. They range from repurposed small molecules and natural products to proteins and nucleic acids. Platforms range from lipid particles and polymer nanoparticles to gels and delivery devices. Design dials include particle size, surface charge, mucus interaction, and targeting decorations. Translation stalls on species differences in nasal anatomy, tiny dose volumes, device variability, thin human data, and manufacturing and safety hurdles, which the authors catalogue frankly.
pmc-13407931:
Jacob Rosenberg and Kristoffer Andresen ask, in 2026, who will still know how to repair groin hernias the open way in Denmark. Keyhole repair has displaced the open Lichtenstein operation over two decades. The pair analysed the national hernia database's 296,864 elective repairs from 1998 to 2025 to see what that means for training and future services.

By 2025 only 19 percent of one-sided repairs were open, and open work was thinly spread. Of forty departments still doing it, eighteen performed fewer than twenty a year and only four exceeded a hundred. Reoperation rates after open repair have climbed across successive five-year periods while keyhole rates held steady. Maintaining universal open competence through ordinary training no longer looks realistic, so the authors suggest centralising open surgery and leaning into keyhole training.
pmc-13408131:
Raviteja Sista and team built standard Reporting and Data Systems for laparoscopic cholecystectomy, the gold-standard gallbladder removal op. Their 2026 work takes on scattered, free-form pre-, intra-, and post-op data across centers, which hampers filing, retrieval, and quality comparison. Reporting systems already make radiology uniform, but surgical data lacked a like standard.

The proposed LC-RADS logs pre-op findings, ultrasound, operating theatre findings, procedure video, and follow-up, plus a surgeon-bound section on skill. One hundred surgeons of varied skill reviewed the system, with 73 percent agreeing it logs apt data well and 77 percent favoring regular use. The center-neutral proforma aims to make surgical data uniform for better care management, pending uptake and outcome studies.
pmc-13408431:
Seyedeh Zahra Miri and co-authors test in 2026 whether gum from the wild almond kin Amygdalus scoparia can fight the germs behind tooth decay. Plant antimicrobials draw interest as drug resistance spreads. The standard mouthwash drug chlorhexidine also has drawbacks. The team made an alcohol-based extract of the gum, known locally as Zedo gum.

Lab tests measured the clear zones the extract opened around wells. They also found the weakest doses that stopped or killed three oral streptococci plus Staphylococcus aureus. Both lab strains and strains taken from patients were used. Against a patient strain of the main decay germ, the extract's zone beat the zone from chlorhexidine. The mouthwash drug still won on raw strength per dose. Patient strains resisted more than lab strains throughout. The team presents the gum as a hopeful natural option, not a finished swap.
pmc-13409031:
Safronova and co-authors examine in 2026 whether stiff arteries go hand in hand with fading cognition in people whose only diagnosis is high blood pressure. One hundred twenty-eight adults, ninety-six with hypertension and thirty-two without, had their arterial stiffness measured by two indices and their thinking tested with a standard screening tool. The stiffness measures came from the cardio-ankle vascular index and a newer heart-ankle index.

The two indices tracked each other almost perfectly across everyone tested. More importantly, worse scores on the cognitive screen accompanied stiffer arteries by either measure, with moderate correlations in both cases. The newer index had never before been tied to cognitive results, so its parallel behaviour supports it as an alternative gauge. The authors frame arterial stiffness screening as a possible early window on vascular cognitive risk in hypertension clinics.
pmc-13410431:
Chengyi Zhu and colleagues present in 2026 simple carbon-based compounds that keep glowing after the light goes off. The glow lasts close to a second, which is long for such plain molecules. Materials like these could serve in lighting and in marks that expose fake goods.

One lead compound, a six-carbon bis-formamide, glowed in crystals and in plastic films with fair efficiency. Heat scans, X-ray work, and timed light measures pointed to tight hydrogen-bonded packing that traps the excited state. Trials used the materials for decoration, anti-fake marks, and color shifting in white light devices. Warming and cooling restored the glow, a handy trait for reuse.
pmc-13411431:
Minghui Tan and co-authors build in 2026 a chatbot system that trains Chinese health workers to hold advance care planning talks. Facing illness, patients need help stating wishes for future care, and those conversations are delicate. A multi-agent simulator lets staff practice safely before real talks.

Three datasets drive three roles: an assistant, a case presenter, and an evaluator. Thousands of synthetic dialogues, drawn from literature and policy sources, train the team. One open model was fine-tuned, while a commercial mini model got tuning plus crafted prompts. Human and automatic judges scored both under a five-part quality framework. Adapted models beat their baselines, which supports the simulator as a training tool.
pmc-13411931:
Anton Labutin and co-authors trace, in a 2026 field and genome study, how a new hantavirus lineage arose where two vole populations meet. Tula orthohantavirus infects the common vole across Europe, and its genome comes in segments that can swap when two strains infect one host. The researchers trapped voles at 58 sites across a contact zone between two host lineages.

Among 127 infected voles they found 27 reassortant viruses clustered in a band about 12.5 kilometres wide. One reassortant, carrying a swapped middle segment that codes for the surface glycoprotein, dominated most of the zone. Modelling showed its glycoprotein tip has a distinct shape, which the authors read as adaptation to hybrid hosts.
pmc-13412131:
Elisabet Fernandez-Gomez and colleagues studied 306 pregnant women in Melilla, Spain, in 2026 to link eating patterns with pregnancy weight gain and nutrient adequacy. Too much or too little gain raises risks for mother and child, and the team scored diets from food questionnaires against weight change and vitamin and mineral intake.

A Mediterranean pattern tracked with steadier weight gain and better fiber and vitamin B12, D, and E intake, while a Western pattern tracked with higher gain. The paper supports Mediterranean-style eating advice during pregnancy, delivered through clear health education.
pmc-13412331:
Benjamin J. Hazen, Brian P. Staak, and John B. Holcomb argue in 2026 that future large wars will demand a new source of blood for wounded soldiers. Planners project 800 to 3,600 American casualties a day against a near-peer enemy, far beyond recent wars, and bleeding remains the top preventable cause of battlefield death. In Iraq and Afghanistan only about a fifth of the wounded needed transfusions.

The authors propose a formal Walking Wounded Blood Bank: stable casualties who need no transfusion themselves would donate before evacuation. Extrapolating past data, a 72,000-casualty scenario could yield some 57,500 such walking wounded as potential donors. Donation during redeployment processing could add more, and the authors dismiss harvesting blood from the dead as unsound.
pmc-13413731:
Desirée Victoria-Montesinos and co-authors review in 2026 how exercise and food complicate life with type 1 diabetes even when an automated insulin system runs the show. These hybrid closed-loop systems improve glucose control, yet workouts and meals still force users to count carbohydrates, announce food, and flip exercise settings by hand. The narrative review blends trials, observational work, and technical studies across children, adults, and pregnancy.

Glucose swings with exercise depend on insulin still active under the skin, workout type, meal timing, and the body's counter-hormones, which current single-hormone systems cannot fully outguess. Personalizing food strategy around sensor trends and insulin on board is the practical advice offered. Dual-hormone pumps, activity sensors, and metabolite-guided tuning are flagged as promising but unproven in daily life.
pmc-13414831:
Javier Conde-Pipó and colleagues explore whether mouth bacteria predict who gains grip strength from exercise in later life, in a 2026 pilot study. Eighteen community-dwelling older adults completed sixteen weeks of supervised training. Mouth microbes were profiled before training began, using gene sequencing.

Participants whose relative handgrip strength rose were classed as responders. That group began with richer mouth bacteria, averaging about 86 genera against about 72 in non-responders. Richness also tracked the size of strength gains in correlation tests. Some signals faded after correction for many comparisons, which the authors flag openly. Larger studies must confirm whether the mouth offers a useful early marker.
pmc-13415031:
Rita Nocerino leads a 2026 mixed-methods study of eating difficulties in children with food allergy. Seventy children at a specialist allergy center completed questionnaires on restrictive eating symptoms, fear of new foods, and diet quality. Twenty-six children also took part in gentle interviews and drawing tasks about food.

Screening flagged possible avoidant restrictive eating symptoms in three children, about 4 percent of the group. Moderate fear of new foods appeared in about 64 percent, with high levels in about 34 percent. Poorer diet quality scores tracked with stronger selective eating. Interviews surfaced five themes, including fear built on memories of past allergic reactions.
pmc-13415331:
Vishwa Suravaram and colleagues compare two ways to hold a broken, dislocated ankle steady before final surgery, in a 2026 review. Nine cohort studies covered 1,638 patients treated either with a plaster splint or with an external frame pinned to bone. The reviewers graded bias and certainty with standard tools.

Loss of the corrected position occurred in three percent of frame cases, against about fifteen percent with splints. Soft tissue complication rates looked similar in both groups. Timing of final surgery varied too much across studies for a firm answer. Certainty was moderate for the reduction finding and very low for the other outcomes.
pmc-13415531:
Ziyi Zhang and colleagues built a detector in 2026 for crowded radio signals on spectrum maps, where overlapping emitters merge and blurred edges trigger false alarms. Their Separation and Boundary-Aware network splits tangled features with one module and sharpens edges with another, tackling the precision-recall tradeoff head on.

In a dense-emitter dataset the network scored an F1 of 0.988 with recall near 0.991, beating seven rivals at every density level and holding steady across confidence thresholds. Spectrum managers gain a tool for mapping busy airwaves where transmitters crowd together and signals overlap.
pmc-13415831:
Jennifer Steinadler, Christian Minke, and Thomas Bräuniger record boron NMR spectra from a single crystal of the mineral hambergite, in 2026. They used the less common isotope boron-10, whose spin of three splits its signal into three doublets per boron site. Rotating the crystal changed the spectra in a controlled way.

Extracted chemical shift and electric field gradient values matched an earlier boron-11 study of the same crystal closely. Line widths confirmed a long held idea: boron-10 gives cleaner resolution because its weaker magnetism shrinks line broadening from neighbors. Single crystal work sharpens parameters that powder samples blur.
pmc-13418131:
Nora A AbdelMotlb and colleagues compare benzoic acid with salicylic acid as growth regulators for Swiss chard, in a 2026 field study over two seasons. Both acids shape plant growth and defence, yet their side by side effects on leafy vegetables were unclear. The Ruby Red cultivar received each acid at three strengths in a blocked field design with three repeats.

Both acids improved growth, minerals, and health linked compounds over untreated plants. The lowest dose of each worked best overall. Benzoic acid at that dose also cut leaf nitrate the most, a quality plus. The authors recommend the low benzoic dose for high yield with better leaf quality.
pmc-13418431:
Wuping Zhang, Hanping Shi, and Jie Peng are the authors of a sepsis diagnosis paper retracted by the editor of BMC Infectious Diseases, in a 2026 retraction note. The original article, published in 2025, proposed a machine learning model to diagnose sepsis and guide drug discovery. Concerns after publication focused on how the model was built and checked.

Review found likely overfitting and possible data leakage, where information from test data seeps into training and inflates accuracy. The editor judged these flaws serious enough to undermine trust in the model's diagnostic claims and general use. All authors disagreed with the retraction, the note records.
pmc-13418831:
Mingyu Kim and colleagues test whether perfusion numbers from a contrast MRI scan hold steady across the software sold by different vendors. Such scans can act as a stand-in measure of tumor blood vessel growth in prostate cancer. The team drew on records of men who had prostate surgery between December 2021 and September 2022 for confirmed cancer.

Readings from these scans can shift with blood flow, the choice of input artery curve, the math model used, and the vendor's own processing steps. That spread matters when a number guides care or when clinics compare results. The study lays out where vendor systems agree and where they drift apart on the same patients. Its findings support care with cross-vendor checks before perfusion values are pooled or compared.
pmc-13419031:
Junhong Yuan and colleagues found a dual-action compound in 2026 that dismantles the driving program of fusion-positive rhabdomyosarcoma, a childhood muscle cancer with poor outlook. The cancer hinges on the PAX3-FOXO1 transcription factor, sustained by two histone demethylases, KDM4B and KDM5A, in a mutually reinforcing loop.

Their compound, called Compound 01, triggers destruction of both enzymes, collapses the cancer program, and sharply curbs tumor cell growth and metastatic behavior. The paper establishes dual demethylase blockade as a strategy for breaking this cancer's core circuitry and for drug developers seeking new angles.
pmc-13422831:
Margaret A. Kypreos and five colleagues report, in a 2026 study, the real performance of the thinnest available cryobiopsy probe for diagnosing interstitial lung disease. Freezing a tiny piece of lung through a bronchoscope can spare patients open surgery. Yet the larger probes bleed dangerously. The newer slim probe promised similar answers with less risk, on conflicting evidence.

At a Texas medical centre, registry patients who had the procedure between 2022 and 2026 were reviewed. Adding cryobiopsy to a standard lung wash produced a diagnosis in about forty-four percent of patients and changed the working diagnosis just as often. Risks were real but bounded: collapsed lung in about eleven percent and bleeding in about six and a half. Taking more samples raised the yield.
pmc-13422931:
Ana M Pinto and four colleagues argue, in a 2026 paper, that fibromyalgia is best understood as an emotional imbalance written into the body. Their postulate: threat systems run hot while the soothing system runs weak. Early hardship can deepen that imbalance. It leaves epigenetic marks, and those marks sensitise the pathways of pain and stress.

Emotions, they note, are not mere ideas. They shift immune, hormonal and inflammatory processes that keep chronic pain going. The clinical encounter itself becomes a biological intervention, working through expectation effects, neural synchrony and shared calming of the vagus nerve. Care that is kind and validating, restoring a felt sense of safety, should improve outcomes, they argue. That holds in fibromyalgia and in chronic pain generally. The paper is a case for compassionate care as treatment, not decoration.
pmc-13423031:
Md. Shaffiul Alam leads a fourteen-author team applying Bayesian mixture modelling to blood-test thresholds for bovine brucellosis, a bacterial disease of cattle, in dairy herds where the infection is common. Fixed cut-off values, they note, blur the spread of antibody readings and hide differences between herds, so a probabilistic approach may read results more fairly.

Working with 2,696 milk samples, the group fitted a three-part model separating healthy, latent, and diseased animals. Two thresholds emerged, near 10.7 and 82.2 on the antibody scale, yet confirmatory cut-offs varied widely between herds, and herd prevalence ranged from about 1% to 67%. Herd-specific thresholds, the authors conclude, suit endemic settings better than one universal line.
pmc-13423831:
Federico Mazza and seven colleagues borrow a tool from quantum measurement theory, quantum Fisher information, to characterise strange metals. In these materials, electrical resistance falls in a straight line with temperature instead of the usual curve. Physicists lack a positive fingerprint for this state, and heavy-fermion compounds, where electrons behave as if hugely heavy, are a key test bed.

Combining neutron scattering measurements with large computer simulations, the team watched fluctuations tied to the breakdown of the Kondo effect, a screening process in these materials. As temperature dropped and the strange metal formed, the Fisher information climbed steeply with no set scale. That pattern signals deep many-particle entanglement. It offers a concrete hallmark of the strange metal state.
pmc-13424031:
Jeong, Yong, and Park experiment with an unlikely starter culture in this 2026 food study: extracts of Korean traditional fermented soy pastes used to ferment butter. Cream was inoculated with a 0.5 percent extract solution from cheonggukjang, doenjang, or meju, three distinct pastes. The resulting butters were compared against a commercial-starter control. The comparisons covered chemistry, microbes, aroma, taste, and human sensory panels.

The meju butter stood out. It carried the highest lactic acid bacteria counts, along with greater yellowness, fat, and moisture than the other samples. The cheonggukjang batch had the highest total plate counts. Human tasters scored the meju butter highest on most traits, supporting paste extracts as functional starter alternatives.
pmc-13424531:
Wei and Ding pool the trial evidence in this 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. They ask whether giving probiotics to infants prevents atopic dermatitis. That is the itchy eczema that often opens the allergic march of childhood. Eighteen randomized controlled trials enrolling 10,195 infants aged up to 36 months compared probiotic supplements against placebo or nothing.

The pooled result was a shrug: a risk ratio of 0.94 for developing dermatitis, with a confidence interval spanning 0.72 to 1.25 and a p-value of 0.66, meaning no significant protection in the analysis, and the trials disagreed with each other substantially. Sensitivity checks confirmed the null result, and no publication bias showed. The authors draw a careful distinction: earlier positive meta-analyses leaned on regimens starting in pregnancy, treating mother and baby together, whereas starting probiotics only after birth has failed to show consistent benefit.
pmc-13424731:
Junyan Li and four colleagues translate two maternity-care questionnaires into Traditional Chinese and validate them among mothers in Hong Kong. One scale measures how respected mothers felt during childbirth; the other measures how much say they had in decisions. Both were rendered through a strict forward-and-back translation process, then tested with 1,395 women who had given birth locally within five years.

The respect index emerged in a revised thirteen-item, three-factor form after one item was dropped, with perfect content validity ratings and a reliability score of 0.86. The seven-item autonomy scale survived unchanged, fitting a single factor with reliability of 0.91. Both instruments now give Hong Kong researchers dependable tools for studying respectful maternity care.
pmc-13424831:
Nonna Grigoryan and four colleagues publish the first national checklist of thick-headed flies, family Conopidae, for Armenia. They draw on expeditions in 2024 and 2025 plus specimens held in Yerevan's Scientific Center of Zoology and Hydroecology. These flies, many of them parasites of bees and wasps, had never been inventoried for the country.

Distribution follows altitude: most species live in mid-elevation mountain steppe and grassland between about 800 and 2,000 metres, while alpine meadows up to 2,600 metres host their own specialists. Armenia emerges as a Transcaucasian stronghold for the family.
pmc-13425031:
Banda and colleagues reviewed 17 years of light therapy for mycosis fungoides at a British teaching hospital, from 2007 to 2024. Mycosis fungoides is the most common skin T-cell lymphoma. They weighed narrowband ultraviolet B against PUVA. PUVA pairs a drug that makes skin light-sensitive with ultraviolet A. They also searched for traits linked to who responds to phototherapy.

The cohort held 33 patients with a median age of 58 years. Of them, 26 received narrowband treatment, 5 received PUVA, and 2 received both. Complete remission and partial remission were each reached by 15 patients, a 45 percent rate for each outcome. Three patients showed no response. Hypopigmented disease did far better than hyperpigmented disease. Advanced stage at treatment start pointed to poorer outcomes. Side effects appeared in only three patients. That backs both options as effective and well tolerated.
pmc-13425631:
Anderson and colleagues used the New Hampshire Colonoscopy Registry in 2026 to ask what colonoscopy finds after a positive stool test. They compared three groups: 1,089 patients after a positive multi-target stool DNA test, 436 after a positive blood-in-stool test, and 43,379 who went straight to screening colonoscopy. The focus was patients carrying both growth types at once, glandular adenomas and flat serrated polyps.

Patients with a positive DNA stool test had over twice the risk of mixed lesions compared with either other group. Their risk of serrated polyps, the harder-to-see type, was nearly triple that of the colonoscopy-only group. The blood-based stool test group showed no such excess. Most stool-test patients with mixed lesions also had at least one advanced lesion. Most colonoscopy-only patients with mixed lesions had none, so a positive DNA test flags a higher-risk colon.
pmc-13425831:
Jade Y. Moon and a large expert group published 2026 consensus guidance on eye disease in incontinentia pigmenti, a rare genetic condition that can blind. Practice for screening, classifying, and treating retinal problems varied widely despite risks of detachment and vision loss. Guidance came from the International Conference on Incontinentia Pigmenti held in February 2025 and sponsored by the National Foundation for Ectodermal Dysplasias, supported by literature review and author images.

Families and eye specialists gain shared rules for when to examine, how to stage retinal findings, and when to treat. Standard care should reduce missed windows for preventing detachment in affected children.
pmc-13425931:
Alexander S. Dowdell and colleagues study how gut microbes steady a gut-lining switch called HIF, which helps the bowel barrier hold firm. Trillions of microbes live in the gut, and their presence keeps the lining mildly low in oxygen, a state that supports barrier work.

Harmful bacteria were already known to steady HIF without relying on short-chain fatty acids, but the paper tests whether harmless resident bacteria do the same. The question matters for gut health, since a steady barrier keeps microbes and their products on the right side of the wall. Readers get a bridge between microbe ecology and human gut defence.
pmc-13426231:
Asya Achimova and coauthors show that adults with Williams syndrome handle logical language surprisingly well in a 2026 cognition study. Williams syndrome brings mild to moderate intellectual disability with severe spatial and number weaknesses, raising questions about abstract words such as quantifiers, numerals, and connectors such as and, or. Two experiments tested 32 adults with the syndrome against 32 neurotypical English speakers.

Participants with Williams syndrome scored well above chance and near ceiling on set-based meanings of basic quantifiers, numerals, and connectors, and on entailments flowing from them. Preserved logical semantics, despite broad cognitive difficulty, reshapes assumptions about language and intellect in this syndrome. The tests used plain words and short tasks, so the high scores can not be put down to luck or to ease of the work set.
pmc-13427131:
Soppelsa and collaborators report a route to a new class of cyclopentadienes, using copper hydride. Cyclopentadienes are five-membered ring building blocks. Their acidity and rapid hydrogen shifts have long made stable handed versions nearly impossible to obtain. The new route converts simple precursors into cyclopentadienes loaded with extra groups. The products keep their shape and handedness.

The reaction gave the products in high yield with very high enantioselectivity. One mirror-image form ruled almost completely. Computer work traced the selectivity to an unusual step in copper catalysis. A nitrile group gets activated, rarely seen in this chemistry, during the key bond-forming stage. The new rings proved unexpectedly stable. The team credits a conjugated push-pull effect between electron-donating and electron-withdrawing groups. They propose this effect as a general design principle. It could tame the tendency of cyclopentadienes to fall apart.
pmc-13427431:
Ziyu Wang and coauthors probed how brain stimulation sharpens task switching using EEG and machine learning in a 2026 double-blind study of 24 participants. Volunteers performed unpredictable magnitude and parity switching tasks under anodal stimulation over the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex or sham stimulation. Active stimulation improved switch cost accuracy while reducing mixing cost accuracy, a split behavioral pattern needing neural explanation.

Brain wave analysis found larger N1 responses in repeat trials. It also erased N2 latency differences between switch and repeat trials. Power in alpha, beta, and theta bands shifted in specific windows, with central theta gains in women. Machine learning classification helped separate responders, addressing inconsistent stimulation outcomes. Brain waves were read in fine time slices, so the team could track how the pulse shifts thought step by step as each task switch came and went.
pmc-13429131:
Chenxue Wang and co-authors review, in a 2026 paper, how phone-based tools and neighborhood care could jointly tackle diabetic foot disease where resources are scarce. Foot ulcers in diabetes lead to amputations that good early care can prevent, yet poor regions face late arrival, thin specialist cover, and fragmented services. The authors searched literature from 2005 to 2025 across three databases plus policy sources. Sub-Saharan Africa anchors the discussion.

Digital tools can flag high-risk feet early and keep patients connected between visits. Community workers can teach prevention and speed referrals before ulcers worsen. Neither works alone for long: both need primary care links, referral paths, trained staff, and funding that stays. The authors insist on health equity as the design standard, adapting tools to local reality instead of importing high-income models whole.
pmc-13430431:
House and colleagues audit the educational materials given to children awaiting kidney transplants across the United States in this 2026 study. Good materials build partnership between children, caregivers, and clinicians around shared priorities: kidney function, infection, survival, and participation in normal life. The team collected packets from transplant centers and scored their readability, their coverage of the four priorities, and how they portrayed life after transplant.

Of 73 centers approached, only 23 shared materials. That is about a third. Just six packets included anything aimed at children themselves. Reading levels averaged around ninth grade, far above the children concerned, with only one packet written at a sixth-grade level. Infection was covered most, survival least, and the portrayal of normal life mixed hope with caution while emphasizing physical recovery over emotional well-being.
pmc-13430731:
Shungo Kamioka and co-authors found a fresh route in 2026 to ring-shaped iodine compounds that hold two linked aromatic units across a seven-membered ring with an oxygen bridge. Such salts serve as handy tools for building rich aromatic products. Older routes first had to stitch the frame in place before an oxidation step, and mid-sized rings stayed rare.

The new route starts from a ready salt that carries an alcohol arm and a spare ring that later leaves. A fleeting reactive species forms, the oxygen arm reaches across, and the iodine center closes the ring from inside. A final proton step frees the product. The rings then serve as platforms for deeper change, giving access to oxygen-bearing ring systems and a short path to cannabinol.
pmc-13431031:
Nakai, Takeshita, and Komiya test a simple elastic toe tube exercise against the standard short foot exercise to wake the small muscles inside the foot. Those muscles stiffen the arch and pass force during running and jumping. Their 2026 study uses a randomized crossover design in twenty young men. Each man tries the tube exercise, the short foot exercise, and rest, a week apart. Ultrasound scans of three foot muscles and rebound jump tests come before and after.

Only the tube exercise clearly worked on the day. It swelled all three muscles' cross sections by roughly six to thirteen percent. That passed the threshold for a real change, beating the short foot drill and rest. Reactive strength, a jump score that blends air time against ground time, also rose only after the tube work. The authors pitch it as a quick priming drill before sport or rehab sessions.
pmc-13431131:
Lan and colleagues examine the brain's waste-clearance system in children with spinal muscular atrophy in this 2026 study. The disease is known for killing lower motor neurons, but it also affects brain development, and the glymphatic system maintains brain health during growth. The team prospectively recruited 48 children with type 2 or 3 disease and 53 typically developing controls, measuring clearance with three imaging approaches.

Children with the disease had more cerebrospinal fluid than controls. Enlarged perivascular spaces were more frequent. The diffusion-based clearance index was lower. Together, the pattern indicates glymphatic dysfunction. The fluid volume was negatively tied to disease severity, so milder cases carried more fluid in this sample. A subgroup of 22 patients treated for a year with nusinersen, the standard gene-targeting drug, still showed increased fluid and a lower clearance index afterward.
pmc-13431331:
Betül Ay, Mehmet Ata Öztürk, and Galip Aydın taught a computer system in 2026 to name therapy moves of children with autism from body-point tracks alone. Such tracks hide faces and names, which guards privacy, while hand scoring of sessions eats time and varies by scorer. Many therapy moves look near alike, which makes the task hard for software.

Their base system learns a set of motion patterns and blends them to name each move. The team added a training-only step that spots the pairs of moves the system mixes up most and pushes those pairs apart. Scores rose on three test styles, with the largest gain when test children were new to the system. On a held-back set, the system named moves right in most clips and beat recent rival methods.
pmc-13431431:
Song and co-authors surveyed health workers in 2026 about electroacupuncture, needling combined with mild electric current, used to treat hemiplegia, one-sided weakness after stroke. They asked how knowledge, attitudes, and daily practice connect.

The survey at a Chinese medicine hospital in Wuxi collected 311 valid replies during 2023 and 2024, mostly from physicians, and about three in five respondents had used electroacupuncture before. Scores showed insufficient knowledge, favorable attitudes, and moderate practice. Modeling of the answers found that knowledge improved practice both directly and by improving attitudes first. Both links were stronger among workers who already had hands-on experience, so the authors recommend training that pairs theory with supervised clinical practice.
pmc-13432531:
Maurizio De Rocco Ponce and co-authors charted seed quality in 2026 for transgender people born male who banked sperm before starting hormone care that affirms their gender. Two large fertility centers kept the records. The group of thirty-two had not yet begun hormone care, and their reads faced off against men without gender care and against a small group that had paused past care.

Hormone levels sat in normal bands for most. Fewer than half met world norms for healthy seed counts, against three quarters of the comparison men. The paused-care group showed higher female hormone levels and lower seed volume, with more faults that fell short of firm proof. The authors urge early talks on childbearing plans and banking before hormone care starts, since base quality may already run low.
pmc-13432831:
Akingbola and colleagues published a 2026 study mapping hepatitis B vaccine cover across the globe. The third vaccine dose guards children against liver failure and liver cancer. The team tracked coverage in 204 countries from 1980 through 2023. Their data came from a major global disease-burden dataset of estimates.

World coverage rose from near zero in the 1980s to about 82 percent in 2023. Albania led the world at just over 98 percent coverage. Somalia sat lowest, at only 14 percent of children covered. Europe and Oceania ran high, while coverage stayed far lower across sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. Steady yearly gains still leave the 2030 full-coverage goal at risk. Targeted catch-up drives in lagging regions are their chief recommendation.
pmc-13433331:
Murad Ansary and co-authors studied in 2026 how the minds of working mothers in Bangladesh tea gardens fare, and how their strain tracks with their young children's conduct. Field work in one tea district mixed counts from 451 mothers of kids aged two to seven with deep talks and group chats. Set scales read low mood, worry, stress, and child conduct.

Near a third of mothers scored in the mid-to-grave band on each strain scale, and a third showed poor well-being overall. Age tied to stress and to well-being, while child care setups showed no tie to worry. Most children scored in the flagged band for conduct and feeling faults on mother reports. The authors urge better work terms, open child care, and aimed mind care for garden mothers.
pmc-13433931:
Inés Fournon-Berodia and co-authors watched a sea anemone shed skin cells in 2026 under starvation, and tied the loss to a squeeze-out act that may predate most animal lines. Skin sheets likely came before the last shared root of animals, yet how food lack steers their upkeep stayed dim. In the anemone's outer skin, dying cells push out in a ring pose.

A lit ring of kin cells wraps each pushed cell, while grip parts slide to the base. Drug pokes showed death is a must for the act, yet death alone cannot call the ring. One signal chain caps how dense the squeeze-outs pack. Starved skins squeeze more, and kin may eat the shed cells for food scrap. Core marks look old, the authors say.
pmc-13434031:
Brüssow surveys the astonishing variety of bacterial defenses against phages in this 2026 editorial. Phages are viruses that infect bacteria, and computer predictions suggest about thirty genes per E. coli genome belong to anti-phage systems, many still uncharacterized and clustered in defense islands. The editorial highlights recently described examples chosen to show how differently these systems can work at the molecular level.

Some systems sense the phage's own countermeasures and retaliate. Others chop free DNA ends or scan for single-stranded overhangs. A membrane complex called KIWA blocks the phage from injecting its DNA at all. Several build endless DNA or protein products that stall the cell or poison the invader. Strikingly, some bacterial systems resemble animal antiviral defenses such as gasdermin and Argonaute, pointing to an ancient shared origin of immunity.
pmc-13434531:
Deliang Kong and colleagues survey 36,874 adults in Chongqing, China, in 2026, asking how body health and mind health connect. People rated their own health and reported chronic illness. Standard short scales screened for anxiety and low mood, while a quiz weighed how much people know about mental health.

Positive screens came in at 2.72 percent for anxiety and 4.53 percent for low mood, with 2.11 percent showing both. Knowledge about mental health carried part of the link between poor body health and poor mind health. Teaching that knowledge may soften distress tied to chronic illness. District health teams get a low cost lever to test.
pmc-13434631:
Aušra Arlauskienė's team studied organic farms in 2026, asking how handling legume biomass changes the nitrogen and carbon left for the next crop. They grew red clover and alfalfa, alone and mixed with festulolium grass. The cut plants met three fates: hauling it all off, hauling part off with mulch left, and mulching it all. Mulch and root mass, decay, soil nitrogen, and soil carbon were tracked through the season.

Pure legume mulch broke down fast and fed the soil, mixtures held nitrogen better than grass alone, and roots kept feeding soil into autumn. Taking all biomass away lost the most nitrogen, while partial removal with mulching kept soil nitrogen steadier and supported carbon. Organic growers get practical guidance on keeping fertility in the field rather than hauling it off.
pmc-13435431:
Joanna N. Modi's team studied compact breast tissue in 2026, asking how its gene activity differs from looser tissue in the same breast. Dense breasts carry a much higher cancer risk, and compactness is a newer, location-specific way to measure density, but its molecular story was unclear. Eight genes differed, with looser tissue showing immune-calming signals and more regulatory T cells, while compact tissue was rich in cholesterol-making genes, a pathway tied to cancer growth and spread. The paper offers a first molecular sketch, not a risk test, built on only three donors. Breast teams get leads for why compact tissue may behave differently.
pmc-13437231:
Tomohiro Nagano and a large team asked how weight should guide a transplant drug dose in heavier patients.
