Their 2026 study reviewed ninety-four adults who had half-matched transplants at one Japanese hospital.

Seventeen of those patients were overweight or obese, the group the team focused on. Among them, chronic graft-versus-host disease struck far more often when the dose fell below a cutoff set by ideal weight. One-year rates were about 68 percent below that mark against about ten percent at or above it. The authors urge caution, since the heavy subgroup was tiny and the ranges wide. Still, their results hint that ideal weight may be the safer ruler when dosing heavier recipients.
pmc-13437931:

pmc-13438531:
Pérez Velilla and Smaldino build a mathematical theory in this 2026 paper about a familiar instinct: we preferentially copy people who seem like us. Their evolutionary model asks when that similarity bias helps or hurts. Advice from someone facing different circumstances may not transfer. Identity markers also vary in how informative they really are.

The analysis shows learners evolve flexible biases. They favor similar models when in-group knowledge is adaptive. They favor dissimilar ones when the in-group's habits are failing. This adaptiveness can keep social learning worthwhile. It holds even when copying costs more than learning alone. A threshold result also emerges: a minimum supply of reliable cultural information is required before social learning spreads at all. The framework offers a demographic explanation for patterns of cultural segregation and assimilation in diverse populations.
pmc-13438931:
Alessandra Pennisi and colleagues describe three patients whose shared gene defect produced strikingly different illnesses. Their 2026 report covers a six-year-old boy and two adult siblings from two families, each carrying a previously unseen variant.

The boy's disease declared itself before birth: weak fetal movements, profound floppiness, and breathing failure needing a tracheostomy, with no head or trunk control by age six and a spine curving sideways. His muscle biopsy showed too few of the stem cells the gene supports. The siblings ran milder courses: a sister needed a tracheostomy at fourteen, and her brother reached sixteen before needing night-time breathing support. The authors urge clinicians to expect severe, variable breathing involvement and to plan respiratory care early, whatever the opening picture suggests.
pmc-13441531:

In diabetic mice, podocyte-specific silencing of either link lowered suPAR and eased kidney dysfunction and tissue damage.
pmc-13441931:

Radiotherapy use was sorted into consolidation after initial response, salvage at progression, and palliative courses.

Nearly three fifths of patients received some radiotherapy. Whole-cohort survival landmarks landed close to the trial's figures, with a median span near seven months before progression and median survival near sixteen months. Consolidation patients ran longest without progression, while salvage patients posted the longest median survival. Continuing durvalumab past progression alongside radiotherapy tracked with better survival. Treatment side effects touched about two fifths of patients, with immune toxicities uncommon and lung inflammation rare.
pmc-13442631:

Husk samples showed better emulsion stability and cooking yields at 30 days of storage than the control batches tested. Intermediate inclusion levels produced the largest gains in hardness, gumminess, and chewiness on texture profiling. The highest dose tried did not. Sensory panels accepted every formulation. Intermediate levels again earned the most favorable profiles from tasters. The authors present psyllium as a functional ingredient that enriches fiber while supporting acceptable salami quality.
pmc-13442831:
Hajar Erraji and colleagues report womb-lining growths in odd places in a 32-year-old woman in a 2026 case paper. Belly pain cleared fully, and shoulder pain eased to a mild, bearable level. The team calls for joint teams on such spread cases.

The notice fixes a series of numbers. The count of patients classified HER2 3+ rises from 15 to 16. Several response-rate percentages in Tables 4 to 6 are replaced. Two p-values are also corrected. One subgroup's major response rate moves from about six percent to about twenty-five percent. All corrected comparisons remain statistically non-significant.
pmc-13445531:

Drops had long been judged too weak for this condition, which is usually treated with injections into the eye. Stage one aimed to fix the dose plan that a later stage will test.

Patients got the steroid drops or a matching blank, six times a day for six weeks, then three times a day for six more. The main yardstick was change in letter-reading score at week six, with safety tracked in all who got a dose.
pmc-13445631:

The rest sat inside those six as linked local groups. Gene flow, meaning mixing between groups, blurred many borders. Shared genes could also fake deep splits and make close kin look far apart.
pmc-13446131:
Xiaoqin Ji and colleagues report a thirty-five-year-old man whose neck artery stent, placed to stop a catastrophic bleed after cancer surgery, became a suspected source of repeated blood infection, published in 2026. Fever returned again and again, and blood cultures kept growing Pseudomonas aeruginosa despite matched antibiotics and line removal. A scope later showed the stent exposed inside the airway, a strong sign the device itself was colonized. Bleeding through the windpipe opening resumed, his state worsened, and the family chose to stop active care. The case warns against stents in dirty fields.
pmc-13447431:

pmc-13448031:

They close by looking at how big data and linkage may extend registries. Other countries have since adapted the Swedish model for their own systems.
pmc-13448231:
Grażyna Lisowska leads a team testing a standardised ginkgo extract for vertigo and dizziness of mixed causes in a 2026 pragmatic trial. Handicap, symptom and severity scores all improved clearly by six weeks and held at twelve, with roughly two-thirds reaching a meaningful gain. Standing balance normalised in far more patients, and stepping test abnormalities fell steeply. Episodic symptoms and shorter histories predicted stronger gains. Natural recovery cannot be separated from drug effect in this design, the authors state plainly.
pmc-13449431:
Jehan Perera and colleagues demonstrate in 2026 a gentler way to attach the alpha emitter astatine-211 to drug-like molecules for targeted cancer therapy. The authors argue that column-shipped astatine can feed late-stage labeling under mild conditions, widening access to this therapy for centers without their own production.
pmc-13450631:

A second workshop checked the map under stress. The authors offer the map as a tool for groups that want to shift the system, not just add one more test.
pmc-13452231:
Wenwen Su, Yongxiu Song, and Xia Zhang find in 2026 a group of brain cells that brake stress anxiety and cycle upset in female mice. Switching the cells off bred anxiety-like acts, while switching them on blunted the stress reply. Under long stress, females showed both anxiety-like dodging and scrambled fertility cycles, and steady cell activation eased both. The authors cast the cells as a stress-hired buffer node in the brain's fear web.
pmc-13452331:
Dash and colleagues explore in 2026 whether lymphatic endothelium, the lining of the vessels that drain tissues to lymph nodes, can be turned into an anti-tumor ally. These cells normally present antigens in a way that teaches tolerance, which may shield tumors.

The team targeted the sugar chains, called glycans, on the lymphatic surface and reduced their sulfation, a chemical decoration. That change boosted the cells' display of a model antigen. It also strengthened activation of killer CD8 T cells exposed to antigen-carrying lymphatics in laboratory work with the model antigen. In animals, the targeted state raised the number of CD8 T cells in lymph nodes and came with reduced spread of tumors to distant sites. The authors propose glycan targeting as a way to recruit lymphatic tissue into adaptive anti-cancer immunity.
pmc-13454031:
Stergiani Agorastos, Wei Hou, and Echezona T Maduekwe compare three bedside rules for judging how deep a breathing tube should sit in tiny newborns. Placing the tube right matters in babies of 1,500 grams or less, where a few millimetres count. Their 2026 study enrolls 50 such babies in a level IIIC intensive care unit between April 2022 and February 2024, each checked against the depth shown on chest X-ray.

One rule measures from mouth to ear, one from nose to ear flap, and one reads depth off a table by pregnancy age. The mouth to ear rule, called oro-helix length, landed closest to the X-ray depth, with the least bias at 0.15 centimetres. The nose based rule strayed most. The authors back the mouth to ear measure as the preferred first estimate in these smallest babies.
pmc-13454131:
Parviz Malekzadeh and others tried alpha-ketoglutarate to keep cut mums fresh in 2026, a prized cut bloom that wilts fast. Cut bloom life is cut short by fast aging, and a cheap, green cell fuel might slow it. The team set five millimolar AKG next to a zero control.

AKG stretched vase life a lot by lifting water balance and water uptake, while it raised cell guards such as glutathione, vitamin C, phenols, and flavonoids, plus catalase and superoxide dismutase work. Harmful oxygen bits fell, with less malondialdehyde, less salt leak, and less lipoxygenase work. AKG also held back ethylene-making genes. Flower sellers gain a cheap dip to keep mums fresh longer.
pmc-13454231:
Zezhang T Wen, Bo Yang, Lauren C Guillot, and Lin Zeng study a gene switch called SppR in Streptococcus mutans, the mouth bacterium behind tooth decay. The switch was known to repress two sugar handling genes. Their 2026 study builds a broken switch mutant and tests it in biofilm models and stress challenges.

The mutant grew normally in rich broth yet fared badly at low pH and under oxidative attack, with survival after acid and peroxide challenges clearly down. Reporter tests showed the switch also drives a second gene, brpA, tied to cell wall stress handling: losing the switch cut that gene's activity by over half. Pure switch protein bound the gene's control region and boosted its reading in a test tube. Gene wide scans found over 136 genes shifted, including repair and acid tolerance genes.
pmc-13454431:
Yildiz-Ozhan and team linked area opportunity to brain wiring and thinking skills in 6,141 children aged 8 to 10 from the national ABCD study. They used a Child Opportunity Index. It scores schooling, social and economic, and health-environment factors across 29 measures. They paired those area data with matched diffusion MRI of white matter tracts.

Higher area opportunity was linked with greater fractional anisotropy in the superior longitudinal fasciculus I. Fractional anisotropy marks how organized a tract is. That bundle runs from front to parietal regions and supports higher thinking. Opportunity also tracked with better cognitive performance, most strongly for crystallized cognition. That is the knowledge-and-experience ability children build through schooling and surroundings. That tract's microstructure partly mediated the area-to-thinking link in their models. At the measure level, quality schooling access, area employment rates, and health insurance coverage emerged as the strongest single correlates of neurocognitive outcomes.
pmc-13454831:
Claire Shaw and six colleagues compare, in a 2026 analysis, job outcomes from a trial of supported employment in alcohol and drug treatment. They set those results against the same service rolled out across England. The model, called Individual Placement and Support, embeds job coaches inside treatment teams. The trial group held 843 people, while the national expansion served 3,182.

The expansion group did better on every count. Just over half found work, against 30 percent in the trial. Jobs came faster, lasted more than twice as long, and far more people held a job for at least 13 straight weeks. The authors credit delivery refinements, wider entry rules, and a friendlier economy. Their point for policy readers is that trial results can understate what a mature, well-run service achieves at national scale.
pmc-13455231:
Qingting Sun and others tuned shield plans in tube current modulation chest CT in 2026, with a phantom study. Rising public radiation care has put shields in focus, yet shield place, overranging, and scout-view links needed proof. The team used a life-like phantom on a GE Revolution CT scanner.

Lead shields set inside versus outside the overranging zone were set next to a no-shield control. Shields were tagged as scout-seen or scout-unseen, and scan-area dose and edge-organ image grade were scored. Inside-zone shields lifted scan-area dose. Volume CT dose index rose by as much as twenty-two point nine percent by collimation-pitch mix. Edge image grade fell near twice as much as with outside-zone shields. Radiologists gain proof to set shields outside the overranging zone.
pmc-13457031:
Yanli Tan, Shiqi Liu, and Liuhong Zang compare, in a 2026 network meta-analysis, how different exercise styles and doses soften stiff arteries in adults. Artery stiffness was read as the speed of a pulse wave between neck and groin, a stand-in for vessel aging. The team gathered randomized trials from six databases through January 2026, covering seven exercise types.

Sixty-nine trials with 3,422 participants qualified. Exercise overall cut pulse wave speed by about three quarters of a meter per second against control. Aerobic, combined, and interval training each beat doing nothing, yet none beat each other clearly. Evidence confidence peaked at moderate for combined training. A dose curve suggested benefits bend rather than climb forever, with wide doubt at the extremes. The authors warn that mixed study quality makes rankings and dose claims exploratory, not prescriptions.
pmc-13457631:
Ricarda Endemann and colleagues probe the known weak spot of older memory: linking things together. Older adults usually remember single items nearly as well as the young but struggle to link them. Their 2026 study gave 34 Italian younger adults and 17 healthy older adults a word-color recognition task in Italian and German, a foreign language for both groups. Trials ran with or without instructions to picture each object in its color as one unit.

In their native language with no strategy demanded, the older group, reporting high cognitive reserve, showed no associative deficit. The deficit surfaced when demands rose: the foreign language, or the imposed imagery strategy. The strategy helped younger adults more, widening the age gap, paying off more in the native tongue for everyone. Matching younger adults for German proficiency largely erased the language effect. The authors read the pattern as compensation working until the task gets heavy.
pmc-13458531:
Meng-hao Xi and colleagues map how flood danger and nature's services overlap, or fail to, across the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region, China's capital megalopolis. Their 2026 study builds an assessment-association-mechanism framework, running ecosystem models for water yield and soil conservation, an erosion model, random forest analysis, and spatial statistics at scales from local to regional.

A mismatch emerged: flood risk concentrates in piedmont plains and built-up zones; strong ecosystem services hold in the Yanshan and Taihang mountain barriers, producing high-risk, low-service territory where people live. Relationships changed with scale. Water yield flipped from weakly negative against flood risk at fine scales to positive at broader ones, a scale reversal. Soil conservation stayed negatively linked to flood risk, more strongly at larger scales. The authors identify synergy and trade-off zones and argue watershed governance must plan at the scale where each relationship operates.
pmc-13458831:
Ji Won Seo and colleagues track blood sugar with non-stop meters before and after stomach removal surgery in patients with diabetes in a 2026 study. Stomach removal for stomach cancer changes digestion and sugar control, yet glucose patterns after surgery were poorly mapped. Thirty-three patients, with mean illness span 16.9 years, wore non-stop glucose meters before surgery and after discharge, stopping sugar drugs a day before surgery and resuming only after recheck.

Mean glucose and time above range fell while time in range rose, ups and downs stayed stable, and large glucose swings shrank, with 43.8 percent of assessed patients reducing sugar drugs. Low-sugar goals, however, worsened despite no clear rise in time below range. Doctors gain a case for tailored post-surgery drug plans guided by non-stop tracking, rather than automatic restart of prior plans.
pmc-13459031:
Shono argues in 2026 that the time smart note tools hand back to front line doctors is a shared prize that health policy must steer, not leave to chance. Note tools that listen and draft charts save real minutes in some clinics, and ease head load in more. Shono names the saved stock the attention prize. Left loose, it drains to more visits, more forms, and the well served. The piece lays out pay forms that free clinics to spend it on patients.

Prize pay works best when clinics are paid for health worth, not visit counts. Three uses top the list: spot the missed patient, keep one doctor per patient, and close the loop on risks. Shono pairs eight steer asks with marks, tools, and named owners. Seven traps that siphon the prize off get named too, each with a fix. Counts split by group guard the equity aim.
pmc-13459231:
Jianbo Cui and co-authors tested whether patterns hidden in prostate cancer scan images can predict surgical findings before the operation. They used PSMA PET/CT scans, which light up prostate cancer cells, and extracted hundreds of image measurements, a method called radiomics. Their 2026 study covered 243 patients scanned before prostate removal, split into training and test groups. It built nine machine learning models at three different brightness thresholds for defining the tumor region.

The model using a 45 percent threshold, blending scan patterns with clinical data, performed best. It predicted high grade cancer after surgery with a test accuracy score of 0.917 on the standard curve measure. It also reached 80 percent sensitivity and 92.1 percent specificity as reported. Predicting cancer spread beyond the prostate was harder, scoring 0.772 on the same test set. Performance held across patient subgroups, suggesting a useful noninvasive planning aid.
pmc-13459331:
Sonya C. Faber, Amy Bartlett, Monnica T. Williams, and Jude M. Cénat examine in 2026 a governance overhaul inside the Canadian Psychological Association. The changes followed an internal push for a structural voice for Black, Indigenous, and other racialized members. Through a close reading of association papers, the authors trace bylaw changes that shifted authority toward the board and its chief while shrinking the freedom of member sections.

Read through ideas of power hoarding and divided authority, the reforms moved decisions away from the sections that speak for distinct groups within the field. The authors read that shift as a refusal to share structural power. Their case speaks to professional bodies everywhere about how rule changes can quietly blunt equity commitments, and it offers lessons for consultants and leaders alike.
pmc-13459631:
Katarína Šimeková and co-authors followed people living with HIV through the first pandemic year in Slovakia to see how COVID-19 actually affected them. Their 2026 prospective cohort tracked sixty-four patients on antiretroviral therapy at a university hospital in Martin between September 2020 and September 2021, confirming infections by PCR testing. Age, HIV duration, immune cell counts, viral suppression, other illnesses, and vaccination status were compared between those who caught the virus and those who did not.

Infection was common: 54 of the 64 participants, 84.4 percent, tested positive during the year. Illness was generally mild, with no intensive care admissions and no deaths in the cohort. No significant differences in age, HIV history, CD4 counts, or viral suppression separated those infected from those spared. Participants with at least one other chronic condition were more likely to catch COVID-19, yet fared no worse once infected. Vaccination status showed no clear outcome differences.
pmc-13460831:
Clyde T. Matava and colleagues compared in 2026 anesthetic mixtures used during children's airway procedures, where doctors must keep young patients sedated while they keep breathing on their own. Thirty children aged one to twelve underwent rigid bronchoscopy or suspension laryngoscopy between September 2023 and March 2024, all with carbon dioxide monitored through the skin. Regimens paired propofol with dexmedetomidine, remifentanil, or both drugs at different doses.

The parent study found every child developed raised carbon dioxide during the procedure, and most stayed high afterward. Staff recorded breathing pauses, coughing, and any need to assist breathing by mask, plus interruptions to the procedure itself. The dexmedetomidine-only regimen produced the most stable breathing profile of the groups, a finding the authors offer for planning safer anesthesia in shared-airway surgery.
pmc-13461331:
Luisa Heyn, Tina Schwender, Helena Rudi, and Mara Köhntopp reviewed in 2026 whether dance interventions improve body image and self-worth in people living with overweight and obesity. Ten studies spanning children to adults and many dance styles met their criteria after screening by three independent reviewers. Because the studies differed so much in design and length, results were organized through a Wheel of Dance framework grouping what dance offers, from group belonging to mindful flow.

Across formats, dancing was tied to better body image, stronger self-esteem, and improved psychosocial well-being regardless of whether weight changed. Creative dance forms stood out for unlocking emotional expression and social connection. Most included programs leaned on flow and mindfulness elements, five of the ten, while culture, aesthetics, and imagination received thinner attention.
pmc-13461631:
Esra Başer Akın and colleagues test, in a 2026 study from Türkiye, whether a scale that measures stigma linked to dialysis works well in Turkish. Dialysis patients often face shame or unfair treatment, which can harm mood, social life, and willingness to keep up treatment. Nurses need a sound local tool to spot that stigma. The study ran at a private dialysis center in Sivas between July and September 2025.

Ninety-two patients filled in the translated scale and a short background form. Experts rated how well the items fit the topic, and the team checked the scale's structure with factor methods. Scores held together strongly on the standard consistency measures. Repeating the test later gave close results, showing stability. The authors conclude the Turkish version measures dialysis-related stigma validly and steadily, giving clinics a practical tool.
pmc-13461831:
Jennifer E Hibma leads a 2026 drug modeling study of elranatamab, a lab-made antibody for multiple myeloma that has returned or stopped responding. The drug grabs two targets at once, one on cancer cells and one on immune cells, pulling them to attack the tumor. The team built a population model of drug movement through the body. Data came from four studies with 321 people.

Over thirteen thousand measurements fed the model, covering doses given into a vein or under the skin. Drug levels rose in a straight line with dose. Age, sex, weight, and other traits did not shift exposure in ways that mattered. Early peak levels and tumor burden best predicted a flu-like immune reaction that follows the first step-up dose. Simulations backed restarting after breaks of up to twelve weeks without rebuilding the dose, supporting the fixed-dose plan in use.
pmc-13461931:
Suvitesh Luthra discusses, in a 2026 commentary, a three-stage hybrid repair of a long aneurysm running through the chest and belly aorta in a 75-year-old man. An aneurysm is a dangerous swelling of the main artery. The team used a custom-made graft, T-NEXT Thoraflex, in a frozen elephant trunk step for the arch and aorta. Later stages placed branched stent grafts through vessels for the lower parts.

Staging was a must, not a choice, Luthra argues. Opening the chest for the arch work gave a landing zone for later repairs. Without that zone, the lower repair would have needed a huge open operation with high risk. The case shows why custom grafts matter: standard sizes crowd the upper aorta and force joins too high for some body shapes. The commentary praises the mix of open and vessel-based skills demanded.
pmc-13462431:
Xiang Gao and colleagues build, in a 2026 gene study, a prediction model for liver cancer based on genes tied to palmitoylation, a chemical tag that anchors proteins to cell membranes. The tag helps control cancer growth, yet its liver cancer role was unexplored. The team used two cohorts, one of 377 patients from a United States program and one of 231 from an international consortium. They sought tag-related genes that differ in tumors and matter for survival.

Twenty genes were changed, and eight tied to overall survival. A model using three genes, ZDHHC18, ZDHHC23, and PPT1, split patients into high-risk and low-risk groups. Sorting accuracy was fair in the building cohort and better in the checking cohort. The risk groups also differed in immune pathway activity inside tumors. The authors argue the model can sort patients by risk, guide immunotherapy choices, and name three genes as possible targets.
pmc-13463131:
Chen and colleagues test turmeric's active compound, curcumin, on immune signals in depression in this 2026 laboratory study. Major depressive disorder involves an overactive immune-inflammatory system, and curcumin is known to calm inflammation, but its exact targets were unclear. The team took blood from 18 patients and 18 healthy controls, stimulated the samples, and added curcumin at three doses.

Patients' blood showed the expected overactivation of inflammatory pathways and signaling proteins called cytokines. Curcumin selectively turned down those overactive pathways in patient samples, cutting several chemokines, proteins that attract immune cells, and the major inflammatory signal TNF-alpha. It did not fully normalize the profile and barely touched the calming pathways. In healthy blood, by contrast, curcumin mildly stimulated the immune system, and the authors stress that living-body studies must come before any treatment claims.
pmc-13463931:
Yang and co-authors asked in 2026 whether body weight distorts PSA blood tests for prostate cancer. Larger blood volume in heavier men can dilute the marker. The team reviewed 663 patients, split into leaner and heavier groups at a body mass index of 24. Standard PSA measures were compared with a new age-adjusted density measure. The new measure also accounts for prostate size.

The age-adjusted measure won in both groups. Among leaner men it scored about seven tenths on the standard accuracy curve scale. Ordinary density scored lower, and total PSA barely beat chance. Among heavier men the new measure scored higher still, near eight tenths. It again beat both older markers, and the differences were statistically firm. A variable-selection method kept choosing the new measure as a core predictor in both groups. That supports its use when deciding who needs a biopsy.
pmc-13464331:
Zurab Khabadze, Oleg Mordanov, and Ahmad Wehbe test two fully automatic AI systems that measure jaw and face angles from 3D dental scans. Orthodontists use such measures to plan braces and jaw surgery, yet nobody had checked whether the systems treat left and right sides fairly. Thirty-one scans were read by both systems and by careful hand tracing.

Per-side accuracy held up well: errors landed almost equally on both sides, and one angle matched hand work superbly. The catch came with side differences, the very numbers used to judge facial asymmetry. One system showed no link at all to hand-read jaw asymmetry, and both missed most real cases. Side-difference scores from these tools, the authors warn, cannot yet be trusted alone.
pmc-13466031:
Xin Tang, Yunfei Mu, and Hongjun Shi untangle how a common enzyme switches on the Notch1 signal that shapes blood vessel lining cells, in a 2026 study. The enzyme, protein kinase C, was known to stir Notch activity, but the route was unclear. Working with mouse vessel cells, the team found it acts indirectly rather than tagging Notch1 itself.

Two parallel routes did the work: the enzyme raised levels of a Notch partner called Jag1, and it kept another protein, ADAM10, supplied through a hyaluronic acid pathway. That second link helps explain why mouse embryos lacking the acid-making gene resemble embryos lacking Notch1. The authors suggest downstream steps in this chain could serve as drug targets for vessel and heart valve problems.
pmc-13466131:
Tan and a large team compared gut microbes and digestion in yaks and cattle in 2026 on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. Yaks thrive where air is thin; cattle are their lowland cousins. Animals were studied at 2,200 meters and at 3,800 meters. The team profiled the rumen, the fermentation vat where microbes pre-digest food, covering microbe mix, protein output, ammonia, and a liver stress marker.

Yaks rewired their rumen for energy scarcity. Their microbes shifted toward breaking down amino acids and making long-chain fats, squeezing more fuel from less. The bargain had a price. Microbial protein production fell by nearly half under thin air. Ammonia in the rumen more than doubled, and the liver stress marker rose by about a fifth. Cattle showed no comparable trick. The study frames high-altitude survival as a trade: richer energy now, paid for with liver strain over time.
pmc-13466531:
Mercedes Peña-Rodríguez and colleagues report a study, published in 2026. It looks at inflammation and immune action in Fabry disease. This is a rare inherited disorder. A missing enzyme lets fatty substances build up in organs. Fifteen patients gave blood. Fifteen matched healthy controls did the same. A broad panel of markers was measured. It covered inflammation, complement, and vessel markers.

Patients showed a distinct low-grade inflammation pattern. Fibrinogen was among the strongest differences. It is a clotting and inflammation protein. A tumour necrosis factor receptor also stood out. Grouping methods separated patients from controls cleanly. The pattern tracked total organ involvement. It tracked this more than disease subtype. These markers are proposed for monitoring and future treatment ideas.
pmc-13467631:
Wender Alves Silva, Sayuri Cristina Santos Takada, and Saulo Tarso Alves Passos report a 2026 greener route to isocyanides, versatile building blocks for drug discovery and multi-component reactions. These compounds are rarely sold and classically made by hazardous methods. The new protocol generates the reactive intermediate from chloroform and sodium hydroxide in near-stoichiometric amounts, using a biodegradable detergent-like helper called Span 80 to move reactants between liquid phases under microwave heating.

The method produced a wide range of isocyanides, from simple aliphatic and aromatic types to ones built from amino acids, in yields of 43 to 96 percent within 30 minutes. It skips the usual water workup and avoids toxic dehydrating agents such as phosphorus oxychloride. The authors present it as a faster, cleaner way to stock a class of reagents many labs currently avoid making.
pmc-13468531:
Vincenzo Aiello and colleagues test in 2026 whether extracts of the truffle-like fungus Tuber borchii can buffer muscle cells against sarcopenia-like stress. Sarcopenia, the age-related loss of muscle mass and strength, predicts frailty, yet prevention leans almost entirely on exercise, which many patients cannot do. The team stressed cultured mouse muscle tubes with D-galactose, a sugar that mimics atrophy-related aging changes, and treated them with two independently prepared fungal extracts.

The extracts enhanced features tied to muscle maintenance, and the team measured protein synthesis, protein turnover, and cell shape to judge the protection. Earlier work had shown these preparations touch proliferation pathways, including ERK1/2 signaling, giving the test a mechanistic anchor. A food-derived extract that defends muscle protein balance in a dish is far from a therapy, but it marks a candidate worth animal testing for a condition with few options.
pmc-13469031:
Blom and a large consortium appraised in 2026 the questionnaires judging physical function after leg bone sarcoma treatment. Surgery and radiation can change how patients walk, work, and live. A prior review found 42 instruments in use, eight of them more than once. The team graded validation studies of those eight with COSMIN rules, the standard for judging measurement tools. Seventy-three articles qualified.

The verdict was sobering: most instruments never clearly defined what they claim to measure. Only two, the Toronto Extremity Salvage Score and the Reintegration to Normal Living Index, showed adequate content validity, meaning they plausibly cover what matters. Even those faltered elsewhere: one's consistency was indeterminate, the other's evidence base thin. None of the eight earned a recommendation for standard use. The authors urge the field to refine and properly validate what exists rather than inventing yet more scores.
pmc-13469131:
Mukul Machhindra Barwant and colleagues tested weed leaf extracts in 2026 on maize to weigh their harm against any stress-tolerance gain. Five common weeds were applied at 5, 10, and 20% through seed soaking, soil mixing, leaf spray, and root-zone simulation under field-like conditions. Germination fell by 15 to 55% against controls, with shoots and roots shrinking by up to 40 and 50%.

Chlorophyll fell by 20 to 60% under strong treatments, while stress markers rose by 30 to 120% and antioxidant enzymes climbed 1.5 to 2.0-fold. Moderate doses held pigments near control levels, and three treatments stood out for stress tolerance with partial growth kept. Weed chemicals thus mostly suppress maize, with only tuned doses offering a biostimulant path worth pursuing.
pmc-13469331:
Burley and colleagues in the United Kingdom and the United States tested in 2026 a stepped breath hold drill as a cheap boost for endurance. Breath holds are known to squeeze the spleen and push more red cells out, a trick like high camp drills. Their drill stacks holds of growth length. One test gave 11 men the drill or rest, then a hard bike ride and a short time trial. A twin test ran 48 Marine officer hopefuls through three weeks of drills in their base training.

The one off drill paid at once: red cell load rose, and time trial work beat the rest day by a clear mark. In the three week test, run times gained in both arms, but the drill arm gained more. Their red cell load rose while the plain arm's fell. The authors call for big trials.
pmc-13469831:
Gupta and co-authors ran a 2026 qualitative interview study of how people with obsessive-compulsive disorder use technology across their care journey. Digital tools now appear at every stage from spotting symptoms to self-care, yet real world use was barely studied. Twenty-four adults who reported an OCD diagnosis joined semi-structured talks.

Participants, median age twenty-six, were drawn through online OCD communities and support networks during 2024. Gupta found technology central to three parts of the journey across the interviews. Social media and online content first helped people spot symptoms, name the disorder, and seek care. Telehealth, apps, and wearables then bridged gaps in treatment access and steady follow-up for many. Finally, participants saw emerging tools making symptom tracking and support better in future care models.
pmc-13470931:
Basu and Huynh systematically reviewed in 2026 how to stop medical AI chatbots from hallucinating, inventing facts that sound right. Such errors in clinics include fake citations and wrong treatment claims. Following PRISMA review rules, they searched six databases for studies from 2019 to April 2025 testing real fixes. Of 427 studies found, 44 qualified. The team sorted fixes into seven families and compared their measured effects.

Retrieval-augmented generation, where the model checks sources before answering, was the most tested fix, in 18 of 44 studies. It cut hallucinations by roughly 30 to 50 percent. Knowledge graphs and self-reflection frameworks followed in popularity. Human-in-the-loop checking achieved the deepest cuts, up to 95 percent, but scales poorly. Red teaming, deliberate adversarial probing, caught failure types other methods missed. Combined fixes, like retrieval plus verification, generally beat single methods. The authors propose their typology as a deployment checklist for safer clinical AI.
pmc-13471531:
Gedamu Abera Zegeye, Muluemebet Abera Wordofa, and Afework Mulugeta test in 2026 whether teaching birth companions through a belief based program improves childbirth in Ethiopia. Free maternity care has expanded, yet many women still labor without a companion. Companions often doubt their own role, and wards are seen as women only spaces. Twelve public clinics in Addis Ababa were randomized, with first time mothers and their chosen companions assigned by clinic.

The program arm received five teaching sessions for companions, built on the Health Belief Model, running from mid pregnancy to delivery. The comparison arm received standard antenatal care alone. How satisfied mothers felt, measured on a twenty five item survey, rose markedly in the program group. The trial also tracked delivery mode, labor length, and newborn problems. It also costed the program per problem avoided.
pmc-13471631:
Zhou and co-authors used network pharmacology, computational target fishing, to predict how pachymic acid, a fungus-derived compound, attacks triple-negative breast cancer, then checked the predictions in cells. Their 2026 study screened drug and disease databases, filtered hits through cancer survival data, and landed on three key targets: PTGS2, NOS2, and ABCB1.

In MDA-MB-231 cells, the standard triple-negative model, pachymic acid significantly cut proliferation, migration, and invasion in dose tests, and raised lipid peroxidation, a marker of oxidative damage, in treated cells. Docking simulations supported direct binding to the predicted targets. The authors note the stakes: about one million new breast cancer cases arise yearly, nearly 18% of all female cancers, and five-year survival sits under 40% in developing regions.
pmc-13471831:
Tess Levy leads a large consortium estimating in 2026 how common Phelan-McDermid syndrome really is. This genetic neurodevelopmental condition had only rough guesses before, ranging from a few cases per million births. The team gathered counts from ten sources, including testing laboratories and research centers, covering nearly one hundred eighty thousand people tested for autism.

Within those tested groups, the syndrome appeared in one to about two and a half percent, though test sensitivity varied. Adjustments then corrected for patients without autism, for the ages at which autism is diagnosed, and for variant types some tests miss. National autism rates carried the estimate to the general population: about fourteen per hundred thousand people, roughly one person in seventy three hundred. The authors frame the figure as a firmer base for planning testing and care.
pmc-13472731:
Jacob Chang and colleagues introduce PANORAMIC, a statistical framework for analysing how cell types are arranged in tissue across many samples at once. Their 2026 paper addresses spatial omics studies, which map cells in intact tissue but often ignore uncertainty within each sample.

PANORAMIC estimates local colocalization, meaning how often two cell types sit near each other, corrects for tissue edges, and uses repeated resampling to measure within-sample uncertainty. A multilevel meta-analysis then carries that uncertainty into comparisons across samples, patients, and conditions. In simulations it recovered uncertainty and between-sample differences better than simpler estimators. Applied to colorectal cancer tissue imaged with multiplexed fluorescence, it found stronger B-cell and T-cell colocalization in tumours with a Crohn's-like reaction than in diffusely inflamed tumours, a pattern standard methods missed.
pmc-13472931:
Hagner-Derengowska and colleagues pooled in 2026 the trials on compression garments worn after exercise by endurance athletes. Nine controlled studies with 158 athletes were included from 503 screened records. Bias and certainty were graded with standard tools, and soreness scores were pooled while performance was described in words.

At about twenty-four hours, soreness estimates favoured the garments, but the confidence range was wide and crossed no effect. Soreness in the first two hours after exercise was likewise uncertain. Performance results could not be pooled because studies differed too much. Ten of eleven checks carried high risk of bias, and the overall evidence grade was very low. The authors conclude current evidence cannot confirm a real benefit from post-exercise garments. They present the review as a call for better trials rather than praise for the garments.
pmc-13473031:
Fidan and colleagues followed patients with rare pure forms of breast cancer for up to two decades to learn how each subtype behaves over the long term. Their 2026 retrospective cohort covered 117 patients treated at one tertiary center between November 2000 and February 2024, spanning five uncommon histologies.

Mucinous carcinoma was the largest group at 41.9% of cases, followed by metaplastic at 25.6%, micropapillary at 14.5%, tubular at 10.2%, and malignant phyllodes tumors at 7.7% across the cohort. The team calculated five- and ten-year survival for each. Mucinous and tubular tumors mostly ran slow courses with low-grade tumors and strong hormone-receptor positivity, while metaplastic and micropapillary cancers behaved aggressively with higher recurrence risk.
pmc-13473531:
Su-Boon Yong and eight colleagues studied in 2026 COVID-19 vaccination in young people with juvenile idiopathic arthritis, a childhood joint disease. Using the United States TriNetX network from January 2020 through June 2023, they compared infection, service use, and death between matched groups of 652 vaccinated and 652 unvaccinated patients. A further comparison ran against influenza vaccination. The aim was to see whether vaccination protected this group or changed its care needs.

In this database study, vaccinated patients showed a higher recorded risk of SARS-CoV-2 infection and higher overall medical service use, at a hazard ratio of 2.112 for service use. No difference appeared against the influenza vaccine group, and no rise in death was found. Effects during Delta and Omicron periods were not firm. The authors warn that observational data carry confounding and selection bias, so the findings warrant deeper study of immune responses rather than any change in advice.
pmc-13473631:
Mehmet Zülfü Yıldız and fellow researchers revisit the family tree of a small sand boa in Türkiye in 2026. The snake, Eryx jaculus, was once split into three subspecies by region. Some experts have argued it should count as a single form with no subspecies at all. The team gathered twenty-five snakes in field work from 2004 to 2019 and added nine photo records from local helpers.

Body measures from the Turkish snakes were compared with past records across the range. The new sites filled gaps in the known map for the species. On the full evidence, the authors back the single-form view for this snake. Clear naming helps field guides, trade rules, and protection plans stay consistent.
pmc-13474731:
Yang and Hung used the TriNetX medical records network, spanning over 170 healthcare organizations, to ask whether GLP-1 diabetes drugs taken before shoulder surgery compromise tendon healing after rotator cuff repair. Their 2026 study matched 957 diabetic patients who had started a GLP-1 drug within six months before repair against 957 on other diabetes therapy, balancing age, weight, and blood sugar.

Two years out, the feared harm did not appear. Revision surgery occurred in 1.0% of GLP-1 users and 1.1% of comparators, a risk ratio of 0.91 with a confidence interval comfortably crossing no-effect, and retear-proxy events ran 7.3% versus 8.6% in GLP-1 users' favor. Survival curves showed no significant separation on either endpoint. The authors call the drugs structurally safe around this surgery on current evidence, pending imaging-confirmed prospective studies.
pmc-13474831:
Jeyaprakasam and co-authors review zoonotic malaria in Southeast Asia in 2026, meaning malaria parasites that pass from animals to people, above all Plasmodium knowlesi from monkeys. Human malaria has fallen across the region, yet knowlesi cases keep rising as forests are cleared and farms expand toward wildlife habitat. The review centers on the mosquitoes that carry these parasites and why they are so hard to control.

The authors note that global malaria reached 282 million cases in 2024, up 9 million from the year before, while Southeast Asia held under 1 percent of that total. Many local mosquito species look nearly identical, so misidentification distorts records of biting behavior and habitat, and standard indoor spraying misses species that bite outdoors near forests. The team urges joint human, animal, and environment surveillance, often called One Health, with control plans fitted to each local setting.
pmc-13475231:
Isadore M. Budnick and co-authors measure waste toxins in 2026 in critically ill patients with kidney injury on continuous kidney replacement. Twenty-one toxins were read in eighty-nine patients before and during the first three days of therapy. Twenty-six people without kidney disease served as comparison. Death within thirty days was the outcome, and it struck about half the patients.

Before therapy, fifteen toxins ran high versus the comparison group, yet almost none predicted death alone. During therapy, four toxins ran lower in those who died, a counterintuitive twist. A combined score using all toxins and their direction split survivors from others. Single toxin checks mislead; pooled patterns carry the signal.
pmc-13476531: The note is an editorial notice only, issued in 2026 about a 2025 paper on a grain and starch packaging film. A reader raised concerns that two figure panels closely matched panels in a sister journal paper. The publisher integrity team sought author explanations for both matches. One match led the sister journal to publish a correction, while the editor-in-chief accepted the author explanation for the other. No new research findings are presented in the notice itself.
pmc-13478631:
Vila-Viçosa and colleagues modeled the past and future ranges of eight submediterranean oak species in 2026, trees that hold their dead leaves through winter and live where temperate forest meets Mediterranean scrub. They fitted distribution models to 12,450 cleaned occurrence records and high-resolution climate data. Then they projected ranges from the cold Heinrich Stadial, about 17,000 years ago, forward to 2070 and 2100 under three climate scenarios.

The models performed strongly, scoring above 0.97 on the standard accuracy curve, with rainfall and temperature seasonality as the leading predictors of where oaks can live. Past projections showed contrasting east-west histories, with expansions, contractions, and pockets of stability through abrupt climate swings like the Younger Dryas cold snap. Future projections point northward and uphill, with the steepest suitability losses under the highest-emission scenario and for the narrowest-ranged species.
pmc-13479031:
Taylor, Flowers, and Hutchinson told in 2026 how a nurse led calm down model took root in three acute mental health wards over one year. The model, Safe Steps, swaps control first habits for bond first ones. Staff greet stress with tuned talk, soft tone, and clear steps, in place of holds, locks, or forced drugs. The authors led the roll out and wrote a frank account of what helped, what snagged, and what they would change.

Growth of staff skill was the core lever. Short staged drills, team backup pacts, and coaching built nerve for the new way. Boss backing and a felt sense of safety kept the shift alive on hard shifts. The patient voice, heard in plans and reviews, kept the model true to its aim. The authors urge wards that want less force to fund lead time, drills, and true patient input from day one.
pmc-13479831:
Horieh Moosavi and colleagues present a 2026 laboratory study comparing two crown types for children's first permanent molars, teeth often wrecked early by decay. Stainless steel crowns are quick and cheap, while porcelain-fused-to-metal crowns look better but cost more. Forty extracted lower first molars were sorted into four groups crossing crown type with tooth condition.

Half the teeth stayed intact, while the rest received access cavities and side boxes filled with composite, mimicking restored damaged teeth. Fit was measured by a silicone replica method under a digital microscope. Crowns were then cemented and loaded until fracture. The comparison tells pediatric dentists how much strength and fit each option sacrifices in sound versus rebuilt teeth.
pmc-13479931:
Taiki Kobayashi, Kosuke Maekita, and Yusuke Kazama published a 2026 plant development study on Silene latifolia, a species with separate male and female plants. Its sex chromosomes carry unequal copies of two genes that run a feedback loop controlling stem cell pools in the growing tip. That imbalance should, in theory, destabilize the shoot apical meristem, the tiny dome where stems and leaves begin.

The team grew seedlings in liquid medium and measured meristem diameter and area under a contrast microscope across growth stages. Male and female meristems did not differ in size, despite the gene copy imbalance. The authors read this stability as developmental robustness: the feedback loop buffers its own dosage problem. The result clarifies how plants keep growth steady while their sex chromosomes diverge.
pmc-13480031:
Penghong Chen and colleagues describe a 2026 study of stem cells from umbilical cord jelly as a treatment for aged skin. The team used lab-grown human skin cells aged with a sugar compound and also used hairless mice with the same ageing method. They paired hands-on tests with gene activity scans at bulk, array, and single-cell levels to trace how the cells act.

Fluid from the stem cells restored growth and movement in aged skin cells and cut signs of cell wear. In mice, the cells reversed skin thinning, raised collagen levels, and lowered cell ageing marks. They also nudged immune cells toward a calmer state and boosted new vessel growth. Single-cell data pointed to a pro-inflammatory fibroblast group as a key driver of skin ageing, with one rhythm gene dialled down after treatment. Readers get a detailed map of targets for future skin repair work.
pmc-13480131:
Andrew Moussad and co-authors report a 2026 case of a small tear at the tip of the heart found after a valve-in-valve procedure. An 80-year-old man with a failing artificial aortic valve and severe breathlessness had a new valve placed inside the old one through a catheter. Routine scans a day later showed a tiny, contained puncture at the heart tip, likely from a guidewire, with no fluid around the heart.

Repeat scans days later showed the tear held steady, and the man stayed well with stable vital signs. On day eight the team sealed the hole through the skin with a vascular plug device rather than opening the chest. The case shows the value of careful imaging after such procedures, even when patients feel fine. For stable patients with a contained tear, a plug closure may spare high-risk open surgery.
pmc-13481831:
Peng and colleagues report in 2026 a delivery-platform study for skin rejuvenation. Their electrospun nanomembranes are woven from recombinant human collagen type three and hyaluronic acid, two large molecules that normally cannot cross the stratum corneum, the skin's outer barrier.

In pig skin diffusion tests, the membranes delivered about seventy-two percent more hyaluronic acid across the barrier in twenty-four hours than an identical serum. The collagen signal in the dermis ran nearly fourfold higher. A four-week split-face trial in 35 healthy volunteers then showed the membrane side gaining about forty-eight percent in surface hydration. It also lost about forty-one percent of its water-loss measure of barrier leakiness, and improved elasticity and eye-area wrinkle measures, all significantly against the untreated control. The authors present the membranes as a way to ferry oversized active ingredients into skin.
pmc-13482131:
Wang, Yan, and Zhang describe an optical encryption scheme in 2026 that hides several images at once inside ultrafast light springs. These beams twist in brightness and phase like a corkscrew. Each image first receives random phase scrambling, then rides on its own orbital angular momentum mode, a distinct twist pattern of the light beam. A pulse shaper and a liquid crystal modulator then fold the signals into ultrashort pulses carrying all images together.

Layering double random phase encoding over the pulse shaping stretches the time dimension of the encryption, enlarging the key space beyond what single-frame optical systems offer. The authors tested the scheme with standard security checks, including key sensitivity, information entropy, pixel correlation, and resistance to attack, and report it held up across all of them in simulation. They pitch it for high-capacity optical encryption and secure communication where many images travel together.
pmc-13482331:
Najafi and colleagues compare two ionic liquid extractants in 2026 for pulling valuable metals out of zinc plant residues, waste that holds toxic cadmium alongside recoverable zinc, cobalt, and nickel. Ionic liquids are salts that stay liquid at room temperature, and the pair tested, Aliquat IL336 and Cyphos IL101, grab metals from chloride solutions by an ion-pair exchange. The solvent pulling the metals into a separate liquid phase was dichloromethane.

Both extractants proved choosy in the same useful way, taking cadmium and zinc eagerly while largely leaving cobalt and nickel behind in the solutions tested. The selectivity traces to the stronger chlorine-based complexes cadmium and zinc form, and using hydrochloric acid as the chloride source beat sodium chloride for extraction percentages. Stripping the metals back out worked cleanly too, with sodium hydroxide releasing cadmium and ammonia releasing zinc, completing a recovery loop the authors propose for industrial residues.
pmc-13482831:
Eken and colleagues tested whether siderite, an iron-rich mineral, could replace natural stone in heavy concrete built to block radiation. Their 2026 study mixed siderite at 10, 20, 30, and 100 percent shares, using both fine grains and coarse chunks, while the cement blend and water ratio stayed fixed. The team then measured strength, wear, salt-water penetration, freeze and heat damage, and gamma-ray blocking.

Higher siderite shares generally raised strength and density while letting less chloride, a salt ion that rusts steel, move through the concrete. Strength and chloride movement were closely linked in the data the team reported. Coarse siderite blocked gamma rays better than fine siderite did. Eken concludes that siderite mixes suit durable shielding walls, though the gains come from packing and density rather than one proven cause.
pmc-13483031:
Čechová and team asked whether cleaned city wastewater could water lettuce in a water-based growing system, cutting demand for fresh water and fertilizer. Their 2026 study treated wastewater with a new microwave plasma device, which uses energized argon gas to kill microbes. Lettuce then grew in hydroponic trays, meaning roots sat in water instead of soil, watered with plasma-treated or untreated wastewater and plain drinking water.

Plasma treatment cut the total bacterial count in wastewater by more than tenfold, making reuse far safer. Lettuce watered with wastewater gained 27 percent more fresh mass than the comparison plants in the trial. Element scans showed how minerals from the water spread through roots, stems, and leaves. Čechová concludes treated wastewater can suit hydroponic farming when its contents are monitored and extra disinfection is applied.
pmc-13483631:
Ndivho Tshivhula, Elliot Mbunge, and Tebogo Makaba review how to combine deep learning with radiomics for finding lung cancer early across hospitals. Their 2026 framework paper follows standard review guidance and sorts studies into three families, covering handcrafted image features alone, learned features alone, and blended models. Imaging types span standard, low-dose, and combined scans.

Blended models generally beat either approach alone at telling harmless nodules from cancer and at related sorting tasks. Joining the two feature sets late or in hybrid fashion proved sturdier than simply stacking features early, especially in multi-center data where scanners differ. The synthesis gives builders a practical map for systems that must stay accurate, explainable, and portable between hospitals.
pmc-13487231:
Jalali and team translated and validated a survey form measuring how strongly women nurses in Iran perceive gender bias at work. Without a sound local tool, hospitals cannot document the problem credibly. Their 2026 study followed World Health Organization translation guidance. They then surveyed 535 women nurses and stress-tested the Persian scale's structure with two rounds of factor analysis, a method that finds clusters among questions.

The analysis confirmed five underlying factors across 29 items, together explaining about 51 percent of response variation in the survey data. Model fit statistics rated excellent, and consistency scores for the full scale exceeded 0.90 on both reliability coefficients reported. Jalali presents the validated scale as ready for clinical and research use in Iranian nursing, giving managers a defensible way to track perceived bias over time.
pmc-13487631:
Ilaria Boscolo Galazzo asks if gray matter in multiple sclerosis gets too little blood flow past what tissue loss explains. Past small studies found low flow in key brain zones in this disease. This 2026 study scans 170 people at four sites in Europe with one shared scan plan. The group holds 96 patients with the relapsing form, 41 with the steady-worse form, and 33 healthy peers.

The flow scan needs no dye shot, which eases repeat use. The core test is sharp. Flow loss may just track tissue loss in the same spots. Or flow may drop where tissue still looks whole, which would mark an early harm sign. Ties from whole-brain flow to body and thought scores round out the plan. Strict quality checks trimmed the data set first.
pmc-13487931:
Santo and colleagues pooled the evidence on tafamidis, a drug for a heart disease caused by amyloid protein deposits, in patients aged eighty and older. The disease mainly strikes the elderly, but trials under-represent the very old, leaving doctors unsure the benefit survives frailty and short life expectancy. Their 2026 meta-analysis combined three studies totaling 1,866 participants, with an average age of eighty-four.

Patients on tafamidis died at about half the rate of control patients in the pooled hazard analysis reported. Results barely varied between the three studies, and dropping any single study did not change the conclusion in sensitivity checks. About seventy-seven percent of participants received the drug across the included studies. Santo supports using tafamidis in octogenarians while urging caution, since the underlying evidence base remains just three studies with differing designs.
pmc-13488331:
Sabit Ahmed and colleagues mapped how biofilms, slimy bacterial cities stuck to surfaces, differ across 40 strains of Tenacibaculum, a fish disease genus. These bacteria cause tenacibaculosis, a growing threat to marine fish farming, and biofilms may help them persist on farm surfaces.

The team grew strains three ways, as free cells, surface colonies, and submerged films, and measured 17 traits for each. Strains split into four clusters, trading fast growth against thick, complex three-dimensional films. Imaging showed the glue-like material around cells varied in pores and spread from strain to strain. In four test strains, protection against an antibiotic inside biofilms also depended on the strain, Ahmed reports.
pmc-13490531:
Rostami and team compared womb-lining tissue from fifty women with recurrent implanting failure against fifty women with successful pregnancies, tracking a the hormone signaling network. Repeated failure of embryos to implant frustrates fertility treatment, and the lining's readiness is hormonally choreographed. Their 2026 case-control study at a Tehran hospital measured five linked molecules, from the the hormone receptor to a regulatory long RNA, by quantitative PCR.

The receptor's B form and the vessel-growth signal PROK1 both ran clearly low in the failure group, in gene activity and protein alike. Receptor and PROK1's receptor correlated strongly and positively, suggesting they rise and fall together in healthy lining. The regulatory RNAs shifted as well, completing a disrupted network picture. Rostami argues the panel could become a diagnostic fingerprint for lining that will not receive an embryo.
pmc-13490631:
Jahani and Jahani reported a sixty-two-year-old Iranian woman whose brucellosis revealed itself through the loss of all three blood cell lines, in a 2026 case report. Brucellosis is a bacterial infection caught from animals or unpasteurized dairy. She arrived after ten days of fever, chills, muscle and joint pain, and a five-kilogram weight loss, with white cells and hemoglobin low and platelets reduced. That combination is called pancytopenia, and it occurs in a minority.

Jahani's account shows the diagnosis competing with cancers and marrow disorders, which this presentation mimics. Her blood counts recovered during triple-antibiotic therapy, the combination regimen used when two-drug treatment risks relapse. The authors caution that one case cannot prove triple therapy superior. they stress that in regions where brucellosis is endemic, clinicians should suspect it in pancytopenia, since the disorder proved reversible with antimicrobial treatment.
pmc-13490731:
Ivana Hemmelová and colleagues report a rare, sudden gut crisis in an older surgical patient in a 2026 case report. An older woman with heart problems had the Whipple operation for pancreatic cancer. Weeks before, she had been treated for a bad gut infection with Clostridioides difficile, a germ linked to antibiotic use. That infection had stopped just eleven days before surgery. Days after the operation, she grew very ill with a swollen, blocked colon.

Scans and stool tests proved the germ was back in a fulminant, life-threatening form. Drugs through a tube and strong supportive care in the intensive care unit steadied her. She slowly got better and left hospital in stable shape. The team warns that this germ can return fast in weak patients after big surgery.
pmc-13491331:
Krishna S. Gajula and colleagues pool studies of adding a stroke-prevention plug during valve replacement in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Many patients receiving a catheter aortic valve also have atrial fibrillation, which raises clot and bleeding risks under long-term blood thinners. Sealing the left atrial appendage, a small pouch where clots form, during the same procedure might cut both risks. Four studies with 563 patients, half receiving the combined approach, were pooled.

No outcome differed significantly between combined treatment and valve replacement with standard drug care, at thirty days or across follow-up to two years in the pooled estimates. Death, stroke, and major bleeding all sat close. Contrast use and hospital stay matched too. The authors call certainty low.
pmc-13491731:
Xiaolin Jiang, Ruxue Han, and Xin Yang survey in 2026 how women's menstrual cycles changed after COVID-19 infection. Their survey drew on 884 women who had completed at least one cycle since testing positive in early 2023. Periods respond to inflammation, hormone disruption, and psychological strain, so a major infection could plausibly disturb them. Participants compared their cycles before and after illness in an electronic questionnaire.

Three quarters of respondents reported at least one change, most often in cycle length, flow amount, or bleeding duration. Women whose cycles were already irregular before infection reported changes more often than women with regular cycles, and that link survived statistical adjustment. The authors frame menstruation as sensitive to whole-body stress, while warning that self-reported, one-time survey data can show association but not cause.
pmc-13491931:
Lijing Guo leads a fourteen-author team telling in 2026 how a seventy-one-year-old man nearly died from a waterborne bacterium picked up through a minor injury in a paddy field. Aeromonas caviae flooded his bloodstream, causing septic shock and oddly migrating muscle pain. Standard first-line therapy at the referring hospital failed, and cultures revealed a multidrug-resistant strain.

Whole-genome sequencing confirmed the species beyond doubt and exposed its resistance arsenal, including an extended-spectrum enzyme gene, CTX-M-3, rarely seen in this species. The isolate still yielded to a carbapenem antibiotic called biapenem, and switching therapy cleared the infection quickly. The authors note that one carbapenem failed while another worked, possibly due to the patient's low albumin and kidney injury, and they call for surveillance linking environmental and human resistance.
pmc-13492031:
Junyi Wu and seven co-authors argue in 2026 that the lungs are not innocent bystanders after a stroke but active drivers of the damage that follows. Stroke care usually treats lung problems as complications, like pneumonia from swallowing failure. The review instead casts the lung, one of the body's largest immune reservoirs, as an initiator and amplifier of body-wide and brain inflammation.

Signals from the injured brain travel by nerves and blood to prime lung immune cells, which then flood the circulation and home back to the brain, deepening injury in a self-feeding cycle. Aging and diabetes tilt the lung's immune baseline beforehand, making older and diabetic patients more vulnerable to the cascade. The authors propose protecting brain and lung together and flag the gap between animal evidence and human proof.
pmc-13492431:
Balaji Krishnan and three colleagues recount in 2026 how an extra strand of tissue inside the heart nearly cost a patient his life. Ventricular fibrillation with no structural cause explains a slice of cardiac arrest survivors, and stray early beats are often the trigger. In this patient those beats arose where a false cord, a fibrous band, anchored from the tricuspid valve ring to the right ventricular wall.

The authors reason that muscle fibers inside the band either fire spontaneously or grow excitable where mechanical tugging strains the attachment. Because sedatives easily silence right-sided trigger beats during procedures, they used pace mapping, stimulating candidate spots to mimic the guilty beat's signature. Imaging from inside the heart guided the ablation before, during, and after. Freeing the trigger and treating the surrounding substrate, they report, can deliver lasting freedom from arrhythmia.
pmc-13493831:
Cui, Li, and Wang present AdaptiveFrequencyNet, a forecasting model for long runs of time-stamped data such as electricity use or weather. Long-range forecasts are hard because patterns repeat at several scales at once. Older methods split the data into fixed frequency bands that cannot adapt. Their 2026 design learns its own split using adjustable filters, then blends information across scales with attention, the technique that lets a model weigh which parts of the data matter most.

Tested on six standard benchmarks against nine rival models, the new network posted competitive errors while keeping a moderate size. Results varied by dataset: it matched the leading transformer model on one electricity series, while rivals edged it on a weather benchmark. The authors are candid that rankings depend on the dataset and forecast horizon. Their claim is narrower than a clean sweep: learnable decomposition holds its own without rigid frequency splits.
pmc-13494031:
Cillis, Lanorte, and Nolè use satellite images to watch for vegetation stress across two river basins in Basilicata, southern Italy, over seven years. Healthy plants reflect light in a pattern captured by the NDVI index, and places where growth deviates sharply from the norm can signal drought damage, land abandonment, or degradation. Their 2026 study ran a technique called selective principal component analysis over Sentinel-2 records from 2017 to 2023 to pull real change out of ordinary seasonal swings.

Forests mostly improved, with around three fifths of forest area showing significant, mainly positive anomalies over six-month windows. Grasslands told the opposite story: nearly seven tenths of their area showed significant anomalies, and most of those were negative, pointing to declining growth. Shrublands barely changed and proved the most stable cover type. The authors offer the method as a low-cost early-warning framework for land managers under a shifting climate.
pmc-13494531:
Elio Adib and others reply to commentary on radiation therapy after neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy for locally advanced lung cancer in patients who did not reach surgery. In 2026, the letter thanks the commentators and agrees that caution is vital before look-back plans enter routine practice. Surgery was abandoned for very different reasons across patients.

Those whose surgery was aborted for contraindications such as advance or spread fared worse than those blocked by an acute medical event. The groups cannot fairly be compared with patients who underwent resection. Pneumonitis risk from immune priming must also be weighed case by case. The authors urge deliberate upfront selection and multidisciplinary planning, with larger randomized trials still needed before radiation becomes a standard rescue path.
pmc-13499031:
Tang and a team in China tested in 2026 a new drug tactic against retinoblastoma, an eye cancer of young children. Extra copies of the MYCN gene drive the worst cases, yet MYCN has long been hard to drug. Their compound, HLB-0532259, is a PROTAC, a molecule built to tag a target protein for disposal. They tried it on two cell lines and on tumors in mouse eyes.

The compound broke down MYCN in a dose linked way, and one cell line proved more prone to it than the other. Gene and protein scans showed a fast switch on of the p53 to p21 path, a brake that halts cell growth. DNA repair genes fell, damage built up, and cells slid into senescence, a state where growth stops. In mice, shots into the eye shrank tumor load and cut cells still marked for growth.
pmc-13499331:
Lei Huang and colleagues survey in 2026 whether mental resilience softens the link between bad academic events and anxiety among clinical medicine postgraduates in China. These trainees work under heavy pressure, and setbacks such as failed exams or criticism are common. A total of 1,182 postgraduates at one large medical school answered an anonymous online survey using an eight-item setback checklist, a standard anxiety scale, and a ten-item resilience scale.

Students who reported setbacks had far higher odds of probable anxiety disorder, and low resilience alone also raised the odds sharply. Statistical interaction tests showed the two risks amplified each other, since the setback link was much stronger among low-resilience students than among high-resilience peers. The authors suggest that screening for resilience and building coping support could help training programmes protect students after academic blows.
pmc-13499731:
Poddar, an obesity medicine specialist, and Nadglowski, a patient advocate, hold a clinical dialogue about obesity and liver disease for a 2026 journal podcast article. About a billion people worldwide live with obesity, yet the usual body mass index label misses where fat sits, and belly fat drives the worst metabolic harm. The conversation centres on what good, respectful obesity care looks like in practice, and on waist-based measures that capture risk better.

Liver health anchors the discussion, since three quarters of people with obesity have metabolic fatty liver disease. A substantial minority progress within a decade or so to its inflamed, scarring form. Both conditions usually cause no symptoms, so they stay undiagnosed without deliberate screening. Drawing on Nadglowski's lived experience, the pair argue for routine complication checks, including liver assessment, inside holistic obesity care rather than weight lectures alone.
pmc-13499931:
Deepak K Saini and colleagues evaluate in 2026 keyhole screw fixation for burst fractures of the thoracolumbar spine in patients without nerve injury. Open surgery stabilises such fractures well yet strips back muscles and adds surgical harm, so screws placed through small skin punctures aim for equal stability with less tissue damage. Their prospective study treated 46 consecutive adults aged 18 to 50 at a tertiary public hospital over eighteen months, using standard X-ray guidance in the operating room.

Falls from height caused most injuries, and the second lumbar vertebra was the commonest level affected. Operating time averaged under two hours with modest blood loss in the reported figures, hospital stays ran short, and pain scores fell within days. Spine alignment and vertebral height both improved significantly, and most screws sat perfectly placed on post-surgery scans, with no infections, implant failures, or revisions in early follow-up.
pmc-13500531:
Sunil Lavadiya and colleagues design in 2026 a layered solar absorber that harvests sunlight across a wide band while barely caring about the sun's angle. Most absorbers work narrowly and fade in ultraviolet and near-infrared light, so the team stacked iron, silica glass, an advanced carbon material called MXene, and iron again in a repeating patterned structure. Computer simulations with the finite element method tuned the shape, materials, and layer thicknesses for peak performance.

Uptake exceeded ninety percent across three separate wavelength bands in the tuned design, according to the simulations. The design held for both light polarisations across approach angles from straight-on to steeply tilted, a wide-angle strength prized for real rooftops and collectors. Machine learning models were trained to predict absorption behaviour and agreed with the simulations. Head-to-head checks with published designs favoured the new stack for photothermal energy harvesting.
pmc-13500731:
圣莉 程 and others survey nurses on acceptance of AI systems that dynamically assess venous thromboembolism risk in hospital patients. In 2026, the study collects valid surveys from 2,323 nurses at tertiary hospitals in Anhui Province between April and June 2025. It uses latent profile analysis to find distinct acceptance groups and logistic regression to explain them. Nurse acceptance directly shapes whether smart nursing tools work in practice.

Three profiles emerged: low acceptance with concern and resistance at about seventeen percent, medium acceptance with cautious waiting at about fifty-one percent, and high acceptance with active embrace at about thirty-three percent. Professional attitude, night shift frequency, years of service, and prevention knowledge predicted group membership. Managers should target support and training by profile rather than one uniform rollout.
pmc-13500831:
Mahdee Jodayree leads a four-author team with a 2026 framework for predicting which students risk failing, without pooling their records in one place. Schools increasingly want early-warning models, yet centralizing sensitive student data raises privacy and ownership concerns. Their system, called FL-AtRisk-DP-PBT, trains a shared logistic regression model across schools using federated averaging, so records stay local. Client-side differential privacy adds noise for protection, and a proof-before-train protocol logs each school's part so the process can be audited.

The team tested three setups on a main cohort of 14,003 students split into ten simulated schools, plus two public education datasets. The central model reached 99.14 percent accuracy, while the private federated version reached 98.00 percent, a small cost for the added protections. On the two public datasets the private version scored about 93 to 94 percent accuracy. Feature patterns stayed similar across setups, keeping the model interpretable.
pmc-13501631:
Jie Zhou leads a fifteen-author team reporting a 2026 nanomedicine study of eyedrops for uveitis, a sight-threatening inflammation inside the eye. Biologic drugs each block one target and need injections into the eye, which carry risks when repeated. Screening identified two disease drivers, VEGF and tumour necrosis factor alpha. The team engineered one bispecific antibody, V5-3, that blocks both at once, then packaged it with a dithiolane molecule into nanoparticles that cross the eye's surface after topical dosing.

Compared with the free antibody, the nanoparticle drops entered cells better, curbed microglial growth and movement, and cut inflammatory cytokine release. In cell and animal models the dual targeting combined anti-inflammatory and anti-vessel-growth effects, easing symptoms and tissue damage in the retina. Toxicity was negligible across the models tested. The authors present the drops as a noninvasive candidate for a disease where delivery is the bottleneck.
pmc-13501831:
Lili Xie leads a six-author team presenting a 2026 review of questionnaires that measure quality of life in multiple myeloma, judged by the COSMIN standards for measurement quality. Twenty-six studies covering fourteen patient-reported instruments qualified. The myeloma-specific module EORTC QLQ-MY20 was evaluated most often, followed by instruments such as MyPOS, HM-PRO, and FACT-MM. Evidence clustered on internal consistency, structural validity, and construct testing, while measurement error, criterion validity, and cross-cultural validity were rarely examined.

No instrument earned uniformly high-quality evidence across all the properties that matter. The EORTC QLQ-MY20 and MyPOS carried the broadest supportive evidence and look like the most defensible choices for myeloma-specific use. Even they lack strong content validity work and long-term measurement studies. The authors urge future research to involve patients in validating what the forms ask, and to test responsiveness when health changes.
pmc-13503031:
