The authors urge earlier spotting of added illness, better access to facilities, and stronger teamwork between government and aid groups.
pmc-13623631:
Paolo D'Imporzano and Graham A Hagen-Peter published a 2026 study developing a gentler way to read the origin of lead white paint in old paintings. Lead white's isotope pattern, the mix of lead atoms of different weights, can reveal where the lead was mined and traded. The classic method dissolves a scraped sample, wasting most of it and mixing paint layers together.

The new method fires a laser at spots only micrometres wide and feeds the vapour straight into the measuring instrument, leaving the painting nearly untouched. The team made two synthetic lead whites with known isotope mixes to calibrate the setup, and laser results matched the dissolved-sample values. Tests on layered mock-ups showed that pigment-rich zones give clean readings while oil-rich zones wobble. The method then fingerprinted an anonymous painting thought to be Italian and centuries old, and produced layer-by-layer isotope maps.
pmc-13623831:
Eisho Tanida and colleagues solve the structure of the nucleosomes that mark the centromere, the spot where a chromosome is pulled apart during cell division. The mark is a variant protein called CENP-A that replaces a standard building block in the DNA packaging spools. Lab-made versions had been pictured before, but the natural form inside cells was disputed.

The team fished CENP-A nucleosomes out of human cells, without glue-like chemicals, and imaged them with cryogenic electron microscopy, which freezes samples for ultra-clear pictures. Two forms appeared: a pure CENP-A spool and a mixed spool pairing CENP-A with the standard protein. Both held the full set of eight protein parts and wrapped DNA in the expected left-handed coil, settling the shape debate. Signature details seen in the lab versions, including a shortened helix and a loop, survived in the cell versions.
pmc-13624231:
Ben Fabry, Christian Kuster, and Roland C Francis present a way to watch a breathing tube clog up in real time, using only the pressure and flow signals a ventilator measures. Tubes narrow as mucus and biofilm build inside them, adding breathing effort and risking pressure build-up, yet during assisted spontaneous breathing no check catches the change early.

The method filters the natural wiggles in airway pressure and flow, and strips out the slow push of the patient's own muscles and lung stretch. It then solves the motion equations to recover the tube's resistance, split into steady and flow-dependent parts. Across ventilation modes, tube sizes, filters, and breathing patterns, the recovered values stayed within ten percent of the truth with small bias. The estimates update breath by breath, so a rising blockage shows as it forms. The authors see uses in automatic compensation and safer weaning.
pmc-13626331:
Daniela Choukair and colleagues check the inner load carried by teenagers with chronic illness as they move from children's to adult doctors. Ninety-two adolescents starting that transition filled standard questionnaires on mood, anxiety, and body complaints. A family functioning scale came too. So did a survey of what they knew about their own diseases and what help they wanted. Forty-two of the most burdened teens also sat for interviews.

About two in five reported moderate body complaints, one in five showed moderate or worse depression signs, and about one in eight reported strong anxiety. Families mostly functioned well, yet worse family functioning tracked with heavier symptoms. Interviews sorted needs into body, mind, information, and system problems. The authors urge transition programs to screen feelings as routinely as they check organs.
pmc-13628131:
Sandra Kleinau argues in a 2026 review that the isotype of a therapeutic antibody, its class and subclass, deserves far more attention in cancer immunotherapy. Monoclonal antibodies are engineered to flag cancer cells for destruction, yet many tumours escape, and most approved products use the same IgG1 subclass.

Kleinau compares the structure and immune effects of human IgG and IgA subclasses, using the anti-CD20 antibody rituximab in laboratory models of B-cell lymphoma as the test case. Subclasses differ in how they recruit immune cells and the complement system, and their performance shifts with antigen density, tumour shape, and patient factors. The review makes the case for matching isotype to the individual tumour rather than defaulting to one standard choice.
pmc-13629331:
Mika Schneider and three colleagues present a laboratory protocol for switching genes on only in B cells that have entered the mouse brain, leaving the same cells elsewhere in the body untouched. Standard tamoxifen-based genetic switches work everywhere at once, which in their system triggers runaway B cell growth and death.

The trick is local delivery: the activating compound is mixed into bone wax and placed inside the skull, so recombination happens only near the injection site. The worked example turns on a viral protein and a fluorescent marker in brain-infiltrating B cells, letting the team study how a multiple sclerosis-linked viral gene affects those cells. Steps cover virus injection, wax preparation, and dosing in mice.
pmc-13629531:
Anna Scotts and four colleagues ran a memory experiment with 223 people. They tested whether choosing to memorise facts slows the fading of event files. Event files are the mental bundles that link a cue to a response. Repeating only part of a bundle normally disrupts performance. That cost shrinks as time passes. The bundle itself seems to decay within seconds.

Volunteers did a two-stage task at short and long gaps. One group was told to memorise the first cue. Partial repetition costs shrank over time in both groups. Yet they stayed larger in the memorising group. People with better recall showed slower decay. The authors conclude that active memorising props up these fleeting bindings. The finding links binding, attention, and short-term memory.
pmc-13630431:
Takuo Kubota and twelve colleagues present a guide to spotting hypochondroplasia in children. This mild bone condition causes short stature out of proportion. Their guide appeared in 2026. The condition stems from variants in the FGFR3 gene. One common change accounts for most cases. It sits near achondroplasia on the spectrum while staying much milder.

Wider use of prenatal ultrasound has brought many affected babies to attention before birth. The guide sets out the early imaging signs. Those signs now make diagnosis possible in newborns, at times with 3D CT scans. At the mild end, though, the picture blurs into ordinary shortness. The authors recommend genetic testing for a firm answer. The guide aims to speed recognition and improve care for affected children.
pmc-13635231:
Shakib Absar and six colleagues published this 2026 dataset of freshwater fish photographs from Bangladesh for training recognition software. Automated fish identification needs realistic training images, yet earlier sets were shot in tidy studio conditions. This collection holds over nine thousand high-resolution photographs of nine common species. They were gathered over seven months in working fish markets, with natural clutter, mixed lighting, overlapping fish, and vendors' hands in frame.

Every picture holds one clearly centered fish. Each carries a hand-drawn box around the fish and a precise outline mask produced with a modern segmentation tool. Images are standardized to one size and sorted by species, with rich metadata attached. The set supports classification, detection, and outline tasks without extra preparation. The authors aim it at practical uses: aquaculture monitoring, trade transparency, price watching, and inspection in one of the world's busiest fish economies.
pmc-13637631:
Changhao Han and sixteen colleagues published this 2026 review of photonic neural networks, hardware that computes with light instead of electrons. Artificial intelligence workloads keep swelling while conventional chips hit memory, wiring, and heat limits. Photonic networks move key operations into optical circuits, promising lower delay and energy use. Silicon photonics now allows dense integration of these circuits on chips. The review spans the whole stack.

At the base it analyzes the physical devices and the main computing core architectures that multiply signals optically. Middle layers cover integration strategies that marry photonic chips with electronics. System packaging and complete implementations come next, judged against what working AI hardware demands. The authors close with the field's open problems, from fabrication tolerances to scaling, and argue these networks could underpin the next generation of AI infrastructure. Their cross-layer frame is meant to guide specialists working at any single level.
pmc-13641531:
Arpita Bharadwaj and six colleagues present a 2026 study of how the epithelial sodium channel is assembled inside real mouse tissues. This channel controls sodium movement across surface linings and helps govern fluid balance, blood pressure, and airway moisture.

Most knowledge comes from lab-grown cells forced to overproduce channel parts, which may miss how tissues build the channel naturally. The team engineered a mouse line carrying a tagged channel subunit so intact native complexes could be pulled out and examined across different epithelial tissues. Their approach opens a route to tissue-specific regulation that artificial systems cannot show.
pmc-13641731:
Y. Chen and ten colleagues present a Hong Kong study of body and heart measures after pregnancies complicated by high blood pressure disorders. Women flagged as high risk for pre-eclampsia at first-trimester screening were followed after delivery at the Prince of Wales Hospital.

The sample held 201 women in three groups: high risk who developed a disorder, high risk who did not, and low-risk controls. At six to twelve weeks after birth, the disorder group showed higher arterial pressure and heart muscle mass, with weaker heart strain measures. High-risk women were then tracked to twelve months with lifestyle advice at each visit.
pmc-13642231:
Kunlin Liu and ten colleagues present a 2026 research letter on how lithium, a standard mood stabilizer, shifts survival-related choices in stressed mice. Lithium lowers suicide risk in patients, yet the brain mechanism behind that protection is poorly understood.

After two weeks of unpredictable mild stress, mice faced a foraging task where food sat in a zone marked with fox urine scent. Lithium-treated mice spent less time in the risky zone and ate less, while normal movement stayed unchanged. The pattern points to stronger threat avoidance, and the title links the effect to suppression of a small brain region, the lateral habenula.
pmc-13642931:
Yuchao Zhao and eight colleagues present a 2026 study of how grape seed polyphenols cut methane from dairy cows. Methane from ruminant digestion is a major farm greenhouse gas, and plant chemicals are candidate natural suppressants whose workings were vague.

In live cows and lab fermentations, grape seed proanthocyanidins lowered methane output, cutting emission intensity per unit of milk by about one sixth. Gene-level analysis showed methane-making microbes quieted, while other bacteria took up the spare hydrogen through alternative routes. Microbes also ramped up carbohydrate use and antioxidant defenses. The authors frame polyphenols as microbiome steering tools for cleaner milk production.
pmc-13643631:
Steiner and co-authors examine whether less can be more in this 2026 retrospective study of acute myeloid leukemia treatment for older or unfit patients. The standard pairing of a hypomethylating drug with venetoclax works. But venetoclax given for most of each cycle often crushes blood counts. So the team compared cycles using only seven days of venetoclax against fourteen or more.

Among 61 elderly patients, the best overall response rate was 76 percent and did not differ significantly between schedules. Median survival ran numerically longest on the seven-day schedule, at 28.4 months against 11.4 and 6.7 months for the longer ones. An adjusted model kept the seven-day advantage significant against the longest schedule. Shorter exposure also meant fewer infections, fewer severe low-count episodes, and fewer platelet transfusions per cycle. The authors suggest abbreviated venetoclax preserves efficacy while easing toxicity.
pmc-13645531:
Sara Puente-Marin and eight colleagues present a study of the first immune events when classical swine fever virus sets up lifelong persistence in newborn piglets. Persistently infected pigs look healthy while shedding virus, which defeats control programs.

The team compared blood cell gene activity at day seven between piglets infected with a persistence-causing strain and piglets given the protective C-strain vaccine, before symptoms or antibodies appeared. Infected animals carried high virus loads and strong interferon signals, with pathways for killing and immune regulation switched on and antigen display turned down. Persistence, the authors argue, begins despite vigorous antiviral activation, through regulation that blunts control.
pmc-13648031:
Ceyda Sarı and two colleagues tested ways to fix aged bulk-fill resin composite, a tooth filling paste set in thick layers. A repair bonds new paste to old, and the surface prep may decide how strong that bond is. The team made 150 small disks from three brands of the paste.

The disks were aged with heat and cold cycles, then split into five prep groups. One group got no prep at all. The team then glued on repair paste, pulled the bond apart to test its strength, and viewed a few samples under a fine microscope. A trio of sandblast spray, silane, and a universal glue gave the top scores for all three brands. Plain untreated disks scored worst.
pmc-13648831:
Tomko Settgast and six colleagues ask if rest-state brain waves can foretell how well a person will drive a brain-computer link. They study people with ALS, a nerve disease that locks the body, plus healthy peers. Their frame is the critical brain idea: the brain works best when it sits near a knife edge between calm and chaos.

The team read rest waves for bursts, rhythm slopes, and code-like richness, then set them next to later link scores. In the ALS group, all three marks tied to scores in a steady way. In healthy peers, burst marks tied the other way round. The authors sketch a U-shaped rule: both groups near the sweet spot, but from opposed sides. Such marks may one day flag who will thrive with a link.
pmc-13649431:
Annika Ericson and four colleagues studied how children with spastic cerebral palsy see motion and how that links to how they move. Vision guides steps and reaches, yet brain-based vision problems are often missed in this group. The study covered youths aged 8 to 20, with 37 who had cerebral palsy and 36 who did not.

On a screen test of motion sense, the palsy group scored lower, most of all at very slow and very fast speeds. Parents also reported far more signs of brain-based vision problems in that group. Both gaps grew wider in children with greater limits on movement. The authors urge that vision be checked when movement is assessed and supported.
pmc-13651531:
Chia-Hao Liu and six colleagues forge a forked road into angular triquinanes, natural product frameworks of three fused five-membered rings bent at an angle and crowded with stereocenters. Synthetic chemists prize these compact terpenoid skeletons but struggle to set their many handedness centers on demand.

From shared allene starting materials, two complementary cyclizations diverge. A Lewis acid route assembles one fusion pattern through a ring-forming annulation, while a light-driven cycloaddition followed by oxidative ring expansion delivers the mirror arrangement. A single substituent swap on the starting allene flipped the annulation's selectivity outright, granting direct access to the other family. Calculations traced the divergence to the first ring-closing step, where crowding decides the outcome. The team proved the platform by completing a total synthesis of the natural product arnicenone through the photochemical branch, with a second route confirming the strategies complement each other.
pmc-13652531:
Thayna de Assis Barros Thiago and seven colleagues test a prototype device that delivers fluids under the skin, a method called hypodermoclysis. The technique matters for patients who need hydration but have poor veins, yet the equipment in routine use is basic. Nine nurses with experience in subcutaneous therapy tried the new device in a simulated scenario, then discussed it in interviews and a focus group.

A checklist captured how the prototype performed in hands-on use, while the conversations gathered what worked, what felt awkward, and what should change. Results were mixed across tasks, which is the point of a usability trial: weak spots surface before patients are involved. The study feeds those findings back into design, showing how frontline nurses can shape a device while it is still a prototype rather than after it reaches the ward.
pmc-2702831:
Cani, Possemiers, Van de Wiele, and co-authors study how gut microbes control inflammation in obese mice. Obese and diabetic mice show a leakier gut wall and signs of bacterial products entering the blood, feeding metabolic problems. Earlier work hinted that more Bifidobacterium species softened the harms of a high-fat diet.

The team links changes in gut microbes to a gut hormone pathway that improves the gut barrier. A tighter barrier lets fewer inflammatory triggers through. Their findings support the idea that feeding helpful gut microbes could ease obesity-linked inflammation, a route now widely explored.
pmc-3840331:
Lakens offers a practical primer on calculating and reporting effect sizes for common statistical tests. Effect sizes, he argues, matter more than any other outcome of empirical studies. They communicate the practical significance of results, beyond whether an effect merely exists.

For working scientists, effect sizes prove most useful because they let findings accumulate across studies. Lakens walks readers through computing them for t-tests and ANOVAs, with reporting advice. The primer is widely used in psychology teaching, pushing the field from yes-or-no significance toward measured magnitudes.  Worked examples use realistic sample sizes drawn from published psychology experiments throughout.
pmc-3965031:
Lombard, Ramulu, Drula, and their colleagues updated the CAZy database in a 2014 report. CAZy sorts enzymes that build, change, and break down sugars and related chains. Its web site gives free access and is kept up to date as new data arrive.

Each family in CAZy is grouped by protein sequence, and that grouping is tied to what the enzyme acts on and to its three-dimensional shape. Users can move from a gene sequence to a likely function in a few steps. The system helps chemists and biologists who study plant walls, gut microbes, and biofuels find the right enzyme fast.
pmc-4134331:
Feudtner, Feinstein, Zhong, and their co-authors updated a classification system for sick children in 2014. The system groups complex chronic conditions in children, meaning long-term illnesses that need ongoing care. The first version dated from 2000 and had fallen behind medical practice.

Version two was revised for the tenth revision of the International Classification of Diseases. It also adds dependence on complex medical technology and organ transplantation, both now common in children's hospitals. Health services researchers use the system to count and compare care for the sickest children. A shared scheme makes studies across hospitals far easier to align.
pmc-4521131:
Herrett, Gallagher, Bhaskaran, and their co-authors profiled the Clinical Practice Research Datalink in 2015. Known as CPRD, it is an ongoing primary care database of anonymized medical records from general practitioners. It covers millions of patients from hundreds of practices across the United Kingdom.

Because the records come from real daily care, they show illness and treatment as they occur in the population. Researchers use CPRD to study drug safety, disease rates, and outcomes at large scale. Its size gives power to detect rare effects that trials miss. The profile explains coverage and limits so new users can judge whether the data fit their question.
pmc-5664031:
Susan Hewlings and Douglas Kalman reviewed curcumin and human health in 2017. Curcumin is the main active compound in turmeric, a spice long used in cooking and folk medicine. Interest in it has grown among both scientists and home cooks.

The review gathers evidence on how curcumin may help with swelling, joint pain, and damage caused by unstable oxygen molecules. It also notes weak points, such as poor absorption from the gut and small study sizes. Readers get a balanced look at what is known and what is still unproven. That makes it useful for anyone weighing turmeric supplements.
pmc-7005631:
Ygor Silva, Andressa Bernardi, and Rudimar Frozza reviewed gut-brain communication through microbial fatty acids in 2020. Gut microbes govern much of the body's metabolic, hormone, and immune balance. Their role in brain signaling has gained strong recognition.

When microbes ferment fiber they release short-chain fatty acids. These compounds reach the brain directly and through immune and nerve routes. They can affect appetite, mood circuits, and brain inflammation. The review weighs animal evidence against the thinner human record, and marks where diet-based brain claims outrun the proof. The authors also discuss fatty acids made as drugs, and how they differ from the microbial products.
pmc-7619331:
Patrick L. Jambura led a 2026 comment defending a Mediterranean juvenile white shark identification against a reinterpretation as a porbeagle, a dispute with conservation stakes. A recent paper had questioned citizen-science photographic records of lamnid sharks, reinterpreting a Croatian juvenile as a porbeagle based mainly on selected dental traits. Given white sharks' critically endangered status in the Mediterranean and few confirmed sightings, each record matters. The authors argue reinterpretations demand verified sources, contact with the citizen scientists, and multiple diagnostic traits.

Re-examining all visible external and dental characters, the team found the specimen consistent with a white shark. They show that single dental traits vary with age and individual differences and can mislead alone, while the combined pattern across eyes, fins, keels, tooth shape, serration, and cusplets holds firm.
pmc-7672931:
Hisham Kadry, Behnam Noorani, and Luca Cucullo gave an overview in 2020 of the blood-brain barrier, the tightly sealed wall that guards the brain. This barrier controls which substances move between the blood and brain tissue. Its sound structure is essential for the brain's chemical balance and for healthy nerve cell function.

The authors describe how the barrier is built, how it works, and the ways it can break down in injury and disease. They also review the marker molecules that signal whether the barrier is intact or leaking. That knowledge matters far beyond anatomy, since the same wall that protects the brain also blocks most medicines, and judging its state helps doctors assess brain injury and illness.
pmc-8387231:
Seppo Salminen and an expert panel published a consensus statement in 2021 defining postbiotics, a term then used loosely in nutrition science. The panel was convened in 2019 by the international scientific association for this field, drawing specialists in nutrition, gut medicine, food science, and microbiology. Their task was to review the evidence and settle what the word should cover.

The statement fixes a definition and scope, distinguishing true postbiotics, preparations of inanimate microbes that benefit health, from neighboring products that had borrowed the label. Clear naming matters because research funding, product claims, and health guidance all hang on it. The document gives scientists and regulators a shared reference point for a fast growing product category.
pmc-9252731:
Filipe Madeira and colleagues described in 2022 the search and sequence analysis services run by EMBL-EBI, a major European bioinformatics institute. The services give integrated access to the institute's data resources and its core analysis tools through shared frameworks. Its search engine alone spans billions of records across databases of sequences, structures, and literature.

The article explains what a user can do through these frameworks, from finding a gene record to running alignment and analysis jobs online. It also reports updates and usage at the time. For many working biologists, these free services are the front door to public bioinformatics, and this report documents the doors and what lies behind them.
prospectus-francais-et-anglais-treatise-: One scanned leaf in poor shape lists sellers for a Paris medical publisher, J.-B. Baillière, whose shop stood in the Rue de l'École de Médecine, with a sister house in Regent Street, London. Agent names follow for towns across France. Bayonne, Bordeaux, Brest, Dijon, Lille, Lyon, Metz, Montpellier, Nancy, and Nantes appear among the outlets. The leaf belongs to a French and English prospectus for a treatise whose own pages are not shown, a glimpse of how medical books reached buyers.
spee-cautio-criminalis-1631:
Friedrich Spee was a German Jesuit priest who heard the last words of many women judged as witches. In 1631 he put out Cautio Criminalis in Latin, with no name on the title page. The book was the first strong Catholic attack on the witch trials. Spee risked his post and his life to write it.

Spee shows how torture forces false claims from weak and strong alike. He asks judges to test proof with care and to doubt paid witch finders. His calm case helped slow the trials in parts of Germany. Few books of the age speak for the accused with such force.
spee-cautio-criminalis-latin-1631:
Friedrich Spee, a Jesuit priest, published the Cautio Criminalis in Latin in 1631, without his name. Spee had served as confessor to condemned witches in Würzburg, hearing their last words before the fire. What he learned in that cell produced a searing attack on the trials and their tortures.

He argues that torture makes every accusation true by force. Germany, he warns, will burn its whole population if the process runs unchecked. The book is the moral turning point of the persecution. Its anonymity protected a man whose order and church ran the trials he condemned. Few braver books came out of the burning times.
state-of-the-union-addresses-pg5031:
William McKinley gives four yearly addresses, from December 6, 1897, to December 3, 1900, parted by three stars. The first greets the Fifty-fifth Congress in regular session at the seat of government. Many of its members, McKinley notes, served with him in the law-making work of past years. The meeting falls in a glad hour that calls for thanks to a kind heaven.

Peace and good will with all nations hold unbroken, he reports. A true ground of joy is the growing warmth of kin-feeling among all parts of the country, whose lack has too long held back the Union's highest gains. The spirit of love of country runs wide and burns ever stronger. The questions of the day, he adds, rise far above party, bias, and old lines between North and South.
tales-and-novels-volume-10-helen-pg8531:
Volume X of Maria Edgeworth's Tales and Novels, printed in 1857 with engravings on steel, holds Helen, the final novel of the ten-volume set. The contents at hand list the first volume of Helen chapter by chapter, running to thirteen heads before the page ends.

The novel is Edgeworth's last. It follows Helen Stanley, an orphan. Her friend Cecilia takes her into a fashionable household. Cecilia's approaching marriage hides a secret. The secret concerns her mother's past. Helen's ruling passion is truth; the plot asks what she will do when loyalty to her friend seems to require a lie. The question runs through ballrooms and country houses until candor and affection can be reconciled, and the set of tales and novels closes on that testing of a young woman's honesty.
the-great-round-world-and-what-is-going-: Dated June 10, 1897, No. 31 of The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It is a weekly newspaper for boys and girls. Only front matter is present here. It gives the masthead and a premium notice. The notice backs the bicycle offer of the number before this one. A premium catalogue has also been prepared. It lists selected articles for those who gain a smaller number of subscriptions. A copy of the catalogue is mailed on receipt of five cents.
the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-2-part:
In Ormsby's translation, Don Quixote by Miguel de Cervantes moves on to Volume II, Part 31. Chapter forty-four tells how Sancho Panza was conducted to his government. It also tells of a strange adventure in the castle. The narrator pauses first on the state of his source.

In the true original, they say, Cide Hamete complained at this chapter. His story was dry, he felt, and of little variety. He must speak perpetually of Don Quixote and Sancho. He dares not stray to other ground. Cervantes makes even his invented author weary of the pair. Sancho then leaves for his island government. The two lines of the tale part ways.
the-lock-and-key-library-classic-mystery: Only a Project Gutenberg header is present here, so no story text appears. The header names The Lock and Key Library, edited by Julian Hawthorne, and dates the electronic edition July 1999. It also notes that the file was prepared by Donald Lainson. Nothing in what is present identifies which volume of the series this record holds. It names no story and lists no author. No further account of the contents can honestly be given from this record alone.
the-lock-and-key-library-the-most-intere: Only a Project Gutenberg header and a contents list are present here, so the stories do not appear. The header identifies it as Real Life, number two in Hawthorne's Lock and Key Library series. It splits into Part I, Detective Stories from Real Life, and Part II, True Stories of Modern Magic. Part I's contents name Arthur Train's A Flight into Texas and pieces by P. H. Woodward drawn from the Secret Service of the Post-Office Department. Among them are An Erring Shepherd and The Fortune of Seth Savage.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
The Mirror's number for Saturday, March 28, 1829, No. 363, visits Guy's Cliff near Warwick. The county itself is praised first: Kenilworth, Stratford, Leicester, and Shakespeare trail light across the retrospective dream of merry England. Guy's Cliff stands a mile and a half north-east of Warwick, where the Avon winds through fertile meadows. Rock and wood combine there in a singularly picturesque recess.

Tradition places a Saxon hermit's oratory and cell on the spot, and a hermit certainly dwelt there under Edward III and Henry IV. The renowned Guy, Earl of Warwick, is said to have retired here after his duel with the Danish giant Colbrond. His neglected countess Felicia reportedly buried him at the cliff. Henry V, charmed by the place and its legend, meant to found a chantry for two priests, but war and early death prevented him.

Dunheved Castle in Cornwall leads volume 19, No. 553, dated June 23, 1832. The crumbling ruins crown the hill of Launceston, near the eastern side of the county. Launceston's older name, Dunheved, meant the swelling hill, while its newer name is explained as the church of the castle.

Borlase, the antiquarian writer on Cornwall, supplies the detailed survey that follows. A gateway 120 feet long leads to a terrace running beside ramparts nearly twelve feet thick. One round tower bore the name Witches' Tower. A narrow covered passage climbs between pierced walls to the keep, a round work 93 feet across with three wards, or defensive enclosures, inside its walls.

A chapel built on a bridge at Wakefield leads No. 581 of The Mirror, dated December 15, 1832. Bridge chapels, the article begins, were once common, though few survive. Plutarch is cited deriving pontifex, or high priest, from sacrifices performed on bridges, and priests were long charged with keeping bridges in repair.

Wakefield's bridge crosses the Calder at the town's south-east entrance, in the West Riding of Yorkshire, and dates from the reign of Edward III. The chapel projects from its eastern side, about ten yards long and eight wide, in rich Gothic style. Its east window hangs over the river with fine tracery, while the west front carries buttresses, recesses, and five carved relief panels under battlements.
three-books-of-occult-philosophy-book-i-:
Henry Cornelius Agrippa, knight and doctor of both laws, wrote Three Books of Occult Philosophy, or of Magick, and book one opens the work. Chapter one says every inferior thing is governed by its superior. Virtues flow from the first cause through angels, heavens, stars, elements, animals, plants, metals, and stones.

Agrippa divides magic into natural, celestial, and ceremonial kinds across the three books. Chapter two calls magic a faculty full of high mysteries and knowledge of whole nature. Readers get a Renaissance system joining medicine, astrology, mathematics, and religious ceremony, offered cautiously under the church's judgement.
tob-0131:
Harvard's Oriental Series gave Patanjali's Yoga Sutras their scholarly English home in James Haughton Woods's edition. Volume seventeen of the series prints the Sanskrit text, Woods's translation, and the great classical commentaries of Vyasa and Vacaspati Misra. A full scholarly apparatus surrounds the short root text.

Students can follow each aphorism from the original words through centuries of interpretation. Woods weighs variant readings and explains hard terms with care. Yoga teachers and academics alike treat the edition as a gold standard. Verified from a pre-1930 public-domain edition, it remains the serious reader's path into yoga's root scripture and its oldest interpreters.
tob-10631:
John Bunyan turned the human soul into a besieged city in The Holy War, his companion allegory to The Pilgrim's Progress. Diabolus, a fallen giant, tricks his way into Mansoul and seizes its castle. King Shaddai, the city's rightful lord, sends an army to win it back.

Captains named Boanerges, Conviction, and Judgment lay siege, preach at the walls, and fight street by street, while Mansoul wavers, surrenders, backslides, and is besieged again. Bunyan preaches allegory as a military campaign with a tinsmith's plain force. Less famous than Pilgrim's Progress, The Holy War is fiercer, and its picture of a town divided against itself lingers.
tob-13331:
W. Scott-Elliot, a member of the Theosophical Society, set down his movement's account of two lost continents. Atlantis in the Atlantic and Lemuria in the Pacific were, in Theosophical teaching, homes of early human root races. Scott-Elliot drew his picture from what the Society called clairvoyant research.

He describes the lands, their peoples, their customs, and the disasters that sank them beneath the sea. Maps and charts support the story in sober detail. Historians and geologists reject the account, but few books did more to fix the modern myth of Atlantis in the public mind.
tob-14431:
Plato cast his search for justice as a long talk in Athens, led by his teacher Socrates. Benjamin Jowett's translation of the Republic became the standard English version for generations of students. Socrates and his friends ask what justice is, first in a city and then in a single soul.

To answer, they design a city ruled by philosopher-kings and divide the soul into three parts. The famous image of the cave shows prisoners who take shadows for real things. Plato also weighs in on poetry, education, and forms of rule. Political thought in the West still starts from arguments first made here.
tob-4131:
Echoes from the Gnosis opens with the Gnosis of the Mind, Mead's rendering of the Poimandres, the Corpus Hermeticum's great opening dialogue. Mind itself speaks to Hermes, showing him the making of the world and the nature of man. Mead adds commentary for the general reader.

Light and darkness part; the Logos orders the elements; man leans down through the spheres and takes on nature's frame. The vision explains both creation and the soul's way back. Verified from the 1919 edition, this slim first volume serves as the Hermetic primer: the core revelation, clearly set out, with a guide at the reader's elbow.
tob-4231:
Frederick Starr's Korean Buddhism, dated 1918 in this edition, surveys the tradition's history, condition, and art after his journeys through the peninsula. Mountain temples, monastic life, sculpture, and painting receive illustrated, firsthand treatment. Starr wrote as an anthropologist traveling, interviewing, and photographing, not from a library alone.

Buddhism reached Korea from China and flourished under early kingdoms before later dynasties favored Confucian order, pushing temples into the mountains. Starr found a tradition diminished but alive, and documented it lovingly. His survey brought Western readers to a Buddhism overshadowed by China and Japan, and it remains quoted as an early eyewitness record of Korean temples before modern upheavals.
tob-9047-59131:
Plants and farming take over volume three of Pliny's Natural History in Bostock's translation. Grain, vines, and fruit trees get practical treatment: how to plant, graft, prune, and store the harvest. Wine receives the loving detail Romans expected, with famous vintages ranked and praised.

Beyond the farm, Pliny lists plant medicines drawn from field and garden. Some remedies rest on real use; others on pure folk belief. The volume preserves the working knowledge of Roman agriculture better than any other source. Readers who garden will find much that is familiar, and much that is strange, in Rome's countryside.
un-ga-res-2231:
Gibraltar came back before the UN General Assembly in Resolution 2231, passed in December 1966. Spain and Britain, the administering power, had each stated their case, and people from the territory had been heard. The text recalls the 1964 push for talks and the Assembly's own call of the year before.

The Assembly regrets the slow pace of decolonization for the port colony. It calls on both sides to keep talking, with the good of the people of Gibraltar in mind, and asks Britain to speed the process. The sovereignty fight behind the talks, Spain against Britain, runs on to this day.
un-ga-res-57-131: General Assembly Resolution 57/131 takes its number from the Assembly's fifty-seventh session, which met in 2002 and 2003. The catalog dates the record to 1970, a year that cannot fit the numbering, so that date should not be trusted. The record names no subject, and none should be guessed. What stands is a formal decision of the full Assembly, preserved in the UN's official record text, one of the many measures the body adopts in each busy session year.
un-ga-res-a-69-31:
Space belongs to peaceful work, states Resolution A/69/31, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. All states share a stake in the study and use of space, the Moon, and other far bodies, for peaceful ends alone. Such work must serve the good of all lands, rich or poor in wealth and science. The text recalls the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which bars mass-kill arms from orbit and from the Moon.

No state may use or threaten force in its dealings, in space as on earth, the Charter's rule recalled here. The 1978 disarmament session had held that fresh steps are needed to bar an arms race in space. This yearly vote keeps that guard in place.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 2231 (XXI), from the twenty-first session in 1966, returned to the question of Gibraltar a year after resolution 2070 (XX) had urged talks. The Assembly noted that Spain and the United Kingdom, the ruling power, both said they were willing to keep negotiating. But it regretted acts that had harmed the talks.

The text voiced regret at the delay in ending colonial rule in Gibraltar under the 1960 declaration. Both parties were called on to press on with their talks. They were to keep in mind the interests of the territory's people. Britain was asked to speed the process and report back before the next session.

On 9 February 1946, the General Assembly adopted Resolution 31. It was adopted at the twenty-sixth plenary meeting of the first session. It is a single short instruction. The Assembly told the Secretary-General to put one question on the agenda of the second part of that first session. The question was whether to hold an international press conference. The choice itself was left for later debate.

General Assembly resolution 69/31 (2014) concerns preventing an arms race in outer space. The Assembly reaffirms that space exploration must serve peaceful purposes under the Outer Space Treaty. It reaffirms that the existing legal regime alone does not guarantee against an arms race there. It calls on all states, especially major space powers, to work toward that goal and refrain from contrary actions. It invites the Conference on Disarmament to set up a working group on the subject during its 2015 session. The group would pursue negotiated agreements, including verification measures.
un-sc-res-1031:
United Nations Security Council Resolution 1031 put the Dayton peace agreement for Bosnia into force. The Council adopted it on 15 December 1995, one day after the agreement was signed in Paris. The war in Bosnia had killed many thousands and driven many more from their homes.

The text welcomes the peace deal and calls on all sides to keep their promises. It lets member states set up a NATO-led force, called IFOR, to guard the deal. That force could use all needed means to make the parties obey. The Council also backs a High Representative to watch over the civilian side of the peace.
un-sc-res-1231:
Resolution 1231 on Sierra Leone was adopted on 11 March 1999. Rebels had attacked the capital that January and committed grave atrocities against civilians. Most United Nations observers had pulled out to Conakry for safety. Reports kept saying arms and fighters reached the rebels through Liberia.

The Council extends the observer mission, called UNOMSIL, until 13 June 1999. The mission should move back into Freetown as soon as safety allows. More military observers and human rights staff will join it. The text condemns rebel abuse of women and children and the use of child soldiers. All states must honor the arms embargo on rebel forces.
un-sc-res-1331:
Council members took up Cyprus and unanimously adopted Resolution 1331 on Cyprus on 13 December 2000. The peacekeeping force on the island had served since 1964. Cyprus had agreed the force should stay past mid-December. New limits placed on its patrols that June had raised concern.

The Council extends the force, called UNFICYP, until 15 June 2001. It urges the Turkish Cypriot side and Turkish forces to lift the limits set on 30 June 2000. The old military position at Strovilia should be restored. The text also backs urgent work on the fate of missing persons. A fresh report is due by 1 June 2001.
un-sc-res-1431: Formal action by the Council in its numbered series produced Resolution 1431, which the catalog dates to 2002. These short legal texts often sit at turning points, since the Council acts when peace or security is at stake. The text here follows the English Wikisource transcription of the official record, so readers get the Council's own wording. It sits in this library among other public records in the DECLASSIFIED group.
un-sc-res-1531:
Ethiopia and Eritrea's stalled border process framed a mission renewal on 12 March 2004. The Boundary Commission's twelfth report, of 27 February 2004, said it could not move forward with demarcation as things stood. Ethiopia rejected large parts of the commission's binding ruling and was not cooperating. Eritrea refused to deal with the Secretary-General's special envoy.

The Council extended the United Nations Mission in Ethiopia and Eritrea, UNMEE, at its set troop and observer levels to 15 September 2004. It urged both parties to cooperate fully and quickly with the mission and to guard its staff. Final duty for applying the Algiers Agreements and the boundary ruling rested with the two governments, the Council stressed. It backed the special envoy's good offices and pressed both sides to open a direct air route between Asmara and Addis Ababa. Delays, it noted, were raising the mission's costs.
un-sc-res-1631:
Cooperation with regional bodies was set out as doctrine on 17 October 2005. Chapter VIII of the Charter supplied the legal frame. The 2005 World Summit outcome had just been adopted. The sixth high-level meeting with regional organizations had closed in July. The Council recalled its own debates of 2003 and 2004 on working with regional partners.

The Council voiced its resolve to deepen cooperation with regional and subregional organizations. All states and bodies were urged to give money and skills to build their capacity, above all in Africa. Regional strategies inside the United Nations system had to grow. The Council stressed what regional bodies can do in settling disputes, peacekeeping, and rebuilding after war. It meant to hold regular meetings with the heads of regional organizations. Its own committees were praised for drawing such partners into the fight against terrorism and arms spread.
un-sc-res-1731:
Liberia sanctions are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1731, adopted on 20 December 2006. Liberia's new elected government had made real gains since January 2006. A new forestry law had passed, and the ban on timber exports had been lifted. Yet the Council judged that other reforms still fell short.

The text renews the arms and travel bans for twelve more months. The ban on rough diamond exports runs six more months, with a review after four. Liberia must build a clear origin scheme for its diamonds and join the Kimberley Process. The expert panel that checks the sanctions stays on until 20 June 2007.
un-sc-res-1831:
AMISOM's authorization was renewed on 19 August 2008. The African Union had already extended its Somalia mission from 17 July 2008 for six more months. Uganda and Burundi kept troops in Mogadishu. The Council condemned all violence inside Somalia and acts meant to block a peaceful political process. It stressed the need for disarmament and reintegration of fighters.

The Council renewed the authorization of African Union member states to run AMISOM for a further six months. The mission could take all necessary measures to carry out its mandate under resolution 1744 (2007). The arms embargo terms of resolution 733 (1992) would not block supplies meant for the mission. African Union states were urged to send more troops, and all member states were asked for money, staff, and equipment. The Secretary-General was encouraged to keep working with the African Union on plans for a possible United Nations force to follow.
un-sc-res-1931:
Yugoslav tribunal judges had their terms stretched again on 29 June 2010. The tribunal's president had written on 31 May about the bench. Its completion strategy report admitted the work would not end in 2010, as ordered. The loss of experienced staff was slowing the trials. Resolution 1900 (2009) had promised a review by this date.

The Council restated that persons indicted by the tribunal must face trial. It noted the need for the tribunal to be staffed well enough to finish. The terms of the permanent trial judges were extended to 31 December 2011, or to the end of their cases if sooner. Appeals judges' terms ran on in the same way, to the dates set out in the text. Ad litem judges gained matching extensions. Named ad litem judges were allowed to sit past their terms to finish the cases before them.
un-sc-res-2031: From 2011, Resolution 2031 is a Security Council act preserved in this collection in its record wording. The transcription source is English Wikisource. Inside the act, concern and command alternate in the Council's settled rhythm, preamble first and operative paragraphs after. The entry preserves the rhythm and the content together, complete at its sequence number.
un-sc-res-231:
Cyprus's peacekeeping force came up for renewal again in December 1966. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 8 December, said the force was still needed if peace was to be maintained. Cyprus's government agreed it should stay beyond 26 December. Resolution 231 was adopted unanimously on 15 December 1966.

The Council reaffirmed its Cyprus resolutions, reaching back to Resolution 186 of 1964. The parties were urged to show the utmost restraint. They were also told to keep working together toward the Council's goals. The force's stationing was extended for six months, ending on 26 June 1967. The Council hoped that enough progress toward a settlement would be made by then. Such progress might at last allow the force to leave the island.
un-sc-res-31:
Indonesia's fight for independence from the Netherlands brought the Council back to the dispute in August 1947. Resolution 27, passed on 1 August, had called on both sides to stop fighting. It had also pointed them toward a peaceful settlement. One part of that text let the parties ask for the Council's help. Resolution 31, adopted on 25 August 1947, makes that offer in form.

The Council resolved to tender its good offices to the parties. In plain terms, it offered its own help to bring about a peaceful settlement of the dispute. If the parties asked, the help would come through a small committee of the Council. The committee would have three members. Each party would choose one member, and the two chosen would name the third. The offer put the Council's mediation on the table, ready for the Dutch and the Republic of Indonesia to use.
un-sc-res-331: With a catalog date of 1973, Resolution 331 records a decision of the UN Security Council. Council texts of this kind carry weight under the UN Charter, since the Council holds the main duty for peace and security. The entry gives the decision in full, as transcribed on English Wikisource from the records of the United Nations. It sits in this library among other public records in the DECLASSIFIED group.
un-sc-res-431:
Namibia's path to a United Nations settlement plan advanced on 27 July 1978. The Council recalled resolution 385 (1976), which had demanded free elections for the territory. A proposal for a settlement of the Namibian situation had been laid before it on 10 April 1978, in document S/12636. The Western contact group's plan was now on the table.

The Council asked the Secretary-General to appoint a special representative for Namibia. His task was to secure the territory's early independence through free elections under United Nations supervision and control. The Secretary-General also had to report at the earliest date with advice on putting the settlement proposal into effect under resolution 385. All concerned were urged to do their best to bring Namibia to independence as soon as possible. The special representative's work became the core of the settlement effort the Council pursued from that summer on.
un-sc-res-631:
United Nations observers were watching the Iran-Iraq ceasefire in early 1989. On 8 February 1989 the Security Council renewed their mission, UNIIMOG. The Secretary-General had reported on the observer group two days before. The Council took note of his observations. It also recalled resolution 598, the text that had demanded an end to the war.

The renewal ran for seven months and twenty-two days. It ended on 30 September 1989. The Council called on both parties to carry out resolution 598 without delay. The Secretary-General owed a report at the end of the period. It would cover events on the ground and steps taken toward a settlement.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
The Dayton peace deal for Bosnia and Herzegovina is put into force by Resolution 1031, adopted on 15 December 1995. The General Framework Agreement had been signed in Paris the day before by Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. A London conference had set up a Peace Implementation Council to guide the work ahead.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council authorizes a multinational implementation force, IFOR, under unified command, with power to use all needed measures to enforce the military parts of the deal. It ends UNPROFOR's mandate once authority passes to IFOR. It backs elections run by the OSCE, the right of refugees to go home, and full cooperation with the war crimes tribunal. It also endorses a High Representative to oversee the civilian side of the settlement, agreeing to the designation named in the text.

Sierra Leone's observer mission is extended and sent back to the capital in Resolution 1231, adopted on 11 March 1999. The situation remained fragile after the recent escalation of violence. The Secretary-General's fifth report of 4 March 1999 recommended the move. Reports persisted that rebels were receiving arms and mercenaries, in particular from Liberian territory.

The Council extends the mandate of the United Nations Observer Mission in Sierra Leone, UNOMSIL, until 13 June 1999. It welcomes the plan to re-establish UNOMSIL in Freetown as soon as possible with more military observers and human rights personnel, subject to strict attention to security. It condemns rebel atrocities against civilians, especially women and children, including recruiting children as soldiers, and demands full humanitarian access. It reaffirms the Resolution 1171 (1998) arms embargo, commends ECOMOG, and asks the Secretary-General to report by 5 June 1999 with recommendations on UNOMSIL's future deployment.

Guinea's break with France brought its bid to the Council within weeks in 1958. On 9 December, it adopted Resolution 131. Guinea had voted that autumn for instant freedom in a referendum. It was the only French colony to choose that path in 1958. A republic was proclaimed at once under its new leaders.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit the Republic of Guinea. Admission followed days later. Guinea's arrival marked an early sign of the wave to come. African decolonization would reshape the UN's ranks and its politics within a few short years.

Cyprus, again, is the real subject of Resolution 1331. Some digests mislabel it as a Golan Heights text. In fact it was adopted unanimously on 13 December 2000, after the Secretary-General's report on the Cyprus operation. UNFICYP peacekeepers had guarded the island's buffer zone for decades.

The Council extended UNFICYP's mandate to 15 June 2001. It asked for an implementation report by 1 June. It also pressed the Turkish Cypriot side and Turkish forces on a sore point. Restrictions imposed in June 2000 had hampered the peacekeepers. Members demanded those limits be lifted. They wanted the former military position restored at Strovilia, a village inside the buffer zone.

Short-term judges come to the Rwanda war crimes tribunal in this text of 14 August 2002. The tribunal's president had asked for the change so trials could finish sooner. A similar ad litem system already existed at the tribunal for the former Yugoslavia.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council amended the Rwanda tribunal's Statute to create the pool, and adjusted related articles of the Yugoslavia tribunal's Statute too. The Secretary-General is asked to arrange the election of 18 ad litem judges for Rwanda as soon as possible. Staff and facilities for the new judges were to follow, so the extra courtroom capacity could actually be used.

Resolution 1531, adopted unanimously on 12 March 2004, voices frustration at a peace process stuck between Ethiopia and Eritrea. The boundary commission had reported in February that it could not move ahead with marking the border under present conditions. The Council blamed the impasse mainly on missing progress in demarcation, and singled out Ethiopia's refusal to accept key parts of the binding ruling, and its weak cooperation.

The Council kept UNMEE, the UN mission in both countries, in place for a further six months. It restated support for the Algiers Agreements and the commission's 2002 ruling, which both sides had accepted as final. The text warned, in effect, that a peace both governments had signed was being undone by delay.

How the UN should work with regional bodies on peace and security is the theme of Resolution 1631, adopted on 17 October 2005. It rests on Chapter VIII of the UN Charter, which covers regional arrangements. The 2005 World Summit had urged a bigger role for regional groups, and a new Peacebuilding Commission was about to be created.

The Council invites regional and subregional groups with peacekeeping skill to place that strength in the UN Standby Arrangements System. It urges states to help build up such groups, above all in Africa, with people, training, and money. It stresses fast deployment in support of UN missions and the role of regional groups against the illegal small arms trade and terrorism. It also plans regular meetings with regional heads and asks for a report on the chances and problems in this teamwork.

Liberia's sanctions are renewed in Resolution 1731, adopted on 20 December 2006. The new government had made real progress since January 2006, passing a forestry reform law, and the timber measures had already been lifted. Diamond controls were not yet in place, though work toward the Kimberley Process was under way. The expert panel found that the conditions for ending the remaining measures were not yet met.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews the arms embargo and travel ban for 12 months, with an exemption for non-lethal equipment for vetted, trained Liberian police and security forces. It renews the rough-diamond ban for six months, with a review after four, to give Liberia time to build a transparent certificate-of-origin regime. The asset freeze from Resolution 1532 stays in force. The Panel of Experts is extended to 20 June 2007, reporting by 6 June 2007.

Resolution 1831, passed on 19 August 2008, keeps the African force in Somalia for six more months. The force, AMISOM, was small and based in Mogadishu. It worked in the midst of a fierce revolt. The Council condemned bids to block peace talks by force. It deplored fresh calls to arms and fresh attacks on aid staff and peace staff alike.

The force won six more months of cover from the Council. Calm in Somalia, the text says, needs arms laid down and ex-fighters brought back to civil life. The Council restated its respect for the land's unity and its borders. It also wove this grant into its web of past texts on guards for the weak, for children, and for aid teams.

Resolution 1931, adopted on 29 June 2010, deals with the judges and timetable of the International Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. The tribunal had been told to finish its work in 2010, but its own report said that goal could not be met. Skilled staff were leaving, and a string of trials and appeals still had years to run.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends the terms of the appeals judges until 31 December 2012 and of the trial judges until 31 December 2011, or until their cases end. It lets nine short-term ad litem judges serve past the usual three-year limit. It presses states, above all those of the former Yugoslavia, to help the tribunal and arrest those still indicted. It also urges the tribunal to finish its work as fast as it can.

The Central African Republic had held elections in 2011, but armed groups still controlled much of the country outside the capital. One of them, the Lord's Resistance Army, crossed borders to raid villages. Resolution 2031, adopted on 21 December 2011, concerns BINUCA, the United Nations peacebuilding office in the country.

The Council extended BINUCA's mandate until 31 January 2013. It pushed the government to set up a permanent, independent body to run future elections. The electoral code also had to be revised. The office would keep backing the peace agreement process and disarmament work. Regional efforts against the Lord's Resistance Army received support as well. The aim was to help the state extend its authority beyond the capital.

A year of Cyprus renewals closed with one more in December 1966. On the fifteenth, the Council adopted Resolution 231 without dissent. The Secretary-General's report held that the force was still needed to keep peace. The Cyprus government agreed it should stay past late December.

The text restates the long list of earlier Cyprus decisions. It urges all parties to show the utmost restraint. It also asks them to keep working together toward the Council's goals. The posting then runs on for a further period. By late 1966, the pattern was fixed. The force could neither solve the Cyprus problem nor leave it.

Mediation, not troops, was the Council's offer in the Indonesia dispute of 1947. On 25 August, it adopted Resolution 31. Eight members voted yes and none voted no. Three members held back from the vote. Three weeks before, Resolution 27 had called for a halt to the fighting.

The Council now tenders its good offices to both sides. It offers help through a panel of three Council members. Each party would pick one member of the panel. Those two would then choose the third. The offer grew into the Committee of Good Offices. That body walked with Indonesia toward full independence in 1949.

Egypt's foreign minister addressed the Council on the Middle East in April 1973, and Resolution 331 followed on 20 April. The short text asks the Secretary-General for a full report. The report had to cover every effort the United Nations had made on the Middle East situation since June 1967. It was to reach the Council as early as possible. Once the report arrived, the Council would meet to examine the situation. The Secretary-General's special envoy for the region was to be on hand to assist during that debate.

Resolution 431, adopted on 27 July 1978, puts a negotiator in charge of Namibia's road to independence. A settlement proposal for the territory, prepared by five Western governments and circulated that April, was on the table. The Council's 1976 resolution had already laid down the goal: a free Namibia, chosen by its own people.

The Council asked the UN chief to name a special envoy for Namibia. His task was to make sure independence came early, through free elections under UN supervision and control. The Secretary-General also had to report back as soon as possible with recommendations for carrying out the proposal. The appointment set up the UN operation that, after long delays, finally ran Namibia's founding election in 1989.

An odd, precise span marks this Iran-Iraq observer renewal of 1989. On 8 February, the Council adopted Resolution 631. The observer group had watched the truce line since August 1988. The peace text behind it, Resolution 598, was still not carried out. The Secretary-General's February report grounded the step.

The text calls once again on the parties to act on Resolution 598 at once. It renews the mandate for seven months and twenty-two days. The term ends on 30 September 1989. A report on the state of play is due from the Secretary-General then. The odd end date matched the UN planning calendar, not a round half-year.
widger-s-quotations-from-the-project-gut: Only a Project Gutenberg header stands in this record, with none of Lord Chesterfield's quoted lines shown. The set is DW number 06 in David Widger's Quotations series. Its header follows the older Gutenberg pattern of about 2000, ending in a state list for donations. Chesterfield's letters were famed for worldly advice to his son, but no line of them appears here. Readers get the set's number, its compiler, and its source, plus the standard header cautions on copying and law.
